rows.finding: Tesla, Inc. was incorporated in Delaware on 2003-07-01 and converted to a Texas corporation on 2024-06-13; it has one class of common stock with 3,952,648,559 shares outstanding at 2026-09-30, listed on Nasdaq under TSLA.
rows.mechanism: Domicile and single-class structure mean voting power is proportional to economic ownership; there is no dual-class charter for a founder to fall back on, so control must be built through equity awards.
rows.benchmark: Ford's Class B shares carry 16 votes each and give the family about 40% of voting power on roughly 2% of shares [S95].
rows.weakens: Single class is the minority-shareholder-friendly feature; the reincorporation to Texas moved litigation to a court with no precedent on the 2025 award.
rows.implication: Governance risk is not a permanent dual-class wedge; it is contestable and tied to how much of the CEO award is earned, so model dilution rather than a fixed control discount.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: Which Texas state court would hear a challenge to the 2025 award, and has one been filed?

rows.finding: Elon Musk beneficially owns 699,580,882 shares, 19.8% of the 2026-09-30 count, including 286,428,773 restricted shares from the 2018 award and 207,498,721 shares pledged as collateral; the 423,743,904 unearned 2025 award shares are excluded from his beneficial ownership.
rows.mechanism: A 19.8% stake plus CEO office and board seat delivers effective control; the pledge means a margin call or forced sale could hit the register at the same time as bad news.
rows.benchmark: Ford family: ~40% of votes on ~2% economic [S95]; Vanguard holds 5.3% of Tesla, the only other disclosed 5% holder [S5].
rows.weakens: Unearned award shares vote proportionately to all other shares, so Musk's voting share does not rise until tranches are earned.
rows.implication: Treat the 207.5M pledged shares as a tail risk that would amplify a drawdown; free float is at most ~74.9% after Musk and Vanguard.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: Loan-to-value and lender identity of the pledge; not disclosed.

rows.finding: The 2025 CEO Performance Award is 423,743,904 shares (10.7% of shares outstanding) in 12 tranches tied to market-cap milestones from $2.0 trillion to $8.5 trillion and 12 operational milestones; none earned as of 2026-10-19; unrecognised stock compensation is $9.74bn for the one probable milestone and $105.82bn-$120.37bn for the improbable ones.
rows.mechanism: Dilution is contingent but real: each $0.5 trillion band from $2.0 trillion releases 35,311,992 shares, and a change of control drops the operational test, paying on deal price alone [S78].
rows.benchmark: The 2018 award, reinstated by the Delaware Supreme Court on 2025-12-19, delivered 286,428,773 restricted shares and was exercised in June 2026.
rows.weakens: At a $2.0 trillion market cap no tranche is earned and no shares are issued; tranches 11 and 12 also require board approval of a succession framework Musk writes.
rows.implication: Underwrite a 10.7% overhang above a $2.0 trillion valuation and a governance mechanism that pays the CEO on a merger without any robotaxi or Optimus milestone.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: How would a Tesla-SpaceX exchange ratio be set and who negotiates for Tesla?

rows.finding: Related-party flows: Tesla agreed on 2026-01-16 to invest about $2.00bn in xAI Series E, converted into SpaceX Class A stock when SpaceX acquired xAI on 2026-02-02 and funded on 2026-03-12; 2025 revenue from xAI was $430.1mn and from SpaceX $143.3mn, and Tesla paid a Musk-owned security firm $4.8mn.
rows.mechanism: The CEO sits on both sides of a $2bn capital allocation and of the largest trading counterparties, so minority holders rely on an Audit Committee whose members include directors with SpaceX ties.
rows.benchmark: The related-party policy review threshold is $120,000, so every one of these flows passed an Audit Committee review [S5].
rows.weakens: Combined 2025 revenue from both parties is ~0.6% of Tesla's $94.8bn, and the $2.00bn is ~4.4% of cash and investments, so the economics are small next to the governance signal.
rows.implication: Price a standing related-party discount: capital can be directed to Musk entities at valuations minority holders do not set.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: What valuation was used for the xAI Series E and did any independent adviser opine on it?

rows.finding: The nine-seat board is classified into three classes; six directors are independent under Nasdaq rules, but compensation and governance committee chair Ira Ehrenpreis has sat on SpaceX's board since February 2026, Kimbal Musk is the CEO's brother, and JB Straubel runs Redwood, a Tesla counterparty with $3.3mn of 2025 purchases.
rows.mechanism: Conflicts sit exactly where a merger or pay decision would be decided: the committees that set CEO pay and police conflicts are chaired by a director with a seat on the likely merger counterparty.
rows.benchmark: Tesla labels Ehrenpreis independent; a shareholder-approved 2025 proposal to declassify the board drew 39.4% of shares outstanding, short of the bar, and the board will not bring it back [S78].
rows.weakens: The Special Committee that designed the 2025 award used only Denholm and Wilson-Thompson, and compensation consultants advised it.
rows.implication: Board independence cannot be relied on to stop a value-extractive transaction; require a special committee with no SpaceX ties as a condition of holding.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: Will the 2026 say-on-pay vote show a minority of support, and do large index holders disclose votes against Denholm?

rows.finding: Delaware litigation ended in the CEO's favour (Supreme Court 2025-12-19, Chancery order 2026-03-18) and the 96,000,000-share 2025 interim award was forfeited on 2026-04-21; a securities class action filed 2025-08-04 in the Western District of Texas covers purchasers from 2023-04-19 to 2025-06-22 over Autopilot, FSD and Robotaxi statements.
rows.mechanism: Removing the Delaware overhang converted a contingent governance risk into a realised 19.8% stake plus a live disclosure claim, shifting legal risk from compensation to product claims.
rows.benchmark: The certified 2025 vote approving the award was 1,892,235,822 for and 564,940,908 against, about 77% of votes cast [S26].
rows.weakens: The class action is at pleading stage and no liability is recorded; the company describes the claims as alleging violations, not admitted facts [S3].
rows.implication: Litigation is a disclosure and damages risk, not a control risk; the bigger control event is a potential SpaceX combination.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: Docket status of the W.D. Tex. class action and any motion to dismiss ruling in 2026.

rows.finding: Capital allocation: no dividend has ever been paid, no shares were repurchased in 2025 (Item 5 shows none), cash and short-term investments were $45.45bn at 2026-09-30, 2026 capex is guided above $20bn, and in September 2026 Tesla signed three credit agreements with aggregate commitments of $30bn.
rows.mechanism: Growth capex plus debt commitments replace buybacks and dividends, so per-share value depends on the return on AI, robot and energy investment rather than on capital returns.
rows.benchmark: Nine-month 2026 operating cash flow $14.90bn against capex $13.01bn leaves $1.9bn of free cash flow before the Q3 figure of $1.5bn for the quarter [S4, S6].
rows.weakens: The balance sheet is still net-cash-like with $45.45bn of liquidity, so the $30bn commitments are optionality rather than distress borrowing.
rows.implication: An investor is funding a capex programme with no capital-return floor; the buyback authorisation is nil, so dilution from stock compensation is not offset.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: Terms, pricing and drawdown of the three September 2026 credit agreements.

rows.finding: Insiders filed no open-market purchases in the 12 months to 2026-09-09 and sold 207,882 shares for $87.69mn, of which directors Wilson-Thompson ($29.95mn), Murdoch ($26.72mn) and Kimbal Musk ($25.61mn) accounted for most; the CFO's $5.41mn was tax-withholding.
rows.mechanism: Director sales into a $360-$450 price range with zero insider buying signal that the people closest to the 2027-2028 milestones are not adding exposure.
rows.benchmark: Zero purchases against $87.69mn of sales is a one-sided tape; Form 4 filings in the same window include the 423,743,904-share CEO grant and the 96,000,000-share forfeiture.
rows.weakens: Director sales are small relative to holdings and several were 10b5-1 plans set in advance, so they are weak evidence of a view.
rows.implication: Do not treat insider activity as a positive signal; it is at best neutral and at worst a warning about near-term conviction.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: Any 2026 Form 4 purchases after 2026-09-09, and 10b5-1 plan adoption dates.

plan.decision_question: Is Tesla's legal, capital and control structure one a public-equity investor can underwrite for a multi-year hold — who owns it, who controls capital allocation, and how much dilution is outstanding or contingent?
plan.thesis_sentence: Tesla is a single-class Texas corporation whose control rests on a 19.8% CEO stake plus a 423.7 million-share contingent award, so a public-equity holder is underwriting Elon Musk's capital allocation rather than a board-governed company — acceptable only at a governance discount, not at a premium.
plan.why_different: This section covers identity, control and contingent dilution; it does not re-argue growth, margins or valuation, which belong to the financial, market and valuation sections.
plan.mechanism: Control is built through equity: a 19.8% stake, a 10.7% contingent award whose unearned shares vote proportionately and whose change-of-control terms pay on deal price, and a board whose conflict committees include directors tied to SpaceX, the likely merger counterparty. Dilution and related-party capital allocation are therefore the two channels through which minority value is transferred.
plan.comparison_set: Ford (dual-class family control at ~40% of votes on ~2% of shares), GM and Alphabet (single- or multi-class peers), and Tesla's own 2018 award, which delivered 286.4 million shares after a Delaware reversal.
plan.counter_evidence: Tesla has one share class with proportional votes, no poison pill disclosed, a special committee that used an outside consultant, and a $45bn liquidity cushion; the related-party flows are under 1% of revenue and no award tranche has been earned, so the control discount may be smaller than the bear case assumes.
plan.visual: kpi component plus the legal-entity table and cap table, with the timeline covering 2003-2026 legal, award and litigation milestones.
plan.prohibited: Do not call the board 'independent' without qualification, do not present the award as certain dilution, do not use 'Musk discount' as a substitute for a mechanism, and do not state a share price or market cap without a timestamped source.

Hybrid-electric vehicles ranked as the most popular powertrain choice amongst buyers, while battery-electric cars accounted for 21.7% of new EU car registrations. Meanwhile, plug-in hybrids captured 10% of the EU market.

New EU car registrations by power source

Up until August 2026, battery-electric cars held a 21.7% share of the EU market, up from 15.8% a year earlier. Hybrid-electric car registrations captured 36.6% of the market, remaining the preferred choice among EU consumers. At the same time, the combined market share of petrol and diesel cars fell to 29%, compared with 37.5% a year earlier.

Electric cars

In the first eight months of 2026, 1,641,333 new battery-electric cars were registered, capturing 21.7% of the EU market. Three of the four largest EU markets, which together accounted for 64% of all battery-electric car registrations, recorded strong growth: France (+74.2%), Germany (+53.1%), and Denmark (+40.9%). Belgium also posted an increase (+13.1%), albeit at a slower pace.

August 2026 YTD’s figures also showed new EU hybrid-electric car registrations rising to 2,759,718 units, supported by growth in Spain (+21%) and Italy (+20.5%), with Germany (+5.2%) and France (+1.8%) also recording increases. Overall, hybrid-electric models accounted for 36.6% of the total EU market.

Plug-in-hybrid electric car registrations continued to grow, reaching 758,082 units in January-August 2026. This was driven by rising volumes in key markets such as Italy (+77.6%), Spain (+33.9%), and Germany (+15.6%). New plug-in-hybrid electric cars now represent 10% of EU registrations, up from 8.8% over the same period in 2025.

Petrol and diesel cars

By the end of August 2026, petrol car registrations fell 18.6%, experiencing significant downturns across all major European markets. France saw the sharpest decline, with volumes plunging by 35.8%, while other key markets also posted double-digit losses: Spain (-18.5%), Germany (-21.9%), and Italy (-16.7%).

Accounting for 1,634,733 new cars registered over the past eight months, petrol’s market share fell to 21.7% from 28% last year. In addition, the diesel car market continued its downward trend, with registrations declining by 18.6% and representing 7.3% of new EU car registrations, down from 9.4%.

 New EU car registrations increased by 5.3% year-to-date, against a backdrop of rising energy prices and persistent geopolitical uncertainty. Demand for a range of electrified vehicles remained strong, driven by market support measures and a broader model offering.

rows.finding: Automotive revenue excluding regulatory credits was $67,533M in FY2025, $74,307M in FY2024 and $80,629M in FY2023; regulatory credits were $1,993M, $2,763M and $1,790M; energy revenue rose from $6,035M (FY2023) to $12,771M (FY2025) and services from $8,319M to $12,530M. In Q3 2026 services revenue reached $4,605M (+33% YoY) while automotive revenue ex-credits was $20,447M and energy $2,881M.
rows.mechanism: The revenue base is rebalancing: the car business is flat to shrinking in dollars per unit while energy storage and the services layer (Supercharging, insurance, used cars, collision) grow double digits off a smaller base, so consolidated revenue can grow while vehicle units fall.
rows.benchmark: FY2023 mix: automotive 85.1% of revenue, energy 6.2%, services 8.6%. Q3 2026: automotive 72.9%, energy 10.3%, services 16.4%.
rows.implication: Value the segments separately; a single blended multiple hides that the 33%-margin energy business is now 17% of gross profit and services 13%.
rows.weakens: Q3 2026 energy revenue fell 16% YoY on tariff refunds and lower Megapack ASP, so the mix shift is not yet monotonic.
rows.confidence: high, from audited segment disclosure and the Q3 2026 release
rows.follow_up: What share of services revenue is recurring (Supercharging, insurance, FSD) versus used-vehicle resale, which carries thin margin?

rows.finding: Regulatory credits contributed $1,993M of FY2025 operating income of $4,355M (45.8%), $2,763M of $7,076M in FY2024 (39.0%) and $1,790M of $8,891M in FY2023 (20.1%). Q3 2026 credits were $113M, down 73% YoY and 15.7% of operating income; 9M 2026 credits were $639M (31.1% of operating income) versus $1,451M a year earlier.
rows.mechanism: Credits carry no cost of revenue, so a dollar of credit revenue is close to a dollar of operating profit; as the compliance obligation on other automakers disappears, that profit disappears without any change in vehicle volumes.
rows.benchmark: FY2024 peak of $2,763M and 39% of operating income; the US DOT finalized the CAFE rollback in late September 2026, removing the compliance driver.
rows.implication: Treat credit revenue as zero in any valuation beyond 2027; the FY2025 operating margin of 4.6% was really 2.5% without credits.
rows.weakens: Credits held up in Q4 2025 ($542M implied) after the consumer credit lapsed, so the decline is regulatory-calendar driven and could stall rather than go to zero in any single quarter.
rows.confidence: high on the figures; medium on the 2027 trajectory
rows.follow_up: How much of the remaining $639M of 9M 2026 credits is non-US (EU/China) and thus outside the CAFE rollback?

rows.finding: Q3 2026 automotive revenue per delivery was $42,026 excluding credits against cost of revenue of $34,436, giving gross profit of $7,591 per vehicle (18.1%); a year earlier the same figures were $41,818, $35,385 and $6,433 (15.4%). Company gross profit per delivery was $11,292 across all three segments, SG&A $4,142, R&D $5,675, operating profit $1,476 (Q3 2025: $3,267).
rows.mechanism: Price was flat (+0.5%) and cost per vehicle fell 2.7%, so the entire 270bp margin recovery came from cost and regional mix (Asia-Pacific), not pricing power; company-level profit per vehicle halved because R&D per delivery rose from $3,279 to $5,675.
rows.benchmark: Rivian's automotive gross profit was a $(36)M loss in Q2 2026; BYD's automotive gross margin was 20.49% in FY2025 (from 22.31%).
rows.implication: Tesla's per-vehicle cost advantage over pure EV peers is real but is being spent on AI R&D, so unit economics no longer translate into company margin.
rows.weakens: Management attributes the 18.1% to regional mix, which can reverse; part of the 2026 cost relief is tariff refunds that peers (Rivian) also booked.
rows.confidence: high on arithmetic from disclosed segment revenue, cost of revenue and deliveries
rows.follow_up: What is the ex-credit automotive gross margin in North America alone, where tariffs and the lost consumer credit hit hardest?

rows.finding: Energy storage revenue was $210M per GWh deployed in Q3 2026 (13.7 GWh) against $273M in Q3 2025 and $273M for FY2025 (46.7 GWh); gross profit per GWh fell only from $85.8M to $69.6M because cost per GWh fell from $187M to $141M, lifting segment gross margin from 31.4% to 33.1% and to 30.2% for 9M 2026.
rows.mechanism: Megapack pricing is deflating faster than the bill of materials as Tesla substitutes its own LFP cells (first Megapacks with Nevada LFP cells shipped in Q3 2026) and adds Megafactory Texas capacity of 50 GWh, so vertical integration defends margin per unit while revenue per unit falls.
rows.benchmark: Fluence, the listed pure-play integrator, earned about 13.1% GAAP gross margin in FY2025.
rows.implication: Energy is the highest-margin dollar of growth and deserves a separate valuation, but 2026 margin is flattered by one-offs.
rows.weakens: Management said the 33.1% was helped by tariff refunds for Megapack customers and cell-related warranty cost reimbursements; excluding those the margin is closer to 30%.
rows.confidence: high on segment arithmetic; medium on the durability of the margin
rows.follow_up: What is the energy gross margin excluding tariff refunds and warranty reimbursements, and what ASP is contracted for 2027 backlog?

rows.finding: FSD (Supervised) active subscriptions rose from 1.04M (Q3 2025) to 1.74M (Q3 2026); deferred revenue tied to FSD, connectivity and software was $4.08B at 2026-09-30 against $3.87B at 2025-12-31; $668M of revenue was recognized in 9M 2026 from prior deferred balances, and total unsatisfied performance obligations over one year were $10.73B, of which $4.80B is due within 12 months.
rows.mechanism: Software is sold as a stand-ready obligation recognised over the vehicle's ownership life, so cash arrives before revenue; the balance sheet therefore carries a growing but slow-release software annuity rather than a high-margin licence.
rows.benchmark: Deferred revenue $4.08B versus 9M 2026 revenue of $78,669M is about 5% of annual revenue, small relative to the valuation premium attributed to autonomy.
rows.implication: FSD is not yet a material revenue line and cannot be verified as one; the robotaxi and Optimus optionality is not in the current financials.
rows.weakens: The company's >75% North American attach rate implies deferred revenue should grow faster than it has; FSD revenue is not disclosed as a separate line, so the attach rate cannot be reconciled to revenue.
rows.confidence: medium: filings disclose balances, not FSD revenue
rows.follow_up: Will Tesla disclose FSD revenue separately once robotaxi rides scale, and how is Robotaxi revenue recognised?

rows.finding: Operating expenses rose to $4,776M in Q3 2026 (+39% YoY) against gross profit of $5,494M, so opex absorbed 86.9% of gross profit; R&D alone was $2,761M (+69%) and SG&A $2,015M (+29%), of which $293M was stock-based compensation tied to the 2025 CEO Performance Award. Depreciation rose 17% to $1,580M in the quarter.
rows.mechanism: Tesla is converting a hardware gross-profit pool into a fixed AI cost base (compute, silicon, Optimus, robotaxi fleet) before the associated revenue exists, so operating leverage runs backwards: gross margin up 160bp, operating margin down 322bp.
rows.benchmark: FY2025 R&D was $6,411M; 9M 2026 R&D alone is $7,078M, already 10% above the full prior year.
rows.implication: The break-even question is not unit economics but whether energy and services gross profit can outgrow the AI cost base; at 2.6% operating margin the model does not cover its capital cost.
rows.weakens: Part of the opex increase is equity compensation, not cash; the cash cost base grows more slowly than GAAP opex.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: What is the 2027 R&D and capex plan once Cortex and Austin Fab are commissioned, and when does AI spending stop expanding as a share of revenue?

rows.finding: The warranty reserve rose to $10,138M at 2026-09-30 from $8,075M a year earlier (+26%) while quarterly deliveries fell 2%; the quarterly provision fell to $597M from $727M but costs incurred rose to $1,614M for 9M 2026 from $1,254M. Inventory rose to $14,092M from $12,392M at 2025-12-31 (+13.7%) with 11 days of vehicle supply.
rows.mechanism: A growing warranty reserve against falling unit volume means either the fleet is ageing into claims (services cost) or accruals are being built for recalls and new products; inventory growth ahead of deliveries absorbs cash and signals launch build-up for Semi, Cybercab and Optimus.
rows.benchmark: Warranty provision per delivery fell to $1,227 from $1,463; reserve per trailing-twelve-month delivery rose to about $5,816 from $4,713.
rows.implication: Watch warranty and inventory as the two places where future margin can be silently pre-spent; they are small relative to revenue but trending the wrong way.
rows.weakens: The reserve covers energy storage warranties of up to 25 years, so growth in the storage fleet mechanically raises it; the per-vehicle comparison is therefore imperfect.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: What portion of the warranty reserve relates to energy storage versus vehicles, and were there recall accruals in 2026?

plan.decision_question: Where does Tesla actually make its money in 2026, and how much of operating profit depends on regulatory credits or one-off items rather than vehicle gross profit?
plan.thesis_sentence: Tesla still makes most of its gross profit selling cars, but after regulatory credits the car business earns almost nothing at the operating line: the credit stream that supplied 45.8% of FY2025 operating income had fallen to $113M in Q3 2026, and the incremental profit is now coming from a 33%-margin energy-storage business and a 15.9%-margin services business while AI spending absorbs 87% of gross profit.
plan.why_different: The market and competition sections describe the addressable market and rivals; this section is the only place that decomposes the P&L into who pays, for what, per unit, and how much profit survives each layer of cost.
plan.mechanism: Credits are a zero-cost revenue line that converts almost one-for-one into operating profit, so their withdrawal mechanically subtracts margin with no volume change; meanwhile energy storage deflates in price but falls faster in cost through LFP vertical integration, and services scale on an installed fleet without proportional unit cost.
plan.comparison_set: Rivian (pure EV, still negative automotive gross profit), BYD (20.49% auto gross margin, FY2025), Fluence (13.1% storage gross margin), GM (FY2025 EBIT-adjusted $12.7B) and Ford (2026 capex guidance $9.5-10.5B).
plan.counter_evidence: The 18.1% ex-credit automotive margin may be a regional-mix and tariff-refund artefact rather than a cost step-down; the 33.1% energy margin contains tariff refunds and warranty reimbursements; opex is rising 39% and R&D 69%, so the operating margin (2.6%) may keep falling even as gross margin improves.
plan.visual: Two tables: revenue and gross margin by segment FY2023-FY2025, 9M 2026 and Q3 2026; and a per-delivery unit-economics waterfall Q3 2026 against Q3 2025.
plan.prohibited: 'clear business model', 'strong team', 'huge market', 'well positioned', 'risks are manageable', 'fierce competition', vague counts, and any sentence describing how the section is written.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Tesla, Inc. 10-K for the period ending 2025-12-31, filed 2026-01-29 (accession 0001628280-26-003952): Item 7 (Management's Discussion and Analysis), paragraphs mentioning deliveries, market share, competition, demand. Page 1 of 2 (12,106 characters).

As a result of rapidly evolving trade and fiscal policy, uncertainty in the automotive and energy markets continues, posing risks to our global supply chain and cost structure which could have a meaningfully adverse impact on demand for our products and our profitability. The current tariff regime will have a relatively larger impact on our energy generation and storage business compared to our automotive business. While we prepare for near-term challenges to our business under current policies, we are focused on long-term growth opportunities as we continue to make prudent investments.
In 2025, we recognized total revenues of $94.83 billion, representing a decrease of $2.86 billion compared to the prior year. In 2025, our net income attributable to common stockholders was $3.79 billion, representing a decrease of $3.30 billion compared to the prior year. We continue to ramp production and build and optimize our manufacturing capacity, expand our operations while focusing on further cost reductions and operational efficiencies to enable increased deliveries and deployments of our products, and invest in research and development to accelerate our AI, software and fleet-based profits for further revenue growth.
Automotive and AI Enabled Products—Demand, Sales, Deliveries and Infrastructure
Our cost reduction efforts, cost innovation strategies, and additional localized procurement and manufacturing are key to our vehicles’ affordability and have allowed us to competitively price our vehicles. We will also continue to generate demand by improving our vehicles’ performance and functionality, including through product offerings and features utilizing artificial intelligence such as FSD (Supervised) and other software, and delivering new vehicles and vehicle options. In addition, we believe the launch of our Robotaxi service unlocks the potential for significant business growth to advance a service-driven business model. We will continue to improve safety and profitability while scaling the network. In addition, we have been increasing awareness, and expanding our vehicle financing programs, including attractive leasing terms for our customers. We will also continue to work on developing our robotics offerings.
Changes in government and economic policies, incentives or tariffs may also impact our production, cost structure and the competitive landscape. For instance, while the final scope and application of recently announced changes in trade policy remain uncertain at this time, higher tariffs on imports and subsequent retaliatory tariffs could adversely impact consumer spending and demand for durable goods and related services. Furthermore, certain provisions of the OBBBA, including the removal of tax credits for electric vehicles, may also impact consumer demand for electric vehicles in general. We will continue to adjust accordingly to such developments, and we believe our ongoing cost reduction efforts, including through production innovation, process improvements and logistics optimization, and focus on operating leverage, vertical integration and supply chain localization will continue to benefit us in relation to our competitors. Our new products and our advances in autonomy and robotics, position us for future growth.
As our vehicle production increases, we must work constantly to similarly increase vehicle delivery capability so that it does not become a bottleneck on our total deliveries. As we expand our manufacturing operations globally, we will also have to continue to increase and staff our delivery, servicing and charging infrastructure accordingly, maintain our vehicle reliability and optimize our Supercharger locations to ensure cost effectiveness and customer satisfaction. In particular, as other automotive manufacturers have announced their adoption of NACS and agreements with us to utilize our Superchargers, we must correspondingly expand our network in order to ensure adequate availability to meet customer demands. We also remain focused on continued enhancements of the capability and efficiency of our servicing operations. In tandem with the launch of our Robotaxi business, we are focused on developing and optimizing dedicated infrastructure, including in relation to vehicle cleaning and maintenance, charging, security, teleoperations and fleet management, to ensure service quality as we continue to scale.
Energy Generation and Storage Demand, Production and Deployment
The long-term success of this business is dependent upon incremental volume growth. We continue to increase the production and capabilities of our energy storage products to meet high levels of demand, including the ramps of our Megafactories in Shanghai and Lathrop, California, and the construction of a new Megafactory near Houston, Texas. In 2025, we introduced Megapack 3 and Megablock, our next-generation industrial storage product, and began manufacturing a new residential retrofit solar panel. For Megapack, energy storage deployments can vary meaningfully quarter to quarter depending on the timing of specific project milestones and logistics. As these product lines grow, we will have to maintain adequate battery cell supply for our energy storage products. At the same time, changes in government and economic incentives or tariffs may also impact our sales, cost structure and the competitive landscape. For instance, import tariffs by the US government and the provisions of the OBBBA could significantly increase battery cell expenses and impact costs for our consumers, negatively impacting consumer demand. Despite these challenges, as AI infrastructure drives rapid load growth, we see opportunities for our energy storage products to stabilize the grid, shift energy when it is needed most and provide additional power capacity.
Automotive sales revenue includes revenues related to cash and financing deliveries of new vehicles, and specific other features and services that meet the definition of a performance obligation under Accounting Standards Codification 606, Revenue from Contracts with Customers (“ASC 606”), including access to our internet connectivity, access to our FSD (Supervised) features and their ongoing maintenance, free Supercharging programs and over-the-air software updates. We recognize revenue on automotive sales, net of any discounts or financial subsidies, upon delivery to the customer, which is when the control of a vehicle transfers. Payments are typically received at the point control transfers or in accordance with payment terms customary to the business, except sales we finance for which payments are collected over the contractual loan term. We also recognize a sales return reserve based on historical experience plus consideration for expected future market values when we offer resale value guarantees or similar buyback terms. Other features and services such as access to our internet connectivity, unlimited free Supercharging and over-the-air software updates are provisioned upon transfer of control of a vehicle and recognized over time on a straight-line basis as we have a stand-ready obligation to deliver such services to the customer. Other limited free Supercharging incentives are recognized based on actual usage or expiration, whichever is earlier. We recognize revenue related to these other features and services over the performance period, which is generally the expected ownership life of the vehicle. Revenue related to FSD (Supervised) features is recognized when functionality is delivered to the customer and their ongoing maintenance is recognized over time. For our obligations related to automotive sales, we estimate standalone selling price by considering costs used to develop and deliver the service, third-party pricing of similar options and other information that may be available. Customers may purchase subscriptions, including FSD (Supervised) and premium connectivity, after taking delivery of their vehicles. Revenue from subscriptions is recognized either over time or point in time depending on the nature of contractual terms.
Inventories are stated at the lower of cost or net realizable value. Cost is computed using standard cost for vehicles and energy products, which approximates actual cost on a first-in, first-out basis. We record inventory write-downs for excess or obsolete inventories based upon assumptions about current and future demand forecasts. If our inventory on-hand is in excess of our future demand forecast, the excess amounts are written-off.
Automotive sales revenue includes revenues related to cash and financing deliveries of new vehicles, including internet connectivity, access to our FSD (Supervised) features and their ongoing maintenance, free Supercharging programs and over-the-air software updates. These deliveries are vehicles that are not subject to lease accounting.

plan.comparison_set: Waymo's autonomy operating bench, BYD's engineering depth and Tesla's own 2017-2018 Model 3 ramp, plus the 2024-2026 departure list as a base rate for a company running four simultaneous programmes.
plan.counter_evidence: Internal promotions (Joe Ward to global sales, AJ Booth to energy VP), Elluswamy's 12-year retention and Straubel's return to the board show the bench is not empty; the 2025 award and $158bn grant value are explicitly retention tools, and the 10 millionth vehicle and 3 September Cybercab launch show shipping capability.
plan.decision_question: Does the team's execution record and bandwidth support the vehicle, energy, autonomy and Optimus roadmap at the same time?
plan.mechanism: Tesla's model concentrates decision rights in one CEO while distributing execution to a thin layer of long-tenured engineers; when a programme leader leaves, the knowledge does not transfer to a peer but up to Musk, which slows each of the four programmes that compete for his attention and for the same AI talent pool.
plan.prohibited: No 'strong team', no 'visionary', no unqualified claim that departures are normal attrition; do not present the 2025 award as retention certainty; no ratings without a stated dimension.
plan.thesis_sentence: Tesla's execution machine still ships — 10.2 million cumulative vehicles, fare-paying Cybercab rides from 2026-09-03 and Optimus off a high-volume Fremont line — but the bench beneath Elon Musk has thinned to three named executive officers and at least 17 senior departures since April 2024, so the four-front roadmap depends on one man and a handful of engineers paid to stay rather than on a management team that could be handed the plan.
plan.visual: Team assessment matrix with each leader plus the evidence component on the strongest proof and the strongest doubt; education and career tables carry the CV record.
plan.why_different: This section judges people and execution capacity, not the products themselves or their markets; the same departure facts belong here as retention evidence, while the product section owns technical feasibility.

rows.benchmark: Ford and GM run multi-layer executive benches with named segment presidents; Tesla discloses three executive officers for a $94.8bn-revenue group [S5].
rows.confidence: high
rows.finding: Tesla discloses only three executive officers as of 2026-10-19: Elon Musk (CEO and Technoking), Vaibhav Taneja (CFO, since August 2023) and Xiaotong (Tom) Zhu (SVP APAC and Global Vehicle Manufacturing, since June 2025).
rows.follow_up: Who runs vehicle engineering, energy and Optimus below the SVP layer, and are they disclosed anywhere?
rows.implication: Key-person risk is structural, not incidental: an investor owns Musk's attention allocation across Tesla, SpaceX/xAI and politics, with no disclosed COO to absorb operations.
rows.mechanism: With no COO and no segment CEOs, every programme leader reports into a CEO who also runs SpaceX and chairs xAI's successor; decision rights concentrate at the top while execution capacity sits in a thin layer of long-tenured engineers.
rows.weakens: Titles understate the real bench: unnamed VPs such as Ashok Elluswamy run FSD, Robotaxi and Optimus [S94], and Joe Ward was promoted to global sales chief in February 2026 [S93].

rows.benchmark: The 2018 award delivered 286,428,773 restricted shares after the Delaware Supreme Court reversed the rescission on 2025-12-19 [S5].
rows.confidence: high
rows.finding: Elon Musk, age 55, has been CEO since October 2008; prior exits Zip2 (sold to Compaq, March 1999) and PayPal (sold to eBay, October 2002); concurrently SpaceX CEO since May 2002, xAI CEO since March 2023, X CTO since October 2022 and Neuralink CEO; education B.A. Physics, University of Pennsylvania and B.S. Business, Wharton.
rows.follow_up: How many days per quarter does Musk spend at Tesla, and does any board process measure it?
rows.implication: Founder-market fit is unusually strong on product and capital raising and unusually weak on succession and focus; size the position for headline and key-person volatility rather than for management continuity.
rows.mechanism: The same person sets product direction, raises capital and negotiates related-party transactions, so his attention is the binding constraint on four simultaneous programmes and his departure or distraction re-prices the equity.
rows.weakens: Musk's record of shipping against scepticism (Model 3 ramp, 10 millionth vehicle in Q3 2026 [S6]) argues against discounting his operating involvement.

rows.benchmark: Musk's 2025 reported compensation was $158,359,009,867 against a median employee of $62,786, a ratio of 2,522,203:1 [S78]; 2025 say-on-pay support was 78.2% [S5].
rows.confidence: high
rows.finding: The other two NEOs are paid almost entirely in equity on modest salaries: Taneja $400,000 and Zhu $364,338 at end-2025, with Taneja holding 1,362,518 exercisable options and Zhu 2,195,673 options at 2026-09-30.
rows.follow_up: What are the retention terms for the engineers below VP level who actually build FSD and Optimus?
rows.implication: Retention is bought with stock, not cash, so a falling share price removes the retention mechanism exactly when the programmes are most at risk.
rows.mechanism: Equity-heavy pay aligns the top three with the share price but leaves the VP and director layer, where the departed leaders sat, exposed to a volatile stock and to offers from better-capitalised AI labs.
rows.weakens: The board says it does not make annual grants to NEOs and that options carry no intrinsic value at grant, which is a pay-for-performance design rather than a retention guarantee.

rows.benchmark: A 30-month window in which the Cybercab programme lost its program manager, its new-product-introduction head, two assembly leads and the robotaxi-software director, and energy lost its VP two weeks before this report.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.finding: At least 17 senior leaders left between April 2024 and 2026-10-15, including Drew Baglino (SVP powertrain and energy, April 2024), Rebecca Tinucci (Supercharging, April 2024), Omead Afshar (operations, fired 2025-06-26), Raj Jegannathan (VP IT and AI infrastructure, 2026-02-09), Sendil Palani (VP finance after 17 years, 2026-03-10) and Mike Snyder (VP energy and charging, 2026-10-15).
rows.follow_up: Do the 2026 departures map to a specific programme slipping, and did any join a competitor with Tesla IP knowledge?
rows.implication: Turnover in the Cybercab and energy programmes is a direct execution risk to the two growth engines outside autos; a diligence team should ask for programme-level staffing and attrition data.
rows.mechanism: Departures cluster where the roadmap is newest (Cybercab, Optimus, energy) and where the labour market is hottest, so the programmes with the least institutional memory lose the most of it.
rows.weakens: Several exits were dismissals or planned retirements and internal promotions filled key roles (AJ Booth for Snyder, Joe Ward for global sales), so the net loss of capability is smaller than the headline count.

rows.benchmark: Battery Day (2020-09-22) promised a step-change in cell cost and volume; the dry-electrode process reached production about five years later, and battery availability still capped Q3 2026 volumes [S6].
rows.confidence: medium
rows.finding: The 4680 cell programme reached dry-electrode production for both anode and cathode at Giga Texas, disclosed in the Q4 2025 update on 2026-01-28, roughly five years after the 2020 Battery Day target; Tesla nonetheless described battery availability as the limiting factor for auto volumes in Q3 2026.
rows.follow_up: What is 4680 output in GWh and what share of 2026 vehicle cells is in-house?
rows.implication: The team eventually solves hard manufacturing problems but consistently later than promised; discount management timelines on Optimus and Cybercab by a similar factor.
rows.mechanism: Tesla's method is to attack the limiting component in-house; that works but the learning curve is long, so each new vertical (cells, AI silicon, robots) consumes years of engineering bandwidth before it pays.
rows.weakens: The disclosure shows the problem was solved rather than abandoned, and Tesla Semi volume production and Megafactory Texas started in Q3 2026 [S6], evidence the manufacturing bench can still deliver.

rows.benchmark: Waymo's fleet data show a scaled driverless operation with no steering-wheel exemption fight, a reminder that autonomy execution is an operating discipline, not only a model problem [S59].
rows.confidence: medium
rows.finding: Autonomy execution has shipped on a shorter cycle than the 4680 effort: Robotaxi launched in June 2025 with Model Y, safety monitors began coming out in Austin in January 2026, commercial Cybercab rides started 2026-09-03, and active FSD subscriptions reached 1.74 million at 2026-09-30.
rows.follow_up: What are absolute unsupervised Robotaxi miles and fleet size, and what is the incidents-per-mile record?
rows.implication: The autonomy team, led by Elluswamy, is the strongest evidence for the team's ability to execute; it also makes him the single most acute retention risk after Musk.
rows.mechanism: One engineer's organisation owns FSD, Robotaxi software and Optimus AI, so a departure or a split of his attention would hit all three programmes at once.
rows.weakens: Tesla discloses cumulative unsupervised miles only as an eightfold quarter-on-quarter increase, not an absolute figure, and NHTSA issued a Special Order in September 2026 demanding proof the driverless Cybercab meets federal standards [S93].

rows.benchmark: A public company of Tesla's scale normally discloses a CEO succession plan; Tesla's own award makes the CEO the author of the framework that unlocks his last two tranches.
rows.confidence: high
rows.finding: No COO or president sits below Musk, the two most senior operating roles are a CFO who came up through accounting and an SVP who built Shanghai, and tranches 11 and 12 of the 2025 award vest only after the board approves a CEO succession framework developed by Musk himself.
rows.follow_up: Has the board seen a succession framework, and is it conditioned on Musk remaining CEO through 2032?
rows.implication: A multi-year hold carries unhedgeable key-person risk: the plan, the capital allocation and the succession are all the same person, and the award pays him to stay rather than to build a successor.
rows.mechanism: The succession condition turns a governance safeguard into an award trigger, so the board has an incentive to approve a framework that keeps Musk in place rather than one that replaces him.
rows.weakens: Straubel, a co-founder and former CTO, sits on the board and could plausibly step into a technical leadership role, and Denholm has chaired the board since 2018.

arguments.markdown:
Tesla's technology is proven where it is a manufacturing problem — dry-electrode cells, Megapack integration — and unproven where the valuation sits. About 2.0 million cumulative unsupervised robotaxi miles, a 300-plus Cybercab fleet in Austin and a Texas-only paid driverless permit sit against Waymo's roughly 4,000 vehicles and 500,000 paid rides a week; autonomy is a 2027-2029 option, not a 2026 capability [S6, S59]. The judgement that follows: the technology justifies a premium to a capital-intensive manufacturer in energy and process engineering, and does not yet justify the multiple of a software platform.

### How FSD works, and where it stops

FSD (Supervised) is vision-only. Eight cameras feed an end-to-end neural network that outputs steering, acceleration and braking; it learns from video harvested from a fleet that has delivered 10.2 million vehicles and runs on Tesla's in-house inference silicon. There is no lidar, no radar and no dependence on pre-mapped corridors of the kind Waymo uses — the wager is that fleet-scale data substitutes for sensor redundancy. Training runs on the Cortex clusters at Gigafactory Texas (Cortex 1 above 105 MW, Cortex 2 above 120 MW, 400 MW targeted by 2026-12-31). Two problems stay unsolved. The first is degradation detection when cameras are blinded by rain, fog or low sun: NHTSA's Engineering Analysis EA26002, opened 2026-03-19 over 13 crashes and about 2.88 million vehicles, asks exactly whether the system notices and warns the driver. The second is the reliability increment that permits removing the supervisor, which is why customer-owned unsupervised driving moved to about Q2 2027 [S58, S80].

| Metric | Value | Method | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| FSD miles per major collision | 6,006,200 (North America, October 2026) | Company safety report, FSD-engaged miles | S58 |
| US driving miles per major collision | 660,164 | Company comparison basis | S58 |
| Cumulative unsupervised robotaxi miles | ~2.0 million (to 2026-09-30) | Company quarterly update | S6 |
| Active FSD subscriptions | 1.74 million (Q3 2026) | Company KPI, excludes free trials | S6 |
| FSD attach rate, North America | >75% of deliveries (Q3 2026, from 55% in Q2 2026) | Company disclosure | S6 |
| 4680 cell output | >1 million cells/week; >40 GWh installed | Giga Texas line data | S56 |
| 4680 energy density | 272 Wh/kg (Cybercell, Gen 2) | Cell teardown estimates | S56 |
| Energy storage deployed | 13.7 GWh (Q3 2026); 36.0 GWh (9M 2026) | Company KPI | S6 |
| Megapack segment gross margin | 33.1% (Q3 2026) | Segment accounts | S4 |

### Robotaxi: a real service, on one state's terms

Paid Cybercab rides began in Austin on 2026-09-03, and Tesla claimed 300-plus Cybercabs serving the city on 2026-10-10. Texas registration records showed 319 authorised Cybercab VINs, and the company has not said how many run without a safety monitor, what a ride costs or what the service earns. The permit position is the constraint: Texas allows self-certified commercial driverless operation under its 2026 law, while California lists Tesla Robotaxi LLC only for testing with a driver and omits it from both the driverless-testing and deployment lists (2026-10-22) [S73, S74]. NHTSA's defect petition DP26010, opened 2026-10-09 on school-zone speeding, puts the monitored fleet at about 1,000 vehicles — larger than the Austin count the company promotes.

| Dimension | Tesla | Benchmark | What it means | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Autonomy sensing | Vision-only cameras, no lidar or radar | Waymo: lidar, radar and cameras with high-definition maps | Lower bill of materials, higher tail risk in degraded conditions | S59 |
| Weekly paid rides | Not disclosed; ~2.0 million cumulative unsupervised miles | Waymo: 500,000 paid rides a week on ~4,000 vehicles | At ~5 miles a ride, Waymo runs roughly 2.5 million rider-only miles a week, more than Tesla's cumulative total | S59, S6 |
| Cities with paid driverless service | Austin (Cybercab), Dallas (Model Y, company claim) | Waymo: 15 US cities | Tesla's revenue base is one state | S74, S59 |
| Cell performance | 4680: 272 Wh/kg, 10-80% charge in 35-40 minutes | CATL Qilin 3 claims a full charge in six minutes | Tesla leads on cost, trails on density and charging | S56 |
| Cell scale | 27.1% of H1 2026 global ESS cells held by CATL (125.0 GWh of 461.3 GWh) | Tesla does not disclose a cell share | Tesla is a niche cell maker, not a scale leader | S81 |
| Storage integrator rank | Tesla second | Sungrow first, CATL third, BYD fourth, Fluence seventh | Integration and bankability, not cells, carry Megapack | S72 |
| BEV volume, Q3 2026 | 486,532 units | BYD 762,478 passenger BEVs (+30.89% YoY) | Cost leadership has moved to China | S76 |

### Cells and manufacturing: a cost moat, not a performance one

Giga Texas runs above one million 4680 cells a week at more than 40 GWh of installed capacity, and since January 2026 both electrodes use the dry process in production — a step CATL, Panasonic, LG and Samsung SDI have not taken to commercial scale. The economics are real: electrode cost toward 50% lower, roughly 41% less line capex, more than 30% less factory energy. The product is not: energy density trails by 10-15%, charging is slower than Panasonic 2170 packs, yields above 90% sit below the 98% of mature producers, and Tesla still buys CATL LFP and Panasonic or LG 2170 cells for Shanghai and Fremont Model Y. Battery availability, not demand, remained the stated limit on 2026 volume [S56].

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why it is hard | Time to replicate |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fleet data and training set | 7 | 10.2 million vehicles and billions of FSD miles, but data only compounds with compute and labelling | 3-4 years |
| Dry-electrode process | 7 | Both electrodes dry at >90% yield; no competitor at commercial scale | 3 years |
| Vertical integration (cells, packs, chips, charging) | 6 | Process know-how and capital; AI6 foundry dependence caps it | 3-5 years |
| Energy integration and Autobidder software | 5 | Utility relationships, bankability and US localisation | 2 years |
| Supercharger and NACS network | 5 | 8,904 stations and 84,465 connectors at 2026-09-30 | 3 years |
| Driverless permits | 4 | Texas self-certification is easy; California and the EU are not | 1-2 years Texas, 3+ California |
| **Composite** | **6/10** | | **~3 years of lead time** |

The replication test: a funded team of 50 with all published Tesla material would need about three years to match the dry-electrode line and two to match Megapack integration, because both rest on process know-how that patents do not disclose. The autonomy stack is harder to copy but also harder to prove.

### Patents: thin disclosure, deliberate

| Patent or application | Title | Jurisdiction | Filed | Granted | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Four international filings published 2026-04-16 | Optimus Gen 3 forearm, wrist, joint and hand assemblies | WIPO/PCT | Priority 2024-10-10 | — | Published, national phase pending | 22 degrees of freedom per hand, 25 forearm actuators, tendon-driven | S75 |
| US20260310299A1 | Flexible touch sensors for robotic hands | US | Not disclosed | — | Published 2025-10-08 | Tactile sensing for manipulation | S75 |
| Maxwell Technologies portfolio (acquired 2019, ~$235m) | Dry electrode manufacturing IP | US | Pre-2019 | Granted, owned | In force | Underpins the 4680 dry process | S56 |

Patent protection is not presented as a competitive advantage in the 10-K business description, which rests the case on data, manufacturing cost and vertical integration [S3]. The Optimus filings illustrate the limit: Musk said in April 2026 that the V3 hand would not use the patented design because it "ultimately didn't work", so the public record trails the programme by design cycles. Freedom-to-operate risk is not publicly disclosed; no blocking third-party claim appears in the sources reviewed, which is not the same as none existing.

### Product inventory

| Product | Stage | Launch | Revenue or share | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Model 3/Y | Commercial | 2017-2020 | $20.09bn automotive sales Q3 2026; 478,237 units (98.3%) | 18.5% total automotive | Next-generation platform, no date disclosed | S6, S76 |
| Cybertruck and other models | Commercial | 2023-11 | 8,295 units Q3 2026 | Not disclosed | Utilise >125,000 capacity | S6 |
| Cybercab and Robotaxi | Early commercial | 2026-09-03 Austin | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Unsupervised customer cars ~Q2 2027 | S6, S57 |
| FSD (Supervised) | Commercial | 2020-10 | 1.74m subscriptions; >75% North America attach | Inside services; not disclosed | China approval pending | S6 |
| Megapack, Megablock | Commercial | 2019; Megapack 3 in 2025 | $2.881bn segment Q3 2026 | 33.1% | Ramp 50 GWh Texas | S4, S6 |
| Optimus | Early production | 2026-10 | None | None | 20,000 units a week by end-2027, company claim | S57 |
| Tesla Semi | Volume production | 2026 Q3 | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | 25,000-unit Nevada capacity | S6 |

Two products carry the equity: Model 3/Y, which is 98.3% of volume and flat, and Megapack, which earns a third of revenue as gross profit on a fraction of the capital. Cybercab and Optimus carry the narrative and, so far, no disclosed revenue [S6, S57].

### Energy is the proven technology

Megapack is the one line where Tesla holds a genuine integration advantage and prices it: 13.7 GWh deployed in Q3 2026, a 33.1% gross margin and record order rate and backlog, with 50 GWh of Texas capacity starting production and packs now built from Tesla-made LFP cells in Nevada. The counterweight is pricing: revenue fell 16% year over year to $2.881bn even as volume rose, on lower Megapack average selling prices and tariff refunds [S4, S72]. A business whose volume grows while revenue falls is winning on cost and losing on price, which is what a commoditising integrator market looks like.

::: evidence
**The headline safety statistic is a company measurement, not an audited record.**

Tesla's October 2026 report puts FSD (Supervised) at 6,006,200 miles per major collision against 660,164 for US driving overall, but the ratio is not fault-based, is computed from Tesla telemetry and has not been verified by the regulator, which is running an engineering analysis over 13 reduced-visibility crashes instead [S58, S80].
:::

### What would change the judgement

The strongest case against my caution is that FSD is already a monetised product: attach reached more than 75% of North American deliveries, subscriptions reached 1.74 million and deferred revenue rose $1.24bn in Q3 2026 to $8.79bn across current and non-current balances, while services and other gross profit hit a record $734m. That is real software revenue without a single unsupervised mile, and it argues the data flywheel is working even if the robotaxi is late. Against it: eight NHTSA recall campaigns on the 2026 Model Y since 2025-05-30 show launch quality is slipping on the highest-volume car, none of them ADAS-related, and the FSD attach rate is a North American figure that cannot be reproduced in China, where sales fell 16% in Q3 2026 and approval is still pending [S7, S77].

Diligence questions: what did the Austin robotaxi service earn per vehicle per week, and how many Cybercabs ran without a monitor? What is the blended pack cost per kWh and the share of packs bought rather than built? Does EA26002 end in a recall, and what would that do to the unsupervised release date? Until the first two are answered, the honest position is that Tesla owns the best-proven manufacturing technology in the sector and has not yet proven the one that the share price pays for.

{"url":"https://www.coxautoinc.com/insights/ev-market-monitor-august-2026/","title":"EV Market Monitor – August 2026 - Cox Automotive Inc.","text":"August brought further evidence of a steadily maturing electric vehicle (EV) market. New and used EV sales increased from July, inventory levels moved closer to ICE+ vehicles and growing off-lease returns continued to expand used EV availability. At the same time, lower-priced models gained share in the new market, helping narrow the price gap between EVs and ICE+ vehicles.

New and Used EV Sales – August

New EV Sales: New EV sales totaled an estimated 78,895 units in August, up 2.5% from July but down 46.9% from a year earlier. The sizeable decline was expected, as August 2025 set a record for new EV volume in the U.S. Growth across several automakers more than offset Tesla’s decline in August, highlighting a market that is becoming less dependent on a single brand for sales growth. EVs accounted for 5.7% of total new-vehicle sales, essentially unchanged from July.

Tesla remained the dominant player with 40,816 units sold, followed by Toyota, Rivian, Hyundai and Cadillac. Tesla sales declined 3.8% from July, reducing its share of EV sales to 51.7%, down 3.4 percentage points from the prior month. Meanwhile, Toyota continued to gain momentum, with sales climbing 34.9% month over month to 4,964 units, led by the Toyota bZ, whose sales increased 39.6% from July and boosted its share of EV sales by a full percentage point. Chevrolet (+30.3%), Cadillac (+13.1%) and Kia (+12%) also posted solid gains.

Used EV Sales: Used EV sales increased 25.9% month over month and 14.7% year over year in August to 44,350 units. Growing off-lease returns continue to expand used EV availability, providing a larger pool of vehicles for consumers and supporting strong sales growth. EV market share edged up slightly to 2.8%. Tesla, Ford, Hyundai, BMW and Chevrolet were the top five brands by used EV sales.

Tesla continued to be the primary driver of market growth, with sales of used Tesla products increasing 26.5% from July; nearly 30% of used EVs sold in August were Tesla models. Several legacy brands also recorded outsized gains, led by Nissan (+45.1%), Cadillac (+37.7%), and Kia (+32.1%). At the model level, the Tesla Model 3, Tesla Model Y and Ford Mustang Mach-E generated the largest month-over-month volume increases.

New and Used EV Days’ Supply – August

New EV Days’ Supply: Days’ supply decreased to 78 days in August, down 9.6% month over month but higher by 24% year over year. EV inventory now sits just two days above ICE+ levels, marking the narrowest inventory gap of the year.

While the overall market continues to rebalance, inventory levels remain highly uneven across brands. Subaru remained the leanest brand by a wide margin, with supply falling to 26 days in August from 47 in July. Porsche and Toyota also recorded large inventory reductions, with supply declining by 35 and 33 days, respectively, though both remain above the industry average. Meanwhile, Cadillac, Mercedes-Benz and Audi were among the few brands to see supply rise.

Used EV Days’ Supply: Used EV supply and demand moved into balance in August, with days’ supply reaching parity with ICE+ levels for the first time this year. Days’ supply fell to 42 days in August, down 15.4% month over month, though still up 20.2% year over year. Availability tightened broadly across brands, suggesting demand remains healthy, with used Hyundai EVs among the leanest, at 36 days. Availability of used Cadillacs and BMWs tightened in August, while availability of Mercedes-Benz EVs recorded the highest days’ supply among major brands at 57 days.

Note: Tesla and Rivian figures reflect only vehicles available through traditional dealerships and exclude vehicles at factory-owned outlets.

New and Used EV Prices – August

New EV ATP: The EV price gap continued to narrow in August as lower-priced models gained share and EV demand increasingly shifted toward products priced closer to comparable ICE+ alternatives. The average transaction price (ATP) for a new EV declined to $54,754 in August, down 1.3% month over month and 2.8% year over year. Incentives averaged 12% of ATP, or approximately $6,594 per vehicle, down 2.2% from July and 19.9% from a year ago. The EV price premium over ICE+ vehicles narrowed to $4,847, or 9.7%, continuing the trend toward price parity between EVs and ICE+ vehicles.

Three years earlier automotive was 85.1% of revenue; in Q3 2026 automotive supplied $3,806 million of gross profit (69%), energy $954 million (17%) and services $734 million (13%), against 91%/6%/3% in FY2023. Money arrives at three rhythms: cash when a vehicle changes hands, milestone prepayments on storage projects ($3.30 billion of customer prepayments sat in deferred revenue at 2026-09-30 against $2.04 billion at 2025-12-31), and recurring charges for Supercharging, insurance and FSD subscriptions [S3, S4, S6].

| Segment | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 | 9M 2026 | Q3 2026 | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Automotive revenue excluding credits ($M) | 80,629 | 74,307 | 67,533 | 56,671 | 20,447 | S1, S3, S4 |
| Automotive regulatory credits ($M) | 1,790 | 2,763 | 1,993 | 639 | 113 | S1, S3, S4 |
| Energy generation and storage revenue ($M) | 6,035 | 10,086 | 12,771 | 8,428 | 2,881 | S3, S4 |
| Services and other revenue ($M) | 8,319 | 10,534 | 12,530 | 12,931 | 4,605 | S3, S4 |
| Total revenue ($M) | 96,773 | 97,690 | 94,827 | 78,669 | 28,046 | S1, S2, S3, S4 |
| Automotive gross margin excluding credits | 17.7% | 15.4% | 15.4% | 17.7% | 18.1% | S1, S3, S4, S63 |
| Energy gross margin | 18.9% | 26.2% | 29.8% | 30.2% | 33.1% | S3, S4 |
| Services gross margin | 5.9% | 5.8% | 7.4% | 13.4% | 15.9% | S3, S4 |
| Credits as % of operating income | 20.1% | 39.0% | 45.8% | 31.1% | 15.7% | S3, S4 |

The credit franchise is ending, and it outlived the consumer subsidy by about a year. Tesla booked $2,763 million of automotive regulatory credits in FY2024, $1,993 million in FY2025 and $639 million in the first nine months of 2026; the third quarter alone was $113 million, down 73% from $417 million. Because credits carry no cost of revenue, a credit dollar is almost a dollar of operating profit: 45.8% of FY2025 operating income, 39.0% in FY2024 and 20.1% in FY2023, still 31.1% in 9M 2026 but only 15.7% in Q3 2026. The implied Q4 2025 figure of $542 million shows the collapse was not the lapse of the US consumer credit after September 2025 but the removal of the compliance obligation in 2026: the Department of Transportation finalised its rollback of the CAFE standards on 2026-10-01, removing the requirement that made legacy automakers buy zero-emission credits. Stripping credits, FY2025's 4.6% operating margin becomes 2.5%, and Q3 2026's 2.6% becomes 2.2% [S4, S64, S66].

Per vehicle, the business improved even as credits disappeared. Q3 2026 automotive revenue per delivery excluding credits was $42,026, up 0.5% on $41,818; cost of revenue per delivery fell 2.7% to $34,436 from $35,385, so gross profit per vehicle rose 18.0% to $7,591 (18.1% margin) from $6,433 (15.4%). The gain is cost and regional mix, not price: management attributes the 270 basis points to a higher Asia-Pacific delivery mix, where Shanghai is the lowest-cost plant, and Tesla has no disclosed list-price increase in the filings. Tesla does not disclose customer acquisition cost; SG&A per delivery of $4,142 is an upper bound that also carries Supercharging, insurance and corporate cost, against which the first vehicle's gross profit covers 1.8 times the SG&A attributed to its sale. A three-year LTV estimate of about $8,455 adds three years of services gross profit per vehicle in the fleet (roughly $288 a year on 10.2 million cumulative deliveries), giving LTV:CAC of about 2.0:1 on that overstated proxy and payback inside the delivery quarter. Against peers Tesla is the only one of the three with positive per-vehicle automotive gross profit after credits: BYD's automotive gross margin was 20.49% in FY2025, down from 22.31%, and Rivian's automotive gross profit was still a $(36) million loss in Q2 2026 [S63, S65, S68].

| Per unit, Q3 2026 | Q3 2025 | Q3 2026 | Change | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Deliveries (units) | 497,099 | 486,532 | -2.1% | S6 |
| Automotive revenue per delivery, excluding credits | $41,818 | $42,026 | +0.5% | S4, S6 |
| Automotive cost of revenue per delivery | $35,385 | $34,436 | -2.7% | S4, S6 |
| Automotive gross profit per delivery, excluding credits | $6,433 | $7,591 | +18.0% | S4, S6 |
| Energy gross profit per delivery | $2,158 | $1,961 | -9.1% | S4, S6 |
| Services gross profit per delivery | $736 | $1,508 | +105% | S4, S6 |
| SG&A per delivery (acquisition-cost upper bound) | $3,142 | $4,142 | +31.8% | S4, S6 |
| R&D per delivery | $3,279 | $5,675 | +73.1% | S4, S6 |
| Operating profit per delivery | $3,267 | $1,476 | -54.8% | S4, S6 |
| LTV estimate, three years / payback | n/a | $8,455 / under one quarter | n/a | S6, S4 |

| Product | Pricing metric | Q3 2025 | Q3 2026 | Peer benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Model 3/Y, Cybertruck and other vehicles, net of credits | realised revenue per delivery | $41,818 | $42,026 | BYD automotive gross margin 20.49%, FY2025 | S4, S6, S65 |
| Megapack and Powerwall | realised revenue per GWh deployed | $273 million | $210 million | Fluence GAAP gross margin 13.1%, FY2025 | S3, S6, S67 |
| Services and other | revenue per delivery | $6,991 | $9,465 | no comparable peer disclosure | S6 |
| FSD (Supervised) | deferred balance per active subscription | not disclosed | $2,345 | none disclosed | S4, S6 |

Energy is now the highest-margin dollar of growth. Storage revenue per GWh fell 23% to $210 million from $273 million, but gross profit per GWh fell only 19% to $69.6 million from $85.8 million because cost per GWh fell 25% to $141 million from $187 million, lifting segment gross margin to 33.1% from 31.4%. The mechanism is vertical integration into cells: the first Megapacks built with Tesla's own Nevada LFP cells shipped in Q3 2026, Megafactory Texas began production with 50 GWh of planned capacity, and management says the Megapack backlog is nearly sold out through 2027. Fluence, the listed pure-play integrator, earned about 13.1% gross margin in FY2025, so Tesla's advantage is roughly two and a half times the systems-integrator benchmark and comes from owning the cell, not from pricing power, since its own price per GWh is falling. The caveat is that management attributed part of the 33.1% to tariff refunds for Megapack customers and to cell-related warranty cost reimbursements, which are not repeatable. Services is the quieter engine: revenue rose 33% to $4,605 million on 2% fewer deliveries, gross margin reached 15.9% from 10.5% (13.4% for 9M 2026), and the mix is Supercharging, insurance, collision and used vehicles rather than high-margin software. Each additional $1 billion of energy revenue at a 30% margin adds $300 million of gross profit; each $1 billion of automotive revenue at 18% adds $180 million [S67, S4].

FSD and software are growing but still too small to see in the income statement. Active FSD subscriptions rose to 1.74 million from 1.04 million a year earlier; deferred revenue tied to FSD, connectivity and over-the-air software was $4.08 billion against $3.87 billion at 2025-12-31; $668 million of revenue was recognised in 9M 2026 from balances already deferred; and unsatisfied performance obligations longer than one year were $10.73 billion, of which $4.80 billion falls due within twelve months. Management's claim that FSD is attached to more than 75% of North American new deliveries is company-reported and cannot be tied to a revenue line: Tesla does not disclose FSD revenue, so the only observable is $2,345 of deferred balance per active subscription, a stock rather than an annual price. In the second quarter of 2026 Tesla paid $1.95 billion in stock and equity awards for an AI hardware company, of which $222 million went to developed technology and $1.73 billion is contingent on service and performance conditions judged improbable, so no expense has been recognised [S4, S6].

The counter-case is that gross margin is improving while the company gets less profitable. Operating expenses of $4,776 million rose 39% against $5,494 million of gross profit, R&D alone rose 69% to $2,761 million, and depreciation rose 17% to $1,580 million and will accelerate as more than $20 billion of 2026 capital expenditure is commissioned. The warranty reserve rose 26% to $10,138 million against 2% fewer deliveries, with claims incurred up 29% to $1,614 million for the nine months while the provision per delivery fell to $1,227 from $1,463, a cost that may migrate back into cost of revenue if claim rates hold. Inventory rose 13.7% to $14,092 million with only 11 days of vehicle supply, consistent with launch build-up for Semi, Cybercab and Optimus rather than unsold cars [S4, S6].

The vehicle line covers its own costs today, so the break-even question is about the cost base rather than the unit. Quarterly operating expenses of $4,776 million need roughly $27 billion of revenue at a 17.7% blended gross margin to break even; Q3 2026 delivered $28.0 billion and $718 million of operating profit. Normalise energy to a 30% margin and take credits to zero and the same quarter earns about $515 million, a 1.8% operating margin, which is the number a buyer is paying for. Confidence is high on the segment arithmetic, which comes from audited segment disclosure, and medium on how much of the 2026 cost relief is structural rather than tariff and mix effects. Four questions would settle it: the North American automotive gross margin excluding credits, where tariffs and the lost consumer credit bite hardest; the energy margin excluding tariff refunds and the contracted average selling price of the 2027 backlog; the FSD revenue line and how robotaxi rides will be recognised; and the year in which R&D and capital expenditure stop rising as a share of revenue.

::: evidence
**Tesla's profit now rests on energy and services gross profit, not on credits or on the car**

Energy storage and services supplied $1,688 million of Q3 2026 gross profit at 33.1% and 15.9% margins, while regulatory credits fell to $113 million, 15.7% of operating income, from 45.8% of FY2025 operating income, and operating expenses absorbed 86.9% of gross profit [S4, S6].
:::
