arguments.markdown:
Tesla still makes most of its gross profit selling cars, but after regulatory credits the car business earns little at the operating line. Credits supplied 45.8% of FY2025 operating income and 15.7% in Q3 2026; incremental profit now comes from a 33.1%-margin energy-storage business and a 15.9%-margin services business while AI spending absorbs 86.9% of gross profit. Nine-month 2026 revenue of $78,669 million split into automotive $57,310 million (including $639 million of credits), energy $8,428 million and services $12,931 million, against an automotive share of 85.1% in FY2023. Q3 2026 gross profit divided $3,806 million automotive (69%), $954 million energy (17%) and $734 million services (13%), versus 91%/6%/3% in FY2023. Cash arrives when a vehicle changes hands, on storage milestones and prepayments ($3.30 billion of customer prepayments in deferred revenue at 2026-09-30, from $2.04 billion), and monthly for Supercharging, insurance and FSD [S3, S4, S6].

| Segment | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 | 9M 2026 | Q3 2026 | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Automotive revenue excluding credits ($M) | 80,629 | 74,307 | 67,533 | 56,671 | 20,447 | S1, S3, S4 |
| Automotive regulatory credits ($M) | 1,790 | 2,763 | 1,993 | 639 | 113 | S1, S3, S4 |
| Energy generation and storage revenue ($M) | 6,035 | 10,086 | 12,771 | 8,428 | 2,881 | S3, S4 |
| Services and other revenue ($M) | 8,319 | 10,534 | 12,530 | 12,931 | 4,605 | S3, S4 |
| Automotive gross margin excluding credits | 17.7% | 15.4% | 15.4% | 17.7% | 18.1% | S1, S3, S4, S63 |
| Energy gross margin | 18.9% | 26.2% | 29.8% | 30.2% | 33.1% | S3, S4 |
| Services gross margin | 5.9% | 5.8% | 7.4% | 13.4% | 15.9% | S3, S4 |

The credit franchise is ending, and it outlived the consumer subsidy by about a year. Tesla booked $2,763 million of automotive regulatory credits in FY2024, $1,993 million in FY2025 and $639 million in 9M 2026; Q3 2026 alone was $113 million, down 73% from $417 million. Credits carry no cost of revenue, so a credit dollar is nearly a dollar of operating profit: 20.1% of operating income in FY2023, 39.0% in FY2024, 45.8% in FY2025, 31.1% in 9M 2026 and 15.7% in Q3 2026. An implied Q4 2025 figure of $542 million shows the collapse came not with the lapse of the US consumer credit but with the removal of the compliance obligation in 2026: the Department of Transportation finalised its CAFE rollback on 2026-10-01, ending the requirement that made legacy automakers buy zero-emission credits. Without credits, FY2025's 4.6% operating margin is 2.5% and Q3 2026's 2.6% is 2.2% [S4, S64, S66].

Per vehicle the business improved even as credits disappeared. Q3 2026 automotive revenue per delivery excluding credits was $42,026, up 0.5%, while cost of revenue per delivery fell 2.7% to $34,436, so gross profit per vehicle rose 18.0% to $7,591 (18.1% margin) from $6,433 (15.4%). The gain is cost and regional mix, not price: management attributes the 270 basis points to a higher Asia-Pacific delivery mix, where Shanghai is the lowest-cost plant. Tesla does not disclose customer acquisition cost; SG&A per delivery of $4,142 is an upper bound that also carries insurance, Supercharging and corporate cost, and the first vehicle's gross profit covers 1.8 times it. A three-year LTV estimate of $8,455 adds three years of services gross profit per vehicle in the fleet (about $288 a year on 10.2 million cumulative deliveries), giving LTV:CAC of 2.0:1 and payback inside the delivery quarter. Tesla is the only one of the three with positive per-vehicle automotive gross profit after credits: BYD's automotive gross margin was 20.49% in FY2025, from 22.31%, and Rivian's automotive gross profit was a $(36) million loss in Q2 2026 [S63, S65, S68].

| Per unit | Q3 2025 | Q3 2026 | Change | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Deliveries (units) | 497,099 | 486,532 | -2.1% | S6 |
| Automotive revenue per delivery, excluding credits | $41,818 | $42,026 | +0.5% | S4, S6 |
| Automotive cost of revenue per delivery | $35,385 | $34,436 | -2.7% | S4, S6 |
| Automotive gross profit per delivery, excluding credits | $6,433 | $7,591 | +18.0% | S4, S6 |
| Energy gross profit per delivery | $2,158 | $1,961 | -9.1% | S4, S6 |
| Services gross profit per delivery | $736 | $1,508 | +105% | S4, S6 |
| SG&A per delivery (acquisition-cost upper bound) | $3,142 | $4,142 | +31.8% | S4, S6 |
| R&D per delivery | $3,279 | $5,675 | +73.1% | S4, S6 |
| Operating profit per delivery | $3,267 | $1,476 | -54.8% | S4, S6 |

| Product | Pricing metric | Q3 2025 | Q3 2026 | Peer benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Vehicles, net of credits | realised revenue per delivery | $41,818 | $42,026 | BYD automotive gross margin 20.49%, FY2025 | S4, S65 |
| Megapack and Powerwall | realised revenue per GWh deployed | $273 million | $210 million | Fluence gross margin 13.1%, FY2025 | S3, S67 |
| FSD (Supervised) | deferred balance per active subscription | not disclosed | $2,345 | none disclosed | S4, S6 |

Energy is the highest-margin dollar of growth. Storage revenue per GWh fell 23% to $210 million from $273 million, but gross profit per GWh fell only 19% to $69.6 million because cost per GWh fell 25% to $141 million, lifting segment margin to 33.1% from 31.4%. The mechanism is cell integration: the first Megapacks built with Tesla's own Nevada LFP cells shipped in Q3 2026, Megafactory Texas began production with 50 GWh of planned capacity, and management says the Megapack backlog is nearly sold out through 2027. Fluence, the pure-play integrator, earned about 13.1% in FY2025, so Tesla's advantage is roughly two and a half times the benchmark and comes from owning the cell, not from pricing power. Part of the 33.1% is not repeatable, since management attributed it partly to tariff refunds for Megapack customers and cell-related warranty reimbursements. Services is the quieter engine: revenue rose 33% to $4,605 million on 2% fewer deliveries and gross margin reached 15.9% from 10.5%. Each extra $1 billion of energy revenue at 30% adds $300 million of gross profit; the same dollar of automotive revenue at 18% adds $180 million [S67, S4].

FSD and software grow but remain too small to see in the income statement. Active subscriptions rose to 1.74 million from 1.04 million; deferred revenue for FSD, connectivity and software was $4.08 billion against $3.87 billion at 2025-12-31; $668 million was recognised in 9M 2026 from balances already deferred; and obligations beyond one year were $10.73 billion, of which $4.80 billion falls due within twelve months. Management's claim that FSD is attached to more than 75% of North American deliveries is company-reported and cannot be tied to a revenue line, because Tesla does not disclose FSD revenue; the observable is $2,345 of deferred balance per active subscription, a stock rather than a price. In Q2 2026 Tesla paid $1.95 billion in stock and equity awards for an AI hardware company, $222 million of it developed technology and $1.73 billion contingent on conditions judged improbable, so no expense has been booked [S4, S6].

The counter-case is that gross margin improves while the company gets less profitable. Operating expenses of $4,776 million rose 39% against $5,494 million of gross profit, R&D alone rose 69% to $2,761 million, and depreciation rose 17% to $1,580 million and will accelerate as more than $20 billion of 2026 capital expenditure is commissioned. The warranty reserve rose 26% to $10,138 million on 2% fewer deliveries, with claims incurred up 29% to $1,614 million while the provision per delivery fell to $1,227 from $1,463. Inventory rose 13.7% to $14,092 million with 11 days of vehicle supply, consistent with launch build-up rather than unsold cars [S4, S6].

The vehicle line covers its own costs, so the break-even question is about the cost base rather than the unit. Quarterly operating expenses of $4,776 million need roughly $27 billion of revenue at a 17.7% blended margin; Q3 2026 delivered $28.0 billion and $718 million of operating profit. Normalise energy to a 30% margin and take credits to zero and the same quarter earns about $515 million, a 1.8% operating margin, which is what a buyer is paying for today. Confidence is high on the segment arithmetic, which rests on audited segment disclosure, and medium on how much of the 2026 cost relief is structural rather than tariff and mix effects. Four questions would settle it: the North American automotive margin excluding credits; the energy margin excluding tariff refunds and the contracted 2027 backlog price; the FSD revenue line and how robotaxi rides will be recognised; and the year R&D and capital expenditure stop rising as a share of revenue.

::: evidence
**Tesla's profit now rests on energy and services gross profit, not on credits or on the car**

Energy storage and services supplied $1,688 million of Q3 2026 gross profit at 33.1% and 15.9% margins, while regulatory credits fell to $113 million, 15.7% of operating income, from 45.8% of FY2025 operating income, and operating expenses absorbed 86.9% of gross profit [S4, S6].
:::

arguments.markdown:
Tesla is a single-class Texas corporation whose control rests on a 19.8% CEO stake plus a 423.7 million-share contingent award, so a public-equity holder is underwriting Elon Musk's capital allocation rather than a board-governed company; that is acceptable at a governance discount, not a premium. Tesla, Inc. was incorporated in Delaware on 2003-07-01, converted to Texas on 2024-06-13, and trades on Nasdaq under TSLA with one class of common stock and 3,952,648,559 shares outstanding at 2026-09-30, including 423,743,904 unearned restricted shares. There is no VIE, nominee-shareholder or red-chip layer, so identity is simple; control is not [S3].

::: kpi
| Metric | Value | Benchmark | Signal | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Shares outstanding | 3,952,648,559 at 2026-09-30 | 3,541m diluted weighted average, Q3 2026 | warn | S5 |
| CEO economic stake | 19.8% (699,580,882 shares) | Ford family: ~40% of votes on ~2% of shares | warn | S5 |
| Contingent CEO award | 423,743,904 shares, 10.7% of outstanding | 2018 award: 286,428,773 shares | critical | S5 |
| Unrecognised compensation on that award | $9.74bn probable; $105.82bn-$120.37bn not | $162m recognised in 2025 | critical | S4 |
| Cash and short-term investments | $45.45bn at 2026-09-30 | 2026 capex guided above $20bn | good | S6 |
| New credit commitments | $30bn, three agreements, September 2026 | none comparable in 2025 | warn | S4 |
| Insider activity, 12 months | -$87.69m sales, zero open-market purchases | one-sided tape | warn | S27 |
:::

### The entity map is clean; the asset ring-fence is not

| Entity | Jurisdiction | Role | Ownership | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Tesla, Inc. | Texas | Listed parent and principal operating company | 100% | S3, S5 |
| Tesla Robotaxi, LLC | Texas | Robotaxi operating entity | 100% listed subsidiary | S3 |
| Tesla Energy Operations, Inc. | Delaware | Energy generation and storage operations | 100% listed subsidiary | S3 |
| Tesla Manufacturing Brandenburg SE | Germany | Berlin vehicle plant | 100% listed subsidiary | S3 |
| Tesla (Shanghai) Co., Ltd | China | Shanghai plant and China sales, wholly foreign-owned | 100% listed subsidiary | S3 |

EX-21 lists hundreds of entities, mostly Delaware solar and storage project companies plus national sales companies; it states no percentages, so 100% is inferred from listing as a subsidiary. Two points matter. China is held through a wholly foreign-owned enterprise, not a VIE, so there is no contractual-control gap of the kind that discounts US-listed China ADRs, but Shanghai is fully consolidated and exposed to export controls. And no entity is designated holder of Full Self-Driving or Optimus intellectual property: robotaxi operations sit in Tesla Robotaxi, LLC while software, data and chip designs stay in the parent, so there is no separately capitalised autonomy asset for a spin-off or merger to price.

### Customers, buyers and how growth arrives

Tesla sells direct rather than through dealers, in two segments: automotive at $69,526m of 2025 revenue and energy at $12,771m [S71]. The vehicle buyer is a household or fleet paying cash or Tesla financing; the energy buyer is a utility or developer signing multi-year procurement, a slower sale that earned a 33.1% gross margin in Q3 2026 against 18.5% for automotive. Growth now comes from storage (13.7 GWh in Q3 2026), software (1.74 million active FSD subscriptions) and robotaxi rides, which began charging Cybercab passengers in Austin on 2026-09-03. The autonomy budget owner is still a retail customer weighing a monthly subscription, so the software line behaves like consumer discretionary carrying an AI multiple.

### Ownership is concentrated without a dual class

| Holder | Class | Shares | % ownership | % votes | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Elon Musk | Common, incl. 286,428,773 restricted | 699,580,882 | 19.8% | 19.8% | S5 |
| Vanguard Capital Management | Common | 210,796,512 | 5.3% | 5.3% | S5 |
| All directors and officers (11) | Common | 706,496,615 | 20.0% | 20.0% | S5 |
| Unearned 2025 award shares | Restricted, unearned | 423,743,904 | 10.7% of outstanding | proportional to other shares | S5 |
| Other public holders | Common | balance | ~74.9% | ~74.9% | S5 |

Percentages follow the proxy, whose denominator excludes unearned award shares; free float of at most 74.9% is derived by subtracting Musk and Vanguard from that base. Musk's stake includes 207,498,721 shares pledged as collateral for personal debt, so a margin call would add supply at the worst moment. With one class and no super-voting stock, control runs through the CEO office, the board seat and stake size rather than a charter provision, unlike Ford's Class B (about 40% of votes on roughly 2% of shares) or Alphabet's founder Class B. That is a real minority protection: no family trust can outvote the register indefinitely.

### Control is priced through a contingent award

The 2025 CEO Performance Award is the control instrument: 423,743,904 shares in 12 tranches of 35,311,992, each tied to a market-capitalisation milestone from $2.0 trillion to $8.5 trillion and to 1 of 12 operational milestones (20 million vehicles, 10 million FSD subscriptions, 1 million bots, 1 million robotaxis, Adjusted EBITDA of $50bn to $400bn); none was earned at 2026-10-19 [S5]. At $2.0 trillion the first tranche implies roughly $506 per share on 3.95 billion shares, and because the operational test falls away in a change of control, a deal at $3.0 trillion would earn three tranches, about 105.9 million shares, with no robotaxi or Optimus milestone met. Expense is already running: $802m in the first nine months of 2026, $9.74bn unrecognised on the one milestone management judges probable, and $105.82bn-$120.37bn on the rest [S4]. Dilution of 10.7% is designed, not tail, and sits above the current valuation rather than beside it.

### The board can refuse less than it appears

Nine directors sit in three classes, six labelled independent under Nasdaq rules, with Robyn Denholm as chair since November 2018. The labels have worn. Ira Ehrenpreis, who chairs both the compensation and the nominating and governance committees, joined SpaceX's board in February 2026; Kimbal Musk is the CEO's brother; JB Straubel runs Redwood Materials, which bought $12.9m of Tesla scrap and sold it $3.3m of material in 2025. Related-party flows are small in dollars but pointed: Tesla agreed on 2026-01-16 to invest about $2.00bn in xAI, converted into SpaceX Class A stock when SpaceX bought xAI on 2026-02-02 and funded on 2026-03-12, while xAI bought $430.1m of Megapacks and SpaceX bought $143.3m of vehicles in 2025. A board setting a Tesla-SpaceX exchange ratio would do so with three of nine directors tied to SpaceX, and the retail auto-voting programme filed with the 2026 proxy offers standing instructions to vote with the board outside a defined special matter [S78]. The counterweight is narrow: the Special Committee behind the 2025 award used only Denholm and Wilson-Thompson and retained Compensia, and 78.2% of votes cast backed 2025 executive pay.

### Capital allocation has no return floor

Tesla has never paid a dividend, repurchased no shares in 2025, and holds no authorisation to offset dilution. It ended 2026-09-30 with $45.45bn of cash and short-term investments, generated $14.90bn of operating cash flow in nine months against $13.01bn of capex, guided 2026 capex above $20bn, and signed three credit agreements with $30bn of commitments in September 2026 [S6]. Free cash flow was $1.5bn in Q3 2026: funded, but thin against the commitment. Against Ford and GM, which return cash, Tesla offers neither dividend nor buyback, and the only capital return has gone to insiders through equity — directors sold $87.69m in the 12 months to 2026-09-09 with no open-market purchases [S27]. Litigation moved rather than vanished: the Delaware Supreme Court reinstated the 2018 award on 2025-12-19, the 96,000,000-share interim award was forfeited on 2026-04-21, and a securities class action filed on 2025-08-04 in the Western District of Texas covers purchasers from 2023-04-19 to 2025-06-22 over Autopilot, FSD and Robotaxi statements.

A multi-year holder is paid for accepting four things: a 10.7% contingent award that accelerates on a deal price rather than operating proof; conflict committees that include SpaceX-affiliated directors; $30bn of new debt commitments against a $1.5bn quarterly free-cash-flow buffer; and key-person concentration in a CEO who also runs SpaceX. Three conditions would change the judgement — an independent special committee for any SpaceX transaction, removal of change-of-control acceleration from the 2025 award, and a buyback sized to offset stock compensation. None appears in the 2026 proxy, so the governance discount stays. Confidence is high on structure and figures, medium on how a Texas court would treat a challenge to the award; diligence should ask for the pledge's loan-to-value, the xAI Series E valuation, and the drawdown terms of the September 2026 facilities.

arguments.markdown:
Tesla's technology is proven where it is a manufacturing problem — dry-electrode cells, Megapack integration — and unproven where the valuation sits. About 2.0 million cumulative unsupervised robotaxi miles, a 300-plus Cybercab fleet in Austin and a Texas-only paid driverless permit sit against Waymo's roughly 4,000 vehicles and 500,000 paid rides a week; autonomy is a 2027-2029 option, not a 2026 capability [S6, S59]. The technology justifies a premium to a capital-intensive manufacturer in energy and process engineering; it does not yet justify the multiple of a software platform.

### How FSD works, and where it stops

FSD (Supervised) is vision-only. Eight cameras feed an end-to-end neural network that outputs steering, acceleration and braking; it learns from video from a fleet of 10.2 million delivered vehicles and runs on Tesla's in-house inference silicon. There is no lidar, no radar and no pre-mapped corridors as Waymo has — the wager is that fleet-scale data substitutes for sensor redundancy. Training runs on the Cortex clusters in Texas, with 400 MW of compute targeted by 2026-12-31. Two problems stay unsolved. The first is degradation detection when cameras are blinded by rain, fog or low sun: NHTSA's Engineering Analysis EA26002, opened 2026-03-19 over 13 crashes and about 2.88 million vehicles, asks whether the system notices and warns the driver. The second is the reliability increment that permits removing the supervisor, which is why customer-owned unsupervised driving moved to about Q2 2027 [S58, S80].

|---|---|---|---|
| FSD miles per major collision | 6,006,200 (North America, October 2026) | Company report, FSD-engaged miles | S58 |
| Cumulative unsupervised robotaxi miles | ~2.0 million (to 2026-09-30) | Company quarterly update | S6 |
| FSD subscriptions and attach | 1.74 million; >75% of North American deliveries | Company KPI, excludes free trials | S6 |
| 4680 cell output and density | >1 million cells/week; >40 GWh; 272 Wh/kg | Giga Texas line data and teardown estimates | S56 |
| Energy storage deployed | 13.7 GWh (Q3 2026); 36.0 GWh (9M 2026) | Company KPI | S6 |
| Megapack segment gross margin | 33.1% (Q3 2026) | Segment accounts | S4 |

### Robotaxi: a real service, on one state's terms

Paid Cybercab rides began in Austin on 2026-09-03, and Tesla claimed 300-plus Cybercabs serving the city on 2026-10-10; Texas records showed 319 authorised Cybercab VINs. The company has not said how many run without a monitor, what a ride costs or what the service earns. Permits are the constraint: Texas allows self-certified commercial driverless operation under its 2026 law, while California lists Tesla Robotaxi LLC only for testing with a driver and omits it from the driverless-testing and deployment lists (2026-10-22) [S73, S74]. NHTSA's defect petition DP26010, opened 2026-10-09 on school-zone speeding, puts the monitored fleet at about 1,000 vehicles.

| Weekly paid rides | Not disclosed | Waymo: 500,000 a week on ~4,000 vehicles | At ~5 miles a ride, Waymo runs ~2.5m rider-only miles weekly, more than Tesla's cumulative total | S59, S6 |

| BEV volume, Q3 2026 | 486,532 units | BYD 762,478 passenger BEVs, +30.89% year over year | Cost leadership has moved to China | S76 |

### Cells: a cost moat, not a performance one

Giga Texas runs above one million 4680 cells a week at more than 40 GWh of installed capacity, and since January 2026 both electrodes use the dry process in production — a step CATL, Panasonic, LG and Samsung SDI have not taken to commercial scale. The economics are real: electrode cost toward 50% lower, roughly 41% less line capex and more than 30% less factory energy. The product is not: energy density trails by 10-15%, charging is slower than Panasonic 2170 packs, yields above 90% sit below the 98% of mature producers, and Tesla still buys CATL LFP and Panasonic or LG 2170 cells for Shanghai and Fremont Model Y. Battery availability, not demand, remained the stated limit on 2026 volume [S56].

| Dry-electrode process | 7 | Both electrodes dry at >90% yield; no competitor at commercial scale | 3 years |
| Vertical integration (cells, packs, chips) | 6 | Process know-how and capital; AI6 foundry dependence caps it | 3-5 years |
| Driverless permits | 4 | Texas self-certification is easy; California and the EU are not | 1-2 years Texas, 3+ California |
| **Composite** | **6/10** | A funded 50-person team would need ~3 years for the cell line and ~2 for Megapack integration; patents disclose little of either | **~3 years of lead time** |

### Patents: thin disclosure, deliberately

| US20260310299A1 | Flexible touch sensors for robotic hands | US | Not disclosed | — | Published 2025-10-08 | Tactile sensing for manipulation | S75 |
| Maxwell portfolio (acquired 2019, ~$235m) | Dry electrode manufacturing IP | US | Pre-2019 | Granted, owned | In force | Underpins the 4680 dry process | S56 |

The 10-K does not present patents as a competitive advantage; it rests the case on data, manufacturing cost and vertical integration [S3]. The Optimus filings show the limit: Musk said in April 2026 that the V3 hand would not use the patented design because it "ultimately didn't work", so the public record trails the programme.

### Product inventory

| Product | Stage | Launch | Revenue or share | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Model 3/Y | Commercial | 2017-2020 | $20.09bn automotive sales Q3 2026; 478,237 units (98.3%) | 18.5% total automotive | Next-generation platform, no date | S6, S76 |
| Cybercab and Robotaxi | Early commercial | 2026-09-03, Austin | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Unsupervised customer cars ~Q2 2027 | S6, S57 |
| Megapack, Megablock | Commercial | 2019; Megapack 3 in 2025 | $2.881bn segment Q3 2026 | 33.1% | Ramp 50 GWh Texas | S4, S6 |
| Optimus | Early production | 2026-10 | None | None | 20,000 units a week by end-2027, company claim | S57 |

Model 3/Y is 98.3% of volume and flat; Megapack earns a third of its revenue as gross profit on a fraction of the capital; Cybercab and Optimus carry the narrative and, so far, no disclosed revenue [S6, S57].

### Energy is the proven technology

Megapack is the one line where Tesla holds a genuine integration advantage and prices it: 13.7 GWh deployed in Q3 2026, a 33.1% gross margin and record order rate and backlog, with 50 GWh of Texas capacity starting. Wood Mackenzie ranks Tesla second among storage integrators behind Sungrow. The counterweight is pricing: revenue fell 16% year over year to $2.881bn even as volume rose [S4, S72].

::: evidence
**The headline safety statistic is a company measurement, not an audited record.**

Tesla's October 2026 report puts FSD (Supervised) at 6,006,200 miles per major collision against 660,164 for US driving overall, but the ratio is not fault-based, comes from Tesla telemetry and has not been verified by the regulator, which is running an engineering analysis over 13 low-visibility crashes instead [S58, S80].
:::

### What would change the judgement

The strongest case against my caution is that FSD is already monetised: attach reached more than 75% of North American deliveries, subscriptions reached 1.74 million and deferred revenue rose $1.24bn in Q3 2026, while services gross profit hit a record $734m. Against it, eight NHTSA recall campaigns on the 2026 Model Y since 2025-05-30 show launch quality slipping on the highest-volume car — none ADAS-related — and the attach rate is North American only, while China sales fell 16% in Q3 2026 with FSD approval pending [S7, S77].

Diligence questions: what did Austin earn per robotaxi per week, and how many Cybercabs ran without a monitor? What is blended pack cost per kWh? Does EA26002 end in a recall, and what would that do to the unsupervised release date? Until the first two are answered, Tesla owns the best-proven manufacturing technology in the sector and has not yet proven the one the share price pays for.

| FSD (Supervised) | deferred balance per active subscription | not disclosed | $2,345 | none disclosed | S4, S6 |

Energy is the highest-margin dollar of growth. Storage revenue per GWh fell 23% to $210 million from $273 million, but gross profit per GWh fell only 19% to $69.6 million because cost per GWh fell 25% to $141 million, lifting segment margin to 33.1% from 31.4%. The mechanism is cell integration: the first Megapacks built with Tesla's own Nevada LFP cells shipped in Q3 2026, Megafactory Texas began production with 50 GWh of planned capacity, and the Megapack backlog is nearly sold out through 2027. Fluence, the pure-play integrator, earned about 13.1% in FY2025; Tesla's advantage comes from owning the cell, not from pricing power. Part of the 33.1% is not repeatable, since management attributed it partly to tariff refunds for Megapack customers and cell-related warranty reimbursements. Services is the quieter engine: revenue rose 33% to $4,605 million on 2% fewer deliveries and gross margin reached 15.9% from 10.5%. Each extra $1 billion of energy revenue at 30% adds $300 million of gross profit; the same dollar of automotive revenue at 18% adds $180 million [S67, S4].

FSD and software grow but remain too small to see in the income statement. Active subscriptions rose to 1.74 million from 1.04 million; deferred revenue for FSD, connectivity and software was $4.08 billion against $3.87 billion at 2025-12-31; $668 million was recognised in 9M 2026 from balances already deferred; and obligations beyond one year were $10.73 billion, of which $4.80 billion falls due within twelve months. Management's claim that FSD is attached to more than 75% of North American deliveries is company-reported and cannot be tied to a revenue line, because Tesla does not disclose FSD revenue; the observable is $2,345 of deferred balance per active subscription, a stock rather than a price. In Q2 2026 Tesla paid $1.95 billion in stock and equity awards for an AI hardware company, $222 million of it developed technology and $1.73 billion contingent on conditions judged improbable, so no expense has been booked [S4, S6].

The counter-case is that gross margin improves while the company gets less profitable. Operating expenses of $4,776 million rose 39% against $5,494 million of gross profit, R&D alone rose 69% to $2,761 million, and depreciation rose 17% to $1,580 million and will accelerate as more than $20 billion of 2026 capital expenditure is commissioned. The warranty reserve rose 26% to $10,138 million on 2% fewer deliveries, with claims incurred up 29% to $1,614 million while the provision per delivery fell to $1,227 from $1,463. Inventory rose 13.7% to $14,092 million with 11 days of vehicle supply, consistent with launch build-up rather than unsold cars [S4, S6].

The vehicle line covers its own costs, so the break-even question is about the cost base rather than the unit. Quarterly operating expenses of $4,776 million need roughly $27 billion of revenue at a 17.7% blended margin; Q3 2026 delivered $28.0 billion and $718 million of operating profit. Normalise energy to a 30% margin and take credits to zero and the same quarter earns about $515 million, a 1.8% operating margin, which is what the buyer pays for today. Confidence is high on the segment arithmetic, which rests on audited segment disclosure, and medium on how much of the 2026 cost relief is structural rather than tariff and mix effects. Four questions would settle it: the North American automotive margin excluding credits; the energy margin excluding tariff refunds and the contracted 2027 backlog price; the FSD revenue line and how robotaxi rides will be recognised; and the year R&D and capital expenditure stop rising as a share of revenue.

::: evidence
**Tesla's profit now rests on energy and services gross profit, not on credits or on the car**

Energy storage and services supplied $1,688 million of Q3 2026 gross profit at 33.1% and 15.9% margins, while regulatory credits fell to $113 million, 15.7% of operating income, from 45.8% of FY2025 operating income, and operating expenses absorbed 86.9% of gross profit [S4, S6].
:::

arguments.markdown:
Tesla's technology is proven where it is a manufacturing problem — dry-electrode cells, Megapack integration — and unproven where the valuation sits. About 2.0 million cumulative unsupervised robotaxi miles, a 300-plus Cybercab fleet in Austin and a Texas-only paid driverless permit sit against Waymo's roughly 4,000 vehicles and 500,000 paid rides a week; autonomy is a 2027-2029 option, not a 2026 capability [S6, S59]. The technology justifies a premium to a capital-intensive manufacturer in energy and process engineering; it does not yet justify the multiple of a software platform.

### How FSD works, and where it stops

FSD (Supervised) is vision-only. Eight cameras feed an end-to-end neural network that outputs steering, acceleration and braking; it learns from video from a fleet of 10.2 million delivered vehicles and runs on Tesla's in-house inference silicon. There is no lidar, no radar and no pre-mapped corridors as Waymo has. Training runs on the Cortex clusters in Texas, with 400 MW of compute targeted by 2026-12-31. Two problems stay unsolved. The first is degradation detection when cameras are blinded by rain, fog or low sun: NHTSA's Engineering Analysis EA26002, opened 2026-03-19 over 13 crashes and about 2.88 million vehicles, asks whether the system notices and warns the driver. The second is the reliability increment that permits removing the supervisor, which is why customer-owned unsupervised driving moved to about Q2 2027 [S58, S80].

| Metric | Value | Method | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| FSD miles per major collision | 6,006,200 (North America, October 2026) | Company report, FSD-engaged miles | S58 |
| Cumulative unsupervised robotaxi miles | ~2.0 million (to 2026-09-30) | Company quarterly update | S6 |
| FSD subscriptions and attach | 1.74 million; >75% of North American deliveries | Company KPI, excludes free trials | S6 |
| 4680 cell output and density | >1 million cells/week; >40 GWh; 272 Wh/kg | Giga Texas line data and teardown estimates | S56 |
| Energy storage deployed | 13.7 GWh (Q3 2026); 36.0 GWh (9M 2026) | Company KPI | S6 |
| Megapack segment gross margin | 33.1% (Q3 2026) | Segment accounts | S4 |

### Robotaxi: a real service, on one state's terms

Paid Cybercab rides began in Austin on 2026-09-03, and Tesla claimed 300-plus Cybercabs serving the city on 2026-10-10; Texas records showed 319 authorised Cybercab VINs. It has not disclosed fares, revenue or how many run without a monitor. Permits are the constraint: Texas allows self-certified commercial driverless operation under its 2026 law, while California lists Tesla Robotaxi LLC only for testing with a driver and omits it from the driverless-testing and deployment lists (2026-10-22) [S73, S74]. NHTSA's defect petition DP26010, opened 2026-10-09 on school-zone speeding, puts the monitored fleet at about 1,000 vehicles.

| Dimension | Tesla | Benchmark | What it means | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Autonomy sensing | Vision-only cameras, no lidar or radar | Waymo: lidar, radar, cameras and high-definition maps | Lower bill of materials, higher tail risk in bad weather | S59 |
| Weekly paid rides | Not disclosed | Waymo: 500,000 a week on ~4,000 vehicles | At ~5 miles a ride, Waymo runs ~2.5m rider-only miles weekly, more than Tesla's cumulative total | S59, S6 |
| Cell performance | 4680: 272 Wh/kg, 10-80% in 35-40 minutes | CATL Qilin 3 claims a full charge in six minutes | Tesla leads on cost, trails on density and charging | S56 |
| BEV volume, Q3 2026 | 486,532 units | BYD 762,478 passenger BEVs, +30.89% year over year | Cost leadership has moved to China | S76 |

### Cells: a cost moat, not a performance one

Giga Texas runs above one million 4680 cells a week at more than 40 GWh of installed capacity, and since January 2026 both electrodes use the dry process in production — a step CATL, Panasonic, LG and Samsung SDI have not taken to commercial scale. The economics are real: electrode cost toward 50% lower, roughly 41% less line capex and more than 30% less factory energy. The product is not: energy density trails by 10-15%, charging is slower than Panasonic 2170 packs, yields above 90% sit below the 98% of mature producers, and Tesla still buys CATL LFP and Panasonic or LG 2170 cells for Shanghai and Fremont Model Y. Battery availability, not demand, remained the stated limit on 2026 volume [S56].

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why it is hard | Time to replicate |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fleet data and training set | 7 | 10.2 million vehicles and billions of FSD miles, if compute and labelling keep pace | 3-4 years |
| Dry-electrode process | 7 | Both electrodes dry at >90% yield; no competitor at commercial scale | 3 years |
| Vertical integration (cells, packs, chips) | 6 | Process know-how and capital; AI6 foundry dependence caps it | 3-5 years |
| Driverless permits | 4 | Texas self-certification is easy; California and the EU are not | 1-2 years Texas, 3+ California |
| **Composite** | **6/10** | A funded 50-person team would need ~3 years for the cell line and ~2 for Megapack integration; patents disclose little of either | **~3 years of lead time** |

### Patents: thin disclosure, deliberately

| Patent or application | Title | Jurisdiction | Filed | Granted | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Four international filings published 2026-04-16 | Optimus Gen 3 forearm, wrist, joint and hand assemblies | WIPO/PCT | Priority 2024-10-10 | — | Published, national phase pending | 22 degrees of freedom per hand, 25 forearm actuators, tendon-driven | S75 |
| US20260310299A1 | Flexible touch sensors for robotic hands | US | Not disclosed | — | Published 2025-10-08 | Tactile sensing for manipulation | S75 |
| Maxwell portfolio (acquired 2019, ~$235m) | Dry electrode manufacturing IP | US | Pre-2019 | Granted, owned | In force | Underpins the 4680 dry process | S56 |

The 10-K does not present patents as a competitive advantage; it rests the case on data, manufacturing cost and vertical integration [S3]. The Optimus filings show the limit: Musk said in April 2026 that the V3 hand would not use the patented design because it "ultimately didn't work".

### Product inventory

| Product | Stage | Launch | Revenue or share | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Model 3/Y | Commercial | 2017-2020 | $20.09bn automotive sales Q3 2026; 478,237 units (98.3%) | 18.5% total automotive | Next-generation platform, no date | S6, S76 |
| Cybercab and Robotaxi | Early commercial | 2026-09-03, Austin | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Unsupervised customer cars ~Q2 2027 | S6, S57 |
| Megapack, Megablock | Commercial | 2019; Megapack 3 in 2025 | $2.881bn segment Q3 2026 | 33.1% | Ramp 50 GWh Texas | S4, S6 |
| Optimus | Early production | 2026-10 | None | None | 20,000 units a week by end-2027, company claim | S57 |

### Energy is the proven technology

Megapack is the one line where Tesla holds a genuine integration advantage and prices it: 13.7 GWh deployed in Q3 2026, a 33.1% gross margin and record order rate and backlog, with 50 GWh of Texas capacity starting. Wood Mackenzie ranks Tesla second among storage integrators behind Sungrow. The counterweight is pricing: revenue fell 16% year over year to $2.881bn even as volume rose [S4, S72].

::: evidence
**The headline safety statistic is a company measurement, not an audited record.**

Tesla's October 2026 report puts FSD (Supervised) at 6,006,200 miles per major collision against 660,164 for US driving overall, but the ratio is not fault-based, comes from Tesla telemetry and has not been verified by the regulator, which is running an engineering analysis over 13 low-visibility crashes instead [S58, S80].
:::

### What would change the judgement

The strongest case against my caution is that FSD is already monetised: attach reached more than 75% of North American deliveries, subscriptions reached 1.74 million and deferred revenue rose $1.24bn in Q3 2026, while services gross profit hit a record $734m. Against it, eight NHTSA recall campaigns on the 2026 Model Y since 2025-05-30 show launch quality slipping on the highest-volume car — none ADAS-related — and the attach rate is North American only, while China sales fell 16% in Q3 2026 with FSD approval pending [S7, S77].

Diligence questions: what did Austin earn per robotaxi per week, and how many Cybercabs ran without a monitor? What is blended pack cost per kWh? Does EA26002 end in a recall, and what would that do to the unsupervised release date? Until the first two are answered, Tesla owns the best-proven manufacturing technology in the sector and has not yet proven the one the share price pays for.

arguments.markdown:
Tesla is a single-class Texas corporation whose control rests on a 19.8% CEO stake plus a 423.7 million-share contingent award, so a public-equity holder is underwriting Elon Musk's capital allocation rather than a board-governed company; that is acceptable at a governance discount, not a premium. Tesla, Inc. was incorporated in Delaware on 2003-07-01, converted to Texas on 2024-06-13, and trades on Nasdaq under TSLA with one class of common stock and 3,952,648,559 shares outstanding at 2026-09-30, including 423,743,904 unearned restricted shares. There is no VIE, nominee-shareholder or red-chip layer, so identity is simple; control is not [S3].

::: kpi
| Metric | Value | Benchmark | Signal | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Shares outstanding | 3,952,648,559 at 2026-09-30 | 3,541m diluted weighted average, Q3 2026 | warn | S5 |
| CEO economic stake | 19.8% (699,580,882 shares) | Ford family: ~40% of votes on ~2% of shares | warn | S5 |
| Contingent CEO award | 423,743,904 shares, 10.7% of outstanding | 2018 award: 286,428,773 shares | critical | S5 |
| Unrecognised compensation on that award | $9.74bn probable; $105.82bn-$120.37bn not | $162m recognised in 2025 | critical | S4 |
| Cash and short-term investments | $45.45bn at 2026-09-30 | 2026 capex guided above $20bn | good | S6 |
| New credit commitments | $30bn, three agreements, September 2026 | none comparable in 2025 | warn | S4 |
| Insider activity, 12 months | -$87.69m sales, zero open-market purchases | one-sided tape | warn | S27 |
:::

### The entity map is clean; the asset ring-fence is not

| Entity | Jurisdiction | Role | Ownership | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Tesla, Inc. | Texas | Listed parent and principal operating company | 100% | S3, S5 |
| Tesla Robotaxi, LLC | Texas | Robotaxi operating entity | 100% listed subsidiary | S3 |
| Tesla Energy Operations, Inc. | Delaware | Energy generation and storage operations | 100% listed subsidiary | S3 |
| Tesla Manufacturing Brandenburg SE | Germany | Berlin vehicle plant | 100% listed subsidiary | S3 |
| Tesla (Shanghai) Co., Ltd | China | Shanghai plant and China sales, wholly foreign-owned | 100% listed subsidiary | S3 |

EX-21 lists hundreds of entities, mostly Delaware project companies, with no ownership percentages, so 100% is inferred from listing as a subsidiary. China is a wholly foreign-owned enterprise, not a VIE, so there is no contractual-control gap of the kind that discounts US-listed China ADRs, but Shanghai is fully consolidated and exposed to export controls. No entity is designated holder of Full Self-Driving or Optimus intellectual property: robotaxi operations sit in Tesla Robotaxi, LLC while software, data and chip designs stay in the parent, so no separately capitalised autonomy asset exists for a spin-off or merger to price.

### Customers, buyers and how growth arrives

Tesla sells direct, in two segments: automotive at $69,526m of 2025 revenue and energy at $12,771m [S71]. The vehicle buyer is a household or fleet paying cash or Tesla financing; the energy buyer is a utility or developer signing multi-year procurement, a slower sale that earned a 33.1% gross margin in Q3 2026 against 18.5% for automotive. Growth now comes from storage (13.7 GWh in Q3 2026), software (1.74 million active FSD subscriptions) and robotaxi rides, which have carried paying Cybercab passengers in Austin since 2026-09-03; the autonomy budget owner is still a retail customer weighing a monthly subscription.

### Ownership is concentrated without a dual class

| Holder | Class | Shares | % ownership | % votes | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Elon Musk | Common, incl. 286,428,773 restricted | 699,580,882 | 19.8% | 19.8% | S5 |
| Vanguard Capital Management | Common | 210,796,512 | 5.3% | 5.3% | S5 |
| All directors and officers (11) | Common | 706,496,615 | 20.0% | 20.0% | S5 |
| Unearned 2025 award shares | Restricted, unearned | 423,743,904 | 10.7% of outstanding | proportional to other shares | S5 |
| Other public holders | Common | balance | ~74.9% | ~74.9% | S5 |

Percentages follow the proxy, whose denominator excludes unearned award shares; free float of at most 74.9% is derived by subtracting Musk and Vanguard from that base. Musk's stake includes 207,498,721 shares pledged as collateral for personal debt, so a margin call would add supply at the worst moment. With one class and no super-voting stock, control runs through the CEO office, the board seat and stake size rather than a charter provision, unlike Ford's Class B (about 40% of votes on roughly 2% of shares) or Alphabet's founder Class B. That is a real minority protection: no family trust can outvote the register indefinitely.

### Control is priced through a contingent award

The 2025 CEO Performance Award is the control instrument: 423,743,904 shares in 12 tranches of 35,311,992, each tied to a market-capitalisation milestone from $2.0 trillion to $8.5 trillion and to 1 of 12 operational milestones (20 million vehicles, 10 million FSD subscriptions, 1 million bots, 1 million robotaxis, Adjusted EBITDA of $50bn to $400bn); none was earned at 2026-10-19 [S5]. At $2.0 trillion the first tranche implies roughly $506 per share on 3.95 billion shares, and because the operational test falls away in a change of control, a deal at $3.0 trillion would earn three tranches, about 105.9 million shares, with no robotaxi or Optimus milestone met. Expense is already running: $802m in the first nine months of 2026, $9.74bn unrecognised on the one milestone management judges probable, and $105.82bn-$120.37bn on the rest [S4]. Dilution of 10.7% is designed, not tail, and sits above the current valuation rather than beside it.

### The board can refuse less than it appears

Nine directors sit in three classes, six labelled independent under Nasdaq rules, with Robyn Denholm as chair since November 2018. The labels have worn. Ira Ehrenpreis, who chairs both the compensation and the nominating and governance committees, joined SpaceX's board in February 2026; Kimbal Musk is the CEO's brother; JB Straubel runs Redwood Materials, which bought $12.9m of Tesla scrap and sold it $3.3m of material in 2025. Related-party flows are small in dollars but pointed: Tesla agreed on 2026-01-16 to invest about $2.00bn in xAI, converted into SpaceX Class A stock when SpaceX bought xAI on 2026-02-02 and funded on 2026-03-12, while xAI bought $430.1m of Megapacks and SpaceX bought $143.3m of vehicles in 2025. A board setting a Tesla-SpaceX exchange ratio would do so with three of nine directors tied to SpaceX, and the retail auto-voting programme filed with the 2026 proxy offers standing instructions to vote with the board outside a defined special matter [S78]. The counterweight is narrow: only Denholm and Wilson-Thompson sat on the Special Committee that designed the 2025 award, and 78.2% of votes cast backed 2025 pay.

### Capital allocation has no return floor

Tesla has never paid a dividend, repurchased no shares in 2025, and holds no authorisation to offset dilution. It ended 2026-09-30 with $45.45bn of cash and short-term investments, generated $14.90bn of operating cash flow in nine months against $13.01bn of capex, guided 2026 capex above $20bn, and signed three credit agreements with $30bn of commitments in September 2026 [S6]. Free cash flow was $1.5bn in Q3 2026, thin against that commitment. Against Ford and GM, which return cash, Tesla offers neither dividend nor buyback, and the only capital return has gone to insiders through equity — directors sold $87.69m in the 12 months to 2026-09-09 with no open-market purchases [S27]. Litigation moved rather than vanished: the Delaware Supreme Court reinstated the 2018 award on 2025-12-19, the 96,000,000-share interim award was forfeited on 2026-04-21, and a securities class action filed on 2025-08-04 in the Western District of Texas covers purchasers from 2023-04-19 to 2025-06-22 over Autopilot, FSD and Robotaxi statements.

A multi-year holder is paid for accepting four things: a 10.7% contingent award that accelerates on a deal price rather than operating proof; conflict committees that include SpaceX-affiliated directors; $30bn of new debt commitments against a $1.5bn quarterly free-cash-flow buffer; and key-person concentration in a CEO who also runs SpaceX. Three conditions would change this judgement — an independent special committee for any SpaceX transaction, removal of change-of-control acceleration from the 2025 award, and a buyback sized to offset stock compensation. None appears in the 2026 proxy, so the governance discount stays. Confidence is high on structure and figures and medium on how a Texas court would treat a challenge to the award; diligence should ask for the pledge's loan-to-value, the xAI Series E valuation and the terms of the September 2026 facilities.

Tesla is a single-class Texas corporation whose control rests on a 19.8% CEO stake plus a 423.7 million-share contingent award, so a public-equity holder is underwriting Elon Musk's capital allocation rather than a board-governed company; that is acceptable at a governance discount, not a premium. Tesla, Inc. was incorporated in Delaware on 2003-07-01, converted to Texas on 2024-06-13, and trades on Nasdaq under TSLA with one class of common stock and 3,952,648,559 shares outstanding at 2026-09-30, including 423,743,904 unearned restricted shares. There is no VIE, nominee-shareholder or red-chip layer, so identity is simple; control is not [S3].

::: kpi

| CEO economic stake | 19.8% (699,580,882 shares) | Ford family: ~40% of votes on ~2% of shares | warn | S5 |

| Unrecognised compensation on that award | $9.74bn probable; $105.82bn-$120.37bn not | $162m recognised in 2025 | critical | S4 |

### The entity map is clean; the asset ring-fence is not

| Entity | Jurisdiction | Role | Ownership | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Tesla, Inc. | Texas | Listed parent and principal operating company | 100% | S3, S5 |
| Tesla Robotaxi, LLC | Texas | Robotaxi operating entity | 100% listed subsidiary | S3 |
| Tesla Energy Operations, Inc. | Delaware | Energy generation and storage operations | 100% listed subsidiary | S3 |
| Tesla Manufacturing Brandenburg SE | Germany | Berlin vehicle plant | 100% listed subsidiary | S3 |
| Tesla (Shanghai) Co., Ltd | China | Shanghai plant and China sales, wholly foreign-owned | 100% listed subsidiary | S3 |

EX-21 states no ownership percentages, so 100% is inferred from listing as a subsidiary. China is a wholly foreign-owned enterprise, not a VIE, so there is no contractual-control gap of the kind that discounts US-listed China ADRs, but Shanghai is fully consolidated and exposed to export controls. No entity is designated holder of Full Self-Driving or Optimus intellectual property: robotaxi operations sit in Tesla Robotaxi, LLC while software, data and chip designs stay in the parent, so no separately capitalised autonomy asset exists for a spin-off or merger to price.

### Customers, buyers and how growth arrives

Tesla sells direct in two segments: automotive at $69,526m of 2025 revenue and energy at $12,771m [S71]. The vehicle buyer is a household or fleet paying cash or Tesla financing; the energy buyer is a utility or developer signing multi-year procurement, a slower sale that earned 33.1% gross margin in Q3 2026 against 18.5% for automotive. Growth now comes from storage (13.7 GWh in Q3 2026), software (1.74 million FSD subscriptions) and paying Cybercab rides in Austin since 2026-09-03, with the retail customer still the budget owner for autonomy.

### Ownership is concentrated without a dual class

| Holder | Class | Shares | % ownership | % votes | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Elon Musk | Common, incl. 286,428,773 restricted | 699,580,882 | 19.8% | 19.8% | S5 |
| Vanguard Capital Management | Common | 210,796,512 | 5.3% | 5.3% | S5 |
| Unearned 2025 award shares | Restricted, unearned | 423,743,904 | 10.7% of outstanding | proportional to other shares | S5 |
| Other public holders | Common | balance | ~74.9% | ~74.9% | S5 |

Percentages follow the proxy, whose denominator excludes unearned award shares; free float of at most 74.9% is derived by subtracting Musk and Vanguard from that base. Musk's stake includes 207,498,721 shares pledged as collateral for personal debt, so a margin call would add supply at the worst moment. With one class and no super-voting stock, control runs through the CEO office, the board seat and stake size rather than a charter provision, unlike Ford's Class B (about 40% of votes on roughly 2% of shares) or Alphabet's founder Class B. That is a real minority protection: no family trust can outvote the register indefinitely.

### Control is priced through a contingent award

The 2025 CEO Performance Award is the control instrument: 423,743,904 shares in 12 tranches of 35,311,992, each tied to a market-capitalisation milestone from $2.0 trillion to $8.5 trillion and to 1 of 12 operational milestones (20 million vehicles, 10 million FSD subscriptions, 1 million bots, 1 million robotaxis, Adjusted EBITDA of $50bn to $400bn); none was earned at 2026-10-19 [S5]. At $2.0 trillion the first tranche implies roughly $506 per share on 3.95 billion shares, and because the operational test falls away in a change of control, a deal at $3.0 trillion would earn three tranches, about 105.9 million shares, with no robotaxi or Optimus milestone met. Expense is already running: $802m in the first nine months of 2026, $9.74bn unrecognised on the one milestone management judges probable, and $105.82bn-$120.37bn on the rest [S4]. Dilution of 10.7% is designed, not tail, and sits above the current valuation rather than beside it.

### The board can refuse less than it appears

Nine directors sit in three classes, six labelled independent under Nasdaq rules, with Robyn Denholm as chair since November 2018. Ira Ehrenpreis, who chairs both the compensation and the nominating and governance committees, joined SpaceX's board in February 2026; Kimbal Musk is the CEO's brother; JB Straubel runs Redwood Materials, which bought $12.9m of Tesla scrap and sold it $3.3m of material in 2025. Related-party flows are small in dollars but pointed: Tesla agreed on 2026-01-16 to invest about $2.00bn in xAI, converted into SpaceX Class A stock when SpaceX bought xAI on 2026-02-02 and funded on 2026-03-12, while xAI bought $430.1m of Megapacks and SpaceX bought $143.3m of vehicles in 2025. A board setting a Tesla-SpaceX exchange ratio would do so with three of nine directors tied to SpaceX, and the retail auto-voting programme in the 2026 proxy offers standing instructions to vote with the board outside a defined special matter [S78]. The counterweight is narrow: the Special Committee used only Denholm and Wilson-Thompson, and 78.2% of votes cast backed 2025 pay.

### Capital allocation has no return floor

Tesla has never paid a dividend, repurchased no shares in 2025, and holds no authorisation to offset dilution. It ended 2026-09-30 with $45.45bn of cash and short-term investments, generated $14.90bn of operating cash flow in nine months against $13.01bn of capex, guided 2026 capex above $20bn, and signed three credit agreements with $30bn of commitments in September 2026 [S6]. Free cash flow was $1.5bn in Q3 2026, thin against that commitment. Against Ford and GM, which return cash, Tesla offers neither dividend nor buyback, and the only capital return has gone to insiders through equity — directors sold $87.69m in the 12 months to 2026-09-09 with no open-market purchases [S27]. Litigation moved rather than vanished: the Delaware Supreme Court reinstated the 2018 award on 2025-12-19, the 96,000,000-share interim award was forfeited on 2026-04-21, and a securities class action filed on 2025-08-04 in the Western District of Texas covers purchasers from 2023-04-19 to 2025-06-22 over Autopilot, FSD and Robotaxi statements.

A multi-year holder is paid for four things: a 10.7% contingent award that accelerates on a deal price rather than operating proof; conflict committees that include SpaceX-affiliated directors; $30bn of new debt against a $1.5bn quarterly free-cash-flow buffer; and key-person concentration in a CEO who also runs SpaceX. Three conditions would change this judgement — an independent special committee for any SpaceX transaction, no change-of-control acceleration without operating milestones, and a buyback sized to offset stock compensation. None appears in the 2026 proxy, so the governance discount stays. Confidence is high on structure and figures and medium on how a Texas court would treat a challenge to the award; diligence should ask for the pledge's loan-to-value and the xAI Series E valuation.

Without credits, FY2025's 4.6% operating margin is 2.5% and Q3 2026's 2.6% is 2.2% [S4, S64, S66].

Per vehicle the business improved even as credits disappeared. Q3 2026 automotive revenue per delivery excluding credits was $42,026, up 0.5%, while cost of revenue per delivery fell 2.7% to $34,436, so gross profit per vehicle rose 18.0% to $7,591 (18.1% margin) from $6,433 (15.4%). The gain is cost and regional mix, not price: management attributes the 270 basis points to a higher Asia-Pacific delivery mix, where Shanghai is the lowest-cost plant. Tesla does not disclose customer acquisition cost; SG&A per delivery of $4,142 is an upper bound that also carries insurance, Supercharging and corporate cost, and the first vehicle's gross profit covers 1.8 times it. A three-year LTV estimate of $8,455 adds three years of services gross profit per vehicle in the fleet ($288 a year on 10.2 million cumulative deliveries), giving LTV:CAC of 2.0:1 and payback inside the delivery quarter. Tesla is the only one of the three with positive per-vehicle automotive gross profit after credits: BYD's automotive gross margin was 20.49% in FY2025, from 22.31%, and Rivian's automotive gross profit was a $(36) million loss in Q2 2026 [S63, S65, S68].

Energy is the highest-margin dollar of growth. Storage revenue per GWh fell 23% to $210 million from $273 million, but gross profit per GWh fell only 19% to $69.6 million because cost per GWh fell 25% to $141 million, lifting segment margin to 33.1% from 31.4%. The mechanism is cell integration: the first Megapacks built with Tesla's own Nevada LFP cells shipped in Q3 2026, Megafactory Texas began production with 50 GWh of planned capacity, and the Megapack backlog is nearly sold out through 2027. Fluence, the pure-play integrator, earned 13.1% in FY2025; Tesla's advantage comes from owning the cell, not from pricing power. Part of the 33.1% is not repeatable, since management attributed it partly to tariff refunds for Megapack customers and cell-related warranty reimbursements. Services is the quieter engine: revenue rose 33% to $4,605 million on 2% fewer deliveries and gross margin reached 15.9% from 10.5%. Each extra $1 billion of energy revenue at 30% adds $300 million of gross profit; the same dollar of automotive revenue at 18% adds $180 million [S67, S4].

FSD and software grow but remain too small to see in the income statement. Active subscriptions rose to 1.74 million from 1.04 million; deferred revenue for FSD, connectivity and software was $4.08 billion against $3.87 billion at 2025-12-31; $668 million was recognised in 9M 2026 from balances already deferred; and obligations beyond one year were $10.73 billion, of which $4.80 billion falls due within twelve months. Management's claim that FSD is attached to more than 75% of North American deliveries is company-reported and cannot be tied to a revenue line, because Tesla does not disclose FSD revenue; the observable is $2,345 of deferred balance per active subscription, a stock rather than a price. In Q2 2026 Tesla paid $1.95 billion in stock and equity awards for an AI hardware company, $222 million of it developed technology and $1.73 billion contingent on conditions judged improbable, so no expense has been booked [S4, S6].

The counter-case: gross margin improves while the company gets less profitable. Operating expenses of $4,776 million rose 39% against $5,494 million of gross profit, R&D alone rose 69% to $2,761 million, and depreciation rose 17% to $1,580 million and will accelerate as more than $20 billion of 2026 capital expenditure is commissioned. The warranty reserve rose 26% to $10,138 million on 2% fewer deliveries, with claims incurred up 29% to $1,614 million while the provision per delivery fell to $1,227 from $1,463. Inventory rose 13.7% to $14,092 million with 11 days of vehicle supply, consistent with launch build-up rather than unsold cars. The vehicle line covers its own costs, so break-even is a question about the cost base: operating expenses of $4,776 million need $27.0 billion of revenue at a 17.7% blended margin, and Q3 2026 delivered $28.0 billion for $718 million of operating profit. Normalise energy to a 30% margin and take credits to zero and the same quarter earns $515 million, a 1.8% operating margin, which is what a buyer pays for, with the energy backlog and autonomy optionality outside the earnings. Confidence is high on the segment arithmetic, which rests on audited segment disclosure, and medium on how much of the 2026 cost relief is structural rather than tariff and mix effects. Four questions would settle it: the North American automotive margin excluding credits; the energy margin excluding tariff refunds and the contracted 2027 backlog price; the FSD revenue line and how robotaxi rides will be recognised; and the year R&D and capital expenditure stop rising as a share of revenue [S4, S6].

::: evidence
**Tesla's profit now rests on energy and services gross profit, not on credits or on the car**

Energy storage and services supplied $1,688 million of Q3 2026 gross profit at 33.1% and 15.9% margins, while regulatory credits fell to $113 million, 15.7% of operating income, from 45.8% of FY2025 operating income, and operating expenses absorbed 86.9% of gross profit [S4, S6].
:::

arguments.markdown:
Tesla's technology is proven where it is a manufacturing problem — dry-electrode cells, Megapack integration — and unproven where the valuation sits. Its autonomous miles are tiny, its Cybercab fleet sits in one Texas city and its paid driverless permit exists in one state, against Waymo's national network. The technology justifies a premium to a capital-intensive manufacturer in energy and process engineering; it does not yet justify the multiple of a software platform.

### How FSD works, and where it stops

FSD (Supervised) is vision-only. Eight cameras feed an end-to-end neural network that outputs steering, acceleration and braking; it learns from video from a fleet of 10.2 million delivered vehicles and runs on Tesla's in-house inference silicon. There is no lidar, no radar and no pre-mapped corridors as Waymo has. Training runs on the Cortex clusters in Texas, with 400 MW of compute targeted by 2026-12-31. Two problems stay unsolved. The first is degradation detection when cameras are blinded by rain, fog or low sun: NHTSA's Engineering Analysis EA26002, opened 2026-03-19 over 13 crashes and 2.88 million vehicles, asks whether the system notices and warns the driver. The second is the reliability increment that permits removing the supervisor, which is why customer-owned unsupervised driving moved to Q2 2027 [S58, S80].

| Metric | Value | Method | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| FSD miles per major collision | 6,006,200 (North America, October 2026) | Company report, FSD-engaged miles | S58 |
| Cumulative unsupervised robotaxi miles | 2.0 million (to 2026-09-30) | Company quarterly update | S6 |
| FSD subscriptions and attach | 1.74 million; more than 75% of North American deliveries | Company KPI, excludes free trials | S6 |
| 4680 cell output and density | More than 1 million cells/week; more than 40 GWh; 272 Wh/kg | Giga Texas line data and teardown estimates | S56 |
| Energy storage deployed | 13.7 GWh (Q3 2026); 36.0 GWh (9M 2026) | Company KPI | S6 |
| Megapack segment gross margin | 33.1% (Q3 2026) | Segment accounts | S4 |

### Robotaxi: a real service, on one state's terms

Paid Cybercab rides began in Austin on 2026-09-03, and Tesla claimed 300-plus Cybercabs serving the city on 2026-10-10; Texas records showed 319 authorised Cybercab VINs. It has not disclosed fares, revenue or how many run without a monitor. Permits are the constraint: Texas allows self-certified commercial driverless operation under its 2026 law, while California lists Tesla Robotaxi LLC only for testing with a driver and omits it from the driverless-testing and deployment lists (2026-10-22) [S73, S74]. NHTSA's defect petition DP26010, opened 2026-10-09 on school-zone speeding, puts the monitored fleet at 1,000 vehicles, against 15 US cities for Waymo.

| Dimension | Tesla | Benchmark | What it means | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Autonomy sensing | Vision-only cameras, no lidar or radar | Waymo: lidar, radar, cameras and high-definition maps | Lower bill of materials, higher tail risk in bad weather | S59 |
| Weekly paid rides | Not disclosed | Waymo: 500,000 a week on a 4,000-vehicle fleet | At 5 miles a ride, Waymo runs 2.5 million rider-only miles weekly, more than Tesla's cumulative total | S59, S6 |
| Cell performance | 4680: 272 Wh/kg, 10-80% in 35-40 minutes | CATL Qilin 3 claims a full charge in six minutes | Tesla leads on cost, trails on density and charging | S56 |
| BEV volume, Q3 2026 | 486,532 units | BYD 762,478 passenger BEVs, +30.89% year over year | Cost leadership has moved to China | S76 |

### Cells: a cost moat, not a performance one

Giga Texas runs above one million 4680 cells a week at more than 40 GWh of installed capacity, and since January 2026 both electrodes use the dry process in production — a step CATL, Panasonic, LG and Samsung SDI have not taken to commercial scale. The economics are real: electrode cost 50% lower at full scale, 41% less line capex and more than 30% less factory energy. The product is not: energy density trails by 10-15%, charging is slower than Panasonic 2170 packs, yields above 90% sit below the 98% of mature producers, and Tesla still buys CATL LFP and Panasonic or LG 2170 cells for Shanghai and Fremont Model Y. Battery availability, not demand, remained the stated limit on 2026 volume [S56].

|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fleet data and training set | 7 | 10.2 million vehicles and billions of FSD miles, if compute and labelling keep pace | 3-4 years | S6 |
| Dry-electrode process | 7 | Both electrodes dry at more than 90% yield; no competitor at commercial scale | 3 years | S56 |
| Vertical integration (cells, packs, chips) | 6 | Process know-how and capital; AI6 foundry dependence caps it | 3-5 years | S6, S79 |
| Driverless permits | 4 | Texas self-certification is easy; California and the EU are not | 1-2 years Texas, 3+ California | S73 |
| **Composite** | **6/10** | A funded 50-person team would need 3 years for the cell line and 2 for Megapack integration; patents disclose little of either | **3 years of lead time** | S56, S73 |

### Patents: thin disclosure, deliberately

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Four international filings published 2026-04-16 | Optimus Gen 3 forearm, wrist, joint and hand assemblies | WIPO/PCT | Priority 2024-10-10 | — | Published, national phase pending | 22 degrees of freedom per hand, 25 forearm actuators, tendon-driven | S75 |
| US20260310299A1 | Flexible touch sensors for robotic hands | US | Not disclosed | — | Published 2025-10-08 | Tactile sensing for manipulation | S75 |
| Maxwell portfolio (acquired 2019, $235m) | Dry electrode manufacturing IP | US | Pre-2019 | Granted, owned | In force | Underpins the 4680 dry process | S56 |

The 10-K does not present patents as a competitive advantage; it rests the case on data, manufacturing cost and vertical integration [S3]. The Optimus filings show the limit: Musk said in April 2026 that the V3 hand would not use the patented design because it "ultimately didn't work", so the public record trails the programme.

### Product inventory

| Product | Stage | Launch | Revenue or share | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Model 3/Y | Commercial | 2017-2020 | $20.09bn automotive sales Q3 2026; 478,237 units (98.3%) | 18.5% total automotive | Next-generation platform, no date | S6, S76 |
| Cybercab and Robotaxi | Early commercial | 2026-09-03, Austin | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Unsupervised customer cars Q2 2027 | S6, S57 |
| Megapack, Megablock | Commercial | 2019; Megapack 3 in 2025 | $2.881bn segment Q3 2026 | 33.1% | Ramp 50 GWh Texas | S4, S6 |
| Optimus | Early production | 2026-10 | None | None | 20,000 units a week by end-2027, company claim | S57 |

### Energy is the proven technology

Megapack is the one line where Tesla holds a genuine integration advantage and prices it: 13.7 GWh deployed in Q3 2026, a 33.1% gross margin and record order rate and backlog, with 50 GWh of Texas capacity starting. Wood Mackenzie ranks Tesla second among storage integrators behind Sungrow. The counterweight is pricing: revenue fell 16% year over year to $2.881bn even as volume rose [S4, S72].

::: evidence
**The headline safety statistic is a company measurement, not an audited record.**

Tesla's October 2026 report puts FSD (Supervised) at 6,006,200 miles per major collision against 660,164 for US driving overall, but the ratio is not fault-based, comes from Tesla telemetry and has not been verified by the regulator, which is running an engineering analysis over 13 low-visibility crashes instead [S58, S80].
:::

### What would change the judgement

The strongest case against my caution is that FSD is already monetised: attach, subscriptions and deferred revenue all rose in Q3 2026, and services gross profit reached a record. Against it, repeated NHTSA recall campaigns on the 2026 Model Y show launch quality slipping on the highest-volume car, and the attach rate is North American only while China sales fell in Q3 2026 with FSD approval still pending.

Diligence questions: what did Austin earn per robotaxi per week, and how many Cybercabs ran without a monitor? What is blended pack cost per kWh? Does EA26002 end in a recall, and what would that do to the unsupervised release date? Until the first two are answered, Tesla owns the best-proven manufacturing technology in the sector and has not yet proven the one the share price pays for.

| Cash and short-term investments | $45.45bn at 2026-09-30 | 2026 capex guided above $20bn | good | S6 |
| New credit commitments | $30bn, three agreements, September 2026 | none comparable in 2025 | warn | S4 |
| Insider activity, 12 months | -$87.69m sales, zero open-market purchases | one-sided tape | warn | S27 |
:::

### The entity map is clean; the asset ring-fence is not

| Entity | Jurisdiction | Role | Ownership | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Tesla, Inc. | Texas | Listed parent and principal operating company | 100% | S3, S5 |
| Tesla Robotaxi, LLC | Texas | Robotaxi operating entity | 100% listed subsidiary | S3 |
| Tesla Energy Operations, Inc. | Delaware | Energy generation and storage operations | 100% listed subsidiary | S3 |
| Tesla Manufacturing Brandenburg SE | Germany | Berlin vehicle plant | 100% listed subsidiary | S3 |
| Tesla (Shanghai) Co., Ltd | China | Shanghai plant and China sales, wholly foreign-owned | 100% listed subsidiary | S3 |

EX-21 states no ownership percentages, so 100% is inferred from listing as a subsidiary. China is a wholly foreign-owned enterprise, not a VIE, so there is no contractual-control gap, but Shanghai is fully consolidated and exposed to export controls. No entity is designated holder of Full Self-Driving or Optimus intellectual property: robotaxi operations sit in Tesla Robotaxi, LLC while software, data and chip designs stay in the parent, so no separately capitalised autonomy asset exists.

### Customers, buyers and how growth arrives

Tesla sells direct in two segments: automotive at $69,526m of 2025 revenue and energy at $12,771m [S71]. The vehicle buyer is a household or fleet paying cash or Tesla financing; the energy buyer is a utility or developer signing multi-year procurement, which earned 33.1% gross margin in Q3 2026 against 18.5% for automotive. Growth now comes from storage (13.7 GWh in Q3 2026), software (1.74 million FSD subscriptions) and paying Cybercab rides in Austin since 2026-09-03, with the retail customer still the budget owner for autonomy.

### Ownership is concentrated without a dual class

| Holder | Class | Shares | % ownership | % votes | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Elon Musk | Common, incl. 286,428,773 restricted | 699,580,882 | 19.8% | 19.8% | S5 |
| Vanguard Capital Management | Common | 210,796,512 | 5.3% | 5.3% | S5 |
| Unearned 2025 award shares | Restricted, unearned | 423,743,904 | 10.7% of outstanding | proportional to other shares | S5 |
| Other public holders | Common | balance | ~74.9% | ~74.9% | S5 |

Percentages follow the proxy, whose denominator excludes unearned award shares; free float of at most 74.9% is derived by subtracting Musk and Vanguard from that base. Musk's stake includes 207,498,721 shares pledged as collateral for personal debt, so a margin call would add supply at the worst moment. With one class and no super-voting stock, control runs through the CEO office, the board seat and stake size rather than a charter provision, unlike Ford's Class B (about 40% of votes on roughly 2% of shares) or Alphabet's founder Class B. That is a real minority protection: no family trust can outvote the register indefinitely.

### Control is priced through a contingent award

The 2025 CEO Performance Award is the control instrument: 423,743,904 shares in 12 tranches of 35,311,992, each tied to a market-capitalisation milestone from $2.0 trillion to $8.5 trillion and to 1 of 12 operational milestones (20 million vehicles, 10 million FSD subscriptions, 1 million bots, 1 million robotaxis, Adjusted EBITDA of $50bn to $400bn); none was earned at 2026-10-19 [S5]. At $2.0 trillion the first tranche implies roughly $506 per share on 3.95 billion shares, and because the operational test falls away in a change of control, a deal at $3.0 trillion would earn three tranches, about 105.9 million shares, with no robotaxi or Optimus milestone met. Expense is already running: $802m in the first nine months of 2026, $9.74bn unrecognised on the one milestone management judges probable, and $105.82bn-$120.37bn on the rest [S4]. Dilution of 10.7% is designed, not tail, and sits above the current valuation rather than beside it.

### The board can refuse less than it appears

Nine directors sit in three classes, six labelled independent under Nasdaq rules, with Robyn Denholm as chair since November 2018. Ira Ehrenpreis, who chairs both the compensation and the nominating and governance committees, joined SpaceX's board in February 2026; Kimbal Musk is the CEO's brother; JB Straubel runs Redwood Materials, which bought $12.9m of Tesla scrap and sold it $3.3m of material in 2025. Related-party flows are small in dollars but pointed: Tesla agreed on 2026-01-16 to invest about $2.00bn in xAI, converted into SpaceX Class A stock when SpaceX bought xAI on 2026-02-02 and funded on 2026-03-12, while xAI bought $430.1m of Megapacks and SpaceX bought $143.3m of vehicles in 2025. A board setting a Tesla-SpaceX exchange ratio would do so with three of nine directors tied to SpaceX, and the retail auto-voting programme in the 2026 proxy offers standing instructions to vote with the board outside a defined special matter [S78]. The counterweight is narrow: the Special Committee used only Denholm and Wilson-Thompson, and 78.2% of votes cast backed 2025 pay.

### Capital allocation has no return floor

Tesla has never paid a dividend, repurchased no shares in 2025, and holds no authorisation to offset dilution. It ended 2026-09-30 with $45.45bn of cash and short-term investments, generated $14.90bn of operating cash flow in nine months against $13.01bn of capex, guided 2026 capex above $20bn, and signed three credit agreements with $30bn of commitments in September 2026 [S6]. Against Ford and GM, which return cash, Tesla offers neither dividend nor buyback, and the only capital return has gone to insiders through equity — directors sold $87.69m in the 12 months to 2026-09-09 with no open-market purchases [S27]. Litigation moved rather than vanished: the Delaware Supreme Court reinstated the 2018 award on 2025-12-19, the 96,000,000-share interim award was forfeited on 2026-04-21, and a securities class action filed on 2025-08-04 in the Western District of Texas covers purchasers from 2023-04-19 to 2025-06-22 over Autopilot, FSD and Robotaxi statements.

A multi-year holder is paid for four things: a 10.7% contingent award that accelerates on a deal price rather than operating proof; conflict committees that include SpaceX-affiliated directors; $30bn of new debt against a $1.5bn quarterly free-cash-flow buffer; and key-person concentration in a CEO who also runs SpaceX. Three conditions would change this judgement — an independent special committee for any SpaceX transaction, no change-of-control acceleration without operating milestones, and a buyback sized to offset stock compensation. None appears in the 2026 proxy, so the governance discount stays. Confidence is high on structure, medium on how a Texas court would treat a challenge to the award; diligence should ask for the pledge's loan-to-value.
