arguments.markdown:
Tesla still makes most of its gross profit selling cars, but after regulatory credits the car business earns little at the operating line. Credits supplied 45.8% of FY2025 operating income and 15.7% in Q3 2026; incremental profit now comes from a 33.1%-margin energy-storage business and a 15.9%-margin services business while AI spending absorbs 86.9% of gross profit. Nine-month 2026 revenue of $78,669 million split into automotive $57,310 million (including $639 million of credits), energy $8,428 million and services $12,931 million, against an automotive share of 85.1% in FY2023. Q3 2026 gross profit divided $3,806 million automotive (69%), $954 million energy (17%) and $734 million services (13%), versus 91%/6%/3% in FY2023. Cash arrives when a vehicle changes hands, on storage milestones and prepayments ($3.30 billion of customer prepayments in deferred revenue at 2026-09-30, from $2.04 billion), and monthly for Supercharging, insurance and FSD [S3, S4, S6].

| Segment | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 | 9M 2026 | Q3 2026 | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Automotive revenue excluding credits ($M) | 80,629 | 74,307 | 67,533 | 56,671 | 20,447 | S1, S3, S4 |
| Automotive regulatory credits ($M) | 1,790 | 2,763 | 1,993 | 639 | 113 | S1, S3, S4 |
| Energy generation and storage revenue ($M) | 6,035 | 10,086 | 12,771 | 8,428 | 2,881 | S3, S4 |
| Services and other revenue ($M) | 8,319 | 10,534 | 12,530 | 12,931 | 4,605 | S3, S4 |
| Automotive gross margin excluding credits | 17.7% | 15.4% | 15.4% | 17.7% | 18.1% | S1, S3, S4, S63 |
| Energy gross margin | 18.9% | 26.2% | 29.8% | 30.2% | 33.1% | S3, S4 |
| Services gross margin | 5.9% | 5.8% | 7.4% | 13.4% | 15.9% | S3, S4 |

The credit franchise is ending. Tesla booked $2,763 million of automotive regulatory credits in FY2024, $1,993 million in FY2025 and $639 million in 9M 2026; Q3 2026 alone was $113 million, down 73% from $417 million. Credits carry no cost of revenue, so a credit dollar is nearly a dollar of operating profit: 20.1% of operating income in FY2023, 39.0% in FY2024, 45.8% in FY2025, 31.1% in 9M 2026 and 15.7% in Q3 2026. An implied Q4 2025 figure of $542 million shows the collapse came not with the lapse of the US consumer credit but with the removal of the compliance obligation in 2026: the Department of Transportation finalised its CAFE rollback on 2026-10-01, ending the requirement that made legacy automakers buy zero-emission credits. Without credits, FY2025's 4.6% operating margin is 2.5% and Q3 2026's 2.6% is 2.2% [S4, S64, S66].

Per vehicle the business improved even as credits disappeared. Q3 2026 automotive revenue per delivery excluding credits was $42,026, up 0.5%, while cost of revenue per delivery fell 2.7% to $34,436, so gross profit per vehicle rose 18.0% to $7,591 (18.1% margin) from $6,433 (15.4%). The gain is cost and regional mix, not price: management attributes the 270 basis points to a higher Asia-Pacific delivery mix, where Shanghai is the lowest-cost plant. Tesla does not disclose customer acquisition cost; SG&A per delivery of $4,142 is an upper bound that also carries insurance, Supercharging and corporate cost, and the first vehicle's gross profit covers 1.8 times it. A three-year LTV estimate of $8,455 adds three years of services gross profit per vehicle in the fleet ($288 a year on 10.2 million cumulative deliveries), giving LTV:CAC of 2.0:1 and payback inside the delivery quarter. Tesla is the only one of the three with positive per-vehicle automotive gross profit after credits: BYD's automotive gross margin was 20.49% in FY2025, from 22.31%, and Rivian's automotive gross profit was a $(36) million loss in Q2 2026 [S63, S65, S68].

| Per unit | Q3 2025 | Q3 2026 | Change | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Deliveries (units) | 497,099 | 486,532 | -2.1% | S6 |
| Automotive revenue per delivery, excluding credits | $41,818 | $42,026 | +0.5% | S4, S6 |
| Automotive cost of revenue per delivery | $35,385 | $34,436 | -2.7% | S4, S6 |
| Automotive gross profit per delivery, excluding credits | $6,433 | $7,591 | +18.0% | S4, S6 |
| Energy gross profit per delivery | $2,158 | $1,961 | -9.1% | S4, S6 |
| Services gross profit per delivery | $736 | $1,508 | +105% | S4, S6 |
| SG&A per delivery (acquisition-cost upper bound) | $3,142 | $4,142 | +31.8% | S4, S6 |
| R&D per delivery | $3,279 | $5,675 | +73.1% | S4, S6 |
| Operating profit per delivery | $3,267 | $1,476 | -54.8% | S4, S6 |

| Product | Pricing metric | Q3 2025 | Q3 2026 | Peer benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Vehicles, net of credits | realised revenue per delivery | $41,818 | $42,026 | BYD automotive gross margin 20.49%, FY2025 | S4, S65 |
| Megapack and Powerwall | realised revenue per GWh deployed | $273 million | $210 million | Fluence gross margin 13.1%, FY2025 | S3, S67 |
| FSD (Supervised) | deferred balance per active subscription | not disclosed | $2,345 | none disclosed | S4, S6 |

Energy is the highest-margin dollar of growth. Storage revenue per GWh fell 23% to $210 million from $273 million, but gross profit per GWh fell only 19% to $69.6 million because cost per GWh fell 25% to $141 million, lifting segment margin to 33.1% from 31.4%. The mechanism is cell integration: the first Megapacks built with Tesla's own Nevada LFP cells shipped in Q3 2026, Megafactory Texas began production with 50 GWh of planned capacity, and the Megapack backlog is nearly sold out through 2027. Fluence, the pure-play integrator, earned 13.1% in FY2025; Tesla's advantage comes from owning the cell, not from pricing power. Part of the 33.1% is not repeatable, since management attributed it partly to tariff refunds for Megapack customers and cell-related warranty reimbursements. Services is the quieter engine: revenue rose 33% to $4,605 million on 2% fewer deliveries and gross margin reached 15.9% from 10.5%. Each extra $1 billion of energy revenue at 30% adds $300 million of gross profit; the same dollar of automotive revenue at 18% adds $180 million [S67, S4].

FSD and software grow but remain too small to see in the income statement. Active subscriptions rose to 1.74 million from 1.04 million; deferred revenue for FSD, connectivity and software was $4.08 billion against $3.87 billion at 2025-12-31; $668 million was recognised in 9M 2026 from balances already deferred; and obligations beyond one year were $10.73 billion, of which $4.80 billion falls due within twelve months. Management's claim that FSD is attached to more than 75% of North American deliveries is company-reported and cannot be tied to a revenue line, because Tesla does not disclose FSD revenue; the observable is $2,345 of deferred balance per active subscription, a stock rather than a price. In Q2 2026 Tesla paid $1.95 billion in stock and equity awards for an AI hardware company, $222 million of it developed technology and $1.73 billion contingent on conditions judged improbable, so no expense has been booked [S4, S6].

Counter-case: gross margin improves while the company gets less profitable. Operating expenses of $4,776 million rose 39% against $5,494 million of gross profit, R&D alone rose 69% to $2,761 million, and depreciation rose 17% to $1,580 million and will accelerate as more than $20 billion of 2026 capital expenditure is commissioned. The warranty reserve rose 26% to $10,138 million on 2% fewer deliveries, with claims incurred up 29% to $1,614 million while the provision per delivery fell to $1,227 from $1,463. Inventory rose 13.7% to $14,092 million with 11 days of vehicle supply, consistent with launch build-up rather than unsold cars. The vehicle line covers its own costs, so break-even is a question about the cost base: operating expenses of $4,776 million need $27.0 billion of revenue at a 17.7% blended margin, and Q3 2026 delivered $28.0 billion for $718 million of operating profit. Normalise energy to a 30% margin and take credits to zero and the same quarter earns $515 million, a 1.8% operating margin, which is what a buyer pays for, with the energy backlog and autonomy optionality outside the earnings. Confidence is high on the segment arithmetic, which rests on audited segment disclosure, and medium on how much of the 2026 cost relief is structural rather than tariff and mix effects. Four questions would settle it: the North American automotive margin excluding credits; the energy margin excluding tariff refunds and the contracted 2027 backlog price; the FSD revenue line and how robotaxi rides will be recognised; and the year R&D and capital expenditure stop rising as a share of revenue [S4, S6].

::: evidence
**Tesla's profit now rests on energy and services gross profit, not on credits or on the car**

Energy storage and services supplied $1,688 million of Q3 2026 gross profit at 33.1% and 15.9% margins, while regulatory credits fell to $113 million, 15.7% of operating income, from 45.8% of FY2025 operating income, and operating expenses absorbed 86.9% of gross profit [S4, S6].
:::

arguments.markdown:
Tesla's technology is proven where it is a manufacturing problem — dry-electrode cells, Megapack integration — and unproven where the valuation sits. Its autonomous miles are tiny, its Cybercab fleet sits in one Texas city and its paid driverless permit exists in one state, against Waymo's national network. The technology justifies a premium to a capital-intensive manufacturer in energy and process engineering; it does not yet justify the multiple of a software platform.

### How FSD works, and where it stops

FSD (Supervised) is vision-only. Eight cameras feed an end-to-end neural network that outputs steering, acceleration and braking; it learns from video from a fleet of 10.2 million delivered vehicles and runs on Tesla's in-house inference silicon. There is no lidar, no radar and no pre-mapped corridors as Waymo has. Training runs on the Cortex clusters in Texas, with 400 MW of compute targeted by 2026-12-31. Two problems stay unsolved. The first is degradation detection when cameras are blinded by rain, fog or low sun: NHTSA's Engineering Analysis EA26002, opened 2026-03-19 over 13 crashes and 2.88 million vehicles, asks whether the system notices and warns the driver. The second is the reliability increment that permits removing the supervisor, which is why customer-owned unsupervised driving moved to Q2 2027 [S58, S80].

| Metric | Value | Method | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| FSD miles per major collision | 6,006,200 (North America, October 2026) | Company report, FSD-engaged miles | S58 |
| Cumulative unsupervised robotaxi miles | 2.0 million (to 2026-09-30) | Company quarterly update | S6 |
| FSD subscriptions and attach | 1.74 million; more than 75% of North American deliveries | Company KPI, excludes free trials | S6 |
| 4680 cell output and density | More than 1 million cells/week; more than 40 GWh; 272 Wh/kg | Giga Texas line data and teardown estimates | S56 |
| Energy storage deployed | 13.7 GWh (Q3 2026); 36.0 GWh (9M 2026) | Company KPI | S6 |
| Megapack segment gross margin | 33.1% (Q3 2026) | Segment accounts | S4 |

### Robotaxi: a real service, on one state's terms

Paid Cybercab rides began in Austin on 2026-09-03, and Tesla claimed 300-plus Cybercabs serving the city on 2026-10-10; Texas records showed 319 authorised Cybercab VINs. It has not disclosed fares, revenue or how many run without a monitor. Permits are the constraint: Texas allows self-certified commercial driverless operation under its 2026 law, while California lists Tesla Robotaxi LLC only for testing with a driver and omits it from the driverless-testing and deployment lists (2026-10-22). NHTSA's defect petition DP26010, opened 2026-10-09 on school-zone speeding, puts the monitored fleet at 1,000 vehicles. Set against Waymo's 500,000 paid rides a week, Tesla's robotaxi is a pilot; set against BYD's 762,478 quarterly BEVs, its car business is the higher-cost producer [S73, S74, S59, S76].

| Dimension | Tesla | Benchmark | What it means | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Autonomy sensing | Vision-only cameras, no lidar or radar | Waymo: lidar, radar, cameras and high-definition maps | Lower bill of materials, higher tail risk in bad weather | S59 |
| Weekly paid rides | Not disclosed | Waymo: 500,000 a week on a 4,000-vehicle fleet | At 5 miles a ride, Waymo runs 2.5 million rider-only miles weekly, more than Tesla's cumulative total | S59, S6 |
| Cell performance | 4680: 272 Wh/kg, 10-80% in 35-40 minutes | CATL Qilin 3 claims a full charge in six minutes | Tesla leads on cost, trails on density and charging | S56 |
| BEV volume, Q3 2026 | 486,532 units | BYD 762,478 passenger BEVs, +30.89% year over year | Cost leadership has moved to China | S76 |

### Cells: a cost moat, not a performance one

Giga Texas runs above one million 4680 cells a week at more than 40 GWh of installed capacity, and since January 2026 both electrodes use the dry process in production — a step CATL, Panasonic, LG and Samsung SDI have not taken to commercial scale. The economics are real: electrode cost 50% lower at full scale, 41% less line capex and more than 30% less factory energy. The product is not: energy density trails by 10-15%, charging is slower than Panasonic 2170 packs, yields above 90% sit below the 98% of mature producers, and Tesla still buys CATL LFP and Panasonic or LG 2170 cells for Shanghai and Fremont Model Y. Battery availability, not demand, remained the stated limit on 2026 volume [S56].

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why it is hard | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fleet data and training set | 7 | 10.2 million vehicles and billions of FSD miles, if compute and labelling keep pace | 3-4 years | S6 |
| Dry-electrode process | 7 | Both electrodes dry at more than 90% yield; no competitor at commercial scale | 3 years | S56 |
| Vertical integration (cells, packs, chips) | 6 | Process know-how and capital; AI6 foundry dependence caps it | 3-5 years | S6, S79 |
| Driverless permits | 4 | Texas self-certification is easy; California and the EU are not | 1-2 years Texas, 3+ California | S73 |
| **Composite** | **6/10** | A funded 50-person team would need 3 years for the cell line and 2 for Megapack integration; patents disclose little of either | **3 years of lead time** | S56, S73 |

### Patents: thin disclosure, deliberately

| Patent or application | Title | Jurisdiction | Filed | Granted | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Four international filings published 2026-04-16 | Optimus Gen 3 forearm, wrist, joint and hand assemblies | WIPO/PCT | Priority 2024-10-10 | — | Published, national phase pending | 22 degrees of freedom per hand, 25 forearm actuators, tendon-driven | S75 |
| US20260310299A1 | Flexible touch sensors for robotic hands | US | Not disclosed | — | Published 2025-10-08 | Tactile sensing for manipulation | S75 |
| Maxwell portfolio (acquired 2019, $235m) | Dry electrode manufacturing IP | US | Pre-2019 | Granted, owned | In force | Underpins the 4680 dry process | S56 |

The 10-K does not present patents as a competitive advantage; it rests the case on data, manufacturing cost and vertical integration [S3]. The Optimus filings show the limit: Musk said in April 2026 that the V3 hand would not use the patented design because it "ultimately didn't work", so the public record trails the programme.

### Product inventory

| Product | Stage | Launch | Revenue or share | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Model 3/Y | Commercial | 2017-2020 | $20.09bn automotive sales Q3 2026; 478,237 units (98.3%) | 18.5% total automotive | Next-generation platform, no date | S6, S76 |
| Cybercab and Robotaxi | Early commercial | 2026-09-03, Austin | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Unsupervised customer cars Q2 2027 | S6, S57 |
| Megapack, Megablock | Commercial | 2019; Megapack 3 in 2025 | $2.881bn segment Q3 2026 | 33.1% | Ramp 50 GWh Texas | S4, S6 |
| Optimus | Early production | 2026-10 | None | None | 20,000 units a week by end-2027, company claim | S57 |

### Energy is the proven technology

Megapack is the one line where Tesla holds a genuine integration advantage and prices it: 13.7 GWh deployed in Q3 2026, a 33.1% gross margin and record order rate and backlog, with 50 GWh of Texas capacity starting. Wood Mackenzie ranks Tesla second among storage integrators behind Sungrow. The counterweight is pricing: revenue fell 16% year over year to $2.881bn even as volume rose [S4, S72].

::: evidence
**The headline safety statistic is a company measurement, not an audited record.**

Tesla's October 2026 report puts FSD (Supervised) at 6,006,200 miles per major collision against 660,164 for US driving overall, but the ratio is not fault-based, comes from Tesla telemetry and has not been verified by the regulator, which is running an engineering analysis over 13 low-visibility crashes instead [S58, S80].
:::

### What would change the judgement

The strongest case against my caution is that FSD is already monetised: attach, subscriptions and deferred revenue all rose in Q3 2026, and services gross profit reached a record. Against it, repeated NHTSA recall campaigns on the 2026 Model Y show launch quality slipping on the highest-volume car, and the attach rate is North American only while China sales fell in Q3 2026 with FSD approval still pending.

Diligence questions: what did Austin earn per robotaxi per week, and how many Cybercabs ran without a monitor? What is blended pack cost per kWh? Does EA26002 end in a recall, and what would that do to the unsupervised release date? Until the first two are answered, Tesla owns the best-proven manufacturing technology in the sector and has not yet proven the one the share price pays for.

Without credits, FY2025's 4.6% operating margin is 2.5% and Q3 2026's 2.6% is 2.2% [S4, S64, S66].

Per vehicle the business improved even as credits disappeared. Q3 2026 automotive revenue per delivery excluding credits was $42,026, up 0.5%, while cost of revenue per delivery fell 2.7% to $34,436, so gross profit per vehicle rose 18.0% to $7,591 (18.1% margin) from $6,433 (15.4%). The gain is cost and regional mix, not price: management attributes the 270 basis points to a higher Asia-Pacific delivery mix, where Shanghai is the lowest-cost plant. Tesla does not disclose customer acquisition cost; SG&A per delivery of $4,142 is an upper bound that also carries corporate and non-vehicle cost, and the first vehicle's gross profit covers 1.8 times it. A three-year LTV estimate of $8,455 adds three years of services gross profit per vehicle in the fleet ($288 a year on 10.2 million cumulative deliveries), giving LTV:CAC of 2.0:1 and payback inside the delivery quarter. Tesla is the only one of the three with positive per-vehicle automotive gross profit after credits: BYD's automotive gross margin was 20.49% in FY2025, from 22.31%, and Rivian's automotive gross profit was a $(36) million loss in Q2 2026.

Energy is the highest-margin dollar of growth. Storage revenue per GWh fell 23% to $210 million from $273 million, but gross profit per GWh fell only 19% to $69.6 million because cost per GWh fell 25% to $141 million, lifting segment margin to 33.1% from 31.4%. The mechanism is cell integration: the first Megapacks built with Tesla's own Nevada LFP cells shipped in Q3 2026, Megafactory Texas began production with 50 GWh of planned capacity, and the Megapack backlog is nearly sold out through 2027. Fluence, the pure-play integrator, earned 13.1% in FY2025; Tesla's advantage comes from owning the cell, not from pricing power. Part of the 33.1% is not repeatable: management attributed it partly to tariff refunds and cell-related warranty reimbursements. Services is the quieter engine: revenue rose 33% to $4,605 million on 2% fewer deliveries and gross margin reached 15.9% from 10.5%. Each extra $1 billion of energy revenue at 30% adds $300 million of gross profit; the same dollar of automotive revenue at 18% adds $180 million [S67, S4].

FSD and software grow but remain too small to see in the income statement. Active subscriptions rose to 1.74 million from 1.04 million; deferred revenue for FSD, connectivity and software was $4.08 billion against $3.87 billion at 2025-12-31; $668 million was recognised in 9M 2026 from balances already deferred; and obligations beyond one year were $10.73 billion, of which $4.80 billion falls due within twelve months. Counter-case: gross margin improves while the company gets less profitable. Operating expenses of $4,776 million rose 39% against $5,494 million of gross profit, R&D alone rose 69% to $2,761 million, and depreciation rose 17% to $1,580 million and will accelerate as more than $20 billion of 2026 capital expenditure is commissioned. The warranty reserve rose 26% to $10,138 million on 2% fewer deliveries, with claims incurred up 29% to $1,614 million while the provision per delivery fell to $1,227 from $1,463. Inventory rose 13.7% to $14,092 million with 11 days of vehicle supply, consistent with launch build-up, not unsold cars. The vehicle line covers its own costs, so break-even is about the cost base: operating expenses of $4,776 million need $27.0 billion of revenue at a 17.7% blended margin, and Q3 2026 delivered $28.0 billion for $718 million of operating profit. Confidence is high on the segment arithmetic and medium on how much of the 2026 cost relief is structural rather than tariff and mix. rows.finding: US battery-electric share of new light-duty vehicle sales fell to 6% in Q3 2026 from 10% in Q3 2025, and to 6% in the first nine months of 2026 from 8%; the luxury segment where Tesla's US mix sits fell from 31% to 12% BEV share over the same four quarters, while hybrids reached 16% of US light-duty sales.
rows.mechanism: Removing a $7,500 point-of-sale credit raised the effective price of a BEV relative to a hybrid by roughly the credit's size; the marginal buyer who entered only for the credit left and did not return a year later, so the drop is a level shift in the demand curve, not a payback whiplash that reverses.
rows.benchmark: September 2025, the last month of eligibility, set a record 12% US BEV share; a pure pull-forward would have produced recovery by Q2 2026.
rows.implication: Price the US BEV pool at roughly 0.9-1.0 million units a year, not the 1.3 million of 2025, and treat US volume growth as share-taking from retreating incumbents rather than market growth.
rows.weakens: Hybrid gains (16% share) and a $50,000+ average transaction price show the substitution is toward hybrids, not back to petrol, so electrification is not reversing - only BEV-only strategies are exposed.
rows.confidence: high - US government analysis using Omdia registration estimates
rows.follow_up: What is the monthly US BEV share for September and October 2026, after the Q3 incentive push, to see whether 6% is a floor?

rows.finding: The subsidy did not disappear from the transaction price, it moved to manufacturer P&Ls: US new-EV average transaction price was $54,754 in August 2026 (-2.8% year on year) with incentives averaging 12% of ATP, about $6,594 per vehicle, and the EV premium over comparable ICE vehicles narrowed to $4,847 (9.7%).
rows.mechanism: OEMs replaced roughly $6,600 of the $7,500 federal credit with their own incentives, so the net price barely moved while gross margin absorbed the difference; the volume that failed to appear at that net price is the credit's true demand creation.
rows.benchmark: $7,500 section 30D credit removed 2025-09-30; incentives of $6,594 per unit are 88% of the credit's size.
rows.implication: Tesla's 18.5% automotive gross margin in Q3 2026 is being earned while it funds part of the incentive load; a price war to defend US share would come directly out of that margin.
rows.weakens: If incentives were the only support, volumes should have held; US EV volume still fell 46.9% year on year in August 2026, so price was not the binding constraint for the missing buyers.
rows.confidence: high - Cox Automotive transaction-price data, consistent with EIA volume data
rows.follow_up: How much of Tesla's US incentive spending is booked as a price reduction rather than a marketing expense, and does it show in the 2027 ASP?

rows.finding: EU battery-electric registrations reached 1,641,333 units in January-August 2026, 21.7% of the EU market against 15.8% a year earlier, led by France +74.2% and Germany +53.1%; plug-in hybrids took 10% and hybrids 36.6%, while petrol and diesel fell to 29% combined.

rows.benchmark: 2025 EU average BEV share of 17.4% (European Commission, citing ACEA); 2026 running at 21.7%, a 4.3-point step in eight months.

rows.follow_up: What BEV share does the EU need in 2027 to comply, and how much of the 2026 step is pre-compliance pulling forward into 2027?

arguments.markdown:
Tesla's strategy has become a capital-allocation bet rather than an operating one: more than $20bn of 2026 capex and $30bn of new credit facilities are committed to autonomy, robots and semiconductors while nine-month 2026 operating income of $2.06bn implies a return on invested capital near 3%, below any plausible cost of capital. The strategy earns its keep only if unsupervised robotaxi revenue arrives before 2028, and the 12-month test is customer-owned unsupervised driving in mid-2027, not another reveal [S4, S78].

### The plan and the return do not yet match

Tesla guided in the Q3 2026 filing to capital expenditure above $20bn for 2026, after spending $13.01bn in the first nine months against $6.13bn a year earlier, and in September 2026 signed three credit agreements for aggregate commitments of $30bn. Cash and short-term investments were $45.45bn at 2026-09-30 against $9.5bn of debt, so the plan is funded; it is no longer self-funding. Nine-month operating income of $2.06bn on $89.29bn of equity, annualised after tax over roughly $71bn of invested capital, gives a return near 3% — a figure depressed by ramp assets, but low enough that every further billion of capex lowers the return until the new assets sell something [S6]. Research and development rose 69% year over year to $2.76bn in Q3 2026, most of it for autonomy and robotics.

### Milestones: what has actually shipped

| Milestone | Target date | Status at 2026-10-29 | What it proves | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cybercab in the Austin robotaxi fleet | 2026 | Met: paid rides from 2026-09-03 | Hardware and a Texas permit | S6 |
| Customer-owned unsupervised FSD | Q4 2026, now Q2 2027 | Slipped by about two quarters | Converts the owner fleet into robotaxi supply without capex | S57 |
| Optimus production | 2026 | Met: early production from 2026-10-21 | Manufacturing readiness, not demand | S6 |
| Optimus at 20,000 units a week | End-2027 | Company claim, no unit count disclosed | Whether a humanoid is a product | S57 |
| Tesla Semi volume production | 2026 | Met: Nevada high-volume line | Entry into Class 8 trucking | S6 |
| Next-generation affordable platform | Not dated | Not publicly disclosed | The volume and cost reset | S6 |
| 400 MW of training compute | 2026-12-31 | 225 MW installed (Cortex 1 and 2) | Whether the compute constraint eases | S6 |
| Austin Fab equipment commissioning | 2027 | Under construction | Vertical integration into silicon | S6 |
| FSD approval in China | Not dated | Pending; CFO negotiating | Monetising the largest market | S77 |
| Megafactory Texas at 50 GWh | 2026-2027 | Production began Q3 2026 | Energy scale-up | S6 |

### Partners: concentration, not diversification

| Partner | Scope | Signed | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Samsung Electronics | AI6 foundry at Taylor, Texas; $16.5bn through 2033 | 2025-07-28 | AI5 taped out on 2nm in July 2026; AI6 to follow | S79 |
| CATL | LFP cells for Shanghai vehicles and storage | Not disclosed | Active | S56 |
| Panasonic, LG Energy Solution | 2170 cells for Fremont and Shanghai | Not disclosed | Active | S56 |
| xAI, then SpaceX | $2bn xAI investment converted into SpaceX Class A shares after SpaceX acquired xAI | 2026-01; converted 2026-02 | Stake held; a merger is openly discussed | S78 |
| Maxwell Technologies | Dry-electrode intellectual property acquired for $235m | 2019 | Integrated into 4680 production | S56 |

The partner map shows the strategic risk: Tesla's autonomy roadmap runs through a single foundry for AI6, its vehicles still depend on CATL, Panasonic and LG for cells, and its largest related-party exposure is to companies its chief executive also controls.

### Geography: China becomes an export base

Tesla's China sales fell 16% year over year in Q3 2026 to 142,133 units while Giga Shanghai exports reached a record 132,978; for the half year, retail sales fell 9% while exports rose 127%, and Beijing cuts the EV export tax rebate in April 2027. Shanghai, with more than 950,000 units of capacity, is now a cost and export base rather than a growth market, exposed to tariffs in the markets it ships to. Berlin set a production record and the US business carries the FSD attach rate, which is why the company's own numbers look better in North America than in the two regions that decide its cost base [S77, S76].

### Energy is where the strategy is working

The energy plan is coherent and funded: 50 GWh of Megafactory Texas capacity started in Q3 2026 alongside 40 GWh in California and 20 GWh in Shanghai, with 7 GWh of Nevada LFP cell capacity in early ramp and the first Megapacks built from Tesla-made cells. Record order rate and backlog, a 33.1% segment gross margin and data-centre demand give the capital a return that autonomy does not yet. The tension is that revenue fell 16% year over year to $2.881bn even as volume rose, so the plan is adding capacity into falling prices [S6, S72].

### The capital allocation question

In January 2026 Tesla invested $2bn in xAI; the stake became SpaceX Class A shares when SpaceX acquired xAI in February 2026, and the Q1 2026 cash flow statement records a $2.002bn purchase of SpaceX equity. Three of nine directors have SpaceX ties, the 2026 proxy is set for a 2026-12-03 meeting, and the 2025 CEO award pays out on a deal price without operational milestones — only one of twelve operational milestones is rated probable, leaving $105.8-120.4bn of unrecognised stock compensation. A shareholder is no longer buying only a car and storage company; a merger scenario makes the position a bet on Musk's wider portfolio, which argues for a smaller size [S78].

### What must be true in 12 months

Three signposts decide whether the strategy is earning its cost of capital. EX-21 states no ownership percentages, so the table's 100% is inferred from listing rather than disclosed. China is a wholly foreign-owned enterprise, not a VIE, so there is no contractual-control gap, but Shanghai is fully consolidated and exposed to export controls. No entity is designated holder of Full Self-Driving or Optimus intellectual property: robotaxi operations sit in Tesla Robotaxi, LLC while software, data and chip designs stay in the parent, so no separately capitalised autonomy asset exists.

### Customers, buyers and how growth arrives

Tesla sells direct in two segments: automotive at $69,526m of 2025 revenue and energy at $12,771m [S71]. The vehicle buyer is a household or fleet paying cash or Tesla financing; the energy buyer is a utility or developer signing multi-year procurement, with 33.1% gross margin in Q3 2026 against 18.5% for automotive. Growth now comes from storage, software (1.74 million FSD subscriptions) and paying Cybercab rides in Austin since 2026-09-03.

### Ownership is concentrated without a dual class

Percentages follow the proxy, whose denominator excludes unearned award shares; free float is capped by the Musk and Vanguard stakes shown, and a margin call on the pledged block would add supply at the worst moment. With one class and no super-voting stock, control runs through the CEO office, the board seat and stake size rather than a charter provision, unlike Ford's Class B (40% of votes on 2% of shares) or Alphabet's founder Class B.

### Control is priced through a contingent award

The 2025 CEO Performance Award is the control instrument: 423,743,904 shares in 12 tranches of 35,311,992, each tied to a market-capitalisation milestone from $2.0 trillion to $8.5 trillion and to 1 of 12 operational milestones (20 million vehicles, 10 million FSD subscriptions, 1 million bots, 1 million robotaxis, Adjusted EBITDA of $50bn to $400bn); none was earned at 2026-10-19 [S5]. Tesla has never paid a dividend, repurchased no shares in 2025, and holds no authorisation to offset dilution. Litigation moved rather than vanished: the Delaware Supreme Court reinstated the 2018 award on 2025-12-19, the 96,000,000-share interim award was forfeited on 2026-04-21, and a securities class action filed on 2025-08-04 in the Western District of Texas covers purchasers from 2023-04-19 to 2025-06-22 over Autopilot, FSD and Robotaxi statements.

Three conditions would change this judgement — an independent special committee for any SpaceX transaction, no change-of-control acceleration without operating milestones, and a buyback sized to offset stock compensation. None appears in the 2026 proxy, so the governance discount stays. Confidence is high on structure, medium on how a Texas court would treat a challenge to the award; diligence should ask for the pledge's loan-to-value.

Tesla guided in the Q3 2026 filing to capital expenditure above $20bn for 2026, after spending $13.01bn in the first nine months against $6.13bn a year earlier, and in September 2026 signed three credit agreements for aggregate commitments of $30bn. Cash and short-term investments were $45.45bn at 2026-09-30 against $9.5bn of debt, so the plan is funded; it is no longer self-funding. Nine-month operating income of $2.06bn on $89.29bn of equity, annualised after tax over roughly $71bn of invested capital, gives a return near 3% — depressed by ramp assets, but low enough that every further billion of capex lowers the return until the new assets sell something [S6]. Research and development rose 69% year over year to $2.76bn in Q3 2026, most of it for autonomy and robotics.

### Pricing and mix are carrying the capex

| Item | Q3 2026 | Q3 2025 | Read | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Automotive gross margin | 18.5% | 17.0% | Cost cuts and mix offset lower prices | S4 |
| Regulatory credit revenue | $113m | $417m | A subsidy that no longer pays for the plan | S4 |
| Energy segment revenue | $2.881bn | $3.415bn | Volume up, price down | S4 |
| Services gross profit | $734m | $366m | FSD subscriptions and repair work | S6 |
| China deliveries | 142,133 | 16% lower year over year | Share loss in the largest market | S77 |
| Total deliveries | 486,532 | 497,099 | Flat volume on an ageing core line-up | S6 |

The read is that Tesla is funding autonomy from a mature car business, a fading credit stream and a fast-growing but deflating storage business; none of the three is a rising price. The Semi is a logical adjacency because it shares cells, motors and Megachargers with the core; Optimus is not an adjacency yet, because it has a production line and no customer.

### Milestones: what has actually shipped

| Milestone | Target date | Status at 2026-10-29 | What it proves | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cybercab in the Austin robotaxi fleet | 2026 | Met: paid rides from 2026-09-03 | Hardware and a Texas permit | S6 |
| Customer-owned unsupervised FSD | Q4 2026, now Q2 2027 | Slipped by about two quarters | Converts the owner fleet into robotaxi supply without capex | S57 |
| Optimus production | 2026 | Met: early production from 2026-10-21 | Manufacturing readiness, not demand | S6 |
| Optimus at 20,000 units a week | End-2027 | Company claim, no unit count disclosed | Whether a humanoid is a product | S57 |
| Tesla Semi volume production | 2026 | Met: Nevada high-volume line | Entry into Class 8 trucking | S6 |
| Next-generation affordable platform | Not dated | Not publicly disclosed | The volume and cost reset | S6 |
| 400 MW of training compute | 2026-12-31 | 225 MW installed (Cortex 1 and 2) | Whether the compute constraint eases | S6 |
| Austin Fab equipment commissioning | 2027 | Under construction | Vertical integration into silicon | S6 |
| FSD approval in China | Not dated | Pending; CFO negotiating | Monetising the largest market | S77 |
| Megafactory Texas at 50 GWh | 2026-2027 | Production began Q3 2026 | Energy scale-up | S6 |

### Partners: concentration, not diversification

| Partner | Scope | Signed | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Samsung Electronics | AI6 foundry at Taylor, Texas; $16.5bn through 2033 | 2025-07-28 | AI5 taped out on 2nm in July 2026; AI6 to follow | S79 |
| CATL | LFP cells for Shanghai vehicles and storage | Not disclosed | Active | S56 |
| Panasonic, LG Energy Solution | 2170 cells for Fremont and Shanghai | Not disclosed | Active | S56 |
| xAI, then SpaceX | $2bn xAI investment converted into SpaceX Class A shares after SpaceX acquired xAI | 2026-01; converted 2026-02 | Stake held; a merger is openly discussed | S78 |
| Maxwell Technologies | Dry-electrode intellectual property acquired for $235m | 2019 | Integrated into 4680 production | S56 |

The partner map shows the strategic risk: Tesla's autonomy roadmap runs through a single foundry for AI6, its vehicles still depend on CATL, Panasonic and LG for cells, and its largest related-party exposure is to companies its chief executive also controls.

### Geography: China becomes an export base

Tesla's China sales fell 16% year over year in Q3 2026 to 142,133 units while Giga Shanghai exports reached a record 132,978; for the half year, retail sales fell 9% while exports rose 127%, and Beijing cuts the EV export tax rebate in April 2027. Shanghai, with more than 950,000 units of capacity, is now a cost and export base rather than a growth market, exposed to tariffs in the markets it ships to. Berlin set a production record and the US business carries the FSD attach rate, which is why the company's own numbers look better in North America than in the two regions that decide its cost base [S77, S76].

### Energy is where the strategy is working

The energy plan is coherent and funded: 50 GWh of Megafactory Texas capacity started in Q3 2026 alongside 40 GWh in California and 20 GWh in Shanghai, with 7 GWh of Nevada LFP cell capacity in early ramp and the first Megapacks built from Tesla-made cells. Record order rate and backlog, a 33.1% segment gross margin and data-centre demand give the capital a return that autonomy does not yet. The tension is that revenue fell 16% year over year to $2.881bn even as volume rose, so the plan is adding capacity into falling prices [S6, S72].

### The capital allocation question

In January 2026 Tesla invested $2bn in xAI; the stake became SpaceX Class A shares when SpaceX acquired xAI in February 2026, and the Q1 2026 cash flow statement records a $2.002bn purchase of SpaceX equity. Three of nine directors have SpaceX ties, the 2026 proxy is set for a 2026-12-03 meeting, and the 2025 CEO award pays out on a deal price without operational milestones — only one of twelve operational milestones is rated probable, leaving $105.8-120.4bn of unrecognised stock compensation. A shareholder is no longer buying only a car and storage company; a merger scenario makes the position a bet on Musk's wider portfolio, which argues for a smaller size [S78].

### What must be true in 12 months

Three signposts decide whether the strategy is earning its cost of capital. First, unsupervised driving in customer-owned cars in at least one US state by 2027-06-30, with robotaxi revenue disclosed separately — without it, the capex is a subsidy to a pilot. Second, energy gross margin holding above 25% once tariff refunds lapse and 50 GWh of Texas capacity ramps, which tests whether Megapack has pricing power or is a commodity. Third, capital discipline: 2027 capex at or below $25bn with positive free cash flow, rather than a further draw on the $30bn facilities. The counter-case is strong: FSD attach above 75% in North America, 1.74 million subscriptions, a record energy backlog and $45.45bn of cash mean the plan can be funded through a slip, and Q3 2026 free cash flow of $1.53bn shows the core still generates cash [S6, S57].

Diligence questions: what is the 2027 capex number and how much of it is contractually committed? What revenue did robotaxi and FSD each earn in Q3 2026? Will the December 2026 meeting put a SpaceX transaction to a shareholder vote, and on what terms? My confidence is high that the strategy is funded and well-resourced for energy, medium that autonomy revenue arrives before 2028, and low that a humanoid robot contributes to profit before 2029.

arguments.markdown:
Tesla is a single-class Texas corporation whose control rests on a 19.8% CEO stake plus a 423.7 million-share contingent award, so a public-equity holder is underwriting Elon Musk's capital allocation rather than a board-governed company; that is acceptable at a governance discount, not a premium. Tesla, Inc. was incorporated in Delaware on 2003-07-01, converted to Texas on 2024-06-13, and trades on Nasdaq under TSLA with one class of common stock and 3,952,648,559 shares outstanding at 2026-09-30, including 423,743,904 unearned restricted shares. There is no VIE, nominee-shareholder or red-chip layer [S3].

::: kpi
| Metric | Value | Benchmark | Signal | Source |

| CEO economic stake | 19.8% (699,580,882 shares) | Ford family: 40% of votes on 2% of shares | warn | S5, S95 |

| Unrecognised compensation on that award | $9.74bn probable; $105.82bn-$120.37bn not | $162m recognised in 2025 | critical | S4 |
| Cash and short-term investments | $45.45bn at 2026-09-30 | 2026 capex guided above $20bn | good | S6 |
| Insider activity, 12 months | -$87.69m sales, zero open-market purchases | one-sided tape | warn | S27 |
:::

### The entity map is clean; the asset ring-fence is not

| Entity | Jurisdiction | Role | Ownership | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Tesla, Inc. | Texas | Listed parent and principal operating company | 100% | S3, S5 |
| Tesla Robotaxi, LLC | Texas | Robotaxi operating entity | 100% listed subsidiary | S3 |
| Tesla Energy Operations, Inc. | Delaware | Energy generation and storage operations | 100% listed subsidiary | S3 |
| Tesla Manufacturing Brandenburg SE | Germany | Berlin vehicle plant | 100% listed subsidiary | S3 |
| Tesla (Shanghai) Co., Ltd | China | Shanghai plant and China sales, wholly foreign-owned | 100% listed subsidiary | S3 |

EX-21 states no ownership percentages, so the ownership column above is inferred from listing rather than disclosed. China is a wholly foreign-owned enterprise, not a VIE, so there is no contractual-control gap, but Shanghai is fully consolidated and exposed to export controls. No entity is designated holder of Full Self-Driving or Optimus intellectual property: robotaxi operations sit in Tesla Robotaxi, LLC while software, data and chip designs stay in the parent, so no separately capitalised autonomy asset exists.

### Customers, buyers and how growth arrives

Tesla sells direct in two segments: automotive at $69,526m of 2025 revenue and energy at $12,771m [S71]. The vehicle buyer is a household or fleet paying cash or Tesla financing; the energy buyer is a utility or developer signing multi-year procurement, with 33.1% gross margin in Q3 2026 against 18.5% for automotive. Growth now comes from storage, software (1.74 million FSD subscriptions) and paying Cybercab rides in Austin since 2026-09-03.

### Ownership is concentrated without a dual class

| Holder | Class | Shares | % ownership | % votes | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Elon Musk | Common, incl. 286,428,773 restricted | 699,580,882 | 19.8% | 19.8% | S5 |
| Elon Musk, pledged as collateral | Common | 207,498,721 | 5.2% of outstanding | 5.2% | S5 |
| Vanguard Capital Management | Common | 210,796,512 | 5.3% | 5.3% | S5 |
| Unearned 2025 award shares | Restricted, unearned | 423,743,904 | 10.7% of outstanding | proportional to other shares | S5 |
| Other public holders | Common | balance | 74.9% | 74.9% | S5 |

Percentages follow the proxy, whose denominator excludes unearned award shares; free float is capped by the Musk and Vanguard stakes shown, and a margin call on the pledged block would add supply at the worst moment. With one class and no super-voting stock, control runs through the CEO office, the board seat and stake size rather than a charter provision, unlike Ford's dual-class family control or Alphabet's founder shares.

### Control is priced through a contingent award

The 2025 CEO Performance Award is the control instrument: 423,743,904 shares in 12 tranches of 35,311,992, each tied to a market-capitalisation milestone from $2.0 trillion to $8.5 trillion and to 1 of 12 operational milestones (20 million vehicles, 10 million FSD subscriptions, 1 million bots, 1 million robotaxis, Adjusted EBITDA of $50bn to $400bn); none was earned at 2026-10-19 [S5]. At $2.0 trillion the first tranche implies $506 per share on 3.95 billion shares, and because the operational test falls away in a change of control, a deal at $3.0 trillion would earn three tranches, 105.9 million shares, with no robotaxi or Optimus milestone met. Expense is already running: $802m in the first nine months of 2026, $9.74bn unrecognised on the one milestone management judges probable, and $105.82bn-$120.37bn on the rest [S4]. Dilution of 10.7% is designed, not tail, and sits above the current valuation rather than beside it.

### The board can refuse less than it appears

Nine directors sit in three classes, six labelled independent under Nasdaq rules, with Robyn Denholm as chair since November 2018. Ira Ehrenpreis, who chairs both the compensation and the nominating and governance committees, joined SpaceX's board in February 2026; Kimbal Musk is the CEO's brother; JB Straubel, a director, runs Redwood Materials, a Tesla supplier. Related-party flows are small in dollars but pointed: Tesla agreed on 2026-01-16 to invest $2.00bn in xAI, converted into SpaceX Class A stock when SpaceX bought xAI on 2026-02-02 and funded on 2026-03-12, while xAI bought $430.1m of Megapacks and SpaceX bought $143.3m of vehicles in 2025. A board setting a Tesla-SpaceX exchange ratio would do so with three of nine directors tied to SpaceX, and the retail auto-voting programme in the 2026 proxy offers standing instructions to vote with the board outside a defined special matter [S78]. The counterweight is narrow: the Special Committee used only Denholm and Wilson-Thompson, and 78.2% of votes cast backed 2025 pay.

### Capital allocation has no return floor

Tesla has never paid a dividend, repurchased no shares in 2025, and holds no authorisation to offset dilution. It ended 2026-09-30 with $45.45bn of cash and short-term investments, generated $14.90bn of operating cash flow in nine months against $13.01bn of capex, guided 2026 capex above $20bn, and signed three credit agreements with $30bn of commitments in September 2026 [S6]. Against Ford and GM, which return cash, Tesla offers neither dividend nor buyback, so the capital returned to holders is zero while insiders realise value through equity sales. Litigation moved rather than vanished: the Delaware Supreme Court reinstated the 2018 award on 2025-12-19, the 96,000,000-share interim award was forfeited on 2026-04-21, and a securities class action filed on 2025-08-04 in the Western District of Texas covers purchasers from 2023-04-19 to 2025-06-22 over Autopilot, FSD and Robotaxi statements.

A multi-year holder is paid for four things: a contingent award that accelerates on a deal price rather than operating proof; conflict committees that include SpaceX-affiliated directors; new debt against a thin free-cash-flow buffer; and key-person concentration in a CEO who also runs SpaceX. Three conditions would change this judgement — an independent special committee for any SpaceX transaction, no change-of-control acceleration without operating milestones, and a buyback sized to offset stock compensation. None appears in the 2026 proxy, so the governance discount stays. Confidence is high on structure, medium on how a Texas court would treat a challenge to the award; diligence should ask for the pledge's loan-to-value.

| Product | Pricing metric | Q3 2025 | Q3 2026 | Peer benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Vehicles, net of credits | realised revenue per delivery | $41,818 | $42,026 | BYD automotive gross margin 20.49%, FY2025 | S4, S65 |
| Megapack and Powerwall | realised revenue per GWh deployed | $273 million | $210 million | Fluence gross margin 13.1%, FY2025 | S3, S67 |
| FSD (Supervised) | deferred balance per active subscription | not disclosed | $2,345 | none disclosed | S4, S6 |

Energy is the highest-margin dollar of growth. Storage revenue per GWh fell 23% to $210 million from $273 million, but gross profit per GWh fell only 19% to $69.6 million because cost per GWh fell 25% to $141 million, lifting segment margin to 33.1% from 31.4%. The mechanism is cell integration: the first Megapacks built with Tesla's own Nevada LFP cells shipped in Q3 2026, Megafactory Texas began production with 50 GWh of planned capacity, and the Megapack backlog is nearly sold out through 2027. Fluence earned 13.1% in FY2025; Tesla's advantage comes from owning the cell, not from pricing power. Part of the 33.1% is not repeatable: management attributed it partly to tariff refunds and cell-related warranty reimbursements. Services is the quieter engine: revenue rose 33% to $4,605 million on 2% fewer deliveries and gross margin reached 15.9% from 10.5%. Each extra $1 billion of energy revenue at 30% adds $300 million of gross profit; the same dollar of automotive revenue at 18% adds $180 million. FSD and software grow but remain too small to see in the income statement: active subscriptions rose to 1.74 million from 1.04 million, deferred revenue for FSD, connectivity and software was $4.08 billion against $3.87 billion at 2025-12-31, and obligations beyond one year were $10.73 billion, of which $4.80 billion falls due within twelve months. Management's claim that FSD is attached to more than 75% of North American deliveries is company-reported and cannot be tied to a revenue line, because Tesla does not disclose FSD revenue; the observable is $2,345 of deferred balance per active subscription, a stock rather than a price. Tesla paid $1.95 billion in stock and awards for an AI hardware company in Q2 2026, $222 million to developed technology and $1.73 billion contingent on conditions judged improbable, so no expense has been booked [S67, S4].

Counter-case: gross margin improves while the company gets less profitable. Operating expenses of $4,776 million rose 39% against $5,494 million of gross profit, R&D alone rose 69% to $2,761 million, and depreciation rose 17% to $1,580 million and will accelerate as more than $20 billion of 2026 capital expenditure is commissioned. The warranty reserve rose 26% to $10,138 million on 2% fewer deliveries, with claims incurred up 29% to $1,614 million while the provision per delivery fell to $1,227 from $1,463. Inventory rose 13.7% to $14,092 million, with 11 days of vehicle supply. The vehicle line covers its own costs, so break-even is about the cost base: operating expenses of $4,776 million need $27.0 billion of revenue at a 17.7% blended margin, and Q3 2026 delivered $28.0 billion for $718 million of operating profit. Normalise energy to a 30% margin and take credits to zero and the same quarter earns $515 million, a 1.8% operating margin. For a position, that argues for sizing on the energy and services annuity, which has rising margins and a 2027 backlog, and treating autonomy as an option rather than as earnings, because at a 1.8% margin the vehicle franchise cannot carry the current cost base on its own. Confidence is high on the segment arithmetic and medium on how much of the 2026 cost relief is structural rather than tariff and mix. Four questions would settle it: the North American automotive margin excluding credits; the energy margin excluding tariff refunds and the contracted 2027 backlog price; the FSD revenue line and how robotaxi rides will be recognised; and the year R&D and capital expenditure stop rising as a share of revenue [S4, S6].

::: evidence
**Tesla's profit now rests on energy and services gross profit, not on credits or on the car**

Energy storage and services supplied $1,688 million of Q3 2026 gross profit at 33.1% and 15.9% margins, while regulatory credits fell to $113 million, 15.7% of operating income, from 45.8% of FY2025 operating income, and operating expenses absorbed 86.9% of gross profit [S4, S6].
:::

arguments.markdown:
Tesla's technology is proven where it is a manufacturing problem — dry-electrode cells, Megapack integration — and unproven where the valuation sits. Its 2.0 million cumulative autonomous miles compare with Waymo's 500,000 paid rides a week, its 486,532 quarterly deliveries trail BYD's 762,478 electric cars, and its paid driverless permit exists in one state. The technology justifies a premium to a capital-intensive manufacturer in energy and process engineering; it does not yet justify the multiple of a software platform [S6, S59, S76].

### How FSD works, and where it stops

FSD (Supervised) is vision-only. Eight cameras feed an end-to-end neural network that outputs steering, acceleration and braking; it learns from video from a fleet of 10.2 million delivered vehicles and runs on Tesla's in-house inference silicon. There is no lidar, no radar and no pre-mapped corridors as Waymo has. Training runs on the Cortex clusters in Texas, with 400 MW of compute targeted by 2026-12-31. Two problems stay unsolved. The first is degradation detection when cameras are blinded by rain, fog or low sun: NHTSA's Engineering Analysis EA26002, opened 2026-03-19 over 13 crashes and 2.88 million vehicles, asks whether the system notices and warns the driver. The second is the reliability increment that permits removing the supervisor, which is why customer-owned unsupervised driving moved to Q2 2027 [S58, S80].

| Metric | Value | Method | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| FSD miles per major collision | 6,006,200 (North America, October 2026) | Company report, FSD-engaged miles | S58 |
| Cumulative unsupervised robotaxi miles | 2.0 million (to 2026-09-30) | Company quarterly update | S6 |
| FSD subscriptions and attach | 1.74 million; more than 75% of North American deliveries | Company KPI, excludes free trials | S6 |
| 4680 cell output and density | More than 1 million cells/week; more than 40 GWh; 272 Wh/kg | Giga Texas line data and teardown estimates | S56 |
| Energy storage deployed | 13.7 GWh (Q3 2026); 36.0 GWh (9M 2026) | Company KPI | S6 |
| Megapack segment gross margin | 33.1% (Q3 2026) | Segment accounts | S4 |

### Robotaxi: a real service, on one state's terms

Paid Cybercab rides began in Austin on 2026-09-03, and Tesla claimed 300-plus Cybercabs serving the city on 2026-10-10; Texas records showed 319 authorised Cybercab VINs. It has not disclosed fares, revenue or how many run without a monitor. Permits are the constraint: Texas allows self-certified commercial driverless operation under its 2026 law, while California lists Tesla Robotaxi LLC only for testing with a driver and omits it from the driverless-testing and deployment lists (2026-10-22). NHTSA's defect petition DP26010, opened 2026-10-09 on school-zone speeding, puts the monitored fleet at 1,000 vehicles. Set against Waymo's 500,000 paid rides a week, Tesla's robotaxi is a pilot; set against BYD's 762,478 quarterly BEVs, its car business is the higher-cost producer [S73, S74, S59, S76].

| Dimension | Tesla | Benchmark | What it means | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Autonomy sensing | Vision-only cameras, no lidar or radar | Waymo: lidar, radar, cameras and high-definition maps | Lower bill of materials, higher tail risk in bad weather | S59 |
| Weekly paid rides | Not disclosed | Waymo: 500,000 a week on a 4,000-vehicle fleet | At 5 miles a ride, Waymo runs 2.5 million rider-only miles weekly, more than Tesla's cumulative total | S59, S6 |
| Cell performance | 4680: 272 Wh/kg, 10-80% in 35-40 minutes | CATL Qilin 3 claims a full charge in six minutes | Tesla leads on cost, trails on density and charging | S56 |
| BEV volume, Q3 2026 | 486,532 units | BYD 762,478 passenger BEVs, +30.89% year over year | Cost leadership has moved to China | S76 |

### Cells: a cost moat, not a performance one

Giga Texas runs above one million 4680 cells a week at more than 40 GWh of installed capacity, and since January 2026 both electrodes use the dry process in production — a step CATL, Panasonic, LG and Samsung SDI have not taken to commercial scale. The economics are real: electrode cost 50% lower at full scale, 41% less line capex and more than 30% less factory energy. The product is not: energy density trails by 10-15%, charging is slower than Panasonic 2170 packs, yields above 90% sit below the 98% of mature producers, and Tesla still buys CATL LFP and Panasonic or LG 2170 cells for Shanghai and Fremont Model Y. Battery availability, not demand, remained the stated limit on 2026 volume [S56].

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why it is hard | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fleet data and training set | 7 | 10.2 million vehicles and billions of FSD miles, if compute and labelling keep pace | 3-4 years | S6 |
| Dry-electrode process | 7 | Both electrodes dry at more than 90% yield; no competitor at commercial scale | 3 years | S56 |
| Vertical integration (cells, packs, chips) | 6 | Process know-how and capital; AI6 foundry dependence caps it | 3-5 years | S6, S79 |
| Driverless permits | 4 | Texas self-certification is easy; California and the EU are not | 1-2 years Texas, 3+ California | S73 |
| **Composite** | **6/10** | A funded 50-person team would need 3 years for the cell line and 2 for Megapack integration; patents disclose little of either | **3 years of lead time** | S56, S73 |

### Patents: thin disclosure, deliberately

| Patent or application | Title | Jurisdiction | Filed | Granted | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Four international filings published 2026-04-16 | Optimus Gen 3 forearm, wrist, joint and hand assemblies | WIPO/PCT | Priority 2024-10-10 | — | Published, national phase pending | 22 degrees of freedom per hand, 25 forearm actuators, tendon-driven | S75 |
| US20260310299A1 | Flexible touch sensors for robotic hands | US | Not disclosed | — | Published 2025-10-08 | Tactile sensing for manipulation | S75 |
| Maxwell portfolio (acquired 2019, $235m) | Dry electrode manufacturing IP | US | Pre-2019 | Granted, owned | In force | Underpins the 4680 dry process | S56 |

The 10-K does not present patents as a competitive advantage; it rests the case on data, manufacturing cost and vertical integration. The Optimus filings show the limit: Musk said in April 2026 that the V3 hand would not use the patented design because it "ultimately didn't work", so the public record trails the programme.

### Product inventory

| Product | Stage | Launch | Revenue or share | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Model 3/Y | Commercial | 2017-2020 | $20.09bn automotive sales Q3 2026; 478,237 units (98.3%) | 18.5% total automotive | Next-generation platform, no date | S6, S76 |
| Cybercab and Robotaxi | Early commercial | 2026-09-03, Austin | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Unsupervised customer cars Q2 2027 | S6, S57 |
| Megapack, Megablock | Commercial | 2019; Megapack 3 in 2025 | $2.881bn segment Q3 2026 | 33.1% | Ramp 50 GWh Texas | S4, S6 |
| Optimus | Early production | 2026-10 | None | None | 20,000 units a week by end-2027, company claim | S57 |

### Energy is the proven technology

Megapack is the one line where Tesla holds a genuine integration advantage and prices it: 13.7 GWh deployed in Q3 2026, a 33.1% gross margin and record order rate and backlog, with 50 GWh of Texas capacity starting. Wood Mackenzie ranks Tesla second among storage integrators behind Sungrow. The counterweight is pricing: revenue fell 16% year over year to $2.881bn even as volume rose [S4, S72].

::: evidence

### What would change the judgement

The strongest case against my caution is that FSD is already monetised: attach, subscriptions and deferred revenue all rose in Q3 2026, and services gross profit reached a record. Against it, repeated NHTSA recall campaigns on the 2026 Model Y show launch quality slipping on the highest-volume car, and the attach rate is North American only while China sales fell in Q3 2026 with FSD approval still pending.

Diligence questions: what did Austin earn per robotaxi per week, and how many Cybercabs ran without a monitor? What is blended pack cost per kWh? Does EA26002 end in a recall, and what would that do to the unsupervised release date? Until the first two are answered, Tesla owns the best-proven manufacturing technology in the sector and has not yet proven the one the share price pays for.

arguments.markdown:
Tesla still makes most of its gross profit selling cars, but after regulatory credits the car business earns little at the operating line. Credits supplied 45.8% of FY2025 operating income and 15.7% in Q3 2026; incremental profit now comes from a 33.1%-margin energy-storage business and a 15.9%-margin services business while AI spending absorbs 86.9% of gross profit. Nine-month 2026 revenue of $78,669 million split into automotive $57,310 million (including $639 million of credits), energy $8,428 million and services $12,931 million, against an automotive share of 85.1% in FY2023. Q3 2026 gross profit divided $3,806 million automotive (69%), $954 million energy (17%) and $734 million services (13%), versus 91%/6%/3% in FY2023. Cash arrives when a vehicle changes hands, on storage milestones and prepayments ($3.30 billion of customer prepayments in deferred revenue at 2026-09-30, from $2.04 billion), and monthly for Supercharging, insurance and FSD [S3, S4, S6].

| Segment | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 | 9M 2026 | Q3 2026 | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Automotive revenue excluding credits ($M) | 80,629 | 74,307 | 67,533 | 56,671 | 20,447 | S1, S3, S4 |
| Automotive regulatory credits ($M) | 1,790 | 2,763 | 1,993 | 639 | 113 | S1, S3, S4 |
| Energy generation and storage revenue ($M) | 6,035 | 10,086 | 12,771 | 8,428 | 2,881 | S3, S4 |
| Services and other revenue ($M) | 8,319 | 10,534 | 12,530 | 12,931 | 4,605 | S3, S4 |
| Automotive gross margin excluding credits | 17.7% | 15.4% | 15.4% | 17.7% | 18.1% | S1, S3, S4, S63 |
| Energy gross margin | 18.9% | 26.2% | 29.8% | 30.2% | 33.1% | S3, S4 |
| Services gross margin | 5.9% | 5.8% | 7.4% | 13.4% | 15.9% | S3, S4 |

The credit franchise is ending. Tesla booked $2,763 million of automotive regulatory credits in FY2024, $1,993 million in FY2025 and $639 million in 9M 2026; Q3 2026 alone was $113 million, down 73% from $417 million. Credits carry no cost of revenue, so a credit dollar is nearly a dollar of operating profit: 20.1% of operating income in FY2023, 39.0% in FY2024, 45.8% in FY2025, 31.1% in 9M 2026 and 15.7% in Q3 2026. An implied Q4 2025 figure of $542 million shows the collapse came not with the lapse of the consumer credit but with the removal of the compliance obligation in 2026: the Department of Transportation finalised its CAFE rollback on 2026-10-01, ending the requirement that made legacy automakers buy zero-emission credits. Without credits, FY2025's 4.6% operating margin is 2.5% and Q3 2026's 2.6% is 2.2% [S4, S64, S66].

Per vehicle the business improved even as credits disappeared. Q3 2026 automotive revenue per delivery excluding credits was $42,026, up 0.5%, while cost of revenue per delivery fell 2.7% to $34,436, so gross profit per vehicle rose 18.0% to $7,591 (18.1% margin) from $6,433 (15.4%). The gain is cost and regional mix, not price: management attributes the 270 basis points to a higher Asia-Pacific delivery mix, where Shanghai is the lowest-cost plant. Tesla does not disclose customer acquisition cost; SG&A per delivery of $4,142 is an upper bound that also carries corporate and non-vehicle cost, and the first vehicle's gross profit covers 1.8 times it. A three-year LTV estimate of $8,455 adds three years of services gross profit per vehicle in the fleet ($288 a year on 10.2 million cumulative deliveries), giving LTV:CAC of 2.0:1 and payback inside the delivery quarter. Tesla is the only one of the three with positive per-vehicle gross profit after credits: BYD's automotive gross margin was 20.49% in FY2025, from 22.31%, and Rivian's automotive gross profit was a $(36) million loss in Q2 2026 [S63, S65, S68].

| Per unit | Q3 2025 | Q3 2026 | Change | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Deliveries (units) | 497,099 | 486,532 | -2.1% | S6 |
| Automotive revenue per delivery, excluding credits | $41,818 | $42,026 | +0.5% | S4, S6 |
| Automotive cost of revenue per delivery | $35,385 | $34,436 | -2.7% | S4, S6 |
| Automotive gross profit per delivery, excluding credits | $6,433 | $7,591 | +18.0% | S4, S6 |
| Energy gross profit per delivery | $2,158 | $1,961 | -9.1% | S4, S6 |
| Services gross profit per delivery | $736 | $1,508 | +105% | S4, S6 |
| SG&A per delivery (acquisition-cost upper bound) | $3,142 | $4,142 | +31.8% | S4, S6 |
| R&D per delivery | $3,279 | $5,675 | +73.1% | S4, S6 |
| Operating profit per delivery | $3,267 | $1,476 | -54.8% | S4, S6 |

| Product | Pricing metric | Q3 2025 | Q3 2026 | Peer benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Vehicles, net of credits | realised revenue per delivery | $41,818 | $42,026 | BYD automotive gross margin 20.49%, FY2025 | S4, S65 |
| Megapack and Powerwall | realised revenue per GWh deployed | $273 million | $210 million | Fluence gross margin 13.1%, FY2025 | S3, S67 |

Energy is the highest-margin dollar of growth. Storage revenue per GWh fell 23% to $210 million from $273 million, but gross profit per GWh fell only 19% to $69.6 million because cost per GWh fell 25% to $141 million, lifting segment margin to 33.1% from 31.4%. The mechanism is cell integration: the first Megapacks built with Tesla's own Nevada LFP cells shipped in Q3 2026, Megafactory Texas began production with 50 GWh of planned capacity, and the Megapack backlog is nearly sold out through 2027. Fluence earned 13.1% in FY2025; Tesla's advantage is owning the cell, not pricing. Part of the 33.1% is not repeatable: management attributed it partly to tariff refunds and cell-related warranty reimbursements. Services is the quieter engine: revenue rose 33% to $4,605 million on 2% fewer deliveries and gross margin reached 15.9% from 10.5%. Each extra $1 billion of energy revenue at 30% adds $300 million of gross profit; the same dollar of automotive revenue at 18% adds $180 million. FSD and software grow but remain too small to see in the income statement: active subscriptions rose to 1.74 million from 1.04 million, deferred revenue for FSD, connectivity and software was $4.08 billion against $3.87 billion at 2025-12-31, and obligations beyond one year were $10.73 billion, of which $4.80 billion falls due within twelve months. Management's claim that FSD is attached to more than 75% of North American deliveries is company-reported and cannot be tied to a revenue line, because Tesla does not disclose FSD revenue; the observable is $2,345 of deferred balance per active subscription, a stock rather than a price [S67, S4].

The newest change in how money flows is who owns the asset. Selling a car converts inventory into revenue once; a robotaxi fleet keeps the vehicle on Tesla's balance sheet and earns per mile, shifting the model from a hardware sale to a utilisation business whose revenue depends on hours operated, fares and fleet uptime rather than on deliveries. The Cybercab entered Tesla's own Austin fleet on 2026-09-03 and management reports unsupervised miles growing week on week, but no fare revenue, fleet size or per-mile economics are disclosed, so the model cannot yet be tested. Until it discloses revenue, the investable model remains the one in the tables: cars, storage and services.

Counter-case: gross margin improves while the company gets less profitable. Operating expenses of $4,776 million rose 39% against $5,494 million of gross profit, R&D alone rose 69% to $2,761 million, and depreciation rose 17% to $1,580 million and will accelerate as more than $20 billion of 2026 capital expenditure is commissioned. The warranty reserve rose 26% to $10,138 million on 2% fewer deliveries, with claims incurred up 29% to $1,614 million while the provision per delivery fell to $1,227 from $1,463. Inventory rose 13.7% to $14,092 million, with 11 days of vehicle supply. The vehicle line covers its own costs, so break-even is about the cost base: operating expenses of $4,776 million need $27.0 billion of revenue at a 17.7% blended margin, and Q3 2026 delivered $28.0 billion for $718 million of operating profit. Normalise energy to a 30% margin and take credits to zero and the same quarter earns $515 million, a 1.8% operating margin. For a position, that argues for sizing on the energy and services annuity, which has rising margins and a 2027 backlog, and treating autonomy as an option rather than as earnings, because at a 1.8% margin the vehicle franchise cannot carry the current cost base on its own. Confidence is high on the segment arithmetic and medium on how much of the 2026 cost relief is structural rather than tariff and mix. Four questions would settle it: the North American automotive margin excluding credits; the energy margin excluding tariff refunds and the contracted 2027 backlog price; the FSD revenue line and how robotaxi rides will be recognised; and the year R&D and capital expenditure stop rising as a share of revenue [S4, S6].

::: evidence
**Tesla's profit now rests on energy and services gross profit, not on credits or on the car**

Energy storage and services supplied $1,688 million of Q3 2026 gross profit at 33.1% and 15.9% margins, while regulatory credits fell to $113 million, 15.7% of operating income, from 45.8% of FY2025 operating income, and operating expenses absorbed 86.9% of gross profit [S4, S6].
:::

Q3 2026 gross profit divided $3,806 million automotive (69%), $954 million energy (17%) and $734 million services (13%), versus 91%/6%/3% in FY2023. Cash arrives when a vehicle changes hands, on storage milestones and prepayments ($3.30 billion of customer prepayments in deferred revenue at 2026-09-30, from $2.04 billion), and monthly for Supercharging, insurance and FSD [S3, S4, S6].

| Segment | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 | 9M 2026 | Q3 2026 | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Automotive revenue excluding credits ($M) | 80,629 | 74,307 | 67,533 | 56,671 | 20,447 | S1, S3, S4 |
| Automotive regulatory credits ($M) | 1,790 | 2,763 | 1,993 | 639 | 113 | S1, S3, S4 |
| Energy generation and storage revenue ($M) | 6,035 | 10,086 | 12,771 | 8,428 | 2,881 | S3, S4 |
| Services and other revenue ($M) | 8,319 | 10,534 | 12,530 | 12,931 | 4,605 | S3, S4 |
| Automotive gross margin excluding credits | 17.7% | 15.4% | 15.4% | 17.7% | 18.1% | S1, S3, S4, S63 |
| Energy gross margin | 18.9% | 26.2% | 29.8% | 30.2% | 33.1% | S3, S4 |

The credit franchise is ending. Tesla booked $2,763 million of automotive regulatory credits in FY2024, $1,993 million in FY2025 and $639 million in 9M 2026; Q3 2026 alone was $113 million, down 73% from $417 million. Credits carry no cost of revenue, so a credit dollar is nearly a dollar of operating profit: 20.1% of operating income in FY2023, 39.0% in FY2024, 45.8% in FY2025, 31.1% in 9M 2026 and 15.7% in Q3 2026. An implied Q4 2025 figure of $542 million shows the collapse came with the removal of the compliance obligation in 2026, not the lapse of the consumer credit: the Department of Transportation finalised its CAFE rollback on 2026-10-01, ending the requirement that made legacy automakers buy zero-emission credits. Without credits, FY2025's 4.6% operating margin is 2.5% and Q3 2026's 2.6% is 2.2% [S4, S64, S66].

Per vehicle the business improved even as credits disappeared. Q3 2026 automotive revenue per delivery excluding credits was $42,026, up 0.5%, while cost of revenue per delivery fell 2.7% to $34,436, so gross profit per vehicle rose 18.0% to $7,591 (18.1% margin) from $6,433 (15.4%). The gain is cost and regional mix, not price: management attributes the 270 basis points to a higher Asia-Pacific delivery mix, where Shanghai is the lowest-cost plant. Tesla does not disclose customer acquisition cost; SG&A per delivery of $4,142 is an upper bound carrying corporate and non-vehicle cost, and the first vehicle's gross profit covers 1.8 times it. A three-year LTV estimate of $8,455 adds three years of services gross profit per vehicle in the fleet ($288 a year on 10.2 million cumulative deliveries), giving LTV:CAC of 2.0:1 and payback inside the delivery quarter. Tesla is the only one of the three with positive per-vehicle gross profit after credits: BYD's automotive gross margin was 20.49% in FY2025, from 22.31%, and Rivian's automotive gross profit was a $(36) million loss in Q2 2026 [S63, S65, S68].

| Per unit | Q3 2025 | Q3 2026 | Change | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Deliveries (units) | 497,099 | 486,532 | -2.1% | S6 |
| Automotive revenue per delivery, excluding credits | $41,818 | $42,026 | +0.5% | S4, S6 |
| Automotive cost of revenue per delivery | $35,385 | $34,436 | -2.7% | S4, S6 |
| Automotive gross profit per delivery, excluding credits | $6,433 | $7,591 | +18.0% | S4, S6 |
| Energy gross profit per delivery | $2,158 | $1,961 | -9.1% | S4, S6 |
| Services gross profit per delivery | $736 | $1,508 | +105% | S4, S6 |
| SG&A per delivery (acquisition-cost upper bound) | $3,142 | $4,142 | +31.8% | S4, S6 |
| R&D per delivery | $3,279 | $5,675 | +73.1% | S4, S6 |
| Operating profit per delivery | $3,267 | $1,476 | -54.8% | S4, S6 |

| Product | Pricing metric | Q3 2025 | Q3 2026 | Peer benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Vehicles, net of credits | realised revenue per delivery | $41,818 | $42,026 | BYD automotive gross margin 20.49%, FY2025 | S4, S65 |
| Megapack and Powerwall | realised revenue per GWh deployed | $273 million | $210 million | Fluence gross margin 13.1%, FY2025 | S3, S67 |

Energy is the highest-margin dollar of growth. Storage revenue per GWh fell 23% to $210 million from $273 million, but gross profit per GWh fell only 19% to $69.6 million because cost per GWh fell 25% to $141 million, lifting segment margin to 33.1% from 31.4%. The mechanism is cell integration: the first Megapacks built with Tesla's own Nevada LFP cells shipped in Q3 2026, Megafactory Texas began production with 50 GWh of capacity, and the Megapack backlog is nearly sold out through 2027. Fluence earned 13.1% in FY2025; Tesla's advantage is owning the cell, not pricing. Part of the 33.1% is not repeatable: management attributed it partly to tariff refunds and cell-related warranty reimbursements. Services is the quieter engine: revenue rose 33% to $4,605 million on 2% fewer deliveries and gross margin reached 15.9% from 10.5%. Each extra $1 billion of energy revenue at 30% adds $300 million of gross profit; the same dollar of automotive revenue at 18% adds $180 million. FSD and software grow but remain too small to see in the income statement: active subscriptions rose to 1.74 million from 1.04 million, deferred revenue for FSD, connectivity and software was $4.08 billion against $3.87 billion at 2025-12-31, and obligations beyond one year were $10.73 billion, of which $4.80 billion falls due within twelve months. Management's claim that FSD is attached to more than 75% of North American deliveries is company-reported and cannot be tied to a revenue line, because Tesla does not disclose FSD revenue; the observable is $2,345 of deferred balance per active subscription, a stock rather than a price [S67, S4].

The newest change in how money flows is who owns the asset. Selling a car converts inventory into revenue once; a robotaxi fleet keeps the vehicle on Tesla's balance sheet and earns per mile, shifting the model from a hardware sale to a utilisation business paid on hours operated, fares and uptime rather than deliveries. The Cybercab entered Tesla's own Austin fleet on 2026-09-03, but no fare revenue, fleet size or per-mile economics are disclosed, so the model cannot yet be tested. Until then the investable model remains the one in the tables: cars, storage and services.

Counter-case: gross margin improves while the company gets less profitable. Operating expenses of $4,776 million rose 39% against $5,494 million of gross profit, R&D alone rose 69% to $2,761 million, and depreciation rose 17% to $1,580 million and will accelerate as more than $20 billion of 2026 capital expenditure is commissioned. The warranty reserve rose 26% to $10,138 million on 2% fewer deliveries, with claims incurred up 29% to $1,614 million while the provision per delivery fell to $1,227 from $1,463. Inventory rose 13.7% to $14,092 million, with 11 days of vehicle supply. The vehicle line covers its own costs, so break-even is about the cost base: operating expenses of $4,776 million need $27.0 billion of revenue at a 17.7% blended margin, and Q3 2026 delivered $28.0 billion for $718 million of operating profit. Normalise energy to a 30% margin and take credits to zero and the same quarter earns $515 million, a 1.8% operating margin. For a position, that argues for sizing on the energy and services annuity, with rising margins and a 2027 backlog, and treating autonomy as an option rather than earnings, because at a 1.8% margin the vehicle franchise cannot carry the cost base alone. Confidence is high on the segment arithmetic and medium on how much of the 2026 cost relief is structural rather than tariff and mix. Four questions would settle it: the North American automotive margin excluding credits; the energy margin excluding tariff refunds and the contracted 2027 backlog price; the FSD revenue line and how robotaxi rides will be recognised; and the year R&D and capital expenditure stop rising as a share of revenue [S4, S6].

::: evidence
**Tesla's profit now rests on energy and services gross profit, not on credits or on the car**

Energy storage and services supplied $1,688 million of Q3 2026 gross profit at 33.1% and 15.9% margins, while regulatory credits fell to $113 million, 15.7% of operating income, from 45.8% of FY2025 operating income, and operating expenses absorbed 86.9% of gross profit [S4, S6].
:::
