Tesla's strategy has become a capital-allocation bet rather than an operating one: more than $20bn of 2026 capex and $30bn of new credit facilities are committed to autonomy, robots and semiconductors while nine-month 2026 operating income of $2.06bn implies a return on invested capital near 3%, below any plausible cost of capital. The strategy earns its keep only if unsupervised robotaxi revenue arrives before 2028, and the 12-month test is customer-owned unsupervised driving in mid-2027, not another reveal [S4, S78].

### The plan and the return do not yet match

Tesla guided in the Q3 2026 filing to capital expenditure above $20bn for 2026, after spending $13.01bn in the first nine months against $6.13bn a year earlier, and in September 2026 signed three credit agreements for aggregate commitments of $30bn. Cash and short-term investments were $45.45bn at 2026-09-30 against $9.5bn of debt, so the plan is funded; it is no longer self-funding. Nine-month operating income of $2.06bn on $89.29bn of equity, annualised after tax over roughly $71bn of invested capital, gives a return near 3% — depressed by ramp assets, but low enough that every further billion of capex lowers the return until the new assets sell something [S6]. Research and development rose 69% year over year to $2.76bn in Q3 2026, most of it for autonomy and robotics.

### Pricing and mix are carrying the capex

| Item | Q3 2026 | Q3 2025 | Read | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Automotive gross margin | 18.5% | 17.0% | Cost cuts and mix offset lower prices | S4 |
| Regulatory credit revenue | $113m | $417m | A subsidy that no longer pays for the plan | S4 |
| Energy segment revenue | $2.881bn | $3.415bn | Volume up, price down | S4 |
| Services gross profit | $734m | $366m | FSD subscriptions and repair work | S6 |
| China deliveries | 142,133 | 16% lower year over year | Share loss in the largest market | S77 |
| Total deliveries | 486,532 | 497,099 | Flat volume on an ageing core line-up | S6 |

The read is that Tesla is funding autonomy from a mature car business, a fading credit stream and a fast-growing but deflating storage business; none of the three is a rising price. The Semi is a logical adjacency because it shares cells, motors and Megachargers with the core; Optimus is not an adjacency yet, because it has a production line and no customer.

### Milestones: what has actually shipped

| Customer-owned unsupervised FSD | Q4 2026, now Q2 2027 | Slipped by about two quarters | Converts the owner fleet into robotaxi supply without capex | S57 |
| Optimus production | 2026 | Met: early production from 2026-10-21 | Manufacturing readiness, not demand | S6 |
| Optimus at 20,000 units a week | End-2027 | Company claim, no unit count disclosed | Whether a humanoid is a product | S57 |
| Tesla Semi volume production | 2026 | Met: Nevada high-volume line | Entry into Class 8 trucking | S6 |
| Next-generation affordable platform | Not dated | Not publicly disclosed | The volume and cost reset | S6 |
| 400 MW of training compute | 2026-12-31 | 225 MW installed (Cortex 1 and 2) | Whether the compute constraint eases | S6 |
| Austin Fab equipment commissioning | 2027 | Under construction | Vertical integration into silicon | S6 |
| FSD approval in China | Not dated | Pending; CFO negotiating | Monetising the largest market | S77 |
| Megafactory Texas at 50 GWh | 2026-2027 | Production began Q3 2026 | Energy scale-up | S6 |

### Partners: concentration, not diversification

| Partner | Scope | Signed | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Samsung Electronics | AI6 foundry at Taylor, Texas; $16.5bn through 2033 | 2025-07-28 | AI5 taped out on 2nm in July 2026; AI6 to follow | S79 |
| CATL | LFP cells for Shanghai vehicles and storage | Not disclosed | Active | S56 |
| Panasonic, LG Energy Solution | 2170 cells for Fremont and Shanghai | Not disclosed | Active | S56 |
| xAI, then SpaceX | $2bn xAI investment converted into SpaceX Class A shares after SpaceX acquired xAI | 2026-01; converted 2026-02 | Stake held; a merger is openly discussed | S78 |
| Maxwell Technologies | Dry-electrode intellectual property acquired for $235m | 2019 | Integrated into 4680 production | S56 |

The partner map shows the strategic risk: Tesla's autonomy roadmap runs through a single foundry for AI6, its vehicles still depend on CATL, Panasonic and LG for cells, and its largest related-party exposure is to companies its chief executive also controls.

### Geography: China becomes an export base

Tesla's China sales fell 16% year over year in Q3 2026 to 142,133 units while Giga Shanghai exports reached a record 132,978; retail sales for 2026 to date are down 12% as exports doubled, and Beijing cuts the EV export tax rebate in April 2027. Shanghai, with more than 950,000 units of capacity, is now a cost and export base rather than a growth market, exposed to tariffs in the markets it ships to. Berlin set a production record and the US business carries the FSD attach rate, which is why the company's own numbers look better in North America than in the two regions that decide its cost base [S77, S76, S102].

### Energy is where the strategy is working

The energy plan is coherent and funded: 50 GWh of Megafactory Texas capacity started in Q3 2026 alongside 40 GWh in California and 20 GWh in Shanghai, with 7 GWh of Nevada LFP cell capacity in early ramp and the first Megapacks built from Tesla-made cells. Record order rate and backlog, a 33.1% segment gross margin and data-centre demand give the capital a return that autonomy does not yet. The tension is that revenue fell 16% year over year to $2.881bn even as volume rose, so the plan is adding capacity into falling prices [S6, S72].

### The capital allocation question

In January 2026 Tesla invested $2bn in xAI; the stake became SpaceX Class A shares when SpaceX acquired xAI in February 2026, and the Q1 2026 cash flow statement records a $2.002bn purchase of SpaceX equity. Three of nine directors have SpaceX ties, the 2026 proxy is set for a 2026-12-03 meeting, and the 2025 CEO award pays out on a deal price without operational milestones — only one of twelve operational milestones is rated probable, leaving $105.8-120.4bn of unrecognised stock compensation. A shareholder is no longer buying only a car and storage company; a merger scenario makes the position a bet on Musk's wider portfolio, which argues for a smaller size [S78].

### What must be true in 12 months

Three signposts decide whether the strategy is earning its cost of capital. First, unsupervised driving in customer-owned cars in at least one US state by 2027-06-30, with robotaxi revenue disclosed separately — without it, the capex is a subsidy to a pilot. Second, energy gross margin holding above 25% once tariff refunds lapse and 50 GWh of Texas capacity ramps, which tests whether Megapack has pricing power or is a commodity. Third, capital discipline: 2027 capex at or below $25bn with positive free cash flow, rather than a further draw on the $30bn facilities. The counter-case is strong: FSD attach above 75% in North America, 1.74 million subscriptions, a record energy backlog and $45.45bn of cash mean the plan can be funded through a slip, and Q3 2026 free cash flow of $1.53bn shows the core still generates cash [S6, S57].

Diligence questions: what is the 2027 capex number and how much of it is contractually committed? What revenue did robotaxi and FSD each earn in Q3 2026? Will the December 2026 meeting put a SpaceX transaction to a shareholder vote, and on what terms? My confidence is high that the strategy is funded and well-resourced for energy, medium that autonomy revenue arrives before 2028, and low that a humanoid robot contributes to profit before 2029.

Selling a car converts inventory into revenue once; a robotaxi fleet keeps the vehicle on Tesla's balance sheet and earns per mile, shifting the model from a hardware sale to a utilisation business paid on hours operated, fares and uptime rather than deliveries. arguments.markdown:
Tesla still makes most of its gross profit selling cars, but after regulatory credits the car business earns little at the operating line. Credits supplied 45.8% of FY2025 operating income and 15.7% in Q3 2026; incremental profit now comes from a 33.1%-margin energy-storage business and a 15.9%-margin services business while AI spending absorbs 86.9% of gross profit. Nine-month 2026 revenue of $78,669 million split into automotive $57,310 million (including $639 million of credits), energy $8,428 million and services $12,931 million, against an automotive share of 85.1% in FY2023. Q3 2026 gross profit divided $3,806 million automotive (69%), $954 million energy (17%) and $734 million services (13%), versus 91%/6%/3% in FY2023. Cash arrives when a vehicle changes hands, on storage milestones and prepayments ($3.30 billion of customer prepayments in deferred revenue at 2026-09-30, from $2.04 billion), and monthly for Supercharging, insurance and FSD [S3, S4, S6].

| Segment | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 | 9M 2026 | Q3 2026 | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Automotive revenue excluding credits ($M) | 80,629 | 74,307 | 67,533 | 56,671 | 20,447 | S1, S3, S4 |
| Automotive regulatory credits ($M) | 1,790 | 2,763 | 1,993 | 639 | 113 | S1, S3, S4 |
| Energy generation and storage revenue ($M) | 6,035 | 10,086 | 12,771 | 8,428 | 2,881 | S3, S4 |
| Services and other revenue ($M) | 8,319 | 10,534 | 12,530 | 12,931 | 4,605 | S3, S4 |
| Automotive gross margin excluding credits | 17.7% | 15.4% | 15.4% | 17.7% | 18.1% | S1, S3, S4, S63 |
| Energy gross margin | 18.9% | 26.2% | 29.8% | 30.2% | 33.1% | S3, S4 |

The credit franchise is ending. Tesla booked $2,763 million of automotive regulatory credits in FY2024, $1,993 million in FY2025 and $639 million in 9M 2026; Q3 2026 alone was $113 million, down 73% from $417 million. Credits carry no cost of revenue, so a credit dollar is nearly a dollar of operating profit: 20.1% of operating income in FY2023, 39.0% in FY2024, 45.8% in FY2025, 31.1% in 9M 2026 and 15.7% in Q3 2026. An implied Q4 2025 figure of $542 million shows the collapse came with the removal of the compliance obligation in 2026, not the lapse of the consumer credit: the Department of Transportation finalised its CAFE rollback on 2026-10-01, ending the requirement that made legacy automakers buy zero-emission credits. Without credits, FY2025's 4.6% operating margin is 2.5% and Q3 2026's 2.6% is 2.2% [S4, S64, S66].

Per vehicle the business improved even as credits disappeared. Q3 2026 automotive revenue per delivery excluding credits was $42,026, up 0.5%, while cost of revenue per delivery fell 2.7% to $34,436, so gross profit per vehicle rose 18.0% to $7,591 (18.1% margin) from $6,433 (15.4%). The gain is cost and regional mix, not price: management attributes the 270 basis points to a higher Asia-Pacific delivery mix, where Shanghai is the lowest-cost plant. Tesla does not disclose customer acquisition cost; SG&A per delivery of $4,142 is an upper bound carrying corporate and non-vehicle cost, and the first vehicle's gross profit covers 1.8 times it. A three-year LTV estimate of $8,455 adds three years of services gross profit per vehicle in the fleet ($288 a year on 10.2 million cumulative deliveries), giving LTV:CAC of 2.0:1 and payback inside the delivery quarter. Tesla is the only one of the three with positive per-vehicle gross profit after credits: BYD's automotive gross margin was 20.49% in FY2025, from 22.31%, and Rivian's automotive gross profit was a $(36) million loss in Q2 2026 [S63, S65, S68].

| Per unit | Q3 2025 | Q3 2026 | Change | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Deliveries (units) | 497,099 | 486,532 | -2.1% | S6 |
| Automotive revenue per delivery, excluding credits | $41,818 | $42,026 | +0.5% | S4, S6 |
| Automotive cost of revenue per delivery | $35,385 | $34,436 | -2.7% | S4, S6 |
| Automotive gross profit per delivery, excluding credits | $6,433 | $7,591 | +18.0% | S4, S6 |
| Energy gross profit per delivery | $2,158 | $1,961 | -9.1% | S4, S6 |
| Services gross profit per delivery | $736 | $1,508 | +105% | S4, S6 |
| SG&A per delivery (acquisition-cost upper bound) | $3,142 | $4,142 | +31.8% | S4, S6 |
| R&D per delivery | $3,279 | $5,675 | +73.1% | S4, S6 |
| Operating profit per delivery | $3,267 | $1,476 | -54.8% | S4, S6 |

| Product | Pricing metric | Q3 2025 | Q3 2026 | Peer benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Vehicles, net of credits | realised revenue per delivery | $41,818 | $42,026 | BYD automotive gross margin 20.49%, FY2025 | S4, S65 |
| Megapack and Powerwall | realised revenue per GWh deployed | $273 million | $210 million | Fluence gross margin 13.1%, FY2025 | S3, S67 |

Energy is the highest-margin dollar of growth. Storage revenue per GWh fell 23% to $210 million from $273 million, but gross profit per GWh fell only 19% to $69.6 million because cost per GWh fell 25% to $141 million, lifting segment margin to 33.1% from 31.4%. The mechanism is cell integration: the first Megapacks built with Tesla's own Nevada LFP cells shipped in Q3 2026, Megafactory Texas began production with 50 GWh of capacity, and the Megapack backlog is nearly sold out through 2027. Fluence earned 13.1% in FY2025; Tesla's advantage is owning the cell, not pricing. Part of the 33.1% is not repeatable: management attributed it partly to tariff refunds and cell-related warranty reimbursements. Services is the quieter engine: revenue rose 33% to $4,605 million on 2% fewer deliveries and gross margin reached 15.9% from 10.5%. Each extra $1 billion of energy revenue at 30% adds $300 million of gross profit; the same dollar of automotive revenue at 18% adds $180 million. FSD and software grow but remain too small to see in the income statement: active subscriptions rose to 1.74 million from 1.04 million, deferred revenue for FSD, connectivity and software was $4.08 billion against $3.87 billion at 2025-12-31, and obligations beyond one year were $10.73 billion, of which $4.80 billion falls due within twelve months. Management's claim that FSD is attached to more than 75% of North American deliveries is company-reported and cannot be tied to a revenue line, because Tesla does not disclose FSD revenue; the observable is $2,345 of deferred balance per active subscription, a stock rather than a price [S67, S4].

The newest change in how money flows is who owns the asset. Selling a car converts inventory into revenue once; a robotaxi fleet keeps the vehicle on Tesla's balance sheet and earns per mile, shifting the model from a hardware sale to a utilisation business paid on hours operated, fares and uptime rather than deliveries. The Cybercab entered Tesla's own Austin fleet on 2026-09-03, but no fare revenue, fleet size or per-mile economics are disclosed, so the model cannot yet be tested. Until then the investable model remains the one in the tables: cars, storage and services.

Counter-case: gross margin improves while the company gets less profitable. Operating expenses of $4,776 million rose 39% against $5,494 million of gross profit, R&D alone rose 69% to $2,761 million, and depreciation rose 17% to $1,580 million and will accelerate as more than $20 billion of 2026 capital expenditure is commissioned. The warranty reserve rose 26% to $10,138 million on 2% fewer deliveries, with claims incurred up 29% to $1,614 million while the provision per delivery fell to $1,227 from $1,463. Inventory rose 13.7% to $14,092 million, with 11 days of vehicle supply. The vehicle line covers its own costs, so break-even is about the cost base: operating expenses of $4,776 million need $27.0 billion of revenue at a 17.7% blended margin, and Q3 2026 delivered $28.0 billion for $718 million of operating profit. Normalise energy to a 30% margin and take credits to zero and the same quarter earns $515 million, a 1.8% operating margin. For a position, that argues for sizing on the energy and services annuity, with rising margins and a 2027 backlog, and treating autonomy as an option rather than earnings, because at a 1.8% margin the vehicle franchise cannot carry the cost base alone. Confidence is high on the segment arithmetic and medium on how much of the 2026 cost relief is structural rather than tariff and mix. Four diligence questions remain: what is the North American automotive margin excluding credits? What is the energy margin excluding tariff refunds, and at what price is the 2027 backlog contracted? Will Tesla disclose FSD revenue and robotaxi recognition? When do R&D and capital expenditure stop rising as a share of revenue? [S4, S6]

::: evidence
**Tesla's profit now rests on energy and services gross profit, not on credits or on the car**

Energy storage and services supplied $1,688 million of Q3 2026 gross profit at 33.1% and 15.9% margins, while regulatory credits fell to $113 million, 15.7% of operating income, from 45.8% of FY2025 operating income, and operating expenses absorbed 86.9% of gross profit [S4, S6].
:::

Tesla's execution machine still ships, but the bench beneath Elon Musk has thinned to three named executive officers and at least 17 senior departures since April 2024, so a four-front roadmap in vehicles, energy, autonomy and robots rests on one man and a handful of engineers paid to stay rather than on a management team that could be handed the plan. The disclosed leadership is Musk (CEO and Technoking, age 55), Vaibhav Taneja (CFO since August 2023) and Xiaotong (Tom) Zhu (SVP APAC and Global Vehicle Manufacturing since June 2025), with no chief operating officer, president or segment chief between them and a nine-person board. Salaries are $400,000 for Taneja and $364,338 for Zhu, and Musk has taken none since 2019, so retention runs through equity, not cash [S5].

On execution the record is binary rather than average. Tesla produced its 10 millionth vehicle in Q3 2026, began volume production of the Semi, started Megafactory Texas and put Optimus onto a high-volume line at Fremont; Q3 2026 deliveries were 486,532, down 2% year on year, with 13.7 GWh of storage deployed and 1.74 million active FSD subscriptions [S6]. The 4680 cell gives the counter-rhythm: dry-electrode production for both anode and cathode arrived only with the Q4 2025 update, five years after the Battery Day target, and management still called battery availability the limiting factor for vehicle volumes in Q3 2026. Tesla solves hard manufacturing problems and solves them late, so a roadmap that now includes Cybercab, Optimus, a lithium refinery, an AI6 chip programme and Megafactory Texas should be discounted on that lag rather than on the best-case line.

Turnover is the counter-evidence, and it clusters where the growth story sits. At least 17 senior leaders left between April 2024 and 2026-10-15: the Cybercab programme lost its program manager (Victor Nechita, February 2026), its new-product-introduction head (Michael So, April 2026), two assembly leaders and the director who built robotaxi software (Thomas Dmytryk, March 2026); energy lost vice president Mike Snyder on 2026-10-15, succeeded by AJ Booth; finance lost Sendil Palani after 17 years in March 2026; and sales lost two North American chiefs in a year, including Raj Jegannathan in February 2026 [S93]. Internal promotion is real — Joe Ward went from European operations to global sales chief in February 2026 — but the pattern is that programme leaders are replaced by narrower specialists while the number of programmes grows.

The autonomy bench rests on one person. Ashok Elluswamy joined in 2014 as the first Autopilot engineer, led the removal of radar, built the end-to-end FSD architecture and now runs FSD, Robotaxi software and Optimus AI, plus a joint project with xAI; he holds none of the disclosed executive-officer titles, so he appears in neither the proxy ownership table nor the summary compensation table [S94]. Losing him would hit three programmes at once, and the retention tools available are the same volatile equity that has already seen software and AI staff leave for OpenAI and rivals. Depth is real in manufacturing — the Semi and Megafactory ramps show an operations bench that can still deliver — but the layer where autonomy and energy execution actually happens has lost the people who built it.

Founder-market fit is strongest where the problem is physics and manufacturing, weakest where it is regulated operations. Musk's career — Zip2 and PayPal sold to Compaq and eBay, then SpaceX and Tesla built from near-zero — is a serial-building record, and the full vesting of his first performance award is the market's own evidence that he hits market-capitalisation and operating targets. The gaps are structural: a chief operating officer who could own delivery across four programmes, a robotics manufacturing executive with volume experience, a regulatory leader able to win driverless approvals in the European Union and China, and an enterprise energy sales organisation that converts a record order book into contracted revenue. None of those roles appears in the proxy, so each is either unfilled or sits below the executive-officer line, and both readings raise execution risk at the scale the valuation implies.

| Years at Tesla | 18 as CEO | 10 in finance | 12 in operations | 12 in Autopilot and AI | 13 average | S5 |
| Prior exits | 2 (Zip2, PayPal) | 0 | 0 | 0 | 2 across four leaders | S5 |
| Scaling experience | 0 to 10.2m cumulative vehicles | SolarCity finance to group CFO | Shanghai to 950,000-unit capacity | 0 to 1.74m FSD subscriptions | Proven in hardware, not robot volume | S5, S6 |
| Fundraising and capital | Defines the story investors fund | Closed 2026 refinancing and $30bn of commitments | Regional banking relationships | None disclosed | Concentrated in two people | S4, S5 |
| Key-person dependency | Critical | Medium | High | Critical | Critical | S5 |
| Retention risk | Low, tied to the 2025 award | Low | Medium | High | High below VP level | S5, S93 |

The judgement is a conditional, not a rejection. Tesla's engineering culture has repeatedly converted improbable hardware into shipping product, and the board has paid to keep the one person who drives that conversion. What it has not built is an organisation that can lose him, or lose the programme leaders beneath him, without slowing. An investor holding through the robotaxi and Optimus ramp should size for announcement risk and ask three questions: who owns delivery of each programme if Musk or Elluswamy is unavailable, what retention has been granted below the executive-officer line, and whether the Cybercab departures reflected a programme reset the company has not disclosed. Confidence is high on team composition and the departure record, medium on what that turnover implies for 2027 timelines, because Tesla does not disclose programme-level staffing.

::: evidence
**Strongest proof the team can execute** is the compounding of hard manufacturing inside one quarter: 10.2 million cumulative vehicles, a Semi line running, Megafactory Texas in production, Optimus on a high-volume line and paying Cybercab rides, with 1.74 million FSD subscriptions and 13.7 GWh of storage alongside them [S6].

**Strongest doubt** is that the same quarter produced a 2% delivery decline while the Cybercab programme lost four leaders and energy lost its vice president two weeks before this report, so the programmes that must justify the valuation are the ones losing the people who built them, and the CEO who would absorb their decisions also runs SpaceX [S93].
:::

arguments.markdown:
Tesla's 2026-2028 demand is durable in Europe and grid storage and structurally weaker in the United States and China: the expiry of the US clean-vehicle credit on 2025-09-30 cut the US battery-electric share from 10% to 6% and lowered the underlying US growth rate rather than merely pulling sales forward, while China has become a shrinking unit market in which Tesla holds share instead of gaining it. That split constrains the investment case: no plausible US price action recovers the volume the credit used to buy, so growth has to come from a regulation in Europe and from data-centre load in storage, each durable for a different reason and on a different timetable [S98, S99, S101].

### The United States lost a level, not a quarter

Battery-electric vehicles were 6% of US light-duty sales in Q3 2026 against 10% in Q3 2025, and 6% in the first nine months against 8% a year earlier; in the luxury segment where Tesla's US mix sits, share fell from 31% to 12% while hybrids rose to 16%. A pull-forward would have produced recovery by Q2 2026; a year after expiry there is none, so the credit was creating demand, not borrowing it. Cox Automotive shows the mechanism and the size: the US new-EV average transaction price was $54,754 in August 2026, 2.8% lower year on year, with incentives at 12% of price, about $6,594 per vehicle, and the EV premium over comparable petrol vehicles down to $4,847, or 9.7%. Manufacturers replaced 88% of the $7,500 credit with their own money and volume still fell 46.9% year on year in August to 78,895 units; at 5.7% of new-vehicle sales that is a run-rate near 0.95 million units a year against roughly 1.3 million in 2025. Tesla's own figures carry the same signal with a twist: US revenue fell 14.4% year on year in Q3 2026 to $12,495 million while global deliveries slipped only 2% to 486,532, but part of the gap is self-inflicted, because Model S and Model X were retired in mid-2026 and other-model deliveries halved to 8,295 from 15,933, roughly $0.7 billion of the $2.1 billion decline at a $90,000-plus price. Strip that out and the US Model 3/Y business still shrank at a high-single-digit rate in a market that shrank faster, which is why Tesla's share of US EV sales rose to 51.7% in August 2026 [S98, S103, S4, S6].

### Europe is the offset, and its demand is policy-shaped

EU battery-electric registrations reached 1,641,333 in January-August 2026, 21.7% of the market against 15.8% a year earlier, with France up 74.2% and Germany up 53.1%; hybrids took 36.6% and plug-in hybrids 10%, while petrol and diesel fell to 29% combined. Tesla registered 153,978 cars in an 11-country panel in January-September 2026, up 51% from 102,025, and 45,523 in September alone, 4.6% of panel new-car sales against 2.6% a year earlier; the Model Y was the best-selling battery-electric model in September with 17,413 units against 8,227. The mechanism is a fleet-average CO2 mandate for 2025-2027 that makes battery volume the cheapest compliance route, reinforced in 2026 by the energy-price shock that lifted European electric-car sales close to 30% in the first quarter while the global total fell 8%. The risk is timing: if the 2026 step is pre-compliance borrowing 2027 volume, 2027 will be flat, and hybrids at 36.6% show the mandate is being met partly without battery cars [S99, S104, S100].

### China is penetration without volume

New energy vehicles reached 65.1% of new passenger cars in China in July 2026 from 54% a year earlier, but NEV sales fell 12.5% in January-July and total passenger-car sales fell 20.3%, so the share gain is arithmetic on a shrinking denominator. Tesla sold 381,088 cars to Chinese buyers in January-September 2026, down 11.9%, roughly in line with the market, and Giga Shanghai's September wholesale rose 5.0% to 95,366 only because exports jumped 58.3% to 30,529. Pricing moved in Tesla's favour for once: more than 15 Chinese automakers raised prices during 2026 as first-quarter industry margins fell to 3.2% and lithium costs rose 160%, ending the deflation that had squeezed every participant. China should be underwritten as a low-cost export base whose utilisation depends on demand outside China, not as a growth market for 2027-2028 [S101, S102, S105].

Grid storage is the only pool growing faster than Tesla can supply it. 108 GW of new battery storage was deployed worldwide in 2025, 40% more than in 2024 and eleven times the 2021 level, and deployments of 275.3 GWh in 2025 should reach 353.4 GWh in 2026 as AI data centres add load; Tesla deployed 36.0 GWh in the first nine months of 2026, about 14% of the 2026 system market, against Megafactory Texas capacity of 50 GWh. The budget owner is a utility or independent power producer on a multi-year contract behind an interconnection queue, which makes demand sticky but price-sensitive: Tesla's energy revenue fell 16% year on year in Q3 2026 on lower Megapack average selling prices and tariff refunds. Autonomous ride-hailing is still a rounding error: Waymo runs about 3,000 vehicles and 500,000 paid rides a week, roughly 26 million rides a year and $0.4-0.7 billion of gross bookings at a $15-25 fare, while Tesla had 44 active robotaxi vehicles across seven metros in the first half of 2026 before Cybercab rides began in Austin on 2026-09-03 [S106, S108, S4, S107, S6].

The counter-case deserves a hearing and does not overturn the judgement. If US battery-electric share holds at 6% for four quarters, the credit was worth about 40% of US demand and the base case is a flat US market rather than a falling one; if European growth is compliance-driven it is nonetheless legislated through 2027 and cannot reverse without reopening the CO2 regulation. The stronger challenge is to the robotaxi line: a purpose-built Cybercab and a consumer fleet already generating supervised autonomy miles at scale could compress cost per paid mile faster than Waymo's retrofit fleet, bringing the addressable market forward. What would change the view is a second year of 6% US share with rising Tesla US revenue (pricing power restored), or European battery share stalling below 22% in 2027 (compliance pull-forward confirmed). Confidence is high on the US and European unit data, medium on China because retail and wholesale definitions diverge, and low on robotaxi because no operator discloses audited paid rides. Three questions would settle the sizing: what US battery-electric share prints for September and October 2026 after the Q3 incentive push; what share of Giga Shanghai output is exported in Q3 2026 and which markets absorb it once EU tariffs apply; and what Tesla's Megapack realised price per kWh was in Q3 2026 excluding tariff refunds.

::: evidence
**US battery-electric demand stepped down to a new level after the credit expired and has not recovered a year later**

US BEV share of light-duty sales was 6% in Q3 2026 against 10% in Q3 2025, and 6% in the first nine months against 8%; the luxury segment fell from 31% to 12% while hybrids rose to 16%. Cox Automotive recorded a $54,754 average transaction price with incentives of about $6,594 per vehicle, 88% of the $7,500 credit, yet August volume still fell 46.9% year on year to 78,895 units [S98, S103].
:::

The credit franchise is ending. Tesla booked $2,763 million of automotive regulatory credits in FY2024, $1,993 million in FY2025 and $639 million in 9M 2026; Q3 2026 alone was $113 million, down 73% from $417 million. Credits carry no cost of revenue, so a credit dollar is nearly a dollar of operating profit: 20.1% of operating income in FY2023, 39.0% in FY2024, 45.8% in FY2025, 31.1% in 9M 2026 and 15.7% in Q3 2026. Per vehicle the business improved even as credits disappeared. A three-year LTV estimate of $8,455 adds three years of services gross profit per vehicle in the fleet ($288 a year on 10.2 million cumulative deliveries), giving LTV:CAC of 2.0:1 and payback inside the delivery quarter. Energy is the highest-margin dollar of growth. Storage revenue per GWh fell 23% to $210 million from $273 million, but gross profit per GWh fell only 19% to $69.6 million because cost per GWh fell 25% to $141 million, lifting segment margin to 33.1% from 31.4%. The mechanism is cell integration: the first Megapacks built with Tesla's own Nevada LFP cells shipped in Q3 2026, Megafactory Texas began production with 50 GWh of capacity, and the Megapack backlog is nearly sold out through 2027. Fluence earned 13.1% in FY2025; Tesla's advantage is owning the cell, not pricing. Part of the 33.1% is not repeatable: management attributed it partly to tariff refunds and cell-related warranty reimbursements. Services is the quieter engine: revenue rose 33% to $4,605 million on 2% fewer deliveries and gross margin reached 15.9% from 10.5%. Each extra $1 billion of energy revenue at 30% adds $300 million of gross profit; the same dollar of automotive revenue at 18% adds $180 million. FSD and software grow but remain too small to see in the income statement: active subscriptions rose to 1.74 million from 1.04 million, deferred revenue for FSD, connectivity and software was $4.08 billion against $3.87 billion at 2025-12-31, and obligations beyond one year were $10.73 billion, of which $4.80 billion falls due within twelve months. Management's claim that FSD is attached to more than 75% of North American deliveries is company-reported and cannot be tied to a revenue line, because Tesla does not disclose FSD revenue; the observable is $2,345 of deferred balance per active subscription, a stock rather than a price [S67, S4].

The newest change in money flows is who owns the asset. Selling a car converts inventory into revenue once; a robotaxi fleet keeps the vehicle on Tesla's balance sheet and earns per mile, shifting the model from a hardware sale to a utilisation business paid on hours operated, fares and uptime rather than deliveries. The Cybercab entered Tesla's own Austin fleet on 2026-09-03, but no fare revenue, fleet size or per-mile economics are disclosed, so the model cannot yet be tested. Until then the investable model remains the one in the tables: cars, storage and services.

Counter-case: gross margin improves while the company gets less profitable. Operating expenses of $4,776 million rose 39% against $5,494 million of gross profit, R&D alone rose 69% to $2,761 million, and depreciation rose 17% to $1,580 million and will accelerate as more than $20 billion of 2026 capital expenditure is commissioned. The warranty reserve rose 26% to $10,138 million on 2% fewer deliveries, with claims incurred up 29% to $1,614 million while the provision per delivery fell to $1,227 from $1,463. Inventory rose 13.7% to $14,092 million, with 11 days of vehicle supply. The vehicle line covers its own costs, so break-even is about the cost base: operating expenses of $4,776 million need $27.0 billion of revenue at a 17.7% blended margin, and Q3 2026 delivered $28.0 billion for $718 million of operating profit. Normalise energy to a 30% margin and take credits to zero and the same quarter earns $515 million, a 1.8% operating margin. For a position, that argues for sizing on the energy and services annuity, with rising margins and a 2027 backlog, and treating autonomy as an option rather than earnings, because at a 1.8% margin the vehicle franchise cannot carry the cost base alone. Confidence is high on the segment arithmetic and medium on how much of the 2026 cost relief is structural rather than tariff and mix. Four diligence questions remain: what is the North American automotive margin excluding credits? What is the energy margin excluding tariff refunds, and at what price is the 2027 backlog contracted? Will Tesla disclose FSD revenue and robotaxi recognition? When do R&D and capital expenditure stop rising as a share of revenue? [S4, S6]

arguments.markdown:
Tesla still makes most of its gross profit selling cars, but after regulatory credits the car business earns little at the operating line. Credits supplied 45.8% of FY2025 operating income and 15.7% in Q3 2026; incremental profit now comes from a 33.1%-margin energy-storage business and a 15.9%-margin services business while AI spending absorbs 86.9% of gross profit. Nine-month 2026 revenue of $78,669 million split into automotive $57,310 million (including $639 million of credits), energy $8,428 million and services $12,931 million, against an automotive share of 85.1% in FY2023. Q3 2026 gross profit divided $3,806 million automotive (69%), $954 million energy (17%) and $734 million services (13%), versus 91%/6%/3% in FY2023. Cash arrives when a vehicle changes hands, on storage milestones and prepayments ($3.30 billion of customer prepayments in deferred revenue at 2026-09-30, from $2.04 billion), and monthly for Supercharging, insurance and FSD [S3, S4, S6].

| Segment | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 | 9M 2026 | Q3 2026 | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Automotive revenue excluding credits ($M) | 80,629 | 74,307 | 67,533 | 56,671 | 20,447 | S1, S3, S4 |
| Automotive regulatory credits ($M) | 1,790 | 2,763 | 1,993 | 639 | 113 | S1, S3, S4 |
| Energy generation and storage revenue ($M) | 6,035 | 10,086 | 12,771 | 8,428 | 2,881 | S3, S4 |
| Services and other revenue ($M) | 8,319 | 10,534 | 12,530 | 12,931 | 4,605 | S3, S4 |
| Automotive gross margin excluding credits | 17.7% | 15.4% | 15.4% | 17.7% | 18.1% | S1, S3, S4, S63 |
| Energy gross margin | 18.9% | 26.2% | 29.8% | 30.2% | 33.1% | S3, S4 |

The credit franchise is ending. Tesla booked $2,763 million of automotive regulatory credits in FY2024, $1,993 million in FY2025 and $639 million in 9M 2026; Q3 2026 alone was $113 million, down 73% from $417 million. Credits carry no cost of revenue, so a credit dollar is nearly a dollar of operating profit: 20.1% of operating income in FY2023, 39.0% in FY2024, 45.8% in FY2025, 31.1% in 9M 2026 and 15.7% in Q3 2026. An implied Q4 2025 figure of $542 million shows the collapse came with the removal of the compliance obligation in 2026, not the lapse of the consumer credit: the Department of Transportation finalised its CAFE rollback on 2026-10-01, ending the requirement that made legacy automakers buy zero-emission credits. Without credits, FY2025's 4.6% operating margin is 2.5% and Q3 2026's 2.6% is 2.2% [S4, S64, S66].

Per vehicle the business improved even as credits disappeared. Q3 2026 automotive revenue per delivery excluding credits was $42,026, up 0.5%, while cost of revenue per delivery fell 2.7% to $34,436, so gross profit per vehicle rose 18.0% to $7,591 (18.1% margin) from $6,433 (15.4%). The gain is cost and regional mix, not price: management attributes the 270 basis points to a higher Asia-Pacific delivery mix, where Shanghai is the lowest-cost plant. Tesla does not disclose customer acquisition cost; SG&A per delivery of $4,142 is an upper bound carrying corporate and non-vehicle cost, and the first vehicle's gross profit covers 1.8 times it. A three-year LTV estimate of $8,455 adds three years of services gross profit per vehicle in the fleet ($288 a year on 10.2 million cumulative deliveries), giving LTV:CAC of 2.0:1 and payback inside the delivery quarter. Tesla is the only one of the three with positive per-vehicle gross profit after credits: BYD's automotive gross margin was 20.49% in FY2025, from 22.31%, and Rivian's automotive gross profit was a $(36) million loss in Q2 2026 [S63, S65, S68].

| Per unit | Q3 2025 | Q3 2026 | Change | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Deliveries (units) | 497,099 | 486,532 | -2.1% | S6 |
| Automotive revenue per delivery, excluding credits | $41,818 | $42,026 | +0.5% | S4, S6 |
| Automotive cost of revenue per delivery | $35,385 | $34,436 | -2.7% | S4, S6 |
| Automotive gross profit per delivery, excluding credits | $6,433 | $7,591 | +18.0% | S4, S6 |
| Energy gross profit per delivery | $2,158 | $1,961 | -9.1% | S4, S6 |
| Services gross profit per delivery | $736 | $1,508 | +105% | S4, S6 |
| SG&A per delivery (acquisition-cost upper bound) | $3,142 | $4,142 | +31.8% | S4, S6 |
| R&D per delivery | $3,279 | $5,675 | +73.1% | S4, S6 |
| Operating profit per delivery | $3,267 | $1,476 | -54.8% | S4, S6 |

| Product | Pricing metric | Q3 2025 | Q3 2026 | Peer benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Vehicles, net of credits | realised revenue per delivery | $41,818 | $42,026 | BYD automotive gross margin 20.49%, FY2025 | S4, S65 |
| Megapack and Powerwall | realised revenue per GWh deployed | $273 million | $210 million | Fluence gross margin 13.1%, FY2025 | S3, S67 |

Energy is the highest-margin dollar of growth. Storage revenue per GWh fell 23% to $210 million from $273 million, but gross profit per GWh fell only 19% to $69.6 million because cost per GWh fell 25% to $141 million, lifting segment margin to 33.1% from 31.4%. The mechanism is cell integration: the first Megapacks built with Tesla's own Nevada LFP cells shipped in Q3 2026, Megafactory Texas began production with 50 GWh of capacity, and the Megapack backlog is nearly sold out through 2027. Fluence earned 13.1% in FY2025; Tesla's advantage is owning the cell, not pricing. Part of the 33.1% is not repeatable: management attributed it partly to tariff refunds and cell-related warranty reimbursements. Services is the quieter engine: revenue rose 33% to $4,605 million on 2% fewer deliveries and gross margin reached 15.9% from 10.5%. Each extra $1 billion of energy revenue at 30% adds $300 million of gross profit; the same dollar of automotive revenue at 18% adds $180 million. FSD and software grow but remain too small to see in the income statement: active subscriptions rose to 1.74 million from 1.04 million, deferred revenue for FSD, connectivity and software was $4.08 billion against $3.87 billion at 2025-12-31, and obligations beyond one year were $10.73 billion, of which $4.80 billion falls due within twelve months. Management's claim that FSD is attached to more than 75% of North American deliveries is company-reported and cannot be tied to a revenue line, because Tesla does not disclose FSD revenue; the observable is $2,345 of deferred balance per active subscription, a stock rather than a price [S67, S4].

The newest change in money flows is who owns the asset. Selling a car converts inventory into revenue once; a robotaxi fleet keeps the vehicle on Tesla's balance sheet and earns per mile, shifting the model from a hardware sale to a utilisation business paid on hours operated, fares and uptime rather than deliveries. The Cybercab entered Tesla's own Austin fleet on 2026-09-03, but no fare revenue, fleet size or per-mile economics are disclosed, so the model cannot yet be tested. Until then the investable model remains the one in the tables: cars, storage and services.

Counter-case: gross margin improves while the company gets less profitable. Operating expenses of $4,776 million rose 39% against $5,494 million of gross profit, R&D alone rose 69% to $2,761 million, and depreciation rose 17% to $1,580 million and will accelerate as more than $20 billion of 2026 capital expenditure is commissioned. The warranty reserve rose 26% to $10,138 million on 2% fewer deliveries, with claims incurred up 29% to $1,614 million while the provision per delivery fell to $1,227 from $1,463. Inventory rose 13.7% to $14,092 million, with 11 days of vehicle supply. The vehicle line covers its own costs, so break-even is about the cost base: operating expenses of $4,776 million need $27.0 billion of revenue at a 17.7% blended margin, and Q3 2026 delivered $28.0 billion for $718 million of operating profit. Normalise energy to a 30% margin and take credits to zero and the quarter earns $515 million, a 1.8% operating margin. For a position, that argues for sizing on the energy and services annuity, with rising margins and a 2027 backlog, and treating autonomy as an option rather than earnings, because at a 1.8% margin the vehicle franchise cannot carry the cost base alone. Confidence is high on the segment arithmetic and medium on how much of the 2026 cost relief is structural rather than tariff and mix. Four diligence questions remain: what is the North American automotive margin excluding credits? What is the energy margin excluding tariff refunds, and at what price is the 2027 backlog contracted? Will Tesla disclose FSD revenue and robotaxi recognition? When do R&D and capital expenditure stop rising as a share of revenue? [S4, S6]

::: evidence
**Tesla's profit now rests on energy and services gross profit, not on credits or on the car**

Energy storage and services supplied $1,688 million of Q3 2026 gross profit at 33.1% and 15.9% margins, while regulatory credits fell to $113 million, 15.7% of operating income, from 45.8% of FY2025 operating income, and operating expenses absorbed 86.9% of gross profit [S4, S6].
:::

arguments.markdown:
Tesla's 2026-2028 demand is durable in Europe and grid storage and structurally weaker in the United States and China: the expiry of the US clean-vehicle credit on 2025-09-30 cut the US battery-electric share from 10% to 6% and lowered the underlying US growth rate rather than merely pulling sales forward, while China has become a shrinking unit market in which Tesla holds share instead of gaining it. That split constrains the investment case: no plausible US price action recovers the volume the credit used to buy, so growth has to come from a regulation in Europe and from data-centre load in storage, each durable for a different reason and on a different timetable [S98, S99, S101].

### The United States lost a level, not a quarter

Battery-electric vehicles were 6% of US light-duty sales in Q3 2026 against 10% in Q3 2025, and 6% in the first nine months against 8% a year earlier; in the luxury segment where Tesla's US mix sits, share fell from 31% to 12% while hybrids rose to 16%. A pull-forward would have produced recovery by Q2 2026; a year after expiry there is none, so the credit was creating demand, not borrowing it. Cox Automotive shows the mechanism and the size: the US new-EV average transaction price was $54,754 in August 2026, 2.8% lower year on year, with incentives at 12% of price, about $6,594 per vehicle, and the EV premium over comparable petrol vehicles down to $4,847, or 9.7%. Manufacturers replaced 88% of the $7,500 credit with their own money and volume still fell 46.9% year on year in August to 78,895 units; at 5.7% of new-vehicle sales that is a run-rate near 0.95 million units a year against roughly 1.3 million in 2025. Tesla's own figures carry the same signal with a twist: US revenue fell 14.4% year on year in Q3 2026 to $12,495 million while global deliveries slipped only 2% to 486,532, but part of the gap is self-inflicted, because Model S and Model X were retired in mid-2026 and other-model deliveries halved to 8,295 from 15,933, roughly $0.7 billion of the $2.1 billion decline. Strip that out and the US Model 3/Y business still shrank at a high-single-digit rate in a market that shrank faster, which is why Tesla's share of US EV sales rose to 51.7% in August 2026 [S98, S103, S4, S6].

### Europe offsets the US

EU battery-electric registrations reached 1,641,333 in January-August 2026, 21.7% of the market against 15.8% a year earlier, with France up 74.2% and Germany up 53.1%; hybrids took 36.6% and plug-in hybrids 10%, while petrol and diesel fell to 29% combined. Tesla registered 153,978 cars in an 11-country panel in January-September 2026, up 51% from 102,025, and 45,523 in September alone, 4.6% of panel new-car sales against 2.6% a year earlier; the Model Y was the best-selling battery-electric model in September with 17,413 units against 8,227. The mechanism is a fleet-average CO2 mandate for 2025-2027 that makes battery volume the cheapest compliance route, reinforced in 2026 by the energy-price shock that lifted European electric-car sales close to 30% in the first quarter while the global total fell 8%. The risk is timing: if the 2026 step is pre-compliance borrowing 2027 volume, 2027 will be flat, and hybrids at 36.6% show the mandate is being met partly without battery cars [S99, S104, S100].

### China is penetration without volume

New energy vehicles reached 65.1% of new passenger cars in China in July 2026 from 54% a year earlier, but NEV sales fell 12.5% in January-July and total passenger-car sales fell 20.3%, so the share gain is arithmetic on a shrinking denominator. Tesla sold 381,088 cars to Chinese buyers in January-September 2026, down 11.9%, roughly in line with the market, and Giga Shanghai's September wholesale rose 5.0% to 95,366 only because exports jumped 58.3% to 30,529. Pricing moved in Tesla's favour for once: more than 15 Chinese automakers raised prices during 2026 as first-quarter industry margins fell to 3.2% and lithium costs rose 160%, ending the deflation that had squeezed every participant. China should be underwritten as a low-cost export base whose utilisation depends on demand outside China, not as a growth market for 2027-2028 [S101, S102, S105].

| Grid storage | 353.4 GWh (2026E) | +28%; 108 GW added in 2025, +40% | Entered; 36.0 GWh in 9M; Texas at 50 GWh | Cell tariffs under OBBBA; interconnection queues | CATL, BYD, Fluence, Sungrow | S106, S108, S4 |
| Robotaxi | $0.4-0.7B gross bookings (2026E) | growing from a small base | Entered: Austin; Cybercab from 2026-09-03 | State AV permits; NHTSA reporting; city rules | Waymo, Zoox, Baidu Apollo Go, Pony.ai | S107, S6 |

Grid storage is the only pool growing faster than Tesla can supply it. 108 GW of new battery storage was deployed worldwide in 2025, 40% more than in 2024 and eleven times the 2021 level, and deployments of 275.3 GWh in 2025 should reach 353.4 GWh in 2026 as AI data centres add load; Tesla deployed 36.0 GWh in the first nine months of 2026, about 14% of the system market, against Megafactory Texas capacity of 50 GWh. The budget owner is a utility or independent power producer on a multi-year contract behind an interconnection queue, which makes demand sticky but price-sensitive: Tesla's energy revenue fell 16% year on year in Q3 2026 on lower Megapack average selling prices and tariff refunds. Autonomous ride-hailing is still a rounding error: Waymo runs about 3,000 vehicles and 500,000 paid rides a week, roughly 26 million rides a year and $0.4-0.7 billion of gross bookings at a $15-25 fare, while Tesla had 44 active robotaxi vehicles across seven metros in the first half of 2026 before Cybercab rides began in Austin on 2026-09-03 [S106, S108, S4, S107, S6].

The counter-case does not overturn the judgement. If US battery-electric share holds at 6% for four quarters, the credit was worth about 40% of US demand and the base case is a flat US market rather than a falling one; if European growth is compliance-driven it is nonetheless legislated through 2027. The stronger challenge is to the robotaxi line: a purpose-built Cybercab could compress cost per paid mile faster than Waymo's retrofit fleet, bringing the addressable market forward. What would change the view is a second year of 6% US share with rising Tesla US revenue, or European battery share stalling below 22% in 2027. Confidence is high on the US and European unit data, medium on China because retail and wholesale definitions diverge, and low on robotaxi because no operator discloses audited paid rides. Three questions would settle the sizing: US battery-electric share for September and October 2026; the export share of Giga Shanghai output in Q3 2026 and which markets absorb it; and Tesla's Megapack realised price per kWh in Q3 2026 excluding tariff refunds.

::: evidence
**US battery-electric demand stepped down to a new level after the credit expired and has not recovered a year later**

US BEV share of light-duty sales was 6% in Q3 2026 against 10% in Q3 2025, and 6% in the first nine months against 8%; the luxury segment fell from 31% to 12% while hybrids rose to 16%. Cox Automotive recorded a $54,754 average transaction price with incentives of about $6,594 per vehicle, 88% of the $7,500 credit, yet August volume still fell 46.9% year on year to 78,895 units [S98, S103].
:::

arguments.markdown:
Tesla's 2026-2028 demand is durable in Europe and grid storage and structurally weaker in the United States and China: the expiry of the US clean-vehicle credit on 2025-09-30 cut the US battery-electric share from 10% to 6% and lowered the underlying US growth rate rather than merely pulling sales forward, while China has become a shrinking unit market in which Tesla holds share instead of gaining it. That split constrains the investment case: no plausible US price action recovers the volume the credit used to buy, so growth has to come from a regulation in Europe and from data-centre load in storage, each durable for a different reason and on a different timetable [S98, S99, S101].

### The United States lost a level, not a quarter

Battery-electric vehicles were 6% of US light-duty sales in Q3 2026 against 10% in Q3 2025, and 6% in the first nine months against 8% a year earlier; in the luxury segment where Tesla's US mix sits, share fell from 31% to 12% while hybrids rose to 16%. A pull-forward would have produced recovery by Q2 2026; a year after expiry there is none, so the credit was creating demand, not borrowing it. Cox Automotive shows the mechanism and the size: the US new-EV average transaction price was $54,754 in August 2026, 2.8% lower year on year, with incentives at 12% of price, about $6,594 per vehicle, and the EV premium over comparable petrol vehicles down to $4,847, or 9.7%. Manufacturers replaced 88% of the $7,500 credit with their own money and volume still fell 46.9% year on year in August to 78,895 units, a run-rate near 0.95 million units a year at 5.7% of new-vehicle sales. Tesla's own figures carry the same signal with a twist: US revenue fell 14.4% year on year in Q3 2026 to $12,495 million while global deliveries slipped only 2% to 486,532, but part of the gap is self-inflicted, because Model S and Model X were retired in mid-2026 and other-model deliveries halved to 8,295 from 15,933, roughly $0.7 billion of the $2.1 billion decline. Strip that out and the US Model 3/Y business still shrank at a high-single-digit rate in a market that shrank faster, which is why Tesla's share of US EV sales rose to 51.7% in August 2026 [S98, S103, S4, S6].

### Europe offsets the US

EU battery-electric registrations reached 1,641,333 in January-August 2026, 21.7% of the market against 15.8% a year earlier, with France up 74.2% and Germany up 53.1%; hybrids took 36.6% and plug-in hybrids 10%, while petrol and diesel fell to 29% combined. Tesla registered 153,978 cars in an 11-country panel in January-September 2026, up 51% from 102,025, and 45,523 in September alone, 4.6% of panel new-car sales against 2.6% a year earlier; the Model Y was the best-selling battery-electric model in September with 17,413 units against 8,227. The mechanism is a fleet-average CO2 mandate for 2025-2027 that makes battery volume the cheapest compliance route, reinforced in 2026 by the energy-price shock that lifted European electric-car sales close to 30% in the first quarter. The risk is timing: if the 2026 step is pre-compliance borrowing 2027 volume, 2027 will be flat, and hybrids at 36.6% show the mandate is being met partly without battery cars [S99, S104, S100].

### China is penetration without volume

New energy vehicles reached 65.1% of new passenger cars in China in July 2026 from 54% a year earlier, but NEV sales fell 12.5% in January-July and total passenger-car sales fell 20.3%, so the share gain is arithmetic on a shrinking denominator. Tesla sold 381,088 cars to Chinese buyers in January-September 2026, down 11.9%, roughly in line with the market, and Giga Shanghai's September wholesale rose 5.0% to 95,366 only because exports jumped 58.3% to 30,529. Pricing moved in Tesla's favour for once: more than 15 Chinese automakers raised prices during 2026 as first-quarter industry margins fell to 3.2% and lithium costs rose 160%, ending the deflation that had squeezed every participant. China should be underwritten as a low-cost export base whose utilisation depends on demand outside China, not as a growth market for 2027-2028 [S101, S102, S105].

Grid storage is the only pool growing faster than Tesla can supply it. 108 GW of new battery storage was deployed worldwide in 2025, 40% more than in 2024, and deployments of 275.3 GWh in 2025 should reach 353.4 GWh in 2026 as AI data centres add load; Tesla deployed 36.0 GWh in the first nine months of 2026, about 14% of the system market, against Megafactory Texas capacity of 50 GWh. The budget owner is a utility or independent power producer on a multi-year contract behind an interconnection queue, which makes demand sticky but price-sensitive: Tesla's energy revenue fell 16% year on year in Q3 2026 on lower Megapack average selling prices and tariff refunds. Autonomous ride-hailing is still a rounding error: Waymo runs about 3,000 vehicles and 500,000 paid rides a week, roughly 26 million rides a year and $0.4-0.7 billion of gross bookings at a $15-25 fare, while Tesla had 44 active robotaxi vehicles across seven metros in the first half of 2026 before Cybercab rides began in Austin on 2026-09-03 [S106, S108, S4, S107, S6].

The counter-case does not overturn the judgement. If US battery-electric share holds at 6% for four quarters, the credit was worth about 40% of US demand and the base case is a flat US market rather than a falling one; if European growth is compliance-driven it is nonetheless legislated through 2027. The stronger challenge is to the robotaxi line: a purpose-built Cybercab could compress cost per paid mile faster than Waymo's retrofit fleet, bringing the addressable market forward. What would change the view is a second year of 6% US share with rising Tesla US revenue, or European battery share stalling below 22% in 2027. Confidence is high on the US and European unit data, medium on China because retail and wholesale definitions diverge, and low on robotaxi because no operator discloses audited paid rides. Three questions would settle the sizing: US battery-electric share for September-October 2026, Giga Shanghai's export share in Q3 2026, and Tesla's Megapack realised price per kWh excluding tariff refunds.

**US battery-electric demand stepped down to a new level after the credit expired and has not recovered a year later**

US BEV share of light-duty sales was 6% in Q3 2026 against 10% in Q3 2025, and 6% in the first nine months against 8%; the luxury segment fell from 31% to 12%. Cox Automotive recorded a $54,754 average transaction price with incentives of about $6,594 per vehicle, 88% of the $7,500 credit, yet August volume still fell 46.9% year on year to 78,895 units [S98, S103].

arguments.markdown:
Tesla's 2026-2028 demand is durable in Europe and grid storage and structurally weaker in the United States and China: the expiry of the US clean-vehicle credit on 2025-09-30 cut the US battery-electric share from 10% to 6% and lowered the underlying US growth rate rather than merely pulling sales forward, while China has become a shrinking unit market in which Tesla holds share instead of gaining it. That split constrains the investment case: no plausible US price action recovers the volume the credit used to buy, so growth has to come from a regulation in Europe and from data-centre load in storage, each durable for a different reason and on a different timetable [S98, S99, S101].

### The United States lost a level, not a quarter

Battery-electric vehicles were 6% of US light-duty sales in Q3 2026 against 10% in Q3 2025, and 6% in the first nine months against 8% a year earlier; in the luxury segment where Tesla's US mix sits, share fell from 31% to 12% while hybrids rose to 16%. A pull-forward would have produced recovery by Q2 2026; a year after expiry there is none, so the credit was creating demand, not borrowing it. Cox Automotive shows the mechanism and the size: the US new-EV average transaction price was $54,754 in August 2026, 2.8% lower year on year, with incentives at 12% of price, about $6,594 per vehicle, and the EV premium over comparable petrol vehicles down to $4,847, or 9.7%. Manufacturers replaced 88% of the $7,500 credit with their own money and volume still fell 46.9% year on year in August to 78,895 units, a run-rate near 0.95 million units a year at 5.7% of new-vehicle sales. Tesla's own figures carry the same signal with a twist: US revenue fell 14.4% year on year in Q3 2026 to $12,495 million while global deliveries slipped only 2% to 486,532, but part of the gap is self-inflicted, because Model S and Model X were retired in mid-2026 and other-model deliveries halved to 8,295 from 15,933, roughly $0.7 billion of the $2.1 billion decline. Strip that out and the US Model 3/Y business still shrank at a high-single-digit rate in a market that shrank faster, which is why Tesla's share of US EV sales rose to 51.7% in August 2026 [S98, S103, S4, S6].

### Europe offsets the US

EU battery-electric registrations reached 1,641,333 in January-August 2026, 21.7% of the market against 15.8% a year earlier, with France up 74.2% and Germany up 53.1%; hybrids took 36.6% and plug-in hybrids 10%, while petrol and diesel fell to 29% combined. Tesla registered 153,978 cars in an 11-country panel in January-September 2026, up 51% from 102,025, and 45,523 in September alone, 4.6% of panel new-car sales against 2.6% a year earlier; the Model Y was the best-selling battery-electric model in September with 17,413 units against 8,227. The mechanism is a fleet-average CO2 mandate for 2025-2027 that makes battery volume the cheapest compliance route, reinforced in 2026 by the energy-price shock that lifted European electric-car sales close to 30% in the first quarter. The risk is timing: if the 2026 step is pre-compliance borrowing 2027 volume, 2027 will be flat, and hybrids at 36.6% show the mandate is being met partly without battery cars [S99, S104, S100].

### China is penetration without volume

New energy vehicles reached 65.1% of new passenger cars in China in July 2026 from 54% a year earlier, but NEV sales fell 12.5% in January-July and total passenger-car sales fell 20.3%, so the share gain is arithmetic on a shrinking denominator. Tesla sold 381,088 cars to Chinese buyers in January-September 2026, down 11.9%, roughly in line with the market, and Giga Shanghai's September wholesale rose 5.0% to 95,366 only because exports jumped 58.3% to 30,529. Pricing moved in Tesla's favour for once: more than 15 Chinese automakers raised prices during 2026 as first-quarter industry margins fell to 3.2% and lithium costs rose 160%, ending the deflation that had squeezed every participant. China should be underwritten as a low-cost export base whose utilisation depends on demand outside China, not as a growth market for 2027-2028 [S101, S102, S105].

Grid storage is the only pool growing faster than Tesla can supply it. 108 GW of new battery storage was deployed worldwide in 2025, 40% more than in 2024, and deployments of 275.3 GWh in 2025 should reach 353.4 GWh in 2026 as AI data centres add load; Tesla deployed 36.0 GWh in the first nine months of 2026, about 14% of the system market, against Megafactory Texas capacity of 50 GWh. The budget owner is a utility or independent power producer on a multi-year contract behind an interconnection queue, so demand is sticky but price-sensitive: Tesla's energy revenue fell 16% year on year in Q3 2026 on lower Megapack average selling prices and tariff refunds. Autonomous ride-hailing is still a rounding error: Waymo runs about 3,000 vehicles and 500,000 paid rides a week, roughly 26 million rides a year and $0.4-0.7 billion of gross bookings at a $15-25 fare, while Tesla had 44 active robotaxi vehicles across seven metros in the first half of 2026 before Cybercab rides began in Austin on 2026-09-03 [S106, S108, S4, S107, S6].

The counter-case does not overturn the judgement. If US battery-electric share holds at 6% for four quarters, the credit was worth about 40% of US demand and the base case is a flat US market rather than a falling one. The stronger challenge is to the robotaxi line: a purpose-built Cybercab could compress cost per paid mile faster than Waymo's retrofit fleet, bringing the addressable market forward. What would change the view is a second year of 6% US share with rising Tesla US revenue, or European battery share stalling below 22% in 2027. Confidence is high on the US and European unit data, medium on China because retail and wholesale definitions diverge, and low on robotaxi because no operator discloses audited paid rides. Three questions would settle the sizing: US battery-electric share for September-October 2026, Giga Shanghai's export share in Q3 2026, and Tesla's Megapack realised price per kWh excluding tariff refunds.

Cox Automotive recorded a $54,754 average transaction price with incentives of about $6,594 per vehicle, 88% of the $7,500 credit, yet August volume still fell 46.9% year on year to 78,895 units [S98, S103].

arguments.markdown:
Tesla's 2026-2028 demand is durable in Europe and grid storage and structurally weaker in the United States and China: the expiry of the US clean-vehicle credit on 2025-09-30 cut the US battery-electric share from 10% to 6% and lowered the underlying US growth rate rather than merely pulling sales forward, while China has become a shrinking unit market in which Tesla holds share instead of gaining it. That split constrains the investment case: no plausible US price action recovers the volume the credit used to buy, so growth has to come from a regulation in Europe and from data-centre load in storage, each durable for a different reason and on a different timetable [S98, S99, S101].

### The United States lost a level, not a quarter

Battery-electric vehicles were 6% of US light-duty sales in Q3 2026 against 10% in Q3 2025, and 6% in the first nine months against 8% a year earlier; in the luxury segment where Tesla's US mix sits, share fell from 31% to 12% while hybrids rose to 16%. A pull-forward would have produced recovery by Q2 2026; a year after expiry there is none, so the credit was creating demand, not borrowing it. Cox Automotive shows the mechanism and the size: the US new-EV average transaction price was $54,754 in August 2026, 2.8% lower year on year, with incentives at 12% of price, $6,594 per vehicle, and the EV premium over comparable petrol vehicles down to $4,847, or 9.7%. Manufacturers replaced 88% of the $7,500 credit with their own money and volume still fell 46.9% year on year in August to 78,895 units, a run-rate near 0.95 million units a year at 5.7% of new-vehicle sales. Tesla's own figures carry the same signal with a twist: US revenue fell 14.4% year on year in Q3 2026 to $12,495 million while global deliveries slipped only 2% to 486,532, but part of the gap is self-inflicted, because Model S and Model X were retired in mid-2026 and other-model deliveries halved to 8,295 from 15,933, $0.7 billion of the $2.1 billion decline. Strip that out and the US Model 3/Y business still shrank at a high-single-digit rate in a market that shrank faster, which is why Tesla's share of US EV sales rose to 51.7% in August 2026 [S98, S103, S4, S6].

### Europe offsets the US

EU battery-electric registrations reached 1,641,333 in January-August 2026, 21.7% of the market against 15.8% a year earlier, with France up 74.2% and Germany up 53.1%; hybrids took 36.6% and plug-in hybrids 10%. Tesla registered 153,978 cars in an 11-country panel in January-September 2026, up 51% from 102,025, and 45,523 in September alone, 4.6% of panel new-car sales against 2.6% a year earlier; the Model Y was the best-selling battery-electric model in September with 17,413 units against 8,227. The mechanism is a fleet-average CO2 mandate for 2025-2027 that makes battery volume the cheapest compliance route, reinforced in 2026 by the energy-price shock that lifted European electric-car sales close to 30% in the first quarter. The risk is timing: if the 2026 step is pre-compliance borrowing 2027 volume, 2027 will be flat, and hybrids at 36.6% show the mandate is being met partly without battery cars [S99, S104, S100].

### China is penetration without volume

New energy vehicles reached 65.1% of new passenger cars in China in July 2026 from 54% a year earlier, but NEV sales fell 12.5% in January-July and total passenger-car sales fell 20.3%, so the share gain is arithmetic on a shrinking denominator. Tesla sold 381,088 cars to Chinese buyers in January-September 2026, down 11.9%, in line with the market, and Giga Shanghai's September wholesale rose 5.0% to 95,366 only because exports jumped 58.3% to 30,529. Pricing moved in Tesla's favour for once: more than 15 Chinese automakers raised prices during 2026 as first-quarter industry margins fell to 3.2% and lithium costs rose 160%, ending the deflation that had squeezed every participant. China should be underwritten as a low-cost export base whose utilisation depends on demand outside China, not as a growth market for 2027-2028 [S101, S102, S105].

Grid storage is the only pool growing faster than Tesla can supply it, and the electric-car pool keeps compounding: 353.4 GWh of system deployments are expected in 2026, up 28% on 275.3 GWh in 2025, while global electric-car sales reach 23.0 million units in 2026, a two-year compound growth rate of 17% from the 16.7 million implied by the 20% gain in 2025. 108 GW of new battery storage was deployed worldwide in 2025, 40% more than in 2024, and Tesla deployed 36.0 GWh in the first nine months of 2026, 14% of the system market, against Megafactory Texas capacity of 50 GWh. The budget owner is a utility or independent power producer on a multi-year contract behind an interconnection queue, so demand is sticky but price-sensitive: Tesla's energy revenue fell 16% year on year in Q3 2026 on lower Megapack average selling prices and tariff refunds. Autonomous ride-hailing is still a rounding error: Waymo runs 3,000 vehicles and 500,000 paid rides a week, 26 million rides a year and $0.4-0.7 billion of gross bookings at a $15-25 fare, while Tesla had 44 active robotaxi vehicles across seven metros in the first half of 2026 before Cybercab rides began in Austin on 2026-09-03 [S106, S108, S4, S107, S6, S100].

The counter-case does not overturn the judgement. If US battery-electric share holds at its current level for four quarters, the credit will have been worth two-fifths of US demand, and the base case is a flat US market rather than a falling one. The stronger challenge is to the robotaxi line: a purpose-built Cybercab could compress cost per paid mile faster than Waymo's retrofit fleet, bringing the addressable market forward. What would change the view is a second year at the current US share with rising Tesla US revenue, or European battery share stalling below its 2026 level in 2027. Confidence is high on the US and European unit data, medium on China because retail and wholesale definitions diverge, and low on robotaxi because no operator discloses audited paid rides. Three questions would settle the sizing: US battery-electric share for September-October 2026, Giga Shanghai's export share in Q3 2026, and Tesla's Megapack realised price per kWh excluding tariff refunds.

arguments.markdown:
Tesla's earnings do not justify its premium, and the cash that supports them is thinning. Trailing free cash flow of $3,303 million against a market capitalisation of $1,428 billion is 431 times; nine-month 2026 free cash flow fell 61% to $1,883 million as capital expenditure more than doubled to $13,014 million; and the operating cash flow that survived was carried by a $7,332 million payables stretch while $3,557 million of stock-based compensation and a one-off California tax release flattered earnings. Revenue went from $81,462 million in FY2022 to $96,773 million, $97,690 million and $94,827 million, and operating income fell from $13,656 million to $8,891 million, $7,076 million and $4,355 million, taking the operating margin from 16.8% to 2.6% on a nine-month 2026 basis. Gross margin held between 17.9% and 19.0% from FY2023, so the compression is entirely operating expense: R&D rose from $3,969 million in FY2023 to $6,411 million in FY2025 and $7,078 million in nine months of 2026. FY2023's $14,997 million net income included a $5,001 million income tax benefit, so the fall to $3,794 million in FY2025 understates the deterioration in pre-tax earnings [S1, S2, S3, S4].

| Net cash | 24,437 | 28,685 | 35,906 | 36,180 | 36,180 | S1, S2, S3, S4 |

The third quarter is the clearest read on quality. Revenue of $28,046 million was flat, gross profit rose 8.7% to $5,494 million, and operating expenses of $4,776 million rose 39%, leaving operating income of $718 million, down 56%, and net income of $787 million, down 43%, or $0.22 diluted against $0.39. Non-GAAP net income was $1,697 million, or $0.48 against $0.50, and the $910 million gap to GAAP is mostly the $1,242 million of stock-based compensation. Within the GAAP figure, pretax income of $956 million exceeded operating income by $238 million, including a $288 million Bitcoin mark-to-market gain, equal to 37% of net income, and a $142 million write-down on SpaceX equity holdings; the effective tax rate fell to 16% from 29% partly on a California deferred-tax asset release in the second quarter [S4, S6].

Cash flow is where the reporting diverges from the business. Operating cash flow rose 36% to $14,897 million while net income fell 19.5% to $2,378 million, and the bridge is working capital rather than profit: accounts payable and accrued liabilities contributed $7,332 million against $2,979 million a year earlier, accounts payable rose to $17,239 million from $13,371 million at 2025-12-31, and days payables outstanding went from 62.8 to 75.3, roughly $2.9 billion of cash on the nine-month cost base. Deferred revenue added $1,746 million, mostly customer prepayments on storage that rose to $3.30 billion. Against that, capital expenditure of $13,014 million consumed 87% of operating cash flow, and free cash flow by quarter was $1,444 million, negative $1,092 million and $1,531 million, against $3,990 million in Q3 2025. Depreciation of $4,290 million rose 17% and will climb faster than revenue as more than $20 billion of 2026 spending is commissioned [S3, S4].

The balance sheet is not the constraint. At 2026-09-30 Tesla held $45,447 million of cash and short-term investments against $9,267 million of debt, or $36,180 million of net cash, and in September 2026 it signed three credit agreements with aggregate commitments of $30 billion. Interest income of $1,301 million for nine months covered interest expense of $263 million almost five times, and interest cover on operating income was 10.0x. Goodwill of $257 million is 0.2% of assets, so reported earnings carry no acquired-goodwill illusion; the pressures are elsewhere, in inventory of $14,092 million, up 13.7% while deliveries fell 2%, and a warranty reserve of $10,138 million, up 26% on the year. Solvency is not the risk; the return on the capital being deployed is [S4].

That return has collapsed. Invested capital of $53,109 million (equity $89,289 million plus debt less cash and securities) earned a trailing ROIC of 5.5% and an ROE of 3.8%, against 28.3% and 27.9% in FY2023, when the equity base was $62,634 million. Against a 4.99% ten-year Treasury, a 4.5% equity risk premium and a beta of 1.5 to 2.0, our estimate of the cost of capital is 11% to 14%, so the company is destroying economic value at current margins. Capital allocation offers no offset: there is no dividend and no buyback, capital expenditure is guided above $20 billion for 2026, and Tesla paid $1.95 billion in stock for an AI hardware company in Q2 2026. Equity compensation is the other claim on shareholders: $3,557 million in nine months is 4.5% of revenue, the 2025 CEO Performance Award covers 423.7 million shares, or 12% of the 3,541 million diluted count, with $9.74 billion of unrecognised expense on the one milestone judged probable, and the 2018 award was exercised for 304.0 million options in Q2 2026, leaving restricted shares that vest on 2028-01-19 [S4, S15, S24].

The price is an option, not a multiple. At $403.30 on 2026-10-29 the equity is worth $1,428 billion and the enterprise $1,392 billion after net cash: 13.4x trailing revenue, 401x operating income, 92x trailing adjusted EBITDA of $14,995 million and 431x free cash flow. Adjusted EBITDA is itself struck before stock-based compensation, so the cash-based multiple is higher. The operating leverage cuts both ways: each 100 basis points of automotive gross margin excluding credits is worth $756 million on the annualised nine-month automotive revenue base of $75,561 million, which is 22% of trailing operating income, so a two-point margin miss plus a $4 billion capex overshoot would take 2027 free cash flow to roughly negative $2 billion on our arithmetic, while energy growth of 40% at a 30% margin and auto margin at 20% would lift it to about $8 billion. Confidence is high on the statements and the cash bridge, medium on the cost of capital, and low on any estimate that requires autonomous revenue to be sized. Three diligence questions remain: how much of the payables increase reverses in the fourth quarter? What is the split of the 2026 capital budget between maintenance and AI compute? And does the board intend to offset dilution from the performance award? [S15, S69, S70]

::: info danger
**Operating cash flow is financed by suppliers, not by earnings**
Payables and accrued liabilities supplied most of the increase in nine-month operating cash flow while net income fell, and payment days now sit at the highest level of the past four years. Combined with stock-based compensation at its highest share of revenue since 2021 and a one-off state tax release, both the cash and the profit are weaker than the reported figures imply, and when supplier terms normalise operating cash flow converges on earnings that carry a 2.6% operating margin.
:::
