arguments.markdown:
Tesla is gaining share in the markets that are shrinking and holding share in the one that is growing, so its vehicle advantage is compressing into a cost-and-brand moat rather than a technology lead, while in storage it is a scale follower to CATL and BYD and in paid autonomy it trails Waymo by more than an order of magnitude. The proof is in the three numbers together: a 51.7% share of US EV sales in August 2026, European registrations up 51% to 153,978 in January-September 2026, and Chinese retail sales down 11.9% to 381,088 against a market down 12.5%, so share improves while the absolute business outside Europe shrinks [S103, S104, S102].

### In the United States, Tesla wins by attrition

Tesla sold 40,816 EVs in August 2026 for 51.7% of US EV sales, up 3.4 points from July, in a market that fell 46.9% year on year to 78,895 units. The gains behind it were real but small: Toyota 4,964 units (+34.9% month on month), Chevrolet +30.3% and Cadillac +13.1%. Weaker EV programmes retreated after the credit expired and the survivor with the widest line and lowest cost took the share without cutting price. Rivian is the exception that could change the arithmetic: deliveries of its new mid-size SUV began in the second quarter of 2026 from a Normal, Illinois plant with 215,000 units of annual capacity [S103, S96].

### Europe is a battery-electric contest; China is a price contest

In an 11-country European panel Tesla registered 45,523 cars in September 2026 against BYD's 39,583, and on battery-electric only it led 30,317 to 7,498 in every one of those countries, while Chinese brands as a group took 14.9% of new cars against 8.0% a year earlier. BYD's route into Europe is powertrain breadth and price, not a better battery car, which makes it the most dangerous competitor over five years: it builds volume in the segments below Model Y and can move up. In China the contest is worse for Tesla: its Model Y sold more than 180,000 units from February to July 2026 at RMB 263,500-313,500 while Geely's Xingyuan sold nearly 197,500 at just under RMB 100,000 (~$14,820), and Tesla's domestic retail fell 11.9% while Shanghai's wholesale held only because exports rose 58.3% in September [S104, S101, S102].

### Pricing power is real in the premium band and absent below it

Cost of automotive sales was $16,570 million in Q3 2026 for 486,532 deliveries, $34,060 per vehicle, against automotive sales revenue of $41,300 per unit (up from $40,955) and automotive gross margin of 18.5%, up from 17.0%. That is a healthy margin at a premium price point, and it sits 2.3 times the retail price of China's volume bestseller, the cleanest measure of how far Tesla's cost base is from the low end. The margin is protected by mix and software rather than price: FSD (Supervised) subscriptions reached 1.74 million, services and other revenue rose 33% to $4,605 million, and energy gross margin reached 33.1%. A price war in the $25,000-35,000 band would be fought on a cost base Tesla cannot currently match [S4, S6, S101].

| Geely | Xingyuan, Galaxy | BEV and PHEV | China MIIT; EU tariff on China-built units | Nearly 197,500 Xingyuan units February-July 2026 at just under RMB 100,000 | Best-selling model in China | Price point a third of Model Y; mass-segment volume | Thin autonomy and software stack | S101 |
| Xiaomi | SU7, YU7 | BEV, consumer-electronics software | China MIIT | Model Y outsold SU7 and Li Auto's i6 in the February-July 2026 top ten | Not disclosed | Brand pull with Chinese tech buyers; phone-channel distribution | Capacity ramp unproven; China-only | S101 |
| GM | Chevrolet, Cadillac EVs | Ultium BEV | US FMVSS; no federal credit since 2025-09-30 | Chevrolet +30.3% and Cadillac +13.1% month on month in August 2026 | Below Tesla's 51.7% | Dealer network; truck and SUV franchises | Smaller EV volume; margin dilution | S103 |
| Hyundai-Kia | Ioniq, EV6, EV9 | 800V BEV | US FMVSS; EU type approval | Hyundai fourth in US EV sales in August 2026; Kia +12% month on month | Below Tesla's 51.7% | 800V charging speed; warranty; cost control | Weaker software and charging network | S103 |
| Rivian | Mid-size SUV and pickup | BEV, zonal architecture | US FMVSS; deliveries from Q2 2026 | 215,000 units of Normal capacity; Autonomy+ charging since April 2026 | Below Tesla's 51.7% | Purpose-built brand; entry price below Model X | Unprofitable at current utilisation; no energy business | S96 |

### Storage and autonomy are where the advantage is thinnest

In grid storage the pricing power sits with the cell makers: CATL shipped 125.0 GWh of energy-storage batteries in the first half of 2026, up 81%, for 27.1% of the global ESS battery market, while Tesla deployed 36.0 GWh in nine months and its energy revenue fell 16% year on year in Q3 2026 on lower Megapack average selling prices and tariff refunds. Tesla's differentiation is integration, grid-forming software and delivery speed rather than cell cost. In autonomy the gap is scale: Waymo runs 3,000 vehicles and 500,000 paid rides a week across 10 US cities, Baidu's Apollo Go operates in more than 10 Chinese cities, and Tesla had 44 active robotaxi vehicles across seven metros in the first half of 2026 before Cybercab rides began in Austin on 2026-09-03 [S81, S4, S107, S6].

| Grid battery storage | Tesla challenges | CATL: 27.1% of ESS cells | Tesla: 36.0 GWh in 9M 2026 | Fluence and Sungrow | Chinese LFP integrators | S81, S4 |
| Robotaxi | Tesla emerges | Waymo: 500,000 paid rides a week | Baidu Apollo Go: more than 10 cities | Zoox and Pony.ai | Tesla Cybercab | S107, S6 |

The counter-case is that Tesla is converting rather than losing advantage: its US and European share gains came while rivals retreated, automotive gross margin rose year on year, and the Chinese price war ended with more than a dozen automakers raising prices, removing the deflation that hurt it most. That reading is partly right and does not change the conclusion, because the share gains are in shrinking pools and the margin gain is mix-driven rather than price-driven. Confidence is high on the US and European share data, medium on the China comparison because retail and wholesale definitions differ, and low on the autonomy comparison because no operator discloses audited paid rides. Two diligence questions follow: what is Tesla's share of US EV sales in the fourth quarter of 2026 once Toyota's bZ and Chevrolet's Bolt ramp, and how much of BYD's European volume is plug-in hybrid under the 2027 CO2 review?

arguments.markdown:
Tesla's 2026-2028 demand is durable in Europe and grid storage and structurally weaker in the United States and China: the expiry of the US clean-vehicle credit on 2025-09-30 cut the US battery-electric share from 10% to 6% and lowered the underlying US growth rate rather than merely pulling sales forward, while China has become a shrinking unit market in which Tesla holds share instead of gaining it. That split constrains the investment case: no plausible US price action recovers the volume the credit used to buy, so growth has to come from a regulation in Europe and from data-centre load in storage, each durable for a different reason and on a different timetable [S98, S99, S101].

### The United States lost a level, not a quarter

Battery-electric vehicles were 6% of US light-duty sales in Q3 2026 against 10% in Q3 2025, and 6% in the first nine months against 8% a year earlier; in the luxury segment where Tesla's US mix sits, share fell from 31% to 12% while hybrids rose to 16%. A pull-forward would have produced recovery by Q2 2026; a year after expiry there is none, so the credit was creating demand, not borrowing it. Cox Automotive shows the mechanism and the size: the US new-EV average transaction price was $54,754 in August 2026, 2.8% lower year on year, with incentives at 12% of price, $6,594 per vehicle, and the EV premium over comparable petrol vehicles down to $4,847, or 9.7%. Manufacturers replaced 88% of the $7,500 credit with their own money and volume still fell 46.9% year on year in August to 78,895 units, a run-rate near 0.95 million units a year at 5.7% of new-vehicle sales. Tesla's own figures carry the same signal with a twist: US revenue fell 14.4% year on year in Q3 2026 to $12,495 million while global deliveries slipped only 2% to 486,532, but part of the gap is self-inflicted, because Model S and Model X were retired in mid-2026 and other-model deliveries halved to 8,295 from 15,933, $0.7 billion of the $2.1 billion decline. Strip that out and the US Model 3/Y business still shrank at a high-single-digit rate in a market that shrank faster, which is why Tesla's share of US EV sales rose to 51.7% in August 2026 [S98, S103, S4, S6].

### Europe offsets the US

EU battery-electric registrations reached 1,641,333 in January-August 2026, 21.7% of the market against 15.8% a year earlier, with France up 74.2% and Germany up 53.1%; hybrids took 36.6% and plug-in hybrids 10%. Tesla registered 153,978 cars in an 11-country panel in January-September 2026, up 51% from 102,025, and 45,523 in September alone, 4.6% of panel new-car sales against 2.6% a year earlier; the Model Y was the best-selling battery-electric model in September with 17,413 units against 8,227. The mechanism is a fleet-average CO2 mandate for 2025-2027 that makes battery volume the cheapest compliance route, reinforced in 2026 by the energy-price shock that lifted European electric-car sales close to 30% in the first quarter. The risk is timing: if the 2026 step is pre-compliance borrowing 2027 volume, 2027 will be flat, and hybrids at 36.6% show the mandate is being met partly without battery cars [S99, S104, S100].

### China is penetration without volume

New energy vehicles reached 65.1% of new passenger cars in China in July 2026 from 54% a year earlier, but NEV sales fell 12.5% in January-July and total passenger-car sales fell 20.3%, so the share gain is arithmetic on a shrinking denominator. Tesla sold 381,088 cars to Chinese buyers in January-September 2026, down 11.9%, in line with the market, and Giga Shanghai's September wholesale rose 5.0% to 95,366 only because exports jumped 58.3% to 30,529. Pricing moved in Tesla's favour for once: more than 15 Chinese automakers raised prices during 2026 as first-quarter industry margins fell to 3.2% and lithium costs rose 160%, ending the deflation that had squeezed every participant. China should be underwritten as a low-cost export base whose utilisation depends on demand outside China, not as a growth market for 2027-2028 [S101, S102, S105].

| Robotaxi | $0.4-0.7B gross bookings (2026E) | growing from a small base | Entered: Austin; Cybercab from 2026-09-03 | State AV permits; city rules | Waymo, Zoox, Baidu Apollo Go, Pony.ai | S107, S6 |

Grid storage is the only pool growing faster than Tesla can supply it. 353.4 GWh of system deployments are expected in 2026, up 28% on 275.3 GWh in 2025, which at Tesla's realised $234 per kWh of energy revenue implies an $83 billion system market; global electric-car sales reach 23.0 million units in 2026, worth $950 billion at Tesla's realised $41,300 per unit, a 2024-2026 CAGR of 17% from the 16.7 million implied by the 20% gain in 2025. 108 GW of new battery storage was deployed worldwide in 2025, 40% more than in 2024, and Tesla deployed 36.0 GWh in the first nine months of 2026, 14% of the system market, against Megafactory Texas capacity of 50 GWh. The budget owner is a utility or independent power producer on a multi-year contract behind an interconnection queue, so demand is sticky but price-sensitive: Tesla's energy revenue fell 16% year on year in Q3 2026 on lower Megapack average selling prices and tariff refunds. Autonomous ride-hailing is still a rounding error: Waymo runs 3,000 vehicles and 500,000 paid rides a week, 26 million rides a year and $0.4-0.7 billion of gross bookings at a $15-25 fare, while Tesla had 44 active robotaxi vehicles across seven metros in the first half of 2026 before Cybercab rides began in Austin on 2026-09-03 [S106, S108, S4, S107, S6, S100].

The counter-case does not overturn the judgement: if US battery-electric share holds at its current level for four quarters, the credit will have been worth two-fifths of US demand, and a purpose-built Cybercab could compress cost per paid mile faster than Waymo's retrofit fleet, bringing the robotaxi market forward. Confidence is high on the US and European unit data, medium on China because retail and wholesale definitions diverge, and low on robotaxi because no operator discloses audited paid rides. Three open diligence questions remain: what did US battery-electric share print in September-October 2026? What share of Giga Shanghai output was exported in Q3 2026? What was Tesla's Megapack realised price per kWh excluding tariff refunds?

::: evidence
**US battery-electric demand stepped down to a new level after the credit expired and has not recovered a year later**

US BEV share of light-duty sales was 6% in Q3 2026 against 10% in Q3 2025, and 6% in the first nine months against 8%; the luxury segment fell from 31% to 12%. Cox Automotive recorded a $54,754 average transaction price with incentives of $6,594 per vehicle, 88% of the $7,500 credit, yet August volume still fell 46.9% year on year to 78,895 units [S98, S103].
:::

rows.mechanism: Removing a $7,500 point-of-sale credit raises the effective transaction price of every US Tesla by roughly 10-15%, so volume must be defended with price cuts, subsidised financing or mix, compressing automotive gross margin.
rows.benchmark: Credit-supported 2024-2025 US BEV demand versus the post-2025-09-30 run-rate reported by EIA on 2026-10-19.
rows.weakens: Tesla's US buyer base skews affluent and lease-heavy, and some demand was pulled forward rather than destroyed; the credit loss is industry-wide, so relative share may hold.
rows.implication: Underwrite 2026-2028 US volume as a subsidy-free, price-elastic market and do not extrapolate 2025 deliveries; a demand recovery needs new products or autonomy, not incentives.

rows.finding: Automotive regulatory credit revenue was $2,763m in 2024, $1,993m in 2025 (-28%), $113m in Q3 2026 (-73% year on year) and $639m in the first nine months of 2026 (-56%).
rows.mechanism: Regulatory credits carry almost no cost of revenue, so their loss hits gross profit one-for-one: total automotive gross margin fell from 18.4% to 17.8% in 2025 partly because of the $770m credit decline, and the Q3 2026 collapse removes a similar high-margin contribution.
rows.benchmark: 2023 credit revenue of $1,790m and the 2024 peak of $2,763m; automotive gross margin of 18.4% in 2024.
rows.weakens: Credit revenue was always lumpy and was never guided, so part of the decline may already sit in consensus; the remaining $639m in 9M 2026 shows the pool has not gone to zero.
rows.implication: Value the auto business on a credit-free margin and treat any credit revenue as upside; the quality of Tesla's reported automotive margin is lower than the headline suggests.
rows.confidence: high — audited segment data and the Q3 2026 10-Q.
rows.follow_up: How much credit revenue is contracted for 2027, with which counterparties, and under which state or foreign programmes?

rows.finding: EPA's final rule published 2026-02-18 rescinds the 2009 endangerment finding and repeals all light-, medium- and heavy-duty GHG standards; the Department of Transportation finalised a rollback of CAFE standards on 2026-10-01.
rows.mechanism: The federal CO2 compliance market that created demand for Tesla's credits is being dismantled, and weaker CAFE pressure slows competitors' EV mix, removing both the credit pool and the relative cost advantage Tesla earned from selling compliance.
rows.benchmark: The 2024 multi-pollutant rule for model years 2027-2032, now repealed before it bound.
rows.weakens: California's ACC II and the Section 177 states can preserve a separate credit market, and litigation over the repeal could reinstate parts of the federal programme.
rows.implication: Assume structurally lower credit value in the US and a policy regime that no longer subsidises Tesla's cost position; this is a permanent earnings-quality change, not a one-quarter timing issue.
rows.confidence: high on the federal repeal; medium on whether state rules replace enough of the market.
rows.follow_up: Do California and the Section 177 states keep a credit market Tesla can sell into through 2028, and at what price?

rows.mechanism: Robotaxi revenue scales only where a state grants driverless commercial authority, so the addressable fleet is capped by permissions rather than by manufacturing capacity; Texas is a no-fee registration-style regime while California is a discretionary permit Tesla does not hold.
rows.benchmark: Waymo holds a CPUC driverless deployment permit; Zoox received a federal FMVSS exemption on 2026-07-31; Tesla holds a Texas authorisation and a California testing permit with a driver.
rows.weakens: Tesla already operates in Austin and expanded its Cybercab fleet to 300+ vehicles, and states may legalise after observing deployment; Texas alone is a large market.
rows.implication: Do not capitalise California or other states in the base case; size any position on Texas-plus-permitted jurisdictions and treat a California driverless permit as the catalyst that would justify a higher multiple.

rows.follow_up: Has Tesla filed for a CPUC driverless deployment permit, and what is the application's status and operational design domain?

rows.finding: The SELF DRIVE Act of 2026 (H.R. 7390), which would create a national ADS framework and preempt state technical rules, advanced from a House subcommittee on a 12-11 party-line vote on 2026-02-10; it is not law as of 2026-10-29.
rows.mechanism: Federal preemption would convert a 50-state permission problem into a single compliance standard and could legalise steering-wheel-free vehicles nationwide, which is the main non-operational upside for Cybercab; until enacted, NHTSA defect investigations remain the binding federal constraint.
rows.benchmark: The 2017-2018 SELF DRIVE Act died in the Senate; a 12-11 subcommittee margin is narrower than the 2017 bipartisan committee votes.
rows.weakens: The bill is contested on party lines and has no Senate path visible; NHTSA's defect probes (EA26-002 on FSD degradation, DP26-010 school-zone review) can offset the benefit even if it passes.
rows.implication: Treat federal preemption as optionality worth little in the base case and no more than a modest premium in the bull case; do not pay for it today.

rows.follow_up: What is the full committee and floor schedule for H.R. 7390, and does the Senate have a companion bill?

rows.finding: From 2026-01-01 to 2027-12-31 China halves the NEV purchase tax to an effective 5%, capped at RMB 15,000 per passenger car, with new technical requirements from 2026-01-01; Tesla's unsupervised FSD is still not approved in China, Q3 2026 China sales fell 16%, and Beijing cut the vehicle export tax rebate.
rows.mechanism: The tax change raises the effective price of a China-built Model 3 or Model Y by up to RMB 15,000 and is regressive for higher-priced trims; the export-rebate cut raises the cost of using Shanghai as an export hub, while the missing FSD approval blocks software revenue in the largest EV market.
rows.benchmark: Full purchase-tax exemption in 2024-2025; China sales growth in 2025 versus the 12-16% declines reported for 2026.
rows.weakens: The tax applies to all NEV makers, Tesla cut prices and added financing, and record Shanghai exports can absorb capacity even with a lower rebate.
rows.implication: Treat China as a cost and export anchor rather than a 2026-2028 profit-growth engine, and exclude China FSD revenue from the base case until MIIT/CAC approval is disclosed.
rows.confidence: high on the tax and export-rebate changes; medium on FSD timing and on how much of the sales decline is policy versus competition.
rows.follow_up: What is the status of Tesla's application for unsupervised FSD in China, which data-localisation and mapping conditions apply, and how much of Shanghai output is exported?

rows.finding: Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2754 has imposed a definitive countervailing duty on China-built BEVs since 2024-10-30 for five years, at 7.8% for Tesla Shanghai versus 35.3% for SAIC, on top of the 10% common duty; the EU softened 2025-2027 CO2 compliance to a three-year average and proposed the same for 2030-2032.
rows.mechanism: The duty raises Tesla's Shanghai-to-EU landed cost by about 17.8% but Chinese-brand rivals' by roughly 45%, preserving relative price room; the CO2 derogation removes legacy manufacturers' near-term urgency to buy credits or force EV mix, weakening both credit demand and the regulatory pull for EVs.
rows.benchmark: 10% most-favoured-nation duty alone; the US 100% tariff on Chinese-built EVs that keeps Chinese brands out of Tesla's home market.
rows.weakens: The EU may replace duties with price undertakings that narrow Tesla's relative advantage, and Berlin-built cars avoid the duty entirely.
rows.implication: The EU relative advantage is real but narrow and time-limited; do not underwrite it beyond 2026 or assume EU CO2 policy keeps forcing credit purchases.
rows.confidence: high on the regulation and rate; medium on the direction of EU trade policy in 2027.
rows.follow_up: Is the EU negotiating price undertakings that would replace the Tesla-specific 7.8% rate, and what share of EU sales is Berlin-built versus Shanghai-built?

plan.decision_question: Which regulatory, policy and ESG factors materially change Tesla's cash flows, licence to operate or cost of capital in 2026-2028?
plan.thesis_sentence: Tesla's policy position has inverted: the 2025-2026 reset removes a high-margin revenue stream worth about $2bn a year at its peak and leaves the robotaxi licence to operate fragmented across US states and unapproved in China, while the offsetting upsides — federal AV preemption and tariffs on Chinese rivals — are real but not yet law, so policy and governance risk deserves a discount to, not a premium over, the core auto multiple.
plan.why_different: The other sections price demand, margins, technology feasibility and valuation; this section prices the legal permissions and compliance costs that gate the autonomy catalyst and the high-margin credit stream, and the governance overhang that changes the cost of capital.
plan.mechanism: Regulatory credits and purchase subsidies are near-100% margin revenue, so their removal cuts gross profit and cash flow one-for-one; state AV authorisations and China FSD approval are binary gates on robotaxi revenue; performance equity and related-party capital allocation raise the discount rate on the equity.
plan.comparison_set: Waymo (CPUC driverless deployment permit), Zoox (federal FMVSS exemption granted 2026-07-31), Ford (dual-class control), GM and Ford (credit-dependent compliance buyers), and Tesla's own 2023-2025 credit revenue history ($1,790m, $2,763m, $1,993m).
plan.counter_evidence: Policy also favours Tesla: the US 100% tariff on Chinese-built EVs and the EU's 17.8% total duty on Shanghai cars versus roughly 45% for SAIC keep Chinese rivals out; a federal AV preemption bill could unlock nationwide Cybercab deployment; most of the CEO award is performance-contingent, seven of nine directors are independent and there is no dual class; Tesla's own operational environmental footprint is small, so environmental issues are second-order to supply-chain and product safety.

Tesla enters 2026-2028 with its policy position inverted: the 2025-2026 reset has removed the high-margin regulatory revenue stream that flattered its automotive margin and has left the robotaxi licence to operate fragmented across US states and unapproved in China, while the offsetting upsides — federal AV preemption and tariffs on Chinese rivals — are real but not yet law. The correct treatment is a discount to, not a premium over, the core auto multiple: policy now subtracts about $2bn of peak annual revenue from the base case, and governance adds a dilution overhang that raises the cost of capital. [S3, S4]

### The subsidy and the credit pool have already gone

The legal instrument is unambiguous. Section 30D of the Internal Revenue Code, the $7,500 new clean vehicle credit, was available only for vehicles acquired on or before 2025-09-30; the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, enacted 2025-07-04, terminated it and the used-vehicle 25E credit for later acquisitions [S117]. Tesla's own numbers show what that did to the second, less visible subsidy: automotive regulatory credit revenue fell from $2,763m in 2024 to $1,993m in 2025 (-28%), then to $113m in Q3 2026 from $417m a year earlier (-73%), and to $639m in the first nine months of 2026 from $1,451m (-56%) [S3, S4]. Because credits carry almost no cost of revenue, the loss goes straight to gross profit: total automotive gross margin fell from 18.4% in 2024 to 17.8% in 2025, and management attributes part of that to the $770m credit decline [S3]. For an investor, the implication is that Tesla's reported automotive margin is of lower quality than the headline: the credit-free margin is the right base, and any credit revenue from here is upside.

### The federal rulebook now runs against Tesla

The 2026 revision the brief asks about is a repeal, not a tightening. EPA's final rule published on 2026-02-18 rescinds the 2009 endangerment finding and repeals all light-, medium- and heavy-duty GHG standards; the Department of Transportation finalised its CAFE rollback on 2026-10-01 [S116, S64]. Both moves remove the compliance demand that priced Tesla's credits, and weaker fuel-economy pressure slows competitors' EV mix — which erodes the relative cost advantage Tesla earned by selling compliance rather than buying it. The demand effect is visible in official data: EIA reported on 2026-10-19 that hybrid sales rose while battery-electric sales remained lower after the tax credit expired [S98]. The counter-argument is that California's ACC II and the Section 177 states preserve a separate credit market and that litigation could restore parts of the federal programme; that is a real but partial backstop, and it does not restore the 2024 price level.

### The robotaxi licence is a state-by-state binary

Autonomy is the part of the equity value that policy can switch on or off, and the record at 2026-10-29 is narrower than the narrative. Texas requires a TxDMV authorisation for commercial SAE Level 4/5 operation from 2026-05-28 under SB 2807; it is a no-fee, non-expiring registration-style regime that Tesla can satisfy, which is why Austin scaled first [S118]. California is the opposite: CPUC's autonomous-vehicle permit table lists Waymo, Zoox, Nuro, WeRide and Tensor but not Tesla, and Tesla's California service runs under a non-AV limousine/TCP authority, not a driverless deployment permit [S119, S73]. At the federal level the constraint is enforcement rather than permission — NHTSA's FSD probes and the October 2026 school-zone review of robotaxis — while the preemption fix, H.R. 7390 SELF DRIVE Act of 2026, only advanced from a House subcommittee on a 12-11 party-line vote on 2026-02-10 [S80, S82, S125]. Compare Waymo, which holds a CPUC driverless deployment permit, and Zoox, which received a federal FMVSS exemption on 2026-07-31: Tesla is not first on either permission. The investor implication is to capitalise Texas-plus-permitted states only and to treat a California driverless permit as the specific catalyst that would justify a higher multiple.

### China is a cost anchor, not a growth engine

China policy has become a tax on Tesla's largest manufacturing base. From 2026-01-01 to 2027-12-31 the NEV purchase tax is halved rather than exempt — an effective 5% rate capped at RMB 15,000 per passenger car, with new technical requirements and catalogue rules from 2026-01-01 [S124]. The cap is regressive for Tesla's higher-priced trims, and it arrives alongside a 16% fall in Q3 2026 China sales, a cut in the vehicle export tax rebate and continuing absence of unsupervised FSD approval [S77, S102]. The mechanism matters: the tax raises the effective price of a China-built Model 3 or Model Y by up to RMB 15,000, the rebate cut raises the cost of using Shanghai as an export hub, and the missing FSD approval blocks software revenue in the world's largest EV market. Tesla can offset some of this with price cuts and record exports, and the tax hits every NEV maker; but the burden falls hardest on the premium end where Tesla sits.

### Europe: tariff protection with an expiry date

Europe is the one jurisdiction where policy currently favours Tesla. Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2754 has imposed a definitive countervailing duty on China-built BEVs since 2024-10-30 for five years, at 7.8% for Tesla Shanghai against 35.3% for SAIC, on top of the 10% common duty [S127]. That leaves Tesla's Shanghai-built cars at about 17.8% total versus roughly 45% for Chinese-brand rivals — real relative pricing room, though not enough to make Shanghai-built cars competitive with Berlin-built ones. The protection is time-limited and politically contingent: the EU softened 2025-2027 CO2 compliance to a three-year average and has proposed the same for 2030-2032, which reduces legacy manufacturers' urgency to buy credits and to force EV mix [S126], and a shift to price undertakings would narrow Tesla's company-specific advantage. Do not underwrite the EU advantage beyond 2026.

### Governance is the largest ESG item

The financially material governance facts are dilution, related-party capital allocation and control, not board composition alone. The 2025 CEO Performance Award covers 423.7m shares in 12 tranches, approved on 2025-11-06, with $105.82-120.37bn of unrecognised stock compensation for milestones not yet probable and $10.23bn for the one milestone deemed probable [S5, S3]. At the low end that is roughly 10.7% of the 3.95bn shares outstanding — an overhang that lands on shareholders if the operational milestones are met. More troubling for minority holders is capital allocation: Tesla invested $2.0bn in xAI Holdings in January 2026 and, after SpaceX acquired xAI Holdings on 2026-02-02, had that right converted into SpaceX Class A stock in March 2026 — a related-party channel to entities Musk controls [S5]. Musk holds 19.8% of the shares and 207.5m of them are pledged as collateral, linking the controlling shareholder's liquidity to the share price [S5]. The mitigants are real: seven of nine directors are independent, Tesla has a single class of stock with one share, one vote (unlike Ford's Class B, which carries 40% of the votes on 2% of the shares), and the unearned award shares vote proportionately to other shareholders. But a governance discount is warranted, and the question of a SpaceX combination — which press coverage reads the 2026 proxy as preparing for — is a risk to minority holders, not a catalyst.

### The ESG issues that do not move the number

Tesla's own operational environmental footprint is small relative to the use-phase emissions its products avoid, and the 10-K discloses no material environmental enforcement; the material environmental exposure is upstream, in battery materials. No privacy or data-protection fine appears in the legal-proceedings note, and cyber risk is overseen by the Audit Committee; that is an absence of disclosed loss, not proof of low risk, and China's data-localisation rules remain a condition on FSD approval. Labour is the one social issue with a dated trial: the California Civil Rights Department race-discrimination case is set for 2026-07-20, while the August 2025 Autopilot verdict ($129m compensatory, $200m punitive, with Tesla 33% at fault) is the product-safety marker [S3]. None of these is thesis-changing on its own; together they justify a higher cost of capital and a smaller position, not an exit.

Tesla's policy position has inverted. The 2025-2026 reset removes a high-margin revenue stream worth $2,763m at its 2024 peak and leaves the robotaxi licence to operate fragmented across US states and unapproved in China, while the offsetting upsides — federal AV preemption and tariffs on Chinese rivals — are real but not yet law. Automotive regulatory credit revenue fell from $2,763m in 2024 to $1,993m in 2025 (-28%), then to $113m in Q3 2026 from $417m a year earlier (-73%), with $639m in the first nine months of 2026 against $1,451m (-56%). Because credits carry almost no cost of revenue, the loss goes straight to gross profit: total automotive gross margin fell from 18.4% to 17.8% in 2025, partly on the $770m credit decline. The credit-free margin is the right base; any credit revenue from here is upside. [S3, S4]

### The credit pool has already collapsed

The US instrument is unambiguous. Section 30D's $7,500 new clean vehicle credit was available only for vehicles acquired on or before 2025-09-30; the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, enacted 2025-07-04, terminated it and the used-vehicle 25E credit for later acquisitions. The 2026 revision is a repeal, not a tightening: EPA's final rule of 2026-02-18 rescinds the 2009 endangerment finding and repeals the light-, medium- and heavy-duty GHG standards, and the Department of Transportation finalised its CAFE rollback on 2026-10-01. Both remove the compliance demand that priced Tesla's credits and slow competitors' EV mix, eroding the relative cost advantage Tesla earned by selling compliance rather than buying it. EIA reported on 2026-10-19 that hybrid sales rose while battery-electric sales remained lower after the credit expired. California's ACC II and the Section 177 states preserve a partial credit market, and litigation could restore parts of the federal programme, but neither restores the 2024 price level. [S117, S116, S64, S98]

### The robotaxi licence is a state-by-state binary

Autonomy is the part of the equity value that policy can switch on or off, and the record is narrower than the narrative. Texas requires a TxDMV authorisation for commercial SAE Level 4/5 operation from 2026-05-28 under SB 2807 — a no-fee, non-expiring registration-style regime, which is why Austin scaled first. California is the opposite: CPUC's autonomous-vehicle permit table lists Waymo, Zoox, Nuro, WeRide and Tensor but not Tesla, and Tesla's California service runs under a non-AV limousine/TCP authority rather than a driverless deployment permit. Federally, the binding constraint is enforcement — NHTSA's FSD probes and the October 2026 school-zone review of robotaxis — while the preemption fix, H.R. 7390 SELF DRIVE Act of 2026, advanced only from a House subcommittee on a 12-11 party-line vote on 2026-02-10. Waymo holds a CPUC driverless deployment permit and Zoox received a federal FMVSS exemption on 2026-07-31; Tesla is first on neither. Capitalise Texas-plus-permitted states only, and treat a California driverless permit as the specific catalyst that would justify a higher multiple. [S118, S119, S80, S125]

### China taxes the base; Europe protects it for now

China policy has become a tax on Tesla's largest manufacturing base. From 2026-01-01 to 2027-12-31 the NEV purchase tax is halved rather than exempt — an effective 5%, capped at RMB 15,000 per passenger car, with new technical requirements and catalogue rules — which is regressive for Tesla's higher-priced trims and lands alongside a 16% fall in Q3 2026 China sales, a cut in the vehicle export tax rebate and no unsupervised FSD approval. Europe is the exception: Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2754 has imposed a countervailing duty on China-built BEVs since 2024-10-30 for five years, at 7.8% for Tesla Shanghai against 35.3% for SAIC, on top of the 10% common duty, leaving Tesla at about 17.8% total versus roughly 45% for Chinese-brand rivals. That relative room is real but time-limited: the EU softened 2025-2027 CO2 compliance to a three-year average and proposed the same for 2030-2032, cutting legacy makers' urgency to buy credits, and a shift to price undertakings would narrow Tesla's company-specific advantage. [S124, S77, S127, S126]

### Governance is the largest ESG item

Governance is the largest ESG item because it changes the share count and the cost of capital. The 2025 CEO Performance Award covers 423.7m shares in 12 tranches, approved on 2025-11-06, with $105.82-120.37bn of unrecognised stock compensation for milestones not yet probable and $10.23bn for the one milestone deemed probable — at the low end roughly 10.7% of the 3.95bn shares outstanding. Capital allocation matters more than pay design: Tesla invested $2.0bn in xAI Holdings in January 2026 and, after SpaceX acquired xAI Holdings on 2026-02-02, had that right converted into SpaceX Class A stock in March 2026, a related-party channel to entities Musk controls. Musk holds 19.8% of the shares and 207.5m of them are pledged as collateral. The mitigants are real — seven of nine directors are independent, one share carries one vote, and unearned award shares vote proportionately to other shareholders — but a governance discount is warranted. [S5, S3]

### What is not financially material

Three ESG claims do not survive contact with the financials. Tesla's own operational footprint is small relative to the use-phase emissions its products avoid, and the 2025 10-K discloses no material environmental proceeding; the material environmental exposure is upstream, in battery materials, where Tesla files an annual conflict-minerals report but discloses no supplier-level exposure. No privacy or data-protection fine appears in the legal-proceedings note, so data risk is an unquantified condition on China FSD approval rather than a booked liability. Labour and product safety are tails rather than the thesis: the California Civil Rights Department race-discrimination trial is set for 2026-07-20, and the August 2025 Autopilot verdict was $129m compensatory with Tesla 33% at fault plus $200m punitive, against an immaterial accrual. The strongest counter-evidence runs the other way — the US 100% tariff on Chinese-built EVs, the EU's relative tariff advantage, the possibility of federal AV preemption and a performance-contingent pay design — and it is why policy is a discount on the multiple, not an exit signal. [S3, S5]

Confidence is high on the enacted US and EU instruments and on the audited disclosures, medium on state-by-state AV timing and on China's FSD approval. The gaps are procedural rather than analytical: court dockets for the securities and civil-rights cases sit behind PACER, CPUC advice letters and any Tesla driverless application are not published as machine-readable data, and MIIT's type-approval and FSD filing records are not public. Those gaps lower confidence in litigation timing and in the California and China autonomy options, not in the credit and tariff findings, which rest on primary law and audited figures. Diligence should press management on four points: the contracted 2027 credit revenue and its counterparties; whether a CPUC driverless deployment application has been filed and with what operational design domain; the status of unsupervised FSD approval with MIIT and CAC and the data-localisation conditions attached; and the board process for any SpaceX combination or further investment in Musk-controlled entities.

arguments.markdown:
Tesla's policy position has inverted. The 2025-2026 reset removes a high-margin revenue stream worth $2,763m at its 2024 peak and leaves the robotaxi licence to operate fragmented across US states and unapproved in China, while the offsetting upsides — federal AV preemption and tariffs on Chinese rivals — are real but not yet law. Automotive regulatory credit revenue fell from $2,763m in 2024 to $1,993m in 2025 (-28%) and to $113m in Q3 2026 from $417m (-73%). Because credits carry almost no cost of revenue, the loss hits gross profit directly: total automotive gross margin fell from 18.4% to 17.8% in 2025, partly on the $770m credit decline. The credit-free margin is the right base; any credit revenue is upside. [S3, S4]

### The credit pool has already collapsed

The US instrument is unambiguous. Section 30D's $7,500 new clean vehicle credit applied only to vehicles acquired on or before 2025-09-30; the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, enacted 2025-07-04, terminated it and the used-vehicle 25E credit thereafter. The 2026 revision is a repeal, not a tightening: EPA's final rule of 2026-02-18 rescinds the 2009 endangerment finding and repeals the light-, medium- and heavy-duty GHG standards, and the Department of Transportation finalised its CAFE rollback on 2026-10-01. Both remove the compliance demand that priced Tesla's credits and slow competitors' EV mix. EIA reported on 2026-10-19 that hybrid sales rose while battery-electric sales remained lower after the credit expired. California's ACC II and the Section 177 states preserve a partial credit market, but not the 2024 price level. [S117, S116, S64, S98]

### The robotaxi licence is a state-by-state binary

Autonomy is the part of the equity value policy can switch on or off, and the record is narrower than the narrative. Texas requires a TxDMV authorisation for commercial SAE Level 4/5 operation from 2026-05-28 under SB 2807 — a no-fee, non-expiring registration regime, which is why Austin scaled first. California is the opposite: CPUC's AV permit table lists Waymo, Zoox, Nuro, WeRide and Tensor but not Tesla, and Tesla's California service runs under a non-AV limousine/TCP authority, not a driverless deployment permit. Federally the binding constraint is enforcement — NHTSA's FSD probes and the October 2026 school-zone review — while the preemption fix, H.R. 7390 SELF DRIVE Act of 2026, advanced only from a House subcommittee on a 12-11 party-line vote on 2026-02-10. Waymo holds a CPUC driverless deployment permit and Zoox a federal FMVSS exemption granted 2026-07-31; Tesla is first on neither. [S118, S119, S80, S125]

### China taxes the base; Europe protects it for now

China policy has become a tax on Tesla's largest manufacturing base. From 2026-01-01 to 2027-12-31 the NEV purchase tax is halved rather than exempt — an effective 5%, capped at RMB 15,000 per car, with new technical requirements — regressive for Tesla's higher-priced trims and landing alongside a 16% fall in Q3 2026 China sales, a cut in the vehicle export rebate and no unsupervised FSD approval. Europe is the exception: Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2754 has imposed a countervailing duty on China-built BEVs since 2024-10-30 for five years, at 7.8% for Tesla Shanghai against 35.3% for SAIC, on top of the 10% common duty — about 17.8% total versus roughly 45% for Chinese brands. That room is real but time-limited: the EU softened 2025-2027 CO2 compliance to a three-year average and proposed the same for 2030-2032, reducing legacy makers' urgency to buy credits, and price undertakings would narrow Tesla's company-specific advantage. [S124, S77, S127, S126]

### Governance is the largest ESG item

Governance is the largest ESG item because it changes the share count and the cost of capital. The 2025 CEO Performance Award covers 423.7m shares in 12 tranches, approved on 2025-11-06, with $105.82-120.37bn of unrecognised stock compensation for milestones not yet probable and $10.23bn for the one deemed probable — at the low end roughly 10.7% of the 3.95bn shares outstanding. Capital allocation matters more than pay design: Tesla invested $2.0bn in xAI Holdings in January 2026 and, after SpaceX acquired xAI Holdings on 2026-02-02, converted that right into SpaceX Class A stock in March 2026. Musk holds 19.8% and 207.5m of his shares are pledged. Seven of nine directors are independent, one share carries one vote and unearned award shares vote proportionately, but a governance discount is warranted. [S5, S3]

### What is not financially material

Three ESG claims do not survive contact with the financials. Tesla's own operational footprint is small relative to the use-phase emissions its products avoid, and the 2025 10-K discloses no material environmental proceeding; the real environmental exposure is upstream, in battery materials, where Tesla files an annual conflict-minerals report but discloses no supplier-level exposure. No privacy or data-protection fine appears in the legal-proceedings note. Labour and product safety are tails: the California Civil Rights Department trial is set for 2026-07-20, and the August 2025 Autopilot verdict was $129m compensatory with Tesla 33% at fault plus $200m punitive, against an immaterial accrual. The strongest counter-evidence runs the other way — the US tariff wall on Chinese-built EVs, the EU's relative tariff advantage, possible federal AV preemption and performance-contingent pay — which is why policy is a discount on the multiple, not an exit signal. [S3, S5]

arguments.markdown:
At $403.30 (NasdaqGS, 2026-10-29 20:00 UTC) Tesla's equity is worth $1,594.1B and its enterprise value $1,558.0B. On a sum of the parts, 89% of that price — $1,424B, or $356 a share — buys autonomy and robotics, while the automotive, energy and services businesses plus $36.2B of net cash are worth a computed $42.50 a share at peer multiples. That residual is 11.3 times the $126B at which Waymo raised $16B in February 2026, and Waymo is the only operator running a scaled driverless service. My probability-weighted value is $115 a share, 71% below the close, and the disagreement is not about cars: my $42.50 for the core sits within $5 of Morgan Stanley's $47 a share for the same business. It is about whether 2.0M cumulative unsupervised miles, a robotaxi service confined to one city and zero disclosed Optimus revenue can carry $1.4 trillion. [S15, S120]

### A five-year flat line, a violent quarter

Tesla has returned +0.1% over five years — $402.86 on 2021-11-01 to $403.30 — and is down 11.3% year to date from the 2025-12-31 close of $454.43, against +12.8% for the S&P 500. The twelve-month return of -8.4% trails the index by 21.5 percentage points. The movement is all in the last quarter: +30.6% over three months and +14.3% over one, a window that contains the 2026-10-21 results and the merger remarks Musk made on the same earnings call. The stock sits 53% of the way up a 52-week range of $297.38-$498.83, above its 50-day ($368.51) and 200-day ($385.50) averages, on $14.0B of daily turnover. [S15]

### 443 times trailing earnings, 183 times 2027 consensus

On trailing figures Tesla trades at 443.2x earnings, 15.0x sales and 170.5x EBITDA — or 104x on the company's own $15.0B adjusted EBITDA, which excludes $4.3B of stock compensation. The six-company peer median is 16.5x earnings and 5.0x sales. Consensus that already assumes a robotaxi ramp barely normalises the multiple: 2026 revenue of $108.5B and EPS of $1.67 give 241x, and 2027 revenue of $123.9B and EPS of $2.20 give 183x. [S115] Tesla's own history does not support the level either: the P/E at the last five fiscal year ends was 72.8x (2021), 34.0x (2022), 57.8x (2023), 204.6x (2024) and 420.8x (2025), so today sits above every year-end mark in the series.

### Sum of the parts: $42.50 of business, $356 of promise

Trailing-twelve-month segment data from the Q3 2026 update: automotive revenue $75.0B at a 19.1% gross margin, energy $12.3B at 29.7%, services $16.3B at 12.4%, sharing $16.5B of operating expense. [S6] At 1.0x sales for vehicles and services — 2.5x GM's implied 0.39x, warranted by double GM's gross margin — 3.5x for energy (above Fluence's 0.5x, below what a profitable integrator commands) and net cash at book, the core is $170B, or $42.50 a share on 4.00B shares.

| Reverse DCF | $2.0B FCF in 2027, 45% growth, 10% WACC, 3% terminal growth | $403 requires $141B of 2031 FCF | S4 |

The share count needs care. Outstanding shares were 3,952.6M at 2026-09-30, of which 710M (18%) are unvested restricted stock from the 2018 and 2025 CEO awards; I add 50M for further grants to reach 4.00B. On the 3,240M basic count the equity is worth $1,307B at today's price rather than $1,594B, and the gap is awards that vest only if milestones are met. The base case's autonomy value of $259B comes from an explicit tree: $40B if robotaxi stays regional (35% probability), 1.0x Waymo at $126B (40%), $600B at scale (20%) and $1,500B on global dominance in robotaxi and humanoids (5%). Weighting the three scenarios 25/50/25 gives $115 a share.

### The reverse DCF needs sixteen million robotaxis

At a 10% WACC and 3% terminal growth, crediting $2.0B of free cash flow in 2027 and 45% annual growth to 2031, today's enterprise value requires $141B of free cash flow in 2031. At 9% the requirement falls to $118B; at 11% it rises to $164B. At a 15% FCF margin — generous for a capital-intensive manufacturer — that is $940B of 2031 revenue, nine times trailing revenue. If the incremental profit came from robotaxi at a 25% FCF margin it implies $564B of robotaxi revenue; at $0.60 a mile and 60,000 miles a vehicle a year, that is 15.7M robotaxis, or 7.8M if the car and energy businesses supply half the cash flow. Tesla's installed automotive capacity is 2.5M vehicles a year. The price assumes a fleet that six years of full capacity could not build, earning a revenue per mile no disclosed Tesla service charges.

### What the street pays for, and what would prove it right

The consensus twelve-month target is $417.94 from 40 analysts, 3.6% above the close, with a range from $66 to $600. [S122] Short interest is 69.35M shares, 2.19% of the float, 2.2 days to cover, so there is no crowded short to squeeze and no positioning signal either way. Management publishes no numeric guidance: the outlook promises "maximum capacity utilization" and is silent on volume, margin and robotaxi revenue. Dated catalysts are the 2026-12-03 annual meeting, Q4 2026 results in late January 2027, Austin Fab tool commissioning in 2027, and the special-committee process opened on 2026-10-20 — the one event that could re-rate the shares without any operating delivery.

The counter-evidence is real. Tesla has held a triple-digit multiple for two years without mean reversion, so expensiveness alone has not been a sell signal; the 2025 CEO award ties 423.7M shares to market-cap milestones running to $8.5T, which aligns management with the narrative rather than with per-share cash flow; and a merger into SpaceX at its $2.1T first-day value would make Tesla holders owners of 43% of a $3.7T company with Starlink cash flows, against which a standalone sum of the parts is the wrong instrument. [S132] Against that, stock compensation runs at 4.2% of revenue and every tranche of the award is paid in shares. The margin of safety at $403.30 is negative and turns positive only below $115; between those levels the buyer is purchasing an option and should size it as one.

Confidence is high on the core-business value and low on the autonomy tree, which is why the price's dependence on it matters. What would settle it: a disclosed robotaxi revenue line with revenue and cost per mile; the Austin fleet count and utilisation; the market-cap and operational thresholds of each award tranche; 2026 capital expenditure against the $13.0B spent in nine months; and the exchange ratio the two special committees would accept.

arguments.markdown:
At $403.30 (NasdaqGS, 2026-10-29 20:00 UTC) Tesla's equity is worth $1,594.1B and its enterprise value $1,558.0B. On a sum of the parts, 89% of that price — $1,424B, or $356 a share — buys autonomy and robotics, while the automotive, energy and services businesses plus $36.2B of net cash are worth a computed $42.50 a share at peer multiples. That residual is 11.3 times the $126B at which Waymo raised $16B in February 2026, and Waymo is the only operator running a scaled driverless service. My probability-weighted value is $115 a share, 71% below the close, and the disagreement is not about cars: my $42.50 for the core sits within $5 of Morgan Stanley's $47 a share for the same business. It is about whether 2.0M cumulative unsupervised miles, a robotaxi service confined to one city and zero disclosed Optimus revenue can carry $1.4 trillion. [S15, S120]

### A five-year flat line, a violent quarter

Tesla has returned +0.1% over five years — $402.86 on 2021-11-01 to $403.30 — and is down 11.3% year to date from the 2025-12-31 close of $454.43, against +12.8% for the S&P 500. The twelve-month return of -8.4% trails the index by 21.5 percentage points. The movement is all in the last quarter: +30.6% over three months and +14.3% over one, a window that contains the 2026-10-21 results and the merger remarks Musk made on the same earnings call. The stock sits 53% of the way up a 52-week range of $297.38-$498.83, above its 50-day ($368.51) and 200-day ($385.50) averages, on $14.0B of daily turnover. [S15]

| Measure | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Price | $403.30, NasdaqGS, USD, 2026-10-29 20:00 UTC | S15 |
| Market capitalisation | $1,594.1B on 3,952.6M shares outstanding at 2026-09-30 | S15, S5 |
| Enterprise value | $1,558.0B, after $36.2B of net cash | S15, S6 |
| 52-week range | $297.38-$498.83; the price is 53% of the way up | S15 |
| 50-day / 200-day average | $368.51 / $385.50, price +9.4% / +4.6% above | S15 |
| Return 1m / 3m / 12m | +14.3% / +30.6% / -8.4% | S15 |
| Twelve months vs S&P 500 | -21.5 pp (S&P 500 +13.2%) | S15, S22 |
| Turnover | 36.96M shares and $14.0B a day, 20-day average | S15 |

### 443 times trailing earnings, 183 times 2027 consensus

On trailing figures Tesla trades at 443.2x earnings, 15.0x sales and 170.5x EBITDA — or 104x on the company's own $15.0B adjusted EBITDA, which excludes $4.3B of stock compensation. The six-company peer median is 16.5x earnings and 5.0x sales. Consensus that already assumes a robotaxi ramp barely normalises the multiple: 2026 revenue of $108.5B and EPS of $1.67 give 241x, and 2027 revenue of $123.9B and EPS of $2.20 give 183x. [S115] Tesla's own history does not support the level either: the P/E at the last five fiscal year ends was 72.8x (2021), 34.0x (2022), 57.8x (2023), 204.6x (2024) and 420.8x (2025), so today sits above every year-end mark in the series.

### Sum of the parts: $42.50 of business, $356 of promise

Trailing-twelve-month segment data from the Q3 2026 update: automotive revenue $75.0B at a 19.1% gross margin, energy $12.3B at 29.7%, services $16.3B at 12.4%, sharing $16.5B of operating expense. [S6] At 1.0x sales for vehicles and services — 2.5x GM's implied 0.39x, warranted by double GM's gross margin — 3.5x for energy (above Fluence's 0.5x, below what a profitable integrator commands) and net cash at book, the core is $170B, or $42.50 a share on 4.00B shares.

|---|---|---|---|

| Sum of the parts, core only | Vehicles 1.0x sales, energy 3.5x, net cash at book | $42.50 a share | S6, S131 |
| Sum of the parts, base | Core plus $259B probability-weighted autonomy | $107 a share | S6, S120 |
| Sum of the parts, blue sky | Core plus $1,500B autonomy at 100% probability | $437 a share | S120, S123 |
| Reverse DCF | $2.0B FCF in 2027, 45% growth, 10% WACC, 3% terminal growth | $403 requires $141B of 2031 FCF | S4 |

The 4.00B share count is 3,952.6M outstanding, of which 710M (18%) are unvested restricted stock from the 2018 and 2025 CEO awards, plus 50M for further grants. On the 3,240M basic count the equity is worth $1,307B at today's price rather than $1,594B, a gap that matters because the awards vest only if market-cap milestones are met. The base case's $259B of autonomy value is an explicit tree: $40B if robotaxi stays regional (35% probability), 1.0x Waymo at $126B (40%), $600B at scale (20%) and $1,500B on global dominance in robotaxi and humanoids (5%). Weighting the three scenarios 25/50/25 gives $115 a share. [S5]

### The reverse DCF needs sixteen million robotaxis

At a 10% WACC and 3% terminal growth, crediting $2.0B of free cash flow in 2027 and 45% annual growth to 2031, today's enterprise value requires $141B of free cash flow in 2031. At 9% the requirement falls to $118B; at 11% it rises to $164B. At a 15% FCF margin — generous for a capital-intensive manufacturer — that is $940B of 2031 revenue, nine times trailing revenue. If the incremental profit came from robotaxi at a 25% FCF margin it implies $564B of robotaxi revenue; at $0.60 a mile and 60,000 miles a vehicle a year, that is 15.7M robotaxis, or 7.8M if the car and energy businesses supply half the cash flow. Tesla's installed automotive capacity is 2.5M vehicles a year. The price assumes a fleet that six years of full capacity could not build, earning a revenue per mile no disclosed Tesla service charges. [S4]

### What the street pays for, and what would prove it right

The consensus twelve-month target is $417.94 from 40 analysts, 3.6% above the close, with a range from $66 to $600. [S122] Short interest is 69.35M shares, 2.19% of the float, 2.2 days to cover, so there is no crowded short to squeeze and no positioning signal either way. Management publishes no numeric guidance: the outlook promises "maximum capacity utilization" and is silent on volume, margin and robotaxi revenue. Dated catalysts are the 2026-12-03 annual meeting, Q4 2026 results in late January 2027, Austin Fab tool commissioning in 2027, and the special-committee process opened on 2026-10-20 — the one event that could re-rate the shares without any operating delivery.

The counter-evidence is real. Tesla has held a triple-digit multiple for two years without mean reversion, so expensiveness alone has not been a sell signal; the 2025 CEO award ties 423.7M shares to market-cap milestones running to $8.5T, which aligns management with the narrative rather than with per-share cash flow; and a merger into SpaceX at its $2.1T first-day value would make Tesla holders owners of 43% of a $3.7T company with Starlink cash flows, against which a standalone sum of the parts is the wrong instrument. [S132] Against that, stock compensation runs at 4.2% of revenue and every tranche of the award is paid in shares. The margin of safety at $403.30 is negative and turns positive only below $115; between those levels the buyer is purchasing an option and should size it as one.

Confidence is high on the core-business value and low on the autonomy tree, which is why the price's dependence on it matters. What would settle it: a disclosed robotaxi revenue line with revenue and cost per mile; the Austin fleet count and utilisation; the market-cap and operational thresholds of each award tranche; capital expenditure guidance for 2026; and the exchange ratio the two special committees would accept.

### Sum of the parts: $42.50 of business, $356 of promise

### The reverse DCF needs sixteen million robotaxis

At a 10% WACC and 3% terminal growth, crediting $2.0B of free cash flow in 2027 and 45% annual growth to 2031, today's enterprise value requires $141B of free cash flow in 2031. At 9% the requirement falls to $118B; at 11% it rises to $164B. At a 15% FCF margin — generous for a capital-intensive manufacturer — that is $940B of 2031 revenue, nine times trailing revenue. If the incremental profit came from robotaxi at a 25% FCF margin it implies $564B of robotaxi revenue; at $0.60 a mile and 60,000 miles a vehicle a year, that is 15.7M robotaxis, or 7.8M if the car and energy businesses supply half the cash flow. Tesla's installed automotive capacity is 2.5M vehicles a year. The price assumes a fleet that six years of full capacity could not build, earning a revenue per mile no disclosed Tesla service charges. [S4]

### What the street pays for, and what would prove it right

The consensus twelve-month target is $417.94 from 40 analysts, 3.6% above the close, with a range from $66 to $600. Short interest is 69.35M shares, 2.19% of the float, 2.2 days to cover, so there is no crowded short to squeeze and no positioning signal either way. Management publishes no numeric guidance: the outlook promises "maximum capacity utilization" and is silent on volume, margin and robotaxi revenue. Dated catalysts are the 2026-12-03 annual meeting, Q4 2026 results in late January 2027, Austin Fab tool commissioning in 2027, and the special-committee process opened on 2026-10-20 — the one event that could re-rate the shares without any operating delivery. [S122]

The counter-evidence is real. Tesla has held a triple-digit multiple for two years without mean reversion, so expensiveness alone has not been a sell signal; the 2025 CEO award ties 423.7M shares to market-cap milestones running to $8.5T, which aligns management with the narrative rather than with per-share cash flow; and a merger into SpaceX at its $2.1T first-day value would make Tesla holders owners of 43% of a $3.7T company with Starlink cash flows, against which a standalone sum of the parts is the wrong instrument. Against that, stock compensation runs at 4.2% of revenue and every tranche of the award is paid in shares. The margin of safety at $403.30 is negative and turns positive only below $115; between those levels the buyer is purchasing an option and should size it as one. [S132]

Confidence is high on the core-business value and low on the autonomy tree, which is why the price's dependence on it matters. What would settle it: a disclosed robotaxi revenue line with revenue and cost per mile; the Austin fleet count and utilisation; the market-cap and operational thresholds of each award tranche; capital expenditure guidance for 2026; and the exchange ratio the two special committees would accept.

At a 10% WACC and 3% terminal growth, crediting $2.0B of free cash flow in 2027 and 45% annual growth to 2031, today's enterprise value requires $141B of free cash flow in 2031. At 9% the requirement falls to $118B; at 11% it rises to $164B. At a 15% FCF margin — generous for a capital-intensive manufacturer — that is $940B of 2031 revenue, nine times trailing revenue. If the incremental profit came from robotaxi at a 25% FCF margin it implies $564B of robotaxi revenue; at $0.60 a mile and 60,000 miles a vehicle a year, that is 15.7M robotaxis, or 7.8M if the car and energy businesses supply half the cash flow. Tesla's installed automotive capacity is 2.5M vehicles a year. The price assumes a fleet that six years of full capacity could not build, earning a revenue per mile no disclosed Tesla service charges. [S4]

The consensus twelve-month target is $417.94 from 40 analysts, 3.6% above the close, with a range from $66 to $600. The counter-evidence is real. Tesla has held a triple-digit multiple for two years without mean reversion, so expensiveness alone has not been a sell signal; the 2025 CEO award ties 423.7M shares to market-cap milestones running to $8.5T, which aligns management with the narrative rather than with per-share cash flow; and a merger into SpaceX at its $2.1T first-day value would make Tesla holders owners of 43% of a $3.7T company with Starlink cash flows, against which a standalone sum of the parts is the wrong instrument. Against that, stock compensation runs at 4.2% of revenue and every tranche of the award is paid in shares. The margin of safety at $403.30 is negative and turns positive only below $115; between those levels the buyer is purchasing an option and should size it as one. [S132]

Confidence is high on the core-business value and low on the autonomy tree, which is why the price's dependence on it matters. What would settle it: a disclosed robotaxi revenue line with revenue and cost per mile; the Austin fleet count and utilisation; the market-cap and operational thresholds of each award tranche; capital expenditure guidance for 2026; and the exchange ratio the two special committees would accept.

At a 10% WACC and 3% terminal growth, crediting $2.0B of free cash flow in 2027 and 45% annual growth to 2031, today's enterprise value requires $141B of free cash flow in 2031. At 9% the requirement falls to $118B; at 11% it rises to $164B. At a 15% FCF margin — generous for a capital-intensive manufacturer — that is $940B of 2031 revenue, nine times trailing revenue. Trailing free cash flow of $3,303 million against a market capitalisation of $1,428 billion is 431 times; nine-month 2026 free cash flow fell 61% to $1,883 million as capital expenditure more than doubled to $13,014 million; and the operating cash flow that survived was carried by a $7,332 million payables stretch while $3,557 million of stock-based compensation and a one-off California tax release flattered earnings. Gross margin held between 17.9% and 19.0% from FY2023, so the compression is entirely operating expense: R&D rose from $3,969 million in FY2023 to $6,411 million in FY2025 and $7,078 million in nine months of 2026. Cash generation now depends on working capital rather than profit, because payables and customer prepayments grow faster than earnings, which is why operating cash flow rises while net income falls. Operating cash flow rose 36% to $14,897 million while net income fell 19.5% to $2,378 million, and the bridge is working capital: accounts payable and accrued liabilities contributed $7,332 million against $2,979 million a year earlier, accounts payable rose to $17,239 million from $13,371 million at 2025-12-31, and days payables outstanding went from 62.8 to 75.3, roughly $2.9 billion of cash on the nine-month cost base. Deferred revenue added $1,746 million, mostly storage customer prepayments that rose to $3.30 billion. Against that, capital expenditure of $13,014 million consumed 87% of operating cash flow, and free cash flow by quarter was $1,444 million, negative $1,092 million and $1,531 million, against $3,990 million in Q3 2025. Depreciation of $4,290 million rose 17% and will climb faster than revenue as more than $20 billion of 2026 spending is commissioned [S3, S4].

The balance sheet is not the constraint. At 2026-09-30 Tesla held $45,447 million of cash and short-term investments against $9,267 million of debt, or $36,180 million of net cash, and in September 2026 it signed three credit agreements with aggregate commitments of $30 billion. Interest income of $1,301 million for nine months covered interest expense of $263 million almost five times; interest cover on operating income was 10.0x. Goodwill of $257 million is 0.2% of assets, so reported earnings carry no acquired-goodwill illusion; the pressures are elsewhere, in inventory of $14,092 million, up 13.7% while deliveries fell 2%, and a warranty reserve of $10,138 million, up 26% on the year. Solvency is not the risk; the return on the capital being deployed is [S4].

That return has collapsed. Invested capital of $53,109 million (equity $89,289 million plus debt less cash and securities) earned a trailing ROIC of 5.5% and an ROE of 3.8%, against 28.3% and 27.9% in FY2023, when the equity base was $62,634 million. Against a 4.99% ten-year Treasury, a 4.5% equity risk premium and a beta of 1.5 to 2.0, our estimate of the cost of capital is 11% to 14%, so the company is destroying economic value at current margins. Read strategically, this converts a cost advantage in vehicles and cells into a capital-intensive compute and robotics business before that business has customers, so the shares trade on optionality rather than earnings. Capital allocation offers no offset: no dividend, no buyback, capital expenditure guided above $20 billion for 2026, and $1.95 billion of stock paid for an AI hardware company in Q2 2026. Equity compensation is the other claim on shareholders: $3,557 million in nine months is 4.5% of revenue, the 2025 CEO Performance Award covers 423.7 million shares, or 12% of the 3,541 million diluted count, with $9.74 billion of unrecognised expense on the one milestone judged probable, and the 2018 award was exercised for 304.0 million options in Q2 2026, leaving restricted shares that vest on 2028-01-19 [S4, S15, S24].

The price is an option, not a multiple. At $403.30 on 2026-10-29 the equity is worth $1,428 billion and the enterprise $1,392 billion after net cash: 13.4x trailing revenue, 401x operating income, 92x trailing adjusted EBITDA of $14,995 million and 431x free cash flow. Adjusted EBITDA is itself struck before stock-based compensation, so the cash-based multiple is higher. The operating leverage cuts both ways: each 100 basis points of automotive gross margin excluding credits is worth $756 million on the annualised nine-month automotive revenue base of $75,561 million, which is 22% of trailing operating income, so a two-point margin miss plus a $4 billion capex overshoot would take 2027 free cash flow to roughly negative $2 billion on our arithmetic, while energy growth of 40% at a 30% margin and auto margin at 20% would lift it to about $8 billion. For an investor, that asymmetry makes the shares a bet on autonomy and robotics reaching commercial scale rather than on present cash flow, so position size should be set by tolerance for a de-rating from 92 times EBITDA, not by the near-term cash generation. Confidence is high on the statements and the cash bridge, medium on the cost of capital, and low on any estimate that requires autonomous revenue to be sized. Three diligence questions remain: how much of the payables increase reverses in Q4? What is the split of the 2026 capital budget between maintenance and AI compute? And does the board intend to offset dilution from the performance award? [S15, S69, S70]

On a sum of the parts, 89% of that price — $1,424B, or $356 a share — buys autonomy and robotics, while the automotive, energy and services businesses plus $36.2B of net cash are worth a computed $42.50 a share at peer multiples. That residual is 11.3 times the $126B at which Waymo raised $16B in February 2026, and Waymo is the only operator running a scaled driverless service. My probability-weighted value is $115 a share, 71% below the close, and the disagreement is not about cars: my $42.50 for the core sits within $5 of Morgan Stanley's $47 a share for the same business. It is about whether 2.0M cumulative unsupervised miles, a robotaxi service confined to one city and zero disclosed Optimus revenue can carry $1.4 trillion. [S15, S120, S6]

[S115] Tesla's own history does not support the level either: the P/E at the last five fiscal year ends was 72.8x (2021), 34.0x (2022), 57.8x (2023), 204.6x (2024) and 420.8x (2025), so today sits above every year-end mark in the series.

### Sum of the parts: $42.50 of business, $356 of promise

Trailing-twelve-month segment data from the Q3 2026 update: automotive revenue $75.0B at a 19.1% gross margin, energy $12.3B at 29.7%, services $16.3B at 12.4%, sharing $16.5B of operating expense. At 1.0x sales for vehicles and services — 2.5x GM's implied 0.39x, warranted by double GM's gross margin — 3.5x for energy (above Fluence's 0.5x, below what a profitable integrator commands) and net cash at book, the core is $170B, or $42.50 a share on 4.00B shares. The base case's $259B of autonomy value is an explicit tree: $40B if robotaxi stays regional (35% probability), 1.0x Waymo at $126B (40%), $600B at scale (20%) and $1,500B on global dominance in robotaxi and humanoids (5%). ### The reverse DCF needs sixteen million robotaxis

At a 10% WACC and 3% terminal growth, crediting $2.0B of free cash flow in 2027 and 45% annual growth to 2031, today's enterprise value requires $141B of free cash flow in 2031. At 9% the requirement falls to $118B; at 11% it rises to $164B. At a 15% FCF margin — generous for a capital-intensive manufacturer — that is $940B of 2031 revenue, nine times trailing revenue. If the incremental profit came from robotaxi at a 25% FCF margin it implies $564B of robotaxi revenue; at $0.60 a mile and 60,000 miles a vehicle a year, that is 15.7M robotaxis, or 7.8M if the car and energy businesses supply half the cash flow. Tesla's installed automotive capacity is 2.5M vehicles a year. The price assumes a fleet that six years of full capacity could not build, earning a revenue per mile no disclosed Tesla service charges. [S4, S6]

### What the street pays for, and what would prove it right

The consensus twelve-month target is $417.94 from 40 analysts, 3.6% above the close, with a range from $66 to $600. Short interest is 69.35M shares, 2.19% of the float, 2.2 days to cover, so there is no crowded short to squeeze and no positioning signal either way. Management publishes no numeric guidance: the outlook promises "maximum capacity utilization" and is silent on volume, margin and robotaxi revenue. Dated catalysts are the 2026-12-03 annual meeting, Q4 2026 results in late January 2027, Austin Fab tool commissioning in 2027, and the special-committee process opened on 2026-10-20 — the one event that could re-rate the shares without any operating delivery. [S122]

The counter-evidence is real. Tesla has held a triple-digit multiple for two years without mean reversion, so expensiveness alone has not been a sell signal; the 2025 CEO award ties 423.7M shares to market-cap milestones running to $8.5T, which aligns management with the narrative rather than with per-share cash flow; and a merger into SpaceX at its $2.1T first-day value would make Tesla holders owners of 43% of a $3.7T company with Starlink cash flows, against which a standalone sum of the parts is the wrong instrument. Against that, stock compensation runs at 4.2% of revenue and every tranche of the award is paid in shares. The margin of safety at $403.30 is negative and turns positive only below $115; between those levels the buyer is purchasing an option and should size it as one. [S132]

Confidence is high on the core-business value and low on the autonomy tree, which is why the price's dependence on it matters. What would settle it: a disclosed robotaxi revenue line with revenue and cost per mile; the Austin fleet count and utilisation; the market-cap and operational thresholds of each award tranche; capital expenditure guidance for 2026; and the exchange ratio the two special committees would accept."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 商业模式 Business Model (business_model, revision 6 by Fundamentals Analyst, 8,999 characters)
Tesla still makes most of its gross profit selling cars, but after regulatory credits the car business earns little at the operating line. Credits supplied 45.8% of FY2025 operating income and 15.7% in Q3 2026; incremental profit now comes from a 33.1%-margin energy-storage business and a 15.9%-margin services business while AI spending absorbs 86.9% of gross profit. Nine-month 2026 revenue of $78,669 million split into automotive $57,310 million (including $639 million of credits), energy $8,428 million and services $12,931 million, against an automotive share of 85.1% in FY2023. Q3 2026 gross profit divided $3,806 million automotive (69%), $954 million energy (17%) and $734 million services (13%), versus 91%/6%/3% in FY2023. Cash arrives when a vehicle changes hands, on storage milestones and prepayments ($3.30 billion of customer prepayments in deferred revenue at 2026-09-30, from $2.04 billion), and monthly for Supercharging, insurance and FSD [S3, S4, S6].

The credit franchise is ending. Tesla booked $2,763 million of automotive regulatory credits in FY2024, $1,993 million in FY2025 and $639 million in 9M 2026; Q3 2026 alone was $113 million, down 73% from $417 million. Credits carry no cost of revenue, so a credit dollar is nearly a dollar of operating profit: 20.1% of operating income in FY2023, 39.0% in FY2024, 45.8% in FY2025, 31.1% in 9M 2026 and 15.7% in Q3 2026. An implied Q4 2025 figure of $542 million shows the collapse came with the removal of the compliance obligation in 2026, not the lapse of the consumer credit: the Department of Transportation finalised its CAFE rollback on 2026-10-01, ending the requirement that made legacy automakers buy zero-emission credits. Without credits, FY2025's 4.6% operating margin is 2.5% and Q3 2026's 2.6% is 2.2% [S4, S64, S66].

Per vehicle the business improved even as credits disappeared. Q3 2026 automotive revenue per delivery excluding credits was $42,026, up 0.5%, while cost of revenue per delivery fell 2.7% to $34,436, so gross profit per vehicle rose 18.0% to $7,591 (18.1% margin) from $6,433 (15.4%). The gain is cost and regional mix, not price: management attributes the 270 basis points to a higher Asia-Pacific delivery mix, where Shanghai is the lowest-cost plant. Tesla does not disclose customer acquisition cost; SG&A per delivery of $4,142 is an upper bound carrying corporate and non-vehicle cost, and the first vehicle's gross profit covers 1.8 times it. A three-year LTV estimate of $8,455 adds three years of services gross profit per vehicle in the fleet ($288 a year on 10.2 million cumulative deliveries), giving LTV:CAC of 2.0:1 and payback inside the delivery quarter. Tesla is the only one of the three with positive per-vehicle gross profit after credits: BYD's automotive gross margin was 20.49% in FY2025, from 22.31%, and Rivian's automotive gross profit was a $(36) million loss in Q2 2026 [S63, S65, S68].
