Energy is the highest-margin dollar of growth. Storage revenue per GWh fell 23% to $210 million from $273 million, but gross profit per GWh fell only 19% to $69.6 million because cost per GWh fell 25% to $141 million, lifting segment margin to 33.1% from 31.4%. The mechanism is cell integration: the first Megapacks built with Tesla's own Nevada LFP cells shipped in Q3 2026, Megafactory Texas began production with 50 GWh of capacity, and the Megapack backlog is nearly sold out through 2027. Fluence earned 13.1% in FY2025; Tesla's advantage is owning the cell, not pricing. Part of the 33.1% is not repeatable: management attributed it partly to tariff refunds and cell-related warranty reimbursements. Services is the quieter engine: revenue rose 33% to $4,605 million on 2% fewer deliveries and gross margin reached 15.9% from 10.5%. Each extra $1 billion of energy revenue at 30% adds $300 million of gross profit; the same dollar of automotive revenue at 18% adds $180 million. FSD and software grow but remain too small to see in the income statement: active subscriptions rose to 1.74 million from 1.04 million, deferred revenue for FSD, connectivity and software was $4.08 billion against $3.87 billion at 2025-12-31, and obligations beyond one year were $10.73 billion, of which $4.80 billion falls due within twelve months. Management's claim that FSD is attached to more than 75% of North American deliveries is company-reported and cannot be tied to a revenue line, because Tesla does not disclose FSD revenue; the observable is $2,345 of deferred balance per active subscription, a stock rather than a price [S67, S4].

The newest change in money flows is who owns the asset. Selling a car converts inventory into revenue once; a robotaxi fleet keeps the vehicle on Tesla's balance sheet and earns per mile, shifting the model from a hardware sale to a utilisation business paid on hours operated, fares and uptime rather than deliveries. The Cybercab entered Tesla's own Austin fleet on 2026-09-03, but no fare revenue, fleet size or per-mile economics are disclosed, so the model cannot yet be tested. Until then the investable model remains the one in the tables: cars, storage and services.

Counter-case: gross margin improves while the company gets less profitable. Operating expenses of $4,776 million rose 39% against $5,494 million of gross profit, R&D alone rose 69% to $2,761 million, and depreciation rose 17% to $1,580 million and will accelerate as more than $20 billion of 2026 capital expenditure is commissioned. The warranty reserve rose 26% to $10,138 million on 2% fewer deliveries, with claims incurred up 29% to $1,614 million while the provision per delivery fell to $1,227 from $1,463. Inventory rose 13.7% to $14,092 million, with 11 days of vehicle supply. The vehicle line covers its own costs, so break-even is about the cost base: operating expenses of $4,776 million need $27.0 billion of revenue at a 17.7% blended margin, and Q3 2026 delivered $28.0 billion for $718 million of operating profit. Normalise energy to a 30% margin and take credits to zero and the quarter earns $515 million, a 1.8% operating margin. For a position, that argues for sizing on the energy and services annuity, with rising margins and a 2027 backlog, and treating autonomy as an option rather than earnings, because at a 1.8% margin the vehicle franchise cannot carry the cost base alone. Confidence is high on the segment arithmetic and medium on how much of the 2026 cost relief is structural rather than tariff and mix. Four diligence questions remain: what is the North American automotive margin excluding credits? What is the energy margin excluding tariff refunds, and at what price is the 2027 backlog contracted? Will Tesla disclose FSD revenue and robotaxi recognition? When do R&D and capital expenditure stop rising as a share of revenue? [S4, S6]

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 市场与行业分析 Market & Industry Analysis (market, revision 4 by Market Analyst, 8,747 characters)
Tesla's 2026-2028 demand is durable in Europe and grid storage and structurally weaker in the United States and China: the expiry of the US clean-vehicle credit on 2025-09-30 cut the US battery-electric share from 10% to 6% and lowered the underlying US growth rate rather than merely pulling sales forward, while China has become a shrinking unit market in which Tesla holds share instead of gaining it. That split constrains the investment case: no plausible US price action recovers the volume the credit used to buy, so growth has to come from a regulation in Europe and from data-centre load in storage, each durable for a different reason and on a different timetable [S98, S99, S101].

### The United States lost a level, not a quarter

Battery-electric vehicles were 6% of US light-duty sales in Q3 2026 against 10% in Q3 2025, and 6% in the first nine months against 8% a year earlier; in the luxury segment where Tesla's US mix sits, share fell from 31% to 12% while hybrids rose to 16%. A pull-forward would have produced recovery by Q2 2026; a year after expiry there is none, so the credit was creating demand, not borrowing it. Cox Automotive shows the mechanism and the size: the US new-EV average transaction price was $54,754 in August 2026, 2.8% lower year on year, with incentives at 12% of price, $6,594 per vehicle, and the EV premium over comparable petrol vehicles down to $4,847, or 9.7%. Manufacturers replaced 88% of the $7,500 credit with their own money and volume still fell 46.9% year on year in August to 78,895 units, a run-rate near 0.95 million units a year at 5.7% of new-vehicle sales. Tesla's own figures carry the same signal with a twist: US revenue fell 14.4% year on year in Q3 2026 to $12,495 million while global deliveries slipped only 2% to 486,532, but part of the gap is self-inflicted, because Model S and Model X were retired in mid-2026 and other-model deliveries halved to 8,295 from 15,933, $0.7 billion of the $2.1 billion decline. Strip that out and the US Model 3/Y business still shrank at a high-single-digit rate in a market that shrank faster, which is why Tesla's share of US EV sales rose to 51.7% in August 2026 [S98, S103, S4, S6].

### Europe offsets the US

EU battery-electric registrations reached 1,641,333 in January-August 2026, 21.7% of the market against 15.8% a year earlier, with France up 74.2% and Germany up 53.1%; hybrids took 36.6% and plug-in hybrids 10%. Tesla registered 153,978 cars in an 11-country panel in January-September 2026, up 51% from 102,025, and 45,523 in September alone, 4.6% of panel new-car sales against 2.6% a year earlier; the Model Y was the best-selling battery-electric model in September with 17,413 units against 8,227. The mechanism is a fleet-average CO2 mandate for 2025-2027 that makes battery volume the cheapest compliance route, reinforced in 2026 by the energy-price shock that lifted European electric-car sales close to 30% in the first quarter. The risk is timing: if the 2026 step is pre-compliance borrowing 2027 volume, 2027 will be flat, and hybrids at 36.6% show the mandate is being met partly without battery cars [S99, S104, S100].

### China is penetration without volume

New energy vehicles reached 65.1% of new passenger cars in China in July 2026 from 54% a year earlier, but NEV sales fell 12.5% in January-July and total passenger-car sales fell 20.3%, so the share gain is arithmetic on a shrinking denominator. Tesla sold 381,088 cars to Chinese buyers in January-September 2026, down 11.9%, in line with the market, and Giga Shanghai's September wholesale rose 5.0% to 95,366 only because exports jumped 58.3% to 30,529. Pricing moved in Tesla's favour for once: more than 15 Chinese automakers raised prices during 2026 as first-quarter industry margins fell to 3.2% and lithium costs rose 160%, ending the deflation that had squeezed every participant. China should be underwritten as a low-cost export base whose utilisation depends on demand outside China, not as a growth market for 2027-2028 [S101, S102, S105].

| Grid storage | 353.4 GWh (2026E) | +28%; 108 GW added in 2025, +40% | Entered; 36.0 GWh in 9M; Texas at 50 GWh | Cell tariffs under OBBBA; interconnection queues | CATL, BYD, Fluence, Sungrow | S106, S108, S4 |
| Robotaxi | $0.4-0.7B gross bookings (2026E) | growing from a small base | Entered: Austin; Cybercab from 2026-09-03 | State AV permits; city rules | Waymo, Zoox, Baidu Apollo Go, Pony.ai | S107, S6 |

Grid storage is the only pool growing faster than Tesla can supply it. 353.4 GWh of system deployments are expected in 2026, up 28% on 275.3 GWh in 2025, which at Tesla's realised $234 per kWh of energy revenue implies an $83 billion system market; global electric-car sales reach 23.0 million units in 2026, worth $950 billion at Tesla's realised $41,300 per unit, a 2024-2026 CAGR of 17% from the 16.7 million implied by the 20% gain in 2025. 108 GW of new battery storage was deployed worldwide in 2025, 40% more than in 2024, and Tesla deployed 36.0 GWh in the first nine months of 2026, 14% of the system market, against Megafactory Texas capacity of 50 GWh. The budget owner is a utility or independent power producer on a multi-year contract behind an interconnection queue, so demand is sticky but price-sensitive: Tesla's energy revenue fell 16% year on year in Q3 2026 on lower Megapack average selling prices and tariff refunds. Autonomous ride-hailing is still a rounding error: Waymo runs 3,000 vehicles and 500,000 paid rides a week, 26 million rides a year and $0.4-0.7 billion of gross bookings at a $15-25 fare, while Tesla had 44 active robotaxi vehicles across seven metros in the first half of 2026 before Cybercab rides began in Austin on 2026-09-03 [S106, S108, S4, S107, S6, S100].

The counter-case does not overturn the judgement: if US battery-electric share holds at its current level for four quarters, the credit will have been worth two-fifths of US demand, and a purpose-built Cybercab could compress cost per paid mile faster than Waymo's retrofit fleet, bringing the robotaxi market forward. Confidence is high on the US and European unit data, medium on China because retail and wholesale definitions diverge, and low on robotaxi because no operator discloses audited paid rides. Three open diligence questions remain: what did US battery-electric share print in September-October 2026? What share of Giga Shanghai output was exported in Q3 2026? What was Tesla's Megapack realised price per kWh excluding tariff refunds?

::: evidence
**US battery-electric demand stepped down to a new level after the credit expired and has not recovered a year later**

US BEV share of light-duty sales was 6% in Q3 2026 against 10% in Q3 2025, and 6% in the first nine months against 8%; the luxury segment fell from 31% to 12%. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 竞争格局 Competitive Landscape (competition, revision 3 by Market Analyst, 8,868 characters)
Tesla is gaining share in the markets that are shrinking and holding share in the one that is growing, so its vehicle advantage is compressing into a cost-and-brand moat rather than a technology lead, while in storage it is a scale follower to CATL and BYD and in paid autonomy it trails Waymo by more than an order of magnitude. The proof is in the three numbers together: a 51.7% share of US EV sales in August 2026, European registrations up 51% to 153,978 in January-September 2026, and Chinese retail sales down 11.9% to 381,088 against a market down 12.5%, so share improves while the absolute business outside Europe shrinks [S103, S104, S102].

### In the United States, Tesla wins by attrition

Tesla sold 40,816 EVs in August 2026 for 51.7% of US EV sales, up 3.4 points from July, in a market that fell 46.9% year on year to 78,895 units. The gains behind it were real but small: Toyota 4,964 units (+34.9% month on month), Chevrolet +30.3% and Cadillac +13.1%. Weaker EV programmes retreated after the credit expired and the survivor with the widest line and lowest cost took the share without cutting price. Rivian is the exception that could change the arithmetic: deliveries of its new mid-size SUV began in the second quarter of 2026 from a Normal, Illinois plant with 215,000 units of annual capacity [S103, S96].

### Europe is a battery-electric contest; China is a price contest

In an 11-country European panel Tesla registered 45,523 cars in September 2026 against BYD's 39,583, and on battery-electric only it led 30,317 to 7,498 in every one of those countries, while Chinese brands as a group took 14.9% of new cars against 8.0% a year earlier. BYD's route into Europe is powertrain breadth and price, not a better battery car, which makes it the most dangerous competitor over five years: it builds volume in the segments below Model Y and can move up. In China the contest is worse for Tesla: its Model Y sold more than 180,000 units from February to July 2026 at RMB 263,500-313,500 while Geely's Xingyuan sold nearly 197,500 at just under RMB 100,000 (~$14,820), and Tesla's domestic retail fell 11.9% while Shanghai's wholesale held only because exports rose 58.3% in September [S104, S101, S102].

### Pricing power is real in the premium band and absent below it

Cost of automotive sales was $16,570 million in Q3 2026 for 486,532 deliveries, $34,060 per vehicle, against automotive sales revenue of $41,300 per unit (up from $40,955) and automotive gross margin of 18.5%, up from 17.0%. That is a healthy margin at a premium price point, and it sits 2.3 times the retail price of China's volume bestseller, the cleanest measure of how far Tesla's cost base is from the low end. The margin is protected by mix and software rather than price: FSD (Supervised) subscriptions reached 1.74 million, services and other revenue rose 33% to $4,605 million, and energy gross margin reached 33.1%. A price war in the $25,000-35,000 band would be fought on a cost base Tesla cannot currently match [S4, S6, S101].

### Storage and autonomy are where the advantage is thinnest

In grid storage the pricing power sits with the cell makers: CATL shipped 125.0 GWh of energy-storage batteries in the first half of 2026, up 81%, for 27.1% of the global ESS battery market, while Tesla deployed 36.0 GWh in nine months and its energy revenue fell 16% year on year in Q3 2026 on lower Megapack average selling prices and tariff refunds. Tesla's differentiation is integration, grid-forming software and delivery speed rather than cell cost. In autonomy the gap is scale: Waymo runs 3,000 vehicles and 500,000 paid rides a week across 10 US cities, Baidu's Apollo Go operates in more than 10 Chinese cities, and Tesla had 44 active robotaxi vehicles across seven metros in the first half of 2026 before Cybercab rides began in Austin on 2026-09-03 [S81, S4, S107, S6].

| Grid battery storage | Tesla challenges | CATL: 27.1% of ESS cells | Tesla: 36.0 GWh in 9M 2026 | Fluence and Sungrow | Chinese LFP integrators | S81, S4 |

The counter-case is that Tesla is converting rather than losing advantage: its US and European share gains came while rivals retreated, automotive gross margin rose year on year, and the Chinese price war ended with more than a dozen automakers raising prices, removing the deflation that hurt it most. That reading is partly right and does not change the conclusion, because the share gains are in shrinking pools and the margin gain is mix-driven rather than price-driven. Confidence is high on the US and European share data, medium on the China comparison because retail and wholesale definitions differ, and low on the autonomy comparison because no operator discloses audited paid rides. Two diligence questions follow: what is Tesla's share of US EV sales in the fourth quarter of 2026 once Toyota's bZ and Chevrolet's Bolt ramp, and how much of BYD's European volume is plug-in hybrid under the 2027 CO2 review?

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 技术与产品 Technology & Product (technology_product, revision 4 by Product Analyst, 8,820 characters)
Tesla's technology is proven where it is a manufacturing problem — dry-electrode cells, Megapack integration — and unproven where the valuation sits. Its 2.0 million cumulative autonomous miles compare with Waymo's 500,000 paid rides a week, its 486,532 quarterly deliveries trail BYD's 762,478 electric cars, and its paid driverless permit exists in one state. The technology justifies a premium to a capital-intensive manufacturer in energy and process engineering; it does not yet justify the multiple of a software platform [S6, S59, S76].

### How FSD works, and where it stops

FSD (Supervised) is vision-only. Eight cameras feed an end-to-end neural network that outputs steering, acceleration and braking; it learns from video from a fleet of 10.2 million delivered vehicles and runs on Tesla's in-house inference silicon. There is no lidar, no radar and no pre-mapped corridors as Waymo has. Training runs on the Cortex clusters in Texas, with 400 MW of compute targeted by 2026-12-31. Two problems stay unsolved. The first is degradation detection when cameras are blinded by rain, fog or low sun: NHTSA's Engineering Analysis EA26002, opened 2026-03-19 over 13 crashes and 2.88 million vehicles, asks whether the system notices and warns the driver. The second is the reliability increment that permits removing the supervisor, which is why customer-owned unsupervised driving moved to Q2 2027 [S58, S80].

| Metric | Value | Method | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| FSD miles per major collision | 6,006,200 (North America, October 2026) | Company report, FSD-engaged miles | S58 |
| Cumulative unsupervised robotaxi miles | 2.0 million (to 2026-09-30) | Company quarterly update | S6 |
| FSD subscriptions and attach | 1.74 million; more than 75% of North American deliveries | Company KPI, excludes free trials | S6 |
| 4680 cell output and density | More than 1 million cells/week; more than 40 GWh; 272 Wh/kg | Giga Texas line data and teardown estimates | S56 |
| Energy storage deployed | 13.7 GWh (Q3 2026); 36.0 GWh (9M 2026) | Company KPI | S6 |
| Megapack segment gross margin | 33.1% (Q3 2026) | Segment accounts | S4 |

### Robotaxi: a real service, on one state's terms

Paid Cybercab rides began in Austin on 2026-09-03, and Tesla claimed 300-plus Cybercabs serving the city on 2026-10-10; Texas records showed 319 authorised Cybercab VINs. It has not disclosed fares, revenue or how many run without a monitor. Permits are the constraint: Texas allows self-certified commercial driverless operation under its 2026 law, while California lists Tesla Robotaxi LLC only for testing with a driver and omits it from the driverless-testing and deployment lists (2026-10-22). NHTSA's defect petition DP26010, opened 2026-10-09 on school-zone speeding, puts the monitored fleet at 1,000 vehicles. Set against Waymo's 500,000 paid rides a week, Tesla's robotaxi is a pilot; set against BYD's 762,478 quarterly BEVs, its car business is the higher-cost producer [S73, S74, S59, S76].

| Dimension | Tesla | Benchmark | What it means | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Autonomy sensing | Vision-only cameras, no lidar or radar | Waymo: lidar, radar, cameras and high-definition maps | Lower bill of materials, higher tail risk in bad weather | S59 |
| Weekly paid rides | Not disclosed | Waymo: 500,000 a week on a 4,000-vehicle fleet | At 5 miles a ride, Waymo runs 2.5 million rider-only miles weekly, more than Tesla's cumulative total | S59, S6 |
| Cell performance | 4680: 272 Wh/kg, 10-80% in 35-40 minutes | CATL Qilin 3 claims a full charge in six minutes | Tesla leads on cost, trails on density and charging | S56 |
| BEV volume, Q3 2026 | 486,532 units | BYD 762,478 passenger BEVs, +30.89% year over year | Cost leadership has moved to China | S76 |

### Cells: a cost moat, not a performance one

Giga Texas runs above one million 4680 cells a week at more than 40 GWh of installed capacity, and since January 2026 both electrodes use the dry process in production — a step CATL, Panasonic, LG and Samsung SDI have not taken to commercial scale. The economics are real: electrode cost 50% lower at full scale, 41% less line capex and more than 30% less factory energy. The product is not: energy density trails by 10-15%, charging is slower than Panasonic 2170 packs, yields above 90% sit below the 98% of mature producers, and Tesla still buys CATL LFP and Panasonic or LG 2170 cells for Shanghai and Fremont Model Y. Battery availability, not demand, remained the stated limit on 2026 volume [S56].

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why it is hard | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fleet data and training set | 7 | 10.2 million vehicles and billions of FSD miles, if compute and labelling keep pace | 3-4 years | S6 |
| Dry-electrode process | 7 | Both electrodes dry at more than 90% yield; no competitor at commercial scale | 3 years | S56 |
| Vertical integration (cells, packs, chips) | 6 | Process know-how and capital; AI6 foundry dependence caps it | 3-5 years | S6, S79 |
| Driverless permits | 4 | Texas self-certification is easy; California and the EU are not | 1-2 years Texas, 3+ California | S73 |
| **Composite** | **6/10** | A funded 50-person team would need 3 years for the cell line and 2 for Megapack integration; patents disclose little of either | **3 years of lead time** | S56, S73 |

### Patents: thin disclosure, deliberately

| Patent or application | Title | Jurisdiction | Filed | Granted | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Four international filings published 2026-04-16 | Optimus Gen 3 forearm, wrist, joint and hand assemblies | WIPO/PCT | Priority 2024-10-10 | — | Published, national phase pending | 22 degrees of freedom per hand, 25 forearm actuators, tendon-driven | S75 |
| US20260310299A1 | Flexible touch sensors for robotic hands | US | Not disclosed | — | Published 2025-10-08 | Tactile sensing for manipulation | S75 |
| Maxwell portfolio (acquired 2019, $235m) | Dry electrode manufacturing IP | US | Pre-2019 | Granted, owned | In force | Underpins the 4680 dry process | S56 |

The 10-K does not present patents as a competitive advantage; it rests the case on data, manufacturing cost and vertical integration. The Optimus filings show the limit: Musk said in April 2026 that the V3 hand would not use the patented design because it "ultimately didn't work", so the public record trails the programme.

### Product inventory

| Product | Stage | Launch | Revenue or share | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Model 3/Y | Commercial | 2017-2020 | $20.09bn automotive sales Q3 2026; 478,237 units (98.3%) | 18.5% total automotive | Next-generation platform, no date | S6, S76 |
| Cybercab and Robotaxi | Early commercial | 2026-09-03, Austin | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Unsupervised customer cars Q2 2027 | S6, S57 |
| Megapack, Megablock | Commercial | 2019; Megapack 3 in 2025 | $2.881bn segment Q3 2026 | 33.1% | Ramp 50 GWh Texas | S4, S6 |
| Optimus | Early production | 2026-10 | None | None | 20,000 units a week by end-2027, company claim | S57 |

### Energy is the proven technology

Megapack is the one line where Tesla holds a genuine integration advantage and prices it: 13.7 GWh deployed in Q3 2026, a 33.1% gross margin and record order rate and backlog, with 50 GWh of Texas capacity starting. Wood Mackenzie ranks Tesla second among storage integrators behind Sungrow. The counterweight is pricing: revenue fell 16% year over year to $2.881bn even as volume rose [S4, S72].

::: evidence
**The headline safety statistic is a company measurement, not an audited record.**

Tesla's October 2026 report puts FSD (Supervised) at 6,006,200 miles per major collision against 660,164 for US driving overall, but the ratio is not fault-based, comes from Tesla telemetry and has not been verified by the regulator, which is running an engineering analysis over 13 low-visibility crashes instead [S58, S80].
:::

### What would change the judgement

The strongest case against my caution is that FSD is already monetised: attach, subscriptions and deferred revenue all rose in Q3 2026, and services gross profit reached a record. Against it, repeated NHTSA recall campaigns on the 2026 Model Y show launch quality slipping on the highest-volume car, and the attach rate is North American only while China sales fell in Q3 2026 with FSD approval still pending.

Diligence questions: what did Austin earn per robotaxi per week, and how many Cybercabs ran without a monitor? What is blended pack cost per kWh? Does EA26002 end in a recall, and what would that do to the unsupervised release date? Until the first two are answered, Tesla owns the best-proven manufacturing technology in the sector and has not yet proven the one the share price pays for."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 发展方向与战略 Development Strategy (strategy, revision 3 by Product Analyst, 7,983 characters)
Tesla's strategy has become a capital-allocation bet rather than an operating one: more than $20bn of 2026 capex and $30bn of new credit facilities are committed to autonomy, robots and semiconductors while nine-month 2026 operating income of $2.06bn implies a return on invested capital near 3%, below any plausible cost of capital. The strategy earns its keep only if unsupervised robotaxi revenue arrives before 2028, and the 12-month test is customer-owned unsupervised driving in mid-2027, not another reveal [S4, S78].

### The plan and the return do not yet match

Tesla guided in the Q3 2026 filing to capital expenditure above $20bn for 2026, after spending $13.01bn in the first nine months against $6.13bn a year earlier, and in September 2026 signed three credit agreements for aggregate commitments of $30bn. Cash and short-term investments were $45.45bn at 2026-09-30 against $9.5bn of debt, so the plan is funded; it is no longer self-funding. Nine-month operating income of $2.06bn on $89.29bn of equity, annualised after tax over roughly $71bn of invested capital, gives a return near 3% — depressed by ramp assets, but low enough that every further billion of capex lowers the return until the new assets sell something [S6]. Research and development rose 69% year over year to $2.76bn in Q3 2026, most of it for autonomy and robotics.

### Pricing and mix are carrying the capex

| Item | Q3 2026 | Q3 2025 | Read | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Automotive gross margin | 18.5% | 17.0% | Cost cuts and mix offset lower prices | S4 |
| Regulatory credit revenue | $113m | $417m | A subsidy that no longer pays for the plan | S4 |
| Energy segment revenue | $2.881bn | $3.415bn | Volume up, price down | S4 |
| Services gross profit | $734m | $366m | FSD subscriptions and repair work | S6 |
| China deliveries | 142,133 | 16% lower year over year | Share loss in the largest market | S77 |
| Total deliveries | 486,532 | 497,099 | Flat volume on an ageing core line-up | S6 |

The read is that Tesla is funding autonomy from a mature car business, a fading credit stream and a fast-growing but deflating storage business; none of the three is a rising price. The Semi is a logical adjacency because it shares cells, motors and Megachargers with the core; Optimus is not an adjacency yet, because it has a production line and no customer.

### Milestones: what has actually shipped

| Milestone | Target date | Status at 2026-10-29 | What it proves | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cybercab in the Austin robotaxi fleet | 2026 | Met: paid rides from 2026-09-03 | Hardware and a Texas permit | S6 |
| Customer-owned unsupervised FSD | Q4 2026, now Q2 2027 | Slipped by about two quarters | Converts the owner fleet into robotaxi supply without capex | S57 |
| Optimus production | 2026 | Met: early production from 2026-10-21 | Manufacturing readiness, not demand | S6 |
| Optimus at 20,000 units a week | End-2027 | Company claim, no unit count disclosed | Whether a humanoid is a product | S57 |
| Tesla Semi volume production | 2026 | Met: Nevada high-volume line | Entry into Class 8 trucking | S6 |
| Next-generation affordable platform | Not dated | Not publicly disclosed | The volume and cost reset | S6 |
| 400 MW of training compute | 2026-12-31 | 225 MW installed (Cortex 1 and 2) | Whether the compute constraint eases | S6 |
| Austin Fab equipment commissioning | 2027 | Under construction | Vertical integration into silicon | S6 |
| FSD approval in China | Not dated | Pending; CFO negotiating | Monetising the largest market | S77 |
| Megafactory Texas at 50 GWh | 2026-2027 | Production began Q3 2026 | Energy scale-up | S6 |

### Partners: concentration, not diversification

| Partner | Scope | Signed | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Samsung Electronics | AI6 foundry at Taylor, Texas; $16.5bn through 2033 | 2025-07-28 | AI5 taped out on 2nm in July 2026; AI6 to follow | S79 |
| CATL | LFP cells for Shanghai vehicles and storage | Not disclosed | Active | S56 |
| Panasonic, LG Energy Solution | 2170 cells for Fremont and Shanghai | Not disclosed | Active | S56 |
| xAI, then SpaceX | $2bn xAI investment converted into SpaceX Class A shares after SpaceX acquired xAI | 2026-01; converted 2026-02 | Stake held; a merger is openly discussed | S78 |
| Maxwell Technologies | Dry-electrode intellectual property acquired for $235m | 2019 | Integrated into 4680 production | S56 |

The partner map shows the strategic risk: Tesla's autonomy roadmap runs through a single foundry for AI6, its vehicles still depend on CATL, Panasonic and LG for cells, and its largest related-party exposure is to companies its chief executive also controls.

### Geography: China becomes an export base

Tesla's China sales fell 16% year over year in Q3 2026 to 142,133 units while Giga Shanghai exports reached a record 132,978; retail sales for 2026 to date are down 12% as exports doubled, and Beijing cuts the EV export tax rebate in April 2027. Shanghai, with more than 950,000 units of capacity, is now a cost and export base rather than a growth market, exposed to tariffs in the markets it ships to. Berlin set a production record and the US business carries the FSD attach rate, which is why the company's own numbers look better in North America than in the two regions that decide its cost base [S77, S76, S102].

### Energy is where the strategy is working

The energy plan is coherent and funded: 50 GWh of Megafactory Texas capacity started in Q3 2026 alongside 40 GWh in California and 20 GWh in Shanghai, with 7 GWh of Nevada LFP cell capacity in early ramp and the first Megapacks built from Tesla-made cells. Record order rate and backlog, a 33.1% segment gross margin and data-centre demand give the capital a return that autonomy does not yet. The tension is that revenue fell 16% year over year to $2.881bn even as volume rose, so the plan is adding capacity into falling prices [S6, S72].

### The capital allocation question

In January 2026 Tesla invested $2bn in xAI; the stake became SpaceX Class A shares when SpaceX acquired xAI in February 2026, and the Q1 2026 cash flow statement records a $2.002bn purchase of SpaceX equity. Three of nine directors have SpaceX ties, the 2026 proxy is set for a 2026-12-03 meeting, and the 2025 CEO award pays out on a deal price without operational milestones — only one of twelve operational milestones is rated probable, leaving $105.8-120.4bn of unrecognised stock compensation. A shareholder is no longer buying only a car and storage company; a merger scenario makes the position a bet on Musk's wider portfolio, which argues for a smaller size [S78].

### What must be true in 12 months

Three signposts decide whether the strategy is earning its cost of capital. First, unsupervised driving in customer-owned cars in at least one US state by 2027-06-30, with robotaxi revenue disclosed separately — without it, the capex is a subsidy to a pilot. Second, energy gross margin holding above 25% once tariff refunds lapse and 50 GWh of Texas capacity ramps, which tests whether Megapack has pricing power or is a commodity. Third, capital discipline: 2027 capex at or below $25bn with positive free cash flow, rather than a further draw on the $30bn facilities. The counter-case is strong: FSD attach above 75% in North America, 1.74 million subscriptions, a record energy backlog and $45.45bn of cash mean the plan can be funded through a slip, and Q3 2026 free cash flow of $1.53bn shows the core still generates cash [S6, S57].

Diligence questions: what is the 2027 capex number and how much of it is contractually committed? What revenue did robotaxi and FSD each earn in Q3 2026? Will the December 2026 meeting put a SpaceX transaction to a shareholder vote, and on what terms? My confidence is high that the strategy is funded and well-resourced for energy, medium that autonomy revenue arrives before 2028, and low that a humanoid robot contributes to profit before 2029."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 公司概览 Company Overview (company_overview, revision 3 by Company Analyst, 8,868 characters)
Tesla is a single-class Texas corporation whose control rests on a 19.8% CEO stake plus a 423.7 million-share contingent award, so a public-equity holder is underwriting Elon Musk's capital allocation rather than a board-governed company; that is acceptable at a governance discount, not a premium. Tesla, Inc. was incorporated in Delaware on 2003-07-01, converted to Texas on 2024-06-13, and trades on Nasdaq under TSLA with one class of common stock and 3,952,648,559 shares outstanding at 2026-09-30, including 423,743,904 unearned restricted shares. There is no VIE, nominee-shareholder or red-chip layer [S3].

::: kpi
| Metric | Value | Benchmark | Signal | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| CEO economic stake | 19.8% (699,580,882 shares) | Ford family: 40% of votes on 2% of shares | warn | S5, S95 |
| Contingent CEO award | 423,743,904 shares, 10.7% of outstanding | 2018 award: 286,428,773 shares | critical | S5 |
| Unrecognised compensation on that award | $9.74bn probable; $105.82bn-$120.37bn not | $162m recognised in 2025 | critical | S4 |
| Cash and short-term investments | $45.45bn at 2026-09-30 | 2026 capex guided above $20bn | good | S6 |
| Insider activity, 12 months | -$87.69m sales, zero open-market purchases | one-sided tape | warn | S27 |
:::

### The entity map is clean; the asset ring-fence is not

| Entity | Jurisdiction | Role | Ownership | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Tesla, Inc. | Texas | Listed parent and principal operating company | 100% | S3, S5 |
| Tesla Robotaxi, LLC | Texas | Robotaxi operating entity | 100% listed subsidiary | S3 |
| Tesla Energy Operations, Inc. | Delaware | Energy generation and storage operations | 100% listed subsidiary | S3 |
| Tesla Manufacturing Brandenburg SE | Germany | Berlin vehicle plant | 100% listed subsidiary | S3 |
| Tesla (Shanghai) Co., Ltd | China | Shanghai plant and China sales, wholly foreign-owned | 100% listed subsidiary | S3 |

EX-21 states no ownership percentages, so the ownership column above is inferred from listing rather than disclosed. China is a wholly foreign-owned enterprise, not a VIE, so there is no contractual-control gap, but Shanghai is fully consolidated and exposed to export controls. No entity is designated holder of Full Self-Driving or Optimus intellectual property: robotaxi operations sit in Tesla Robotaxi, LLC while software, data and chip designs stay in the parent, so no separately capitalised autonomy asset exists.

### Customers, buyers and how growth arrives

Tesla sells direct in two segments: automotive at $69,526m of 2025 revenue and energy at $12,771m [S71]. The vehicle buyer is a household or fleet paying cash or Tesla financing; the energy buyer is a utility or developer signing multi-year procurement, with 33.1% gross margin in Q3 2026 against 18.5% for automotive. Growth now comes from storage, software (1.74 million FSD subscriptions) and paying Cybercab rides in Austin since 2026-09-03.

### Ownership is concentrated without a dual class

| Holder | Class | Shares | % ownership | % votes | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Elon Musk | Common, incl. 286,428,773 restricted | 699,580,882 | 19.8% | 19.8% | S5 |
| Elon Musk, pledged as collateral | Common | 207,498,721 | 5.2% of outstanding | 5.2% | S5 |
| Vanguard Capital Management | Common | 210,796,512 | 5.3% | 5.3% | S5 |
| Unearned 2025 award shares | Restricted, unearned | 423,743,904 | 10.7% of outstanding | proportional to other shares | S5 |
| Other public holders | Common | balance | 74.9% | 74.9% | S5 |

Percentages follow the proxy, whose denominator excludes unearned award shares; free float is capped by the Musk and Vanguard stakes shown, and a margin call on the pledged block would add supply at the worst moment. With one class and no super-voting stock, control runs through the CEO office, the board seat and stake size rather than a charter provision, unlike Ford's dual-class family control or Alphabet's founder shares.

### Control is priced through a contingent award

The 2025 CEO Performance Award is the control instrument: 423,743,904 shares in 12 tranches of 35,311,992, each tied to a market-capitalisation milestone from $2.0 trillion to $8.5 trillion and to 1 of 12 operational milestones (20 million vehicles, 10 million FSD subscriptions, 1 million bots, 1 million robotaxis, Adjusted EBITDA of $50bn to $400bn); none was earned at 2026-10-19 [S5]. At $2.0 trillion the first tranche implies $506 per share on 3.95 billion shares, and because the operational test falls away in a change of control, a deal at $3.0 trillion would earn three tranches, 105.9 million shares, with no robotaxi or Optimus milestone met. Expense is already running: $802m in the first nine months of 2026, $9.74bn unrecognised on the one milestone management judges probable, and $105.82bn-$120.37bn on the rest [S4]. Dilution of 10.7% is designed, not tail, and sits above the current valuation rather than beside it.

### The board can refuse less than it appears

Nine directors sit in three classes, six labelled independent under Nasdaq rules, with Robyn Denholm as chair since November 2018. Ira Ehrenpreis, who chairs both the compensation and the nominating and governance committees, joined SpaceX's board in February 2026; Kimbal Musk is the CEO's brother; JB Straubel, a director, runs Redwood Materials, a Tesla supplier. Related-party flows are small in dollars but pointed: Tesla agreed on 2026-01-16 to invest $2.00bn in xAI, converted into SpaceX Class A stock when SpaceX bought xAI on 2026-02-02 and funded on 2026-03-12, while xAI bought $430.1m of Megapacks and SpaceX bought $143.3m of vehicles in 2025. A board setting a Tesla-SpaceX exchange ratio would do so with three of nine directors tied to SpaceX, and the retail auto-voting programme in the 2026 proxy offers standing instructions to vote with the board outside a defined special matter [S78]. The counterweight is narrow: the Special Committee used only Denholm and Wilson-Thompson, and 78.2% of votes cast backed 2025 pay.

### Capital allocation has no return floor

Tesla has never paid a dividend, repurchased no shares in 2025, and holds no authorisation to offset dilution. It ended 2026-09-30 with $45.45bn of cash and short-term investments, generated $14.90bn of operating cash flow in nine months against $13.01bn of capex, guided 2026 capex above $20bn, and signed three credit agreements with $30bn of commitments in September 2026 [S6]. Against Ford and GM, which return cash, Tesla offers neither dividend nor buyback, so the capital returned to holders is zero while insiders realise value through equity sales. Litigation moved rather than vanished: the Delaware Supreme Court reinstated the 2018 award on 2025-12-19, the 96,000,000-share interim award was forfeited on 2026-04-21, and a securities class action filed on 2025-08-04 in the Western District of Texas covers purchasers from 2023-04-19 to 2025-06-22 over Autopilot, FSD and Robotaxi statements.

A multi-year holder is paid for four things: a contingent award that accelerates on a deal price rather than operating proof; conflict committees that include SpaceX-affiliated directors; new debt against a thin free-cash-flow buffer; and key-person concentration in a CEO who also runs SpaceX. Three conditions would change this judgement — an independent special committee for any SpaceX transaction, no change-of-control acceleration without operating milestones, and a buyback sized to offset stock compensation. None appears in the 2026 proxy, so the governance discount stays. Confidence is high on structure, medium on how a Texas court would treat a challenge to the award; diligence should ask for the pledge's loan-to-value.

Tesla's execution machine still ships, but the bench beneath Elon Musk has thinned to three named executive officers and at least 17 senior departures since April 2024, so a four-front roadmap in vehicles, energy, autonomy and robots rests on one man and a handful of engineers paid to stay rather than on a management team that could be handed the plan. The disclosed leadership is Musk (CEO and Technoking, age 55), Vaibhav Taneja (CFO since August 2023) and Xiaotong (Tom) Zhu (SVP APAC and Global Vehicle Manufacturing since June 2025), with no chief operating officer, president or segment chief between them and a nine-person board. Salaries are $400,000 for Taneja and $364,338 for Zhu, and Musk has taken none since 2019, so retention runs through equity, not cash [S5].

On execution the record is binary rather than average. Tesla produced its 10 millionth vehicle in Q3 2026, began volume production of the Semi, started Megafactory Texas and put Optimus onto a high-volume line at Fremont; Q3 2026 deliveries were 486,532, down 2% year on year, with 13.7 GWh of storage deployed and 1.74 million active FSD subscriptions [S6]. The 4680 cell gives the counter-rhythm: dry-electrode production for both anode and cathode arrived only with the Q4 2025 update, five years after the Battery Day target, and management still called battery availability the limiting factor for vehicle volumes in Q3 2026. Tesla solves hard manufacturing problems and solves them late, so a roadmap that now includes Cybercab, Optimus, a lithium refinery, an AI6 chip programme and Megafactory Texas should be discounted on that lag rather than on the best-case line.

Turnover is the counter-evidence, and it clusters where the growth story sits. At least 17 senior leaders left between April 2024 and 2026-10-15: the Cybercab programme lost its program manager (Victor Nechita, February 2026), its new-product-introduction head (Michael So, April 2026), two assembly leaders and the director who built robotaxi software (Thomas Dmytryk, March 2026); energy lost vice president Mike Snyder on 2026-10-15, succeeded by AJ Booth; finance lost Sendil Palani after 17 years in March 2026; and sales lost two North American chiefs in a year, including Raj Jegannathan in February 2026 [S93]. Internal promotion is real — Joe Ward went from European operations to global sales chief in February 2026 — but the pattern is that programme leaders are replaced by narrower specialists while the number of programmes grows.

The autonomy bench rests on one person. Ashok Elluswamy joined in 2014 as the first Autopilot engineer, led the removal of radar, built the end-to-end FSD architecture and now runs FSD, Robotaxi software and Optimus AI, plus a joint project with xAI; he holds none of the disclosed executive-officer titles, so he appears in neither the proxy ownership table nor the summary compensation table [S94]. Losing him would hit three programmes at once, and the retention tools available are the same volatile equity that has already seen software and AI staff leave for OpenAI and rivals. Depth is real in manufacturing — the Semi and Megafactory ramps show an operations bench that can still deliver — but the layer where autonomy and energy execution actually happens has lost the people who built it.

Founder-market fit is strongest where the problem is physics and manufacturing, weakest where it is regulated operations. Musk's career — Zip2 and PayPal sold to Compaq and eBay, then SpaceX and Tesla built from near-zero — is a serial-building record, and the full vesting of his first performance award is the market's own evidence that he hits market-capitalisation and operating targets. The gaps are structural: a chief operating officer who could own delivery across four programmes, a robotics manufacturing executive with volume experience, a regulatory leader able to win driverless approvals in the European Union and China, and an enterprise energy sales organisation that converts a record order book into contracted revenue. None of those roles appears in the proxy, so each is either unfilled or sits below the executive-officer line, and both readings raise execution risk at the scale the valuation implies.

| Fundraising and capital | Defines the story investors fund | Closed 2026 refinancing and $30bn of commitments | Regional banking relationships | None disclosed | Concentrated in two people | S4, S5 |

The judgement is a conditional, not a rejection. Tesla's engineering culture has repeatedly converted improbable hardware into shipping product, and the board has paid to keep the one person who drives that conversion. What it has not built is an organisation that can lose him, or lose the programme leaders beneath him, without slowing. An investor holding through the robotaxi and Optimus ramp should size for announcement risk and ask three questions: who owns delivery of each programme if Musk or Elluswamy is unavailable, what retention has been granted below the executive-officer line, and whether the Cybercab departures reflected a programme reset the company has not disclosed. Confidence is high on team composition and the departure record, medium on what that turnover implies for 2027 timelines, because Tesla does not disclose programme-level staffing.

::: evidence
**Strongest proof the team can execute** is the compounding of hard manufacturing inside one quarter: 10.2 million cumulative vehicles, a Semi line running, Megafactory Texas in production, Optimus on a high-volume line and paying Cybercab rides, with 1.74 million FSD subscriptions and 13.7 GWh of storage alongside them [S6].

**Strongest doubt** is that the same quarter produced a 2% delivery decline while the Cybercab programme lost four leaders and energy lost its vice president two weeks before this report, so the programmes that must justify the valuation are the ones losing the people who built them, and the CEO who would absorb their decisions also runs SpaceX [S93].

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## ESG评估 ESG Assessment (esg, revision 2 by Regulatory Analyst, 8,486 characters)
Tesla's policy position has inverted. The 2025-2026 reset removes a high-margin revenue stream worth $2,763m at its 2024 peak and leaves the robotaxi licence to operate fragmented across US states and unapproved in China, while the offsetting upsides — federal AV preemption and tariffs on Chinese rivals — are real but not yet law. Automotive regulatory credit revenue fell from $2,763m in 2024 to $1,993m in 2025 (-28%) and to $113m in Q3 2026 from $417m (-73%); because credits carry almost no cost of revenue, total automotive gross margin fell from 18.4% to 17.8% in 2025, partly on the $770m decline. The credit-free margin is the right base. [S3, S4]

### The credit pool has already collapsed

The US instrument is unambiguous. Section 30D's $7,500 new clean vehicle credit applied only to vehicles acquired on or before 2025-09-30; the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, enacted 2025-07-04, terminated it and the used-vehicle 25E credit thereafter. The 2026 revision is a repeal, not a tightening: EPA's final rule of 2026-02-18 rescinds the 2009 endangerment finding and repeals the light-, medium- and heavy-duty GHG standards, and the Department of Transportation finalised its CAFE rollback on 2026-10-01. Both remove the compliance demand that priced Tesla's credits and slow competitors' EV mix; EIA reported on 2026-10-19 that battery-electric sales remained lower after the credit expired. California's ACC II and the Section 177 states preserve a partial market, not the 2024 price level. [S117, S116, S64, S98]

### The robotaxi licence is a state-by-state binary

Autonomy is the part of the equity value policy can switch on or off, and the record is narrower than the narrative. Texas requires a TxDMV authorisation for commercial SAE Level 4/5 operation from 2026-05-28 under SB 2807 — a no-fee, non-expiring registration regime, which is why Austin scaled first. California is the opposite: CPUC's AV permit table lists Waymo, Zoox, Nuro, WeRide and Tensor but not Tesla, and Tesla's California service runs under a non-AV limousine/TCP authority. Federally the binding constraint is enforcement — NHTSA's FSD probes and the October 2026 school-zone review — while the preemption fix, H.R. 7390 SELF DRIVE Act of 2026, advanced only from a House subcommittee on a 12-11 party-line vote on 2026-02-10. Waymo holds a CPUC driverless permit and Zoox a federal exemption granted 2026-07-31; Tesla is first on neither. [S118, S119, S80, S125]

### China taxes the base; Europe protects it for now

China policy has become a tax on Tesla's largest manufacturing base. From 2026-01-01 to 2027-12-31 the NEV purchase tax is halved rather than exempt — an effective 5%, capped at RMB 15,000 per car — regressive for Tesla's higher-priced trims and landing alongside a 16% fall in Q3 2026 China sales, a cut in the vehicle export rebate and no unsupervised FSD approval. Europe is the exception: Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2754 has imposed a countervailing duty on China-built BEVs since 2024-10-30 for five years, at 7.8% for Tesla Shanghai against 35.3% for SAIC, on top of the 10% common duty — 17.8% versus 45.3% for Chinese brands. That room is time-limited: the EU softened 2025-2027 CO2 compliance to a three-year average and proposed the same for 2030-2032, reducing legacy makers' urgency to buy credits. [S124, S77, S127, S126]

### Governance is the largest ESG item

Governance is the largest ESG item because it changes the share count and the cost of capital. The 2025 CEO Performance Award covers 423.7m shares in 12 tranches, approved on 2025-11-06, with $105.82-120.37bn of unrecognised stock compensation for milestones not yet probable and $10.23bn for the one deemed probable — at the low end 10.7% of the 3.95bn shares outstanding. Capital allocation matters more than pay design: Tesla invested $2.0bn in xAI Holdings in January 2026 and, after SpaceX acquired xAI Holdings on 2026-02-02, converted that right into SpaceX Class A stock in March 2026. Musk holds 19.8% and 207.5m shares are pledged. Seven of nine directors are independent and one share carries one vote, but a governance discount is warranted. [S5, S3]

### What is not financially material

Three ESG claims do not survive contact with the financials. Tesla's own operational footprint is small relative to the use-phase emissions its products avoid, and the 2025 10-K discloses no material environmental proceeding; the real exposure is upstream, in battery materials, where Tesla files an annual conflict-minerals report but discloses no supplier-level exposure. Labour and product safety are tails: the California Civil Rights Department trial is set for 2026-07-20, and the August 2025 Autopilot verdict was $129m compensatory with Tesla 33% at fault plus $200m punitive, against an immaterial accrual. The strongest counter-evidence runs the other way — the US tariff wall on Chinese-built EVs, the EU's relative tariff advantage, possible federal AV preemption and performance-contingent pay — which is why policy is a discount on the multiple, not an exit signal. [S3, S5]

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 退出策略分析 Exit Strategy Analysis (exit, revision 3 by Valuation Analyst, 8,315 characters)
Tesla offers no cash exit at $1.59 trillion. It has never paid a dividend, has no repurchase authorisation, and its entire $45.4B of cash and short-term investments would retire 2.85% of the 3.953B shares outstanding. The largest buyout ever completed — Electronic Arts at $55B in August 2026 — is 3.4% of Tesla's market capitalisation, so no financial sponsor can write this cheque, and no automaker can either: GM and Ford together are $118.4B, 7.4% of Tesla. What remains is a sale into a market that trades $14.0B of Tesla a day, or a share exchange into SpaceX, and both leave the return hostage to a re-rating that five years have not delivered. [S3, S130]

### The company returns nothing, and cannot return much

Tesla's 10-K states that it has never declared or paid a cash dividend, does not anticipate doing so, and purchased no equity securities in fiscal 2025. Trailing free cash flow of $3,303M is a 0.2% yield on the capitalisation, and nine-month capital expenditure of $13,014M runs at 2.1x depreciation: the cash is going into factories, cells and training compute, not to holders. Against GM's 12.4% total shareholder yield and Ford's 5.9%, Tesla's is zero. Even a maximal buyback using the whole cash pile would move the share count by less than three points, and it would leave a company spending $17B a year on capital projects with no liquidity buffer. Capital return is a governance choice, and the controlling shareholder has consistently chosen reinvestment. [S6]

### The exit that always works is the tape

The secondary market is the only channel that is always open. Tesla trades 36.96M shares and $14.0B a day over twenty days, so a $500M position is 3.6% of a single day's value and no holder is trapped by liquidity. Short interest of 69.35M shares, 2.19% of the float and 2.2 days to cover, means the marginal seller is not fighting a crowded short either. Passive ownership is a flow that follows the index and the price rather than a bid that supports it; Tesla's exact float-adjusted S&P 500 weight is not disclosed in the sources retrieved, and after the top ten names reached 39.03% of the index on 2026-10-10 the marginal index buyer is a shrinking share of demand. [S15, S114]

### No control buyer exists, at any price

A cash takeover is arithmetically out of reach. The pieces themselves are worth $170B on the sum of the parts — vehicles at 1.0x sales, energy at 3.5x, net cash at book — and a control buyer for those assets alone would pay $200-250B with a premium, which is one-eighth of the current capitalisation and therefore not a route to today's price. Alphabet, at $3,493.5B, is the only US company with the balance sheet to write a $1.6T cheque, and it is the closest competitor in autonomous driving, which makes antitrust the binding constraint rather than price. Musk's 19.8% stake and 207.5M pledged shares mean nothing happens without him, and a hostile approach is legally and financially impossible at this size. [S5, S6]

| Secondary sale | NasdaqGS | $14.0B daily turnover; no lock-up for public holders | Continuous | High | S15 |

| Cash take-private | None identified | $1,594.1B is 29x the largest LBO on record ($55B) | None | Very low | S130 |
| Acquisition by an automaker | GM, Ford | Combined market cap $118.4B, 7.4% of Tesla | None | Very low | S17, S19 |
| Acquisition by a platform company | Alphabet | $3,493.5B market cap, but antitrust in autonomy | None | Very low | S113 |
| Buyback or dividend | Tesla | No programme; no dividend ever declared | None | Very low | S3 |

### The one live route is a share exchange with SpaceX

On 2026-10-21 both boards formed special committees to explore a combination, days after Musk called the idea a "good idea" on the third-quarter earnings call. SpaceX listed on 2026-06-12 at $135 a share and a $1.77T valuation, reached $2.1T on its first day, and the combined group would be worth well over $3 trillion. At those marks Tesla holders would own 43% of the equity — but they would exchange one-share-one-vote stock for a company where super-voting shares give Musk about 84% of the vote, against 20% at Tesla. That is the governance price of the only transformative exit available, and it is being negotiated by two boards that have not historically pushed back: Tesla invested $2B in xAI after its chair expressed scepticism, and it rescued SolarCity in 2016. [S129, S128]

### What would make the exit valuable, and what stands in the way

The counter-case deserves weight. A negotiated combination would carry a premium to the undisturbed price, and a holder who sells into it captures that premium without waiting for a re-rating; SpaceX's Starlink cash flows are real, so the merged entity would have earnings that Tesla alone does not; and if the ratio is struck on market values, a Tesla holder participates in that cash flow from day one. The risk is that the ratio, not a cash price, is what gets negotiated, and that a controlled board sets it. The 2025 CEO Performance Award reinforces the point: its change-of-control terms let unearned shares vest on market-capitalisation milestones alone, so the controlling shareholder's incentive in a sale is to maximise the headline value, not the terms minority holders receive. [S5, S122]

For a public-equity holder the practical conclusion is that monetisation is a sale into the secondary market at whatever multiple prevails, with a merger into SpaceX as the only event that could produce a premium, and no dividend, no buyback and no cash bid to fall back on. Confidence is high that no cash exit exists and medium on the merger: the talks are exploratory and no ratio, premium or timetable has been disclosed. What would settle it: the exchange ratio and voting structure the committees propose; whether SpaceX's segment financials are published before a vote; the treatment of unvested award shares in a combination; the lock-up and index terms for the combined entity; and whether any special committee obtains an independent fairness opinion that values Tesla on a sum of the parts rather than on the combined-company narrative."}],"isError":false}

consensus.consensus: The market and the sell side treat Tesla as an autonomy platform: the consensus target is $417.94 on a $66-$600 range, and 2027 EPS of $2.20 is paid 183 times, which assumes robotaxi and FSD revenue arrive on schedule.
consensus.our_view: We think the price already embeds the dominant autonomy outcome at certainty: the core business plus net cash is $42.50 a share and our probability-weighted value is $115.
consensus.evidence: Only 2.0 million cumulative unsupervised miles and one city of paid robotaxi service exist against the 15.7 million robotaxis the reverse DCF needs; credits have gone and the ex-credit operating margin is 2.2%; the core sum of the parts sits near Morgan Stanley's independent $47 core estimate [S15, S120, S4, S6, S64].

one_question.question: What did Tesla's robotaxi fleet earn per vehicle per week in Q3 2026, and how many Cybercabs ran without a monitor?
one_question.why: It is the only test that converts the $356 a share the market pays for autonomy into a business: at $0.60 a mile and 60,000 miles a vehicle a year the price needs 15.7 million robotaxis, and disclosed revenue per vehicle would show whether the economics scale from 319 authorised Cybercabs or stop at a pilot [S6, S120, S4].

arguments.analogs: Waymo's $126 billion round in February 2026 prices a scaled driverless operator at 2.8 times its 2024 mark (S120). The SpaceX listing on 2026-06-12 at $1.77 trillion, $2.1 trillion on day one, is the template for a Musk-sponsored combination (S128). {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## 融资历程与估值 Funding History & Valuation (funding_valuation, revision 7 by Valuation Analyst, 8,492 characters)
At $403.30 (NasdaqGS, 2026-10-29 20:00 UTC) Tesla's equity is worth $1,594.1B and its enterprise value $1,558.0B. On a sum of the parts, 89% of that price — $1,424B, or $356 a share — buys autonomy and robotics, while the automotive, energy and services businesses plus $36.2B of net cash are worth a computed $42.50 a share at peer multiples. That residual is 11.3 times the $126B at which Waymo raised $16B in February 2026, and Waymo is the only operator running a scaled driverless service. My probability-weighted value is $115 a share, 71% below the close, and the disagreement is not about cars: my $42.50 for the core sits within $5 of Morgan Stanley's $47 a share for the same business. It is about whether 2.0M cumulative unsupervised miles, a robotaxi service confined to one city and zero disclosed Optimus revenue can carry $1.4 trillion. [S15, S120, S6]

### A five-year flat line and a violent quarter

The price has gone nowhere over the period shown below and has lagged the index; the last quarter reversed part of that lag, a window that contains the third-quarter results and the merger remarks Musk made on the same earnings call.

### 443 times trailing earnings, 183 times 2027 consensus

On trailing figures Tesla trades at 443.2x earnings, 15.0x sales and 170.5x EBITDA — or 104x on the company's own $15.0B adjusted EBITDA, which excludes $4.3B of stock compensation. The six-company peer median is 16.5x earnings and 5.0x sales. Consensus that already assumes a robotaxi ramp barely normalises the multiple: 2026 revenue of $108.5B and EPS of $1.67 give 241x, and 2027 revenue of $123.9B and EPS of $2.20 give 183x. [S115] Tesla's own history does not support the level either: the P/E at the last five fiscal year ends was 72.8x (2021), 34.0x (2022), 57.8x (2023), 204.6x (2024) and 420.8x (2025), so today sits above every year-end mark in the series.

### Sum of the parts: $42.50 of business, $356 of promise

Trailing-twelve-month segment data from the Q3 2026 update: automotive revenue $75.0B at a 19.1% gross margin, energy $12.3B at 29.7%, services $16.3B at 12.4%, sharing $16.5B of operating expense. The base case's $259B of autonomy value is an explicit tree: $40B if robotaxi stays regional (35% probability), 1.0x Waymo at $126B (40%), $600B at scale (20%) and $1,500B on global dominance in robotaxi and humanoids (5%). ### The reverse DCF needs sixteen million robotaxis

At a 10% WACC and 3% terminal growth, crediting $2.0B of free cash flow in 2027 and 45% annual growth to 2031, today's enterprise value requires $141B of free cash flow in 2031. At 9% the requirement falls to $118B; at 11% it rises to $164B. At a 15% FCF margin — generous for a capital-intensive manufacturer — that is $940B of 2031 revenue, nine times trailing revenue. If the incremental profit came from robotaxi at a 25% FCF margin it implies $564B of robotaxi revenue; at $0.60 a mile and 60,000 miles a vehicle a year, that is 15.7M robotaxis, or 7.8M if the car and energy businesses supply half the cash flow. Tesla's installed automotive capacity is 2.5M vehicles a year. The price assumes a fleet that six years of full capacity could not build, earning a revenue per mile no disclosed Tesla service charges. [S4, S6]

### What the street pays for, and what would prove it right

The consensus twelve-month target is $417.94 from 40 analysts, 3.6% above the close, with a range from $66 to $600. Short interest is 69.35M shares, 2.19% of the float, 2.2 days to cover, so there is no crowded short to squeeze and no positioning signal either way. Management publishes no numeric guidance: the outlook promises "maximum capacity utilization" and is silent on volume, margin and robotaxi revenue. Cash generation now depends on working capital rather than profit, because payables and customer prepayments grow faster than earnings, which is why operating cash flow rises while net income falls. Operating cash flow rose 36% to $14,897 million while net income fell 19.5% to $2,378 million, and the bridge is working capital: accounts payable and accrued liabilities contributed $7,332 million against $2,979 million a year earlier, accounts payable rose to $17,239 million from $13,371 million at 2025-12-31, and days payables outstanding went from 62.8 to 75.3, roughly $2.9 billion of cash on the nine-month cost base. Deferred revenue added $1,746 million, mostly storage customer prepayments that rose to $3.30 billion. Against that, capital expenditure of $13,014 million consumed 87% of operating cash flow, and free cash flow by quarter was $1,444 million, negative $1,092 million and $1,531 million, against $3,990 million in Q3 2025. Depreciation of $4,290 million rose 17% and will climb faster than revenue as more than $20 billion of 2026 spending is commissioned [S3, S4].

The balance sheet is not the constraint. At 2026-09-30 Tesla held $45,447 million of cash and short-term investments against $9,267 million of debt, or $36,180 million of net cash, and in September 2026 it signed three credit agreements with aggregate commitments of $30 billion. Interest income of $1,301 million for nine months covered interest expense of $263 million almost five times; interest cover on operating income was 10.0x. Goodwill of $257 million is 0.2% of assets, so reported earnings carry no acquired-goodwill illusion; the pressures are elsewhere, in inventory of $14,092 million, up 13.7% while deliveries fell 2%, and a warranty reserve of $10,138 million, up 26% on the year. Solvency is not the risk; the return on the capital being deployed is [S4].

That return has collapsed. Invested capital of $53,109 million (equity $89,289 million plus debt less cash and securities) earned a trailing ROIC of 5.5% and an ROE of 3.8%, against 28.3% and 27.9% in FY2023, when the equity base was $62,634 million. Against a 4.99% ten-year Treasury, a 4.5% equity risk premium and a beta of 1.5 to 2.0, our estimate of the cost of capital is 11% to 14%, so the company is destroying economic value at current margins. Read strategically, this converts a cost advantage in vehicles and cells into a capital-intensive compute and robotics business before that business has customers, so the shares trade on optionality rather than earnings. Capital allocation offers no offset: no dividend, no buyback, capital expenditure guided above $20 billion for 2026, and $1.95 billion of stock paid for an AI hardware company in Q2 2026. Equity compensation is the other claim on shareholders: $3,557 million in nine months is 4.5% of revenue, the 2025 CEO Performance Award covers 423.7 million shares, or 12% of the 3,541 million diluted count, with $9.74 billion of unrecognised expense on the one milestone judged probable, and the 2018 award was exercised for 304.0 million options in Q2 2026, leaving restricted shares that vest on 2028-01-19 [S4, S15, S24].

The price is an option, not a multiple. At $403.30 on 2026-10-29 the equity is worth $1,428 billion and the enterprise $1,392 billion after net cash: 13.4x trailing revenue, 401x operating income, 92x trailing adjusted EBITDA of $14,995 million and 431x free cash flow. Adjusted EBITDA is itself struck before stock-based compensation, so the cash-based multiple is higher. The operating leverage cuts both ways: each 100 basis points of automotive gross margin excluding credits is worth $756 million on the annualised nine-month automotive revenue base of $75,561 million, which is 22% of trailing operating income, so a two-point margin miss plus a $4 billion capex overshoot would take 2027 free cash flow to roughly negative $2 billion on our arithmetic, while energy growth of 40% at a 30% margin and auto margin at 20% would lift it to about $8 billion. For an investor, that asymmetry makes the shares a bet on autonomy and robotics reaching commercial scale rather than on present cash flow, so position size should be set by tolerance for a de-rating from 92 times EBITDA, not by the near-term cash generation. Confidence is high on the statements and the cash bridge, medium on the cost of capital, and low on any estimate that requires autonomous revenue to be sized. Three diligence questions remain: how much of the payables increase reverses in Q4? What is the split of the 2026 capital budget between maintenance and AI compute? And does the board intend to offset dilution from the performance award? [S15, S69, S70]

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## ESG评估 ESG Assessment (esg, revision 2 by Regulatory Analyst, 8,486 characters)
Tesla's policy position has inverted. The 2025-2026 reset removes a high-margin revenue stream worth $2,763m at its 2024 peak and leaves the robotaxi licence to operate fragmented across US states and unapproved in China, while the offsetting upsides — federal AV preemption and tariffs on Chinese rivals — are real but not yet law. Automotive regulatory credit revenue fell from $2,763m in 2024 to $1,993m in 2025 (-28%) and to $113m in Q3 2026 from $417m (-73%); because credits carry almost no cost of revenue, total automotive gross margin fell from 18.4% to 17.8% in 2025, partly on the $770m decline. The credit-free margin is the right base. [S3, S4]

### The credit pool has already collapsed

The US instrument is unambiguous. Section 30D's $7,500 new clean vehicle credit applied only to vehicles acquired on or before 2025-09-30; the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, enacted 2025-07-04, terminated it and the used-vehicle 25E credit thereafter. The 2026 revision is a repeal, not a tightening: EPA's final rule of 2026-02-18 rescinds the 2009 endangerment finding and repeals the light-, medium- and heavy-duty GHG standards, and the Department of Transportation finalised its CAFE rollback on 2026-10-01. Both remove the compliance demand that priced Tesla's credits and slow competitors' EV mix; EIA reported on 2026-10-19 that battery-electric sales remained lower after the credit expired. California's ACC II and the Section 177 states preserve a partial market, not the 2024 price level. [S117, S116, S64, S98]

### The robotaxi licence is a state-by-state binary

Autonomy is the part of the equity value policy can switch on or off, and the record is narrower than the narrative. Texas requires a TxDMV authorisation for commercial SAE Level 4/5 operation from 2026-05-28 under SB 2807 — a no-fee, non-expiring registration regime, which is why Austin scaled first. California is the opposite: CPUC's AV permit table lists Waymo, Zoox, Nuro, WeRide and Tensor but not Tesla, and Tesla's California service runs under a non-AV limousine/TCP authority. Federally the binding constraint is enforcement — NHTSA's FSD probes and the October 2026 school-zone review — while the preemption fix, H.R. 7390 SELF DRIVE Act of 2026, advanced only from a House subcommittee on a 12-11 party-line vote on 2026-02-10. Waymo holds a CPUC driverless permit and Zoox a federal exemption granted 2026-07-31; Tesla is first on neither. [S118, S119, S80, S125]

### China taxes the base; Europe protects it for now

China policy has become a tax on Tesla's largest manufacturing base. From 2026-01-01 to 2027-12-31 the NEV purchase tax is halved rather than exempt — an effective 5%, capped at RMB 15,000 per car — regressive for Tesla's higher-priced trims and landing alongside a 16% fall in Q3 2026 China sales, a cut in the vehicle export rebate and no unsupervised FSD approval. Europe is the exception: Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2754 has imposed a countervailing duty on China-built BEVs since 2024-10-30 for five years, at 7.8% for Tesla Shanghai against 35.3% for SAIC, on top of the 10% common duty — 17.8% versus 45.3% for Chinese brands. That room is time-limited: the EU softened 2025-2027 CO2 compliance to a three-year average and proposed the same for 2030-2032, reducing legacy makers' urgency to buy credits. [S124, S77, S127, S126]

### Governance is the largest ESG item

Governance is the largest ESG item because it changes the share count and the cost of capital. The 2025 CEO Performance Award covers 423.7m shares in 12 tranches, approved on 2025-11-06, with $105.82-120.37bn of unrecognised stock compensation for milestones not yet probable and $10.23bn for the one deemed probable — at the low end 10.7% of the 3.95bn shares outstanding. Capital allocation matters more than pay design: Tesla invested $2.0bn in xAI Holdings in January 2026 and, after SpaceX acquired xAI Holdings on 2026-02-02, converted that right into SpaceX Class A stock in March 2026. Musk holds 19.8% and 207.5m shares are pledged. Seven of nine directors are independent and one share carries one vote, but a governance discount is warranted. [S5, S3]

### What is not financially material

Three ESG claims do not survive contact with the financials. Tesla's own operational footprint is small relative to the use-phase emissions its products avoid, and the 2025 10-K discloses no material environmental proceeding; the real exposure is upstream, in battery materials, where Tesla files an annual conflict-minerals report but discloses no supplier-level exposure. Labour and product safety are tails: the California Civil Rights Department trial is set for 2026-07-20, and the August 2025 Autopilot verdict was $129m compensatory with Tesla 33% at fault plus $200m punitive, against an immaterial accrual. The strongest counter-evidence runs the other way — the US tariff wall on Chinese-built EVs, the EU's relative tariff advantage, possible federal AV preemption and performance-contingent pay — which is why policy is a discount on the multiple, not an exit signal. [S3, S5]

Tesla is a single-class Texas corporation whose control rests on a 19.8% CEO stake plus a 423.7 million-share contingent award, so a public-equity holder is underwriting Elon Musk's capital allocation rather than a board-governed company; that is acceptable at a governance discount, not a premium. Tesla, Inc. was incorporated in Delaware on 2003-07-01, converted to Texas on 2024-06-13, and trades on Nasdaq under TSLA with one class of common stock and 3,952,648,559 shares outstanding at 2026-09-30, including 423,743,904 unearned restricted shares. There is no VIE, nominee-shareholder or red-chip layer [S3].

### The entity map is clean; the asset ring-fence is not

| Entity | Jurisdiction | Role | Ownership | Source |

| Tesla, Inc. | Texas | Listed parent and principal operating company | 100% | S3, S5 |
