business_model.author: Fundamentals Analyst
queries: 10-K FY2025 item 7: automotive regulatory credits, segment revenue and gross margin, energy storage deployments
10-Q Q3 2026 item 2: segment revenue, cost of revenues, gross margin by segment, capex outlook, $30B credit agreements
8-K 2026-10-21 exhibit 99.1: quarterly revenue by segment, deliveries, storage GWh, FSD subscriptions, inventory days, operating cash flow and capex
10-Q Q3 2026 item 1: deferred revenue, warranty reserve roll-forward, inventory write-downs, SI hardware acquisition, 2025 CEO Performance Award
Tesla Q3 2026 earnings call transcript: auto gross margin 18.1% ex credits, energy margin 33.1% with tariff refunds, FSD attach rate, Megapack backlog
BYD FY2025 gross margin and automotive margin; Rivian Q2 2026 automotive gross profit; Fluence FY2025 gross margin
DOT final CAFE rollback 2026-10 and reporting on Tesla regulatory credit revenue collapse

rows.finding: Automotive revenue excluding regulatory credits was $67,533M in FY2025, $74,307M in FY2024 and $80,629M in FY2023; regulatory credits were $1,993M, $2,763M and $1,790M; energy revenue rose from $6,035M (FY2023) to $12,771M (FY2025) and services from $8,319M to $12,530M. In Q3 2026 services revenue reached $4,605M (+33% YoY) while automotive revenue ex-credits was $20,447M and energy $2,881M.
rows.mechanism: The revenue base is rebalancing: the car business is flat to shrinking in dollars per unit while energy storage and the services layer (Supercharging, insurance, used cars, collision) grow double digits off a smaller base, so consolidated revenue can grow while vehicle units fall.
rows.benchmark: FY2023 mix: automotive 85.1% of revenue, energy 6.2%, services 8.6%. Q3 2026: automotive 72.9%, energy 10.3%, services 16.4%.
rows.weakens: Q3 2026 energy revenue fell 16% YoY on tariff refunds and lower Megapack ASP, so the mix shift is not yet monotonic.
rows.implication: Value the segments separately; a single blended multiple hides that the 33%-margin energy business is now 17% of gross profit and services 13%.
rows.confidence: high, from audited segment disclosure and the Q3 2026 release
rows.follow_up: What share of services revenue is recurring (Supercharging, insurance, FSD) versus used-vehicle resale, which carries thin margin?

rows.finding: Regulatory credits contributed $1,993M of FY2025 operating income of $4,355M (45.8%), $2,763M of $7,076M in FY2024 (39.0%) and $1,790M of $8,891M in FY2023 (20.1%). Q3 2026 credits were $113M, down 73% YoY and 15.7% of operating income; 9M 2026 credits were $639M (31.1% of operating income) versus $1,451M a year earlier.
rows.mechanism: Credits carry no cost of revenue, so a dollar of credit revenue is close to a dollar of operating profit; as the compliance obligation on other automakers disappears, that profit disappears without any change in vehicle volumes.
rows.benchmark: FY2024 peak of $2,763M and 39% of operating income; the US DOT finalized the CAFE rollback in late September 2026, removing the compliance driver.
rows.weakens: Credits held up in Q4 2025 ($542M implied) after the consumer credit lapsed, so the decline is regulatory-calendar driven and could stall rather than go to zero in any single quarter.
rows.implication: Treat credit revenue as zero in any valuation beyond 2027; the FY2025 operating margin of 4.6% was really 2.5% without credits.
rows.confidence: high on the figures; medium on the 2027 trajectory
rows.follow_up: How much of the remaining $639M of 9M 2026 credits is non-US (EU/China) and thus outside the CAFE rollback?

rows.finding: Q3 2026 automotive revenue per delivery was $42,026 excluding credits against cost of revenue of $34,436, giving gross profit of $7,591 per vehicle (18.1%); a year earlier the same figures were $41,818, $35,385 and $6,433 (15.4%). Company gross profit per delivery was $11,292 across all three segments, SG&A $4,142, R&D $5,675, operating profit $1,476 (Q3 2025: $3,267).
rows.mechanism: Price was flat (+0.5%) and cost per vehicle fell 2.7%, so the entire 270bp margin recovery came from cost and regional mix (Asia-Pacific), not pricing power; company-level profit per vehicle halved because R&D per delivery rose from $3,279 to $5,675.
rows.benchmark: Rivian's automotive gross profit was a $(36)M loss in Q2 2026; BYD's automotive gross margin was 20.49% in FY2025 (from 22.31%).
rows.weakens: Management attributes the 18.1% to regional mix, which can reverse; part of the 2026 cost relief is tariff refunds that peers (Rivian) also booked.
rows.implication: Tesla's per-vehicle cost advantage over pure EV peers is real but is being spent on AI R&D, so unit economics no longer translate into company margin.
rows.confidence: high on arithmetic from disclosed segment revenue, cost of revenue and deliveries
rows.follow_up: What is the ex-credit automotive gross margin in North America alone, where tariffs and the lost consumer credit hit hardest?

rows.finding: Energy storage revenue was $210M per GWh deployed in Q3 2026 (13.7 GWh) against $273M in Q3 2025 and $273M for FY2025 (46.7 GWh); gross profit per GWh fell only from $85.8M to $69.6M because cost per GWh fell from $187M to $141M, lifting segment gross margin from 31.4% to 33.1% and to 30.2% for 9M 2026.
rows.mechanism: Megapack pricing is deflating faster than the bill of materials as Tesla substitutes its own LFP cells (first Megapacks with Nevada LFP cells shipped in Q3 2026) and adds Megafactory Texas capacity of 50 GWh, so vertical integration defends margin per unit while revenue per unit falls.
rows.benchmark: Fluence, the listed pure-play integrator, earned about 13.1% GAAP gross margin in FY2025.
rows.weakens: Management said the 33.1% was helped by tariff refunds for Megapack customers and cell-related warranty cost reimbursements; excluding those the margin is closer to 30%.
rows.implication: Energy is the highest-margin dollar of growth and deserves a separate valuation, but 2026 margin is flattered by one-offs.
rows.confidence: high on segment arithmetic; medium on the durability of the margin
rows.follow_up: What is the energy gross margin excluding tariff refunds and warranty reimbursements, and what ASP is contracted for 2027 backlog?

rows.finding: FSD (Supervised) active subscriptions rose from 1.04M (Q3 2025) to 1.74M (Q3 2026); deferred revenue tied to FSD, connectivity and software was $4.08B at 2026-09-30 against $3.87B at 2025-12-31; $668M of revenue was recognized in 9M 2026 from prior deferred balances, and total unsatisfied performance obligations over one year were $10.73B, of which $4.80B is due within 12 months.
rows.mechanism: Software is sold as a stand-ready obligation recognised over the vehicle's ownership life, so cash arrives before revenue; the balance sheet therefore carries a growing but slow-release software annuity rather than a high-margin licence.
rows.benchmark: Deferred revenue $4.08B versus 9M 2026 revenue of $78,669M is about 5% of annual revenue, small relative to the valuation premium attributed to autonomy.
rows.weakens: The company's >75% North American attach rate implies deferred revenue should grow faster than it has; FSD revenue is not disclosed as a separate line, so the attach rate cannot be reconciled to revenue.
rows.implication: FSD is not yet a material revenue line and cannot be verified as one; the robotaxi and Optimus optionality is not in the current financials.
rows.confidence: medium: filings disclose balances, not FSD revenue
rows.follow_up: Will Tesla disclose FSD revenue separately once robotaxi rides scale, and how is Robotaxi revenue recognised?

rows.finding: Operating expenses rose to $4,776M in Q3 2026 (+39% YoY) against gross profit of $5,494M, so opex absorbed 86.9% of gross profit; R&D alone was $2,761M (+69%) and SG&A $2,015M (+29%), of which $293M was stock-based compensation tied to the 2025 CEO Performance Award. Depreciation rose 17% to $1,580M in the quarter.
rows.mechanism: Tesla is converting a hardware gross-profit pool into a fixed AI cost base (compute, silicon, Optimus, robotaxi fleet) before the associated revenue exists, so operating leverage runs backwards: gross margin up 160bp, operating margin down 322bp.
rows.benchmark: FY2025 R&D was $6,411M; 9M 2026 R&D alone is $7,078M, already 10% above the full prior year.
rows.weakens: Part of the opex increase is equity compensation, not cash; the cash cost base grows more slowly than GAAP opex.
rows.implication: The break-even question is not unit economics but whether energy and services gross profit can outgrow the AI cost base; at 2.6% operating margin the model does not cover its capital cost.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: What is the 2027 R&D and capex plan once Cortex and Austin Fab are commissioned, and when does AI spending stop expanding as a share of revenue?

rows.finding: The warranty reserve rose to $10,138M at 2026-09-30 from $8,075M a year earlier (+26%) while quarterly deliveries fell 2%; the quarterly provision fell to $597M from $727M but costs incurred rose to $1,614M for 9M 2026 from $1,254M. Inventory rose to $14,092M from $12,392M at 2025-12-31 (+13.7%) with 11 days of vehicle supply.
rows.mechanism: A growing warranty reserve against falling unit volume means either the fleet is ageing into claims (services cost) or accruals are being built for recalls and new products; inventory growth ahead of deliveries absorbs cash and signals launch build-up for Semi, Cybercab and Optimus.
rows.benchmark: Warranty provision per delivery fell to $1,227 from $1,463; reserve per trailing-twelve-month delivery rose to about $5,816 from $4,713.
rows.weakens: The reserve covers energy storage warranties of up to 25 years, so growth in the storage fleet mechanically raises it; the per-vehicle comparison is therefore imperfect.
rows.implication: Watch warranty and inventory as the two places where future margin can be silently pre-spent; they are small relative to revenue but trending the wrong way.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: What portion of the warranty reserve relates to energy storage versus vehicles, and were there recall accruals in 2026?

plan.decision_question: Where does Tesla actually make its money in 2026, and how much of operating profit depends on regulatory credits or one-off items rather than vehicle gross profit?
plan.thesis_sentence: Tesla still makes most of its gross profit selling cars, but after regulatory credits the car business earns almost nothing at the operating line: the credit stream that supplied 45.8% of FY2025 operating income had fallen to $113M in Q3 2026, and the incremental profit is now coming from a 33%-margin energy-storage business and a 15.9%-margin services business while AI spending absorbs 87% of gross profit.
plan.why_different: The market and competition sections describe the addressable market and rivals; this section is the only place that decomposes the P&L into who pays, for what, per unit, and how much profit survives each layer of cost.
plan.mechanism: Credits are a zero-cost revenue line that converts almost one-for-one into operating profit, so their withdrawal mechanically subtracts margin with no volume change; meanwhile energy storage deflates in price but falls faster in cost through LFP vertical integration, and services scale on an installed fleet without proportional unit cost.
plan.comparison_set: Rivian (pure EV, still negative automotive gross profit), BYD (20.49% auto gross margin, FY2025), Fluence (13.1% storage gross margin), GM (FY2025 EBIT-adjusted $12.7B) and Ford (2026 capex guidance $9.5-10.5B).
plan.counter_evidence: The 18.1% ex-credit automotive margin may be a regional-mix and tariff-refund artefact rather than a cost step-down; the 33.1% energy margin contains tariff refunds and warranty reimbursements; opex is rising 39% and R&D 69%, so the operating margin (2.6%) may keep falling even as gross margin improves.
plan.visual: Two tables: revenue and gross margin by segment FY2023-FY2025, 9M 2026 and Q3 2026; and a per-delivery unit-economics waterfall Q3 2026 against Q3 2025.
plan.prohibited: 'clear business model', 'strong team', 'huge market', 'well positioned', 'risks are manageable', 'fierce competition', vague counts, and any sentence describing how the section is written.

rows.finding: Q3 2026 gross profit split $3,806 million automotive (69%), $954 million energy (17%) and $734 million services (13%), against 91%/6%/3% in FY2023; 9M 2026 revenue $78,669 million, of which automotive $57,310 million including $639 million of credits.
rows.mechanism: The profit pool has moved from vehicle hardware to storage and the installed fleet, so the revenue model now has three engines with different margins and timing.
rows.benchmark: Tesla's own FY2023 segment mix.
rows.weakens: Segment gross profit is before unallocated operating expense, which has grown faster than any segment.
rows.implication: Value energy and services separately from the car business rather than on a single blended multiple.
rows.confidence: high - filed segment data
rows.follow_up: What is the automotive margin excluding credits in North America alone?

rows.finding: Automotive regulatory credits were $1,993 million in FY2025 (45.8% of $4,355 million operating income), $639 million in 9M 2026 and $113 million in Q3 2026, down 73% from $417 million; 15.7% of Q3 2026 operating income.
rows.mechanism: Credits carry no cost of revenue, so each dollar is almost pure operating profit; the compliance demand behind them ends with the 2026 CAFE rollback finalised on 2026-10-01.
rows.benchmark: Credits were 20.1% of operating income in FY2023 and 39.0% in FY2024.
rows.weakens: Credits may persist in Europe and China at a lower level, and the Q4 2025 implied $542 million shows the timing of the collapse is tied to US rules.
rows.implication: Underwrite the company on an ex-credit basis; the credit line is a declining, non-core annuity.
rows.confidence: high - filed revenue and rule-making record
rows.follow_up: How much credit revenue is contracted for 2027 outside the United States?

rows.finding: Q3 2026 automotive revenue per delivery excluding credits was $42,026 (+0.5%) and automotive cost of revenue per delivery $34,436 (-2.7%), so gross profit per vehicle rose 18.0% to $7,591 (18.1% margin) from $6,433 (15.4%).
rows.mechanism: The margin gain came from cost and a higher Asia-Pacific mix (Shanghai), not from pricing, so it is volume- and mix-dependent rather than a pricing power signal.
rows.benchmark: BYD automotive gross margin 20.49% in FY2025 (from 22.31%); Rivian automotive gross profit was a $(36) million loss in Q2 2026.
rows.weakens: Management attributed part of the relief to tariff and commodity timing, and SG&A per delivery rose 31.8% to $4,142.
rows.implication: The car business is viable per unit but thin; the fixed cost base, not the vehicle, is the risk.
rows.confidence: high on the arithmetic; medium on durability of the cost relief
rows.follow_up: How much of the $949 per vehicle cost reduction is structural versus mix and tariff timing?

rows.finding: Storage revenue per GWh fell to $210 million from $273 million on 13.7 GWh deployed (from 12.5 GWh), cost per GWh fell 25% to $141 million and gross profit per GWh was $69.6 million, a 33.1% segment margin; management said on the 2026-10-21 call it is 'almost sold out of all Megapacks for 2027', a company claim (unverified) with no volume, contract value or price disclosed.
rows.mechanism: Owning the LFP cell (first Nevada-built Megapacks shipped in Q3 2026) and 50 GWh of planned Texas capacity lowers cost per GWh faster than price falls, which is the source of the margin advantage over integrators.
rows.benchmark: Fluence gross margin 13.1% in FY2025.
rows.weakens: Part of the 33.1% came from tariff refunds and cell-related warranty reimbursements, so the underlying margin is lower; the backlog is not a reported figure.
rows.implication: Size the energy annuity on reported deployments and contracted revenue, not on an undisclosed 2027 backlog.
rows.confidence: high on segment figures; low on the backlog claim
rows.follow_up: What contracted GWh and price per GWh underpin the claimed 2027 sell-out?

rows.finding: Active FSD subscriptions rose to 1.74 million from 1.04 million, a company operating KPI defined for the 2025 CEO Performance Award rather than an audited or GAAP-reported metric; deferred revenue for FSD, connectivity and software was $4.08 billion against $3.87 billion at 2025-12-31, with $10.73 billion of obligations beyond one year, $4.80 billion due within twelve months.
rows.mechanism: Software revenue is recognised over the subscription or over the life of the vehicle, so cash arrives before revenue and the deferred balance is the only hard evidence of the software annuity.
rows.benchmark: No comparable disclosure from GM, Ford or BYD; Tesla does not disclose FSD revenue.
rows.weakens: The 1.74 million count includes upfront purchases and monthly subscriptions and excludes free trials, so it overstates recurring subscribers.
rows.implication: Treat FSD as an option whose revenue cannot yet be tied to a line item; do not capitalise the KPI in the base case.
rows.confidence: medium - company-defined KPI, deferred balance is audited
rows.follow_up: Will Tesla disclose FSD revenue and its recognition period in the FY2026 10-K?

rows.finding: Operating expenses of $4,776 million rose 39% against $5,494 million of gross profit (86.9% absorbed), R&D rose 69% to $2,761 million, the warranty reserve rose 26% to $10,138 million on 2% fewer deliveries and inventory rose 13.7% to $14,092 million.
rows.mechanism: AI and robotics spending is a fixed cost against a vehicle gross profit that is flat to down, so operating leverage runs against the shareholder until software revenue arrives.
rows.benchmark: FY2023 operating margin 9.2% versus 2.6% in Q3 2026.
rows.weakens: Gross margin itself held at 19.6%, so the deterioration is opex, not pricing.
rows.implication: Break-even requires about $27 billion of quarterly revenue at the current cost base; position sizing must assume opex keeps rising.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: When do R&D and capex stop rising as a share of revenue?

rows.finding: Tesla discloses only three executive officers as of 2026-10-19: Elon Musk (CEO and Technoking), Vaibhav Taneja (CFO, since August 2023) and Xiaotong (Tom) Zhu (SVP APAC and Global Vehicle Manufacturing, since June 2025).
rows.mechanism: With no COO and no segment CEOs, every programme leader reports into a CEO who also runs SpaceX and chairs xAI's successor; decision rights concentrate at the top while execution capacity sits in a thin layer of long-tenured engineers.
rows.benchmark: Ford and GM run multi-layer executive benches with named segment presidents; Tesla discloses three executive officers for a $94.8bn-revenue group [S5].
rows.weakens: Titles understate the real bench: unnamed VPs such as Ashok Elluswamy run FSD, Robotaxi and Optimus [S94], and Joe Ward was promoted to global sales chief in February 2026 [S93].
rows.implication: Key-person risk is structural, not incidental: an investor owns Musk's attention allocation across Tesla, SpaceX/xAI and politics, with no disclosed COO to absorb operations.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: Who runs vehicle engineering, energy and Optimus below the SVP layer, and are they disclosed anywhere?

rows.finding: Elon Musk, age 55, has been CEO since October 2008; prior exits Zip2 (sold to Compaq, March 1999) and PayPal (sold to eBay, October 2002); concurrently SpaceX CEO since May 2002, xAI CEO since March 2023, X CTO since October 2022 and Neuralink CEO; education B.A. Physics, University of Pennsylvania and B.S. Business, Wharton.
rows.mechanism: The same person sets product direction, raises capital and negotiates related-party transactions, so his attention is the binding constraint on four simultaneous programmes and his departure or distraction re-prices the equity.
rows.benchmark: The 2018 award delivered 286,428,773 restricted shares after the Delaware Supreme Court reversed the rescission on 2025-12-19 [S5].
rows.weakens: Musk's record of shipping against scepticism (Model 3 ramp, 10 millionth vehicle in Q3 2026 [S6]) argues against discounting his operating involvement.
rows.implication: Founder-market fit is unusually strong on product and capital raising and unusually weak on succession and focus; size the position for headline and key-person volatility rather than for management continuity.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: How many days per quarter does Musk spend at Tesla, and does any board process measure it?

rows.finding: The other two NEOs are paid almost entirely in equity on modest salaries: Taneja $400,000 and Zhu $364,338 at end-2025, with Taneja holding 1,362,518 exercisable options and Zhu 2,195,673 options at 2026-09-30.
rows.mechanism: Equity-heavy pay aligns the top three with the share price but leaves the VP and director layer, where the departed leaders sat, exposed to a volatile stock and to offers from better-capitalised AI labs.
rows.benchmark: Musk's 2025 reported compensation was $158,359,009,867 against a median employee of $62,786, a ratio of 2,522,203:1 [S78]; 2025 say-on-pay support was 78.2% [S5].
rows.weakens: The board says it does not make annual grants to NEOs and that options carry no intrinsic value at grant, which is a pay-for-performance design rather than a retention guarantee.
rows.implication: Retention is bought with stock, not cash, so a falling share price removes the retention mechanism exactly when the programmes are most at risk.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: What are the retention terms for the engineers below VP level who actually build FSD and Optimus?

rows.finding: At least 17 senior leaders left between April 2024 and 2026-10-15, including Drew Baglino (SVP powertrain and energy, April 2024), Rebecca Tinucci (Supercharging, April 2024), Omead Afshar (operations, fired 2025-06-26), Raj Jegannathan (VP IT and AI infrastructure, 2026-02-09), Sendil Palani (VP finance after 17 years, 2026-03-10) and Mike Snyder (VP energy and charging, 2026-10-15).
rows.mechanism: Departures cluster where the roadmap is newest (Cybercab, Optimus, energy) and where the labour market is hottest, so the programmes with the least institutional memory lose the most of it.
rows.benchmark: A 30-month window in which the Cybercab programme lost its program manager, its new-product-introduction head, two assembly leads and the robotaxi-software director, and energy lost its VP two weeks before this report.
rows.weakens: Several exits were dismissals or planned retirements and internal promotions filled key roles (AJ Booth for Snyder, Joe Ward for global sales), so the net loss of capability is smaller than the headline count.
rows.implication: Turnover in the Cybercab and energy programmes is a direct execution risk to the two growth engines outside autos; a diligence team should ask for programme-level staffing and attrition data.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: Do the 2026 departures map to a specific programme slipping, and did any join a competitor with Tesla IP knowledge?

rows.finding: The 4680 cell programme reached dry-electrode production for both anode and cathode at Giga Texas, disclosed in the Q4 2025 update on 2026-01-28, roughly five years after the 2020 Battery Day target; Tesla nonetheless described battery availability as the limiting factor for auto volumes in Q3 2026.
rows.mechanism: Tesla's method is to attack the limiting component in-house; that works but the learning curve is long, so each new vertical (cells, AI silicon, robots) consumes years of engineering bandwidth before it pays.
rows.benchmark: Battery Day (2020-09-22) promised a step-change in cell cost and volume; the dry-electrode process reached production about five years later, and battery availability still capped Q3 2026 volumes [S6].
rows.weakens: The disclosure shows the problem was solved rather than abandoned, and Tesla Semi volume production and Megafactory Texas started in Q3 2026 [S6], evidence the manufacturing bench can still deliver.
rows.implication: The team eventually solves hard manufacturing problems but consistently later than promised; discount management timelines on Optimus and Cybercab by a similar factor.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: What is 4680 output in GWh and what share of 2026 vehicle cells is in-house?

rows.finding: Autonomy execution has shipped on a shorter cycle than the 4680 effort: Robotaxi launched in June 2025 with Model Y, safety monitors began coming out in Austin in January 2026, commercial Cybercab rides started 2026-09-03, and active FSD subscriptions reached 1.74 million at 2026-09-30.
rows.mechanism: One engineer's organisation owns FSD, Robotaxi software and Optimus AI, so a departure or a split of his attention would hit all three programmes at once.
rows.benchmark: Waymo's fleet data show a scaled driverless operation with no steering-wheel exemption fight, a reminder that autonomy execution is an operating discipline, not only a model problem [S59].
rows.weakens: Tesla discloses cumulative unsupervised miles only as an eightfold quarter-on-quarter increase, not an absolute figure, and NHTSA issued a Special Order in September 2026 demanding proof the driverless Cybercab meets federal standards [S93].
rows.implication: The autonomy team, led by Elluswamy, is the strongest evidence for the team's ability to execute; it also makes him the single most acute retention risk after Musk.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: What are absolute unsupervised Robotaxi miles and fleet size, and what is the incidents-per-mile record?

rows.finding: No COO or president sits below Musk, the two most senior operating roles are a CFO who came up through accounting and an SVP who built Shanghai, and tranches 11 and 12 of the 2025 award vest only after the board approves a CEO succession framework developed by Musk himself.
rows.mechanism: The succession condition turns a governance safeguard into an award trigger, so the board has an incentive to approve a framework that keeps Musk in place rather than one that replaces him.
rows.benchmark: A public company of Tesla's scale normally discloses a CEO succession plan; Tesla's own award makes the CEO the author of the framework that unlocks his last two tranches.
rows.weakens: Straubel, a co-founder and former CTO, sits on the board and could plausibly step into a technical leadership role, and Denholm has chaired the board since 2018.
rows.implication: A multi-year hold carries unhedgeable key-person risk: the plan, the capital allocation and the succession are all the same person, and the award pays him to stay rather than to build a successor.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: Has the board seen a succession framework, and is it conditioned on Musk remaining CEO through 2032?

plan.decision_question: Does the team's execution record and bandwidth support the vehicle, energy, autonomy and Optimus roadmap at the same time?
plan.thesis_sentence: Tesla's execution machine still ships — 10.2 million cumulative vehicles, fare-paying Cybercab rides from 2026-09-03 and Optimus off a high-volume Fremont line — but the bench beneath Elon Musk has thinned to three named executive officers and at least 17 senior departures since April 2024, so the four-front roadmap depends on one man and a handful of engineers paid to stay rather than on a management team that could be handed the plan.
plan.why_different: This section judges people and execution capacity, not the products themselves or their markets; the same departure facts belong here as retention evidence, while the product section owns technical feasibility.
plan.mechanism: Tesla's model concentrates decision rights in one CEO while distributing execution to a thin layer of long-tenured engineers; when a programme leader leaves, the knowledge does not transfer to a peer but up to Musk, which slows each of the four programmes that compete for his attention and for the same AI talent pool.
plan.comparison_set: Waymo's autonomy operating bench, BYD's engineering depth and Tesla's own 2017-2018 Model 3 ramp, plus the 2024-2026 departure list as a base rate for a company running four simultaneous programmes.
plan.counter_evidence: Internal promotions (Joe Ward to global sales, AJ Booth to energy VP), Elluswamy's 12-year retention and Straubel's return to the board show the bench is not empty; the 2025 award and $158bn grant value are explicitly retention tools, and the 10 millionth vehicle and 3 September Cybercab launch show shipping capability.
plan.visual: Team assessment matrix with each leader plus the evidence component on the strongest proof and the strongest doubt; education and career tables carry the CV record.
plan.prohibited: No 'strong team', no 'visionary', no unqualified claim that departures are normal attrition; do not present the 2025 award as retention certainty; no ratings without a stated dimension.

rows.finding: US battery-electric share of new light-duty vehicle sales fell to 6% in Q3 2026 from 10% in Q3 2025, and to 6% in the first nine months of 2026 from 8%; the luxury segment where Tesla's US mix sits fell from 31% to 12% BEV share over the same four quarters, while hybrids reached 16% of US light-duty sales.
rows.mechanism: Removing a $7,500 point-of-sale credit raised the effective price of a BEV relative to a hybrid by roughly the credit's size; the marginal buyer who entered only for the credit left and did not return a year later, so the drop is a level shift in the demand curve, not a payback whiplash that reverses.
rows.benchmark: September 2025, the last month of eligibility, set a record 12% US BEV share; a pure pull-forward would have produced recovery by Q2 2026.
rows.weakens: Hybrid gains (16% share) and a $50,000+ average transaction price show the substitution is toward hybrids, not back to petrol, so electrification is not reversing - only BEV-only strategies are exposed.
rows.implication: Price the US BEV pool at roughly 0.9-1.0 million units a year, not the 1.3 million of 2025, and treat US volume growth as share-taking from retreating incumbents rather than market growth.
rows.confidence: high - US government analysis using Omdia registration estimates
rows.follow_up: What is the monthly US BEV share for September and October 2026, after the Q3 incentive push, to see whether 6% is a floor?

rows.finding: The subsidy did not disappear from the transaction price, it moved to manufacturer P&Ls: US new-EV average transaction price was $54,754 in August 2026 (-2.8% year on year) with incentives averaging 12% of ATP, about $6,594 per vehicle, and the EV premium over comparable ICE vehicles narrowed to $4,847 (9.7%).
rows.mechanism: OEMs replaced roughly $6,600 of the $7,500 federal credit with their own incentives, so the net price barely moved while gross margin absorbed the difference; the volume that failed to appear at that net price is the credit's true demand creation.
rows.benchmark: $7,500 section 30D credit removed 2025-09-30; incentives of $6,594 per unit are 88% of the credit's size.
rows.weakens: If incentives were the only support, volumes should have held; US EV volume still fell 46.9% year on year in August 2026, so price was not the binding constraint for the missing buyers.
rows.implication: Tesla's 18.5% automotive gross margin in Q3 2026 is being earned while it funds part of the incentive load; a price war to defend US share would come directly out of that margin.
rows.confidence: high - Cox Automotive transaction-price data, consistent with EIA volume data
rows.follow_up: How much of Tesla's US incentive spending is booked as a price reduction rather than a marketing expense, and does it show in the 2027 ASP?

rows.finding: EU battery-electric registrations reached 1,641,333 units in January-August 2026, 21.7% of the EU market against 15.8% a year earlier, led by France +74.2% and Germany +53.1%; plug-in hybrids took 10% and hybrids 36.6%, while petrol and diesel fell to 29% combined.
rows.mechanism: The 2025-2027 CO2 mandate makes BEV volume the cheapest compliance route for OEMs, and the 2026 energy-price shock raised the running-cost advantage of electric, so supply push and running-cost pull point the same way; subsidy levels matter far less than in the US because the binding constraint is a fleet-average regulation.
rows.benchmark: 2025 EU average BEV share of 17.4% (European Commission, citing ACEA); 2026 running at 21.7%, a 4.3-point step in eight months.
rows.weakens: Hybrids remain the single largest electrified category at 36.6%, so the mandate is being met partly with hybrids and the BEV step-up may flatten once the 2025-2027 compliance window closes.
rows.implication: Europe is the one large market where Tesla's unit growth (+51% January-September 2026) is market-supported rather than share-bought, and it justifies keeping European capacity and the Berlin ramp.
rows.confidence: high - ACEA is the manufacturers' association publishing national registration data
rows.follow_up: What BEV share does the EU need in 2027 to comply, and how much of the 2026 step is pre-compliance pulling forward into 2027?

rows.finding: China's NEV penetration reached 65.1% of new passenger cars in July 2026 (54% a year earlier) while NEV units fell 12.5% in January-July and total passenger-car sales fell 20.3%; Tesla sold 381,088 cars to Chinese buyers in January-September 2026, down 11.9%, roughly in line with the market, and Giga Shanghai's September wholesale rose 5.0% to 95,366 on exports up 58.3%.
rows.mechanism: Penetration is rising through a shrinking denominator, so a stable share now means falling absolute volume; Tesla is holding share by exporting the Shanghai output rather than by winning Chinese buyers, which caps the value of its China franchise without destroying it.
rows.benchmark: China NEV retail -12.5% January-July 2026 versus Tesla China retail -11.9% January-September 2026: no meaningful share loss.
rows.weakens: The 2026 price-war reversal (more than 15 automakers raised prices, industry margin 3.2% in Q1 2026) means Tesla's China pricing held better than the volume number implies.
rows.implication: Do not underwrite China as a growth market for Tesla in 2027-2028; underwrite it as a low-cost export base whose utilisation depends on demand outside China.
rows.confidence: medium - CPCA figures reported through two independent outlets, retail versus wholesale definitions differ
rows.follow_up: What share of Giga Shanghai output was exported in Q3 2026, and which import markets absorb it after the EU tariff and the US exclusion?

rows.finding: Global electric car sales are expected to reach 23 million in 2026, close to 30% of all cars sold, after 20 million (+20%) in 2025; the first quarter of 2026 fell 8% year on year globally, with Europe up close to 30%, Asia-Pacific excluding China up 80% and Latin America up 75%; H1 2026 volume was 9.4 million, almost a quarter of light-duty sales.
rows.mechanism: Growth has re-weighted from the two subsidy-dependent markets to mandate-driven Europe and price-driven emerging markets, where Chinese imports hold 55-60% of sales; the global total therefore grows while the markets Tesla serves shrink.
rows.benchmark: Tesla's nine-month 2026 deliveries of 1,324,681 units, an annualised ~1.77 million, are about 7.7% of the 23 million global market versus 8.1% in 2025.
rows.weakens: The 23 million figure is an IEA projection made before Q2-Q3 2026 outturn, so the denominator could be 1-2 million lower and Tesla's share correspondingly higher.
rows.implication: Tesla's global share is slipping about half a point a year, not collapsing; the loss is arithmetic, caused by where the market grows, and it is not recoverable with US or Chinese volume alone.
rows.confidence: medium-high - IEA projection cross-checked against ICCT's H1 2026 actuals
rows.follow_up: What is the full-year 2026 outturn in units by region, and does Europe alone cover the US and China shortfall?

rows.finding: Grid storage is the fastest-growing market Tesla sells into: 108 GW of new battery storage was deployed globally in 2025, 40% more than 2024 and eleven times the 2021 level, and system deployments were 275.3 GWh in 2025 with 353.4 GWh expected in 2026; Tesla deployed 36.0 GWh in the first nine months of 2026 (13.7 GWh in Q3) against Megafactory Texas capacity of 50 GWh.
rows.mechanism: AI data-centre load growth plus renewable integration create utility-scale demand that is procured on multi-year contracts and is insensitive to consumer subsidies; Tesla's constraint is cell supply and tariff cost, not orders (record order rate and backlog in Q3 2026).
rows.benchmark: 36.0 GWh in nine months against a 353.4 GWh 2026 market implies roughly 14% of deployments, second to Chinese integrated suppliers.
rows.weakens: Energy revenue fell 16% year on year in Q3 2026 to $2,881 million on lower Megapack ASP and tariff refunds, so GWh growth is not translating into revenue growth: this is a volume market with deflating prices.
rows.implication: Storage is the one segment where the addressable market grows faster than Tesla can supply, which supports capital allocation toward Megafactory Texas and LFP cell localisation.
rows.confidence: medium - IEA GW data is high confidence; the GWh market size rests on one tracker (InfoLink) and Tesla's share is a derived estimate
rows.follow_up: What is Tesla's realised Megapack price per kWh in Q3 2026 versus 2025, and how much of the decline is tariff refunds pass-through?

rows.finding: The robotaxi revenue pool is small today: Waymo runs about 3,000 vehicles and 500,000 paid rides a week across 10 US cities (roughly 26 million rides a year), while Tesla had 44 active robotaxi vehicles across seven metros in H1 2026 and began Cybercab rides in Austin on 2026-09-03; Baidu Apollo Go operates in more than 10 Chinese cities.
rows.mechanism: Autonomous ride-hailing revenue is rides x fare, and both sides of that product are still measured in hundreds of thousands per week industry-wide; a market capitalisation attributed to robotaxis is an option on a 2028-2030 fleet, not a 2026-2027 revenue line.
rows.benchmark: At a $15-25 fare, Waymo's 26 million annual rides imply roughly $0.4-0.7 billion of annual gross bookings for the global leader.
rows.weakens: Tesla's unsupervised miles grew eightfold quarter on quarter and its fare structure undercuts Waymo by about 20%, so the gap is in fleet size and permits, not necessarily in unit economics.
rows.implication: Value Tesla's robotaxi as a call option with a dated milestone (unsupervised paid rides per week), not as a near-term cash flow; the option is real but the current base is under 1% of Tesla's revenue.
rows.confidence: low-medium - fleet and ride counts are third-party aggregations of operator disclosures and NHTSA standing general order filings, not audited
rows.follow_up: How many paid driverless rides per week does Tesla deliver in Austin in Q4 2026, and what is the per-ride contribution margin after remote operations?

plan.decision_question: Is demand for Tesla's products durable in 2026-2028, and how much did the end of US purchase subsidies change the underlying growth rate?
plan.thesis_sentence: Tesla's 2026-2028 demand is durable only in Europe and grid storage: the 2025-09-30 US credit expiry halved the US BEV share from 10% to 6% and cut the underlying US growth rate rather than merely pulling sales forward, while China is now a shrinking unit market in which Tesla holds share instead of gaining it.
plan.why_different: This section sizes the pools Tesla sells into and tests whether demand is organic or subsidy-created; it does not evaluate Tesla's execution (company), its cost structure (financials) or its competitor-by-competitor position (competition).
plan.mechanism: Subsidy removal shifts the demand curve by the size of the credit; CO2 mandates make BEV volume a compliance cost in Europe; China's penetration rises through a shrinking denominator; storage demand is driven by data-centre load and is procured on multi-year contracts; robotaxi revenue equals rides times fare and both are still tiny.
plan.comparison_set: Tesla's own 2024-2025 volumes and share; the US 2025 record BEV share of 12% in September 2025 as the pre-expiry peak; EU 2025 average BEV share of 17.4%; China NEV retail growth of -12.5%; CATL's 27.1% ESS cell share as the storage benchmark; Waymo's 500,000 weekly paid rides as the autonomy benchmark.
plan.counter_evidence: US BEV demand may have found a floor at 6% with incentives replacing the credit; Europe's 2026 step-up may be pre-compliance pulling volume forward; China's price-war reversal could restore Tesla's China margin; storage GWh growth with falling ASP could still compound revenue; robotaxi could scale faster than the fleet count implies.
plan.visual: A market-size table (TAM/SAM/SOM by method and year) plus a regional table (US, China, EU, rest of world, storage, robotaxi) with Tesla's position, barriers and key competitors.
plan.prohibited: huge market; strong demand; well positioned; fierce competition; risks are manageable; clear business model; recently

rows.finding: US battery-electric share of light-duty sales fell from 10% in Q3 2025 to 6% in Q3 2026 and was 6% in 9M 2026 against 8% a year earlier; August 2026 volume was 78,895 units, down 46.9% year on year, despite incentives of $6,594 per vehicle, 88% of the $7,500 credit.
rows.mechanism: The credit cut the effective price of a BEV by up to $7,500; removing it raised the relative cost against petrol and hybrid cars, manufacturers replaced only 88% of it with their own incentives, and quantity demanded fell by roughly two-fifths.
rows.benchmark: Q3 and 9M 2025 share before expiry; no recovery by Q2 2026, which rules out a pure pull-forward.
rows.weakens: One year of data; a new model or a Tesla price cut could lift volume; state ZEV rules and tariffs also move supply.
rows.implication: Underwrite the US at a 0.95 million unit annual BEV run-rate and Tesla's 51.7% share inside a shrinking pool, not at pre-credit growth rates.
rows.confidence: high: EIA and Cox Automotive independently agree on the level and direction.
rows.follow_up: What did US BEV share print in September-October 2026?

rows.finding: EU battery-electric registrations reached 1,641,333 in January-August 2026, 21.7% of the market against 15.8% a year earlier; Tesla registered 153,978 cars in an 11-country panel in January-September 2026, up 51%, and 45,523 in September.
rows.mechanism: The 2025-2027 fleet-average CO2 mandate makes battery volume the cheapest compliance route; the 2026 energy-price shock reinforced the switch, while hybrids at 36.6% show part of the mandate is met without battery cars.
rows.benchmark: 15.8% EU BEV share a year earlier against 6% in the US in Q3 2026.
rows.weakens: If 2026 is pre-compliance borrowing, 2027 will be flat; hybrids at 36.6% and a possible softening of the 2030-2032 proposal cap the upside.
rows.implication: Europe is the one large market carrying Tesla's volume growth in 2026-2028; the case depends on the mandate holding through the 2027 review.
rows.confidence: high on registrations, medium on the durability of the mandate-driven step.
rows.follow_up: Is the 2026 step borrowing 2027 volume, and does the 2027 CO2 review change the trajectory?

rows.finding: China NEV reached 65.1% of new passenger cars in July 2026 from 54% a year earlier, but NEV sales fell 12.5% in January-July and total passenger-car sales fell 20.3%; Tesla sold 381,088 cars in China in January-September 2026, down 11.9%, and Shanghai exports rose 58.3% in September.
rows.mechanism: Penetration rises arithmetically while the denominator shrinks; a price war cut first-quarter industry margins to 3.2% before 15 or more automakers raised prices, and export rebate cuts push Tesla toward overseas sales.
rows.benchmark: 54% NEV share a year earlier; Tesla's decline in line with the market.
rows.weakens: Retail and wholesale definitions diverge; a new stimulus or purchase-tax change could restart volume.
rows.implication: China is a low-cost export base whose utilisation depends on demand outside China, not a growth market for 2027-2028.
rows.confidence: medium: CPCA retail and wholesale series are not directly comparable.
rows.follow_up: What share of Giga Shanghai output was exported in Q3 2026?

rows.finding: The 2026 market size is $950 billion for electric cars (23.0M units at Tesla's $41,300 realised revenue per unit) and $82.7 billion for grid storage (353.4 GWh at $234/kWh); Tesla's obtainable revenue is $72.9 billion of automotive revenue, 7.7% of the TAM, and $11.2 billion of energy revenue, 13.6%; global electric-car units compound at 17.4% from an implied 16.7M in 2024 to 23.0M in 2026.
rows.mechanism: Market value equals units times price per unit; storage value equals GWh times revenue per kWh; Tesla's share of each pool is its realised revenue at the 2026 run-rate.
rows.benchmark: IEA 20.0M electric cars in 2025 and 275.3 GWh of storage in 2025.
rows.weakens: Tesla's realised price is above the market average, so the global and EU TAMs overstate revenue; the BEV/PHEV split is not published, so SAM is bounded rather than measured.
rows.implication: Tesla needs share gains or new pools to grow faster than 15-17%; the car TAM alone does not support the growth in the valuation.
rows.confidence: medium: unit data are sourced, the price basis is a labelled proxy.
rows.follow_up: What is the average BEV transaction price by region, and what is the BEV share of the 23.0M electric-car total?

rows.source_type: independent tracker plus primary (NHTSA) and independent (TechCrunch)
rows.finding: Waymo reports 4,000 vehicles in service and 500,000 paid rides a week, 26 million a year, which at $100 a ride is $2.6 billion, 0.3% of the electric-car TAM; Tesla's Texas fleet stood at 1,051 authorised vehicles on 2026-10-27 (544 Cybercab, 507 Model Y, Texas DMV records), NHTSA's DP26010 puts the population it is reviewing at 1,000, and Tesla discloses no fare, booking or paid-ride figure.
rows.mechanism: Ride-hailing revenue equals paid rides times fare; fleet size and permits cap rides, and registrations are an upper bound on vehicles in service.
rows.benchmark: Waymo's disclosed paid rides; Tesla's 1,051 authorised vehicles against Waymo's 4,000.
rows.weakens: Tesla does not disclose paid rides, Texas registrations are authorisations rather than service, and robotaxi unit economics could improve faster than the fleet count suggests.
rows.implication: Autonomy is optionality, not a 2026-2028 revenue line; the market cannot be sized from operator disclosure.
rows.confidence: medium on fleet counts, low on any robotaxi market size.
rows.follow_up: How many paid rides a week does Tesla run, at what fare and subsidy?

rows.finding: Hybrids took 16% of US luxury sales in Q3 2026 and 36.6% of EU new-car registrations in January-August 2026, while US BEV volume fell 46.9% after the credit expired.
rows.mechanism: When the BEV price premium persists, consumers substitute to hybrids, which meet neither the US credit nor, in part, the EU CO2 target as cheaply; charging availability caps adoption for households without a driveway.
rows.benchmark: Hybrid share gains against BEV share losses in the same markets.
rows.weakens: The counter-case to my own Europe thesis: the mandate is being met partly without battery cars, and US hybridisation could persist.
rows.implication: BEV demand may undershoot forecasts and Tesla's addressable pool is narrower than the electric-car headline.
rows.confidence: high on the shares, medium on the causal weight of charging.
rows.follow_up: How fast is public charging capacity growing relative to the BEV stock in the US and EU?

rows.finding: In the United States Tesla sold 40,816 EVs in August 2026, down 3.8% month on month, for 51.7% of US EV sales (down 3.4 points from July); the market itself fell 46.9% year on year to 78,895 units, with Toyota at 4,964 (+34.9%), Chevrolet +30.3%, Cadillac +13.1% and Kia +12%.
rows.mechanism: When weaker EV programmes (Ford, and GM's early BEV lines) retreat after the credit expiry, the surviving brand with the widest model line and lowest cost takes share without cutting price; Tesla's US share therefore rises as the market contracts.
rows.benchmark: Tesla's US EV share of 49% in 2024 and roughly 54% in Q3 2026 - the direction is up, not down.
rows.weakens: Only half the story: Tesla's US revenue fell 14.4% year on year in Q3 2026 to $12,495 million, so the share gain came with a smaller absolute business.
rows.implication: Tesla is winning a shrinking US pool, which protects revenue per unit but not volume; the correct read is share gain and market loss at the same time, and neither alone summarises the position.
rows.confidence: high - Cox Automotive transaction and registration-based estimates
rows.follow_up: Does Tesla hold above 50% US EV share in Q4 2026 once the Toyota bZ and Chevrolet Bolt ramp, and at what incentive cost?

rows.finding: In an 11-country European panel Tesla registered 153,978 cars in January-September 2026, up 51% from 102,025, and 45,523 in September 2026 alone against BYD's 39,583; on battery-electric only Tesla led 30,317 to 7,498; Chinese brands took 14.9% of new cars in September 2026 against 8.0% a year earlier, or 18.2% including Chinese-owned Volvo, Polestar, smart and Lotus.
rows.mechanism: BYD competes with a two-powertrain range that meets CO2 targets at lower cost per unit, so it takes the price-sensitive buyer Tesla does not serve; Tesla's European recovery is driven by the refreshed Model Y and quarter-end delivery batching rather than by price leadership.
rows.benchmark: Tesla led BYD in battery-electric registrations in every one of the 11 countries in September 2026 (30,317 vs 7,498).
rows.weakens: The +51% European growth sits on a depressed 2025 base after the brand controversy; September is Tesla's quarter-end peak month, so the monthly comparison overstates the trend.
rows.implication: BYD is the most dangerous competitor but not yet in Tesla's segment: it wins on powertrain breadth and low price, while Tesla wins the battery-electric comparison; the risk is that BYD's volume funds a premium BEV push into Model Y's price band.
rows.confidence: medium - country-panel aggregation, quarter-end loaded, not full ACEA totals
rows.follow_up: What share of BYD's European volume is PHEV, and does the 2027 CO2 review penalise that mix?

rows.finding: In China, the best-selling model from February to July 2026 was Geely's Xingyuan at nearly 197,500 units and just under RMB 100,000 (~$14,820), with Tesla's Model Y second at more than 180,000 units priced at RMB 263,500-313,500; Tesla's China retail sales were 381,088 in January-September 2026, down 11.9%, against a Chinese NEV retail market down 12.5% in January-July.
rows.mechanism: Tesla defends a price umbrella roughly three times the volume bestseller because Chinese buyers of Model Y are buying the brand and the software, not the cheapest transport; when 15+ local automakers raised prices in 2026 the umbrella stopped compressing.
rows.benchmark: Tesla's Model Y outsold the Geely Xingyuan and Xiaomi SU7 on price multiples of 2.6-3.1x, which is a brand outcome, not a cost outcome.
rows.weakens: The 11.9% fall in Tesla's China retail sales is a volume loss even if share held, and Shanghai's utilisation now depends on exports (+58.3% in September 2026), which are exposed to tariffs.
rows.implication: Tesla is holding share in China without a price advantage, which is the strongest evidence that its brand and software still carry value; but that position is exposed to any credible Chinese premium entrant at RMB 200,000-300,000.
rows.confidence: medium - CPCA data via CNBC and Electrek, retail versus wholesale definitions differ
rows.follow_up: How much of Tesla's China gross margin is protected by Shanghai export pricing rather than domestic pricing?

rows.finding: Tesla's cost of automotive sales was $16,570 million in Q3 2026 for 486,532 deliveries, about $34,060 per vehicle, against automotive gross margin of 18.5% (17.0% a year earlier) and automotive sales revenue per unit of about $41,300 (up from $40,955).
rows.mechanism: Tesla's cost per vehicle is roughly 2.3 times the retail price of China's volume bestseller, so its margin comes from price and mix rather than from a structural cost lead; vertical integration in cells and casting narrows but does not close that gap.
rows.benchmark: Geely's best-selling Xingyuan retails at just under RMB 100,000 (~$14,820), about 43% of Tesla's derived cost per vehicle.
rows.weakens: Cost per vehicle is calculated on a mix skewed to Model Y and excludes leased units, and Chinese retail prices include local taxes and subsidies, so the ratio overstates the true manufacturing gap.
rows.implication: Tesla earns a healthy margin at a premium price point but cannot match Chinese costs at the low end; its pricing power is real in the $40,000+ band and structurally absent below $25,000.
rows.confidence: medium-high - cost per vehicle derived from Tesla's filed cost of automotive sales and deliveries; the Chinese comparison is a retail price, not a cost
rows.follow_up: What is Tesla's cost per vehicle on the next-generation platform at volume, and can it reach the $25,000-30,000 band profitably?

rows.finding: CATL shipped 125.0 GWh of energy-storage batteries in H1 2026, up 81%, for 27.1% of the global ESS battery market as total BESS cell shipments exceeded 490 GWh in the half; Tesla deployed 36.0 GWh in the first nine months of 2026, and its energy revenue fell 16% year on year in Q3 2026 to $2,881 million on lower Megapack average selling prices and tariff refunds.
rows.mechanism: LFP cells are commoditised and Chinese suppliers hold over 80% of cell production, so integrators compete on software, grid-forming capability and delivery speed; Tesla's response is localising LFP cells in Nevada to escape tariffs rather than raising price.
rows.benchmark: Tesla's 36.0 GWh of nine-month deployments equal about 14% of the 353.4 GWh 2026 system market, against CATL's 27.1% of cells.
rows.weakens: Tesla's energy gross margin rose to 33.1% in Q3 2026 from 31.4%, so falling revenue per GWh is being offset by cost, which is a different and healthier signal than pure price deflation.
rows.implication: Pricing power in storage sits with the cell makers and the cheapest integrators, not with Tesla; the investment case for Tesla energy is capacity and backlog (record order rate in Q3 2026), not price.
rows.confidence: medium - cell and system shares are different denominators and Tesla does not disclose system share
rows.follow_up: What is Tesla's Megapack gross margin excluding tariff refunds, and is the ASP decline structural or a one-off pass-through?

rows.finding: Waymo operates about 3,000 robotaxis and roughly 500,000 paid rides a week across 10 US cities, targeting 1 million a week by December 2026; Baidu's Apollo Go runs in more than 10 Chinese cities, Zoox charges fares in Las Vegas and Pony.ai operates in China; Tesla began Cybercab rides in Austin on 2026-09-03 and its cumulative unsupervised robotaxi miles grew eightfold quarter on quarter.
rows.mechanism: In autonomy, scale compounds: more paid miles produce more training data, lower cost per ride and the permits that follow demonstrated safety records; Tesla is starting that loop four years after Waymo and one year after its own service launch.
rows.benchmark: Waymo's roughly 500,000 weekly paid rides against Tesla's 44 active robotaxi vehicles in H1 2026 is a scale gap of more than two orders of magnitude in paid supply.
rows.weakens: Vehicle counts understate Tesla's position because its consumer fleet of about 1.74 million active FSD subscriptions generates supervised miles at a scale no robotaxi operator has, and Cybercab production only began in September 2026.
rows.implication: Tesla's autonomy advantage is a cost-of-vehicle thesis (Cybercab built for the purpose) that has not yet been tested at scale; until paid rides per week are disclosed, the competitive claim is unproven and should not be paid for in the multiple.
rows.confidence: low-medium - third-party aggregation of operator disclosures and NHTSA filings; Tesla does not disclose paid rides
rows.follow_up: How many paid driverless rides per week does Tesla deliver in Austin in Q4 2026, and what does a ride cost after remote supervision?

rows.finding: Peer-reviewed research finds Tesla's brand politicisation moved with political events in both directions: Democratic assessments fell during the Musk-Trump alliance while Republican assessments soured after the alliance dissolved, consistent with partisan consumerism rather than a permanent brand collapse.
rows.mechanism: Politicisation transfers demand between politically defined buyer segments rather than destroying the total; the net effect depends on which segment is larger and on how much incentive is needed to convert the other.
rows.benchmark: Tesla's US EV share rose to 51.7% in August 2026 while the brand-controversy literature predicted a durable Democratic-buyer boycott.
rows.weakens: Survey attitudes are not sales, and Tesla's US revenue fell 14.4% year on year in Q3 2026, so the brand has clearly cost volume even if the direction of the political effect moved.
rows.implication: Brand damage is a real but cyclical risk priced through demand incentives rather than a structural impairment; the investor should watch repeat purchase and incentive per unit, not headlines.
rows.confidence: high for the academic finding; medium for the sales link, which is correlational
rows.follow_up: What are Tesla's US repeat-purchase and consideration rates in 2026 versus 2023, and does the Republican recovery offset the Democratic loss?

plan.decision_question: Is Tesla gaining or losing competitive advantage in vehicles, energy and autonomy, and what does that do to pricing power?
plan.thesis_sentence: Tesla is gaining share in the markets that are shrinking and holding share in the one that is growing, so its vehicle advantage is compressing into a cost-and-brand moat rather than a technology lead, while in storage it is a scale follower to CATL and BYD and in paid autonomy it trails Waymo by more than an order of magnitude.
plan.why_different: This section compares Tesla with named rivals product by product and measures share and price; it does not size demand (market), test unit economics (financials) or judge execution risk (risk).
plan.mechanism: Share moves with the price of the marginal unit relative to the best local substitute; Tesla's cost per vehicle (~$34,100) sits above the Chinese retail price of the volume bestseller (~$14,800), so it cannot win a price war and instead defends with brand, software and vertical integration; in storage the cell is commoditised by CATL at 27.1% share so integration and software set price; in autonomy scale begets data, permits and cost per ride, and Waymo's 500,000 weekly rides against Tesla's 44 vehicles is the scale gap that determines who sets fares.
plan.comparison_set: Tesla's 2023-2025 share path; BYD as the volume and cost benchmark; Geely's RMB 100,000 bestseller as the price floor; CATL's 27.1% ESS cell share; Waymo's 500,000 weekly paid rides; Tesla's own Q3 2025 gross margin of 17.0%.
plan.counter_evidence: Tesla gained US EV share to 51.7% and European registrations rose 51%, so the share-loss story is wrong in the two markets that pay; Chinese price discipline in 2026 (15+ automakers raising prices) removed the price umbrella argument; Waymo's ride count may not be comparable because Tesla's Cybercab launched only on 2026-09-03.
plan.visual: A per-product competitor table (vehicle, storage, autonomy) with 2026 scale, price, share and strengths and weaknesses versus Tesla, plus a positioning table by product.
plan.prohibited: fierce competition; strong team; clear moat; well positioned; risks are manageable; many competitors

plan.comparison_set: BYD, Geely, Xiaomi, Huawei HIMA, Xpeng, GM, Hyundai-Kia and Rivian in vehicles; CATL in cells; Waymo, Baidu Apollo Go and Zoox in autonomy; Tesla's own 2025 share and margin.
plan.counter_evidence: Tesla's share gains and margin expansion show conversion rather than loss, the Chinese price war is ending, and a purpose-built Cybercab could beat Waymo on cost per mile; HIMA and Xpeng are both shrinking year on year, so the flanking threat is price, not scale.
plan.visual: Competitor table followed by the SWOT quad.
plan.prohibited: huge market; fierce competition; well positioned; clear leader; about/roughly/nearly; vague counts; unsourced share claims

rows.finding: Revenue went $81,462M (FY2022), $96,773M (FY2023), $97,690M (FY2024), $94,827M (FY2025) and $78,669M (9M 2026, +12.5%); operating income fell from $13,656M to $8,891M, $7,076M, $4,355M and $2,057M, so operating margin went 16.8%, 9.2%, 7.2%, 4.6% and 2.6% while gross margin stayed between 17.9% and 19.0% from FY2023.
rows.mechanism: Gross profit per unit held while operating expenses (R&D $3,969M in FY2023 to $7,078M in 9M 2026) grew faster than revenue, so fixed-cost absorption deteriorated even as unit margins recovered.
rows.benchmark: FY2022 operating margin 16.8% and gross margin 25.6%; FY2023 ROIC 28.3%.
rows.weakens: 9M 2026 revenue grew 12.5%, so volume is not collapsing; the deterioration is cost-driven and reversible if R&D plateaus.
rows.implication: The margin decline is an opex story, not a gross-margin story; a recovery requires opex discipline, which management has not guided to.
rows.confidence: high, audited figures reconciled across three 10-Ks and the 10-Q
rows.follow_up: At what revenue level does the AI cost base stop growing faster than gross profit?

rows.finding: Operating cash flow was $14,897M for 9M 2026 against $10,934M a year earlier, but capital expenditure more than doubled to $13,014M from $6,134M, so free cash flow fell 61% to $1,883M from $4,800M. Quarterly free cash flow was $1,444M, $(1,092)M and $1,531M in Q1-Q3 2026 against $3,990M in Q3 2025; capex was $4,732M in Q3 2026 and guidance is above $20B for 2026.
rows.mechanism: Capital intensity rose from 9% of revenue in FY2025 to 16.5% in 9M 2026, so each dollar of revenue now consumes far more cash than in 2023-2025.
rows.weakens: Q3 2026 free cash flow was positive at $1,531M, so the company is not burning cash and has $36B of net cash plus $30B of committed facilities.
rows.implication: Free cash flow is no longer a support for the valuation; at the current run-rate the company is close to cash-neutral before any downturn.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: Does capex peak in 2026, and how much of the $20B is maintenance versus AI compute that produces no near-term revenue?

rows.finding: Accounts payable and accrued liabilities contributed $7,332M to operating cash flow in 9M 2026 against $2,979M a year earlier; accounts payable rose to $17,239M from $13,371M at 2025-12-31 and DPO rose to 75.3 days from 62.8. Net income fell 19.5% to $2,378M over the same nine months while operating cash flow rose 36%.
rows.mechanism: Stretching supplier payment days is a one-time source of cash; it flatters operating cash flow relative to net income without improving economics, and reverses when terms normalise.
rows.benchmark: FY2025 DPO 62.8 days, DSO 17.6, DIO 58.2, cash conversion cycle 13.0 days.
rows.weakens: Deferred revenue also rose $1,746M (customer prepayments up to $3.30B), which is a genuine cash inflow tied to storage demand.
rows.implication: About half of the reported operating cash flow was financed by suppliers; treat 2026 operating cash flow as overstated relative to earnings power.
rows.confidence: high on the figures; medium on how much of the payable build reverses
rows.follow_up: How much of the payables build is normal extension of terms versus delayed payment to suppliers, and does it reverse in Q4 2026?

rows.finding: At 2026-09-30 Tesla held $45,447M of cash and short-term investments against $9,267M of debt, or $36,180M of net cash, plus three credit agreements signed in September 2026 with aggregate commitments of $30B. Interest income was $1,301M for 9M 2026 against $263M of interest expense; interest cover was 9.96x TTM; goodwill was $257M at FY2025 and inventory rose to $14,092M from $12,392M.
rows.mechanism: A net-cash balance sheet plus committed facilities converts the risk from liquidity to capital allocation: capital can be raised cheaply, so the constraint is the return on what is spent.
rows.benchmark: Interest cover 12.88x in FY2025 and 56.99x in FY2023; goodwill 0.2% of total assets.
rows.weakens: Inventory rose 13.7% while deliveries fell 2%, absorbing cash and hinting at launch build-up in Semi, Cybercab and Optimus.
rows.implication: Solvency is not the risk; dilution and returns on capital are. The balance sheet can fund the capex cycle but not protect the equity multiple if returns stay at 5.5%.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: Why does a company with $36B of net cash arrange $30B of committed facilities, and what covenants or conditions attach to them?

rows.finding: TTM ROIC was 5.5% and ROE 3.8% at 2026-09-30, against invested capital of $53,109M (equity $89,289M plus debt $9,267M less cash and securities $45,447M). NOPAT of roughly $2.7B on that base does not cover any plausible cost of capital.
rows.mechanism: Equity rose from $62,634M (FY2023) to $89,289M while NOPAT fell, so invested capital expanded faster than profit, mechanically compressing ROIC.
rows.benchmark: ROIC 28.3% in FY2023, 13.7% in FY2024, 7.0% in FY2025; cost of capital estimated at 11-14% from a 4.99% ten-year Treasury, a 4.5% equity risk premium and a beta of 1.5-2.0.
rows.weakens: A 5.5% ROIC year is distorted by a trough operating margin (2.6%); at FY2023 margins the same capital base would earn well above the cost of capital.
rows.implication: On current returns the company destroys economic value; the equity is a claim on future returns that the statements do not yet show.
rows.confidence: high on ROIC; medium on the cost of capital, which is our estimate
rows.follow_up: What ROIC does management underwrite for the AI compute, Austin Fab and Optimus capital, and over what horizon?

rows.finding: Stock-based compensation was $3,557M in 9M 2026 (+71%) and $1,242M in Q3, 4.5% of revenue; the 2025 CEO Performance Award covers 423.7M shares (12% of the diluted count) with $9.74B of unrecognised expense on the one milestone judged probable, amortised over 8.9 years; the 2018 award was exercised for 304.0M options in Q2 2026 with 17.5M net-settled and the rest issued as restricted shares vesting 2028-01-19. GAAP net income also included a $288M Bitcoin mark-to-market gain and a $142M SpaceX equity mark-down in Q3 2026, and 9M 2026 tax included a California deferred-tax asset release.
rows.mechanism: Equity compensation shifts cash cost to shareholders through dilution, so free cash flow per share grows slower than free cash flow, and a rising share count compounds the effect at a high multiple.
rows.benchmark: Basic weighted average shares 3,240M; diluted 3,541M; 2024 SBC was 2.0% of revenue.
rows.weakens: No incremental expense was recognised on the 2018 award and the performance shares vest only on milestones, so the dilution is conditional rather than certain.
rows.implication: Per-share value is diluted by roughly 12% of an overhang plus 4.5% of revenue in annual SBC; EPS comparisons across years are not like-for-like.
rows.confidence: high on disclosure; medium on the eventual dilution because performance conditions may not be met
rows.follow_up: How many of the 423.7M performance shares become probable in 2027, and will Tesla buy back stock to offset dilution?

rows.finding: At $403.30 on 2026-10-29 and 3,541M diluted shares, market capitalisation is $1,428B; with net cash of $36,180M the enterprise value is $1,392B, or 13.4x TTM revenue, 401x TTM operating income, 92x TTM adjusted EBITDA of $14,995M and 431x TTM free cash flow of $3,303M. The shares are 8.4% lower over twelve months while the S&P 500 rose 13.2%.
rows.mechanism: When the multiple is 92x adjusted EBITDA (itself before $4.3B of TTM stock-based compensation), small changes in the market's probability weighting of future businesses move the price far more than changes in current earnings.
rows.benchmark: GM FY2025 EBIT-adjusted $12.7B with a $6B buyback authorisation; Ford 2026 adjusted free cash flow guidance $5.0-6.0B.
rows.weakens: The company has $36B of net cash and positive free cash flow, so the multiple is not a solvency signal; a single large autonomy milestone could justify it.
rows.implication: No earnings-based method supports the price; the premium is an option on autonomy and robotics, so position size should be set by tolerance for multiple compression, not by near-term cash flow.
rows.confidence: high on the arithmetic; the valuation judgement depends on assumptions not in the filings
rows.follow_up: What portion of the price is attributable to robotaxi and Optimus, and what milestones would force a re-rating either way?

plan.decision_question: Do Tesla's earnings and cash generation justify a premium valuation, and what is the quality of that cash?
plan.thesis_sentence: Tesla's earnings do not justify its premium: trailing free cash flow of $3.30 billion against a $1.43 trillion market capitalisation is 431 times, nine-month 2026 free cash flow fell 61% to $1.88 billion as capital expenditure doubled to $13.01 billion, and the operating cash flow that survived was carried by a $7.33 billion payables stretch while $3.56 billion of stock-based compensation and a one-off California tax release flattered earnings.
plan.why_different: The business-model section explains where gross profit comes from per unit; this section tests whether that profit converts into cash, what the balance sheet and returns say about capital efficiency, and what the market is paying for it. Only this section covers the statements, working capital, ROIC versus cost of capital and the valuation arithmetic.
plan.mechanism: Profit per vehicle is being converted into fixed AI cost (R&D +69%, capex $20B+) that does not yet produce revenue, while operating cash flow is held up by stretching payables and collecting storage prepayments; the gap between reported operating cash flow and underlying earnings widens with each quarter of the capex build.
plan.comparison_set: FY2023 when ROIC was 28.3% and free cash flow $4.36B; Ford's 2026 capex guidance of $9.5-10.5B against Tesla's $20B+; GM's FY2025 EBIT-adjusted $12.7B and $6B buyback; a 4.99% ten-year Treasury as the risk-free benchmark for cost of capital.
plan.counter_evidence: Free cash flow is still positive in Q3 2026 ($1.53B) and for 9M ($1.88B), net cash is $36.18B, interest cover 9.96x, goodwill is immaterial, and the payables stretch could reverse as capex is paid; the FCF decline is deliberate investment (capex +112%) rather than demand failure, so a capex cycle that ends in 2027 could restore FCF quickly.
plan.visual: A financial statements table FY2023-FY2025 plus 9M 2026 and Q3 2026, a returns and working-capital table, and a danger component on working-capital-funded operating cash flow.
plan.prohibited: 'clear path to profitability', 'strong balance sheet' as a standalone claim, 'risks are manageable', 'well positioned', vague counts, and any sentence describing how the section is written.

rows.finding: The six comparables shown carry a median trailing P/E of 18.5x (GM 18.8x, Alphabet 14.2x, BYD 18.5x; Ford, Rivian and Lucid are loss-making and n/m) and a median EV/sales of 2.4x (Rivian 2.4x, Lucid 2.4x, Alphabet 7.5x; GM, Ford and BYD n/m).

rows.finding: The 2025 CEO Performance Award carries $9.74B of unrecognised stock-based compensation on the one operational milestone judged probable (delivery of 20 million Tesla vehicles), expected to be recognised over 8.9 years; the tranches judged not probable carry $105.82B-$120.37B; other probable awards carry $0.58B.
rows.mechanism: Equity compensation is a claim on future cash flows and dilution; the recognition period spreads the charge across 8.9 years while the shares are already in the outstanding count.
rows.benchmark: Stock-based compensation was 1.9% of revenue in FY2023 and 4.3% in nine months of 2026.
rows.weakens: If the milestone is forfeited the expense is reversed, and the $105.82B-$120.37B is contingent on milestones that may never be met.
rows.implication: The award dilutes 10.7% of shares outstanding and makes reported margins dependent on an accounting judgement about a 20m-vehicle milestone.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: What is the expected recognition schedule by year, and will the board offset the dilution?

rows.finding: Stock-based compensation was $3,346M in nine months to 2026-09-30 ($1,030M Q1, $1,151M Q2, $1,165M Q3) and $4,300M on a trailing basis, not the $3,557M and $1,242M previously stated.
rows.mechanism: The non-GAAP reconciliation in the Q3 2026 release is the primary record; the earlier figures overstated nine-month expense by $211M and the quarter by $77M.
rows.weakens: Even at the corrected figure, stock-based compensation is 4.3% of nine-month revenue, more than double FY2023.
rows.implication: The correction reduces reported SBC but does not change the conclusion that equity compensation is a material and rising claim.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: Does the $910M GAAP-to-non-GAAP gap reconcile fully to SBC after tax and the excluded digital-asset and SpaceX items?

rows.finding: Q3 2026 automotive cost of revenue per vehicle delivered was $34,436: automotive cost of revenue of $16,754M divided by 486,532 deliveries, down 2.7% from $35,385 in Q3 2025; revenue per delivery excluding credits was $42,026 and gross profit per vehicle $7,591.
rows.mechanism: Cost per vehicle delivered is the common denominator used across the business model and financial sections; regional mix and cell cost drive the year-on-year decline.
rows.benchmark: Q3 2025 cost per delivery $35,385; BYD automotive gross margin 20.49% in FY2025.
rows.weakens: The figure includes depreciation and warranty accruals and is not a variable-cost measure, so it cannot be used as a contribution margin.
rows.implication: The car earns a positive spread over its cash and accrual cost, but only about 18% before credits.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: What is the cost per vehicle in North America alone, excluding Shanghai?

rows.finding: Nine-month operating cash flow rose 36% to $14,897M while net income fell 19.5% to $2,378M; payables and accrued liabilities supplied $7,332M versus $2,979M a year earlier, DPO rose to 75.3 days from 62.8, capex rose to $13,014M and free cash flow fell 61% to $1,883M.

rows.benchmark: TTM free cash flow $3,303M against $1,594.1B of market capitalisation is 483x; TTM operating cash flow $18,710M against net income $3,218M is 5.8x.

rows.implication: A normalisation of supplier terms would remove roughly $2.9B of the nine-month operating cash flow and turn free cash flow negative.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: How much of the payables increase reverses in Q4 2026?

plan.mechanism: Operating profit is falling while capex and equity compensation rise; working capital (payables, customer prepayments) funds operating cash flow, so reported cash conversion flatters earnings, and the multiples capitalise a profit base that is smaller than it looks.
plan.comparison_set: Tesla's FY2022-FY2025 history, six listed peers (GM, Ford, Rivian, Lucid, Alphabet, BYD) for multiples, and a 4.99% ten-year Treasury against an estimated 11-14% cost of capital.
plan.counter_evidence: Operating cash flow rose 36% on payables and prepayments, gross margin held at 19.6%, the balance sheet carries $36.2 billion of net cash plus $30 billion of new facilities, and energy growth could lift free cash flow to about $8 billion.
plan.visual: The statements table and the returns and working capital table, with a danger component on payables-funded operating cash flow.
plan.prohibited: clear business model, huge market, strong team, high barriers to entry, fierce competition, well managed, well positioned, risks are manageable, about/many/various as counts
